parts.problemMd:
A design company stores a company logo as a vector graphic.

The logo contains a circle.

(i) State what is meant by the term **drawing object**.

(1)

(ii) State **one** property that is stored for the circle.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
(i) A drawing object is one component, or shape, that makes up the image and that is created from a formula. **[1]**

(ii) The radius of the circle. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a definition of a drawing object: one component / shape of the image // a component created using a formula // one of the items stored in the drawing list
> 
> **1 mark** for one property of the circle: radius // diameter // centre point coordinates // position // fill colour // line colour // line thickness / line weight
> 
> Accept "attribute" in place of "property"
> 
> Do not accept "a pixel" or "a group of pixels" for a drawing object, because a vector graphic stores no pixels
> 
> Do not accept "resolution", "colour depth" or "file size" as a property of the circle, because those describe a bitmap image or the whole file, not one drawing object

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often answer part (i) with an example, such as "a circle" or "a line". An example is not a definition. Say that a drawing object is one component or shape that makes up the image, and add that it is created from a formula, which is exactly what separates a vector graphic from a bitmap image.
> 
> The common loss in part (ii) is answering with a bitmap term such as colour depth or resolution. A property belongs to one drawing object, so give something that describes that circle alone, such as its radius or its fill colour.

parts.problemMd:
A vector graphic of a road sign is stored on a computer.

The graphic is enlarged to four times its original width and height.

Explain why the quality of the enlarged graphic does not decrease.
parts.solutionMd:
The drawing list stores the commands and mathematical equations needed to draw each drawing object, rather than a colour for every pixel. **[1]**

No fixed dimensions are stored for the graphic, so when it is enlarged the properties of each drawing object are recalculated for the new size. **[1]**

Each drawing object is then redrawn from its equation at the larger size, so nothing is stretched and no pixelation occurs. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for stating that the file stores commands / mathematical equations / descriptions for each drawing object rather than pixels
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that no fixed dimensions are stored, so the properties of each drawing object are recalculated for the new size
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that each drawing object is redrawn from its equation at the new size, so there is no pixelation / no loss of quality
> 
> Accept "attribute" in place of "property", and "formula" in place of "equation"
> 
> Accept "the objects are scaled by recalculating their coordinates" for the second marking point
> 
> Do not accept "the resolution stays the same", because a vector graphic has no image resolution
> 
> Do not accept "vector graphics are better quality than bitmap images", because it gives no reason

> **[exam-tip]**
> The command word is Explain, so every mark needs a reason. Writing "it does not pixelate" simply repeats the question and scores nothing.
> 
> Many students borrow bitmap vocabulary here and write about resolution, or about the pixels being made bigger. A vector graphic has neither. Keep to the three terms the syllabus names for this topic: drawing list, drawing object and property.

parts.problemMd:
An airport stores a floor plan of a terminal building as a vector graphic.

The plan contains 400 drawing objects.

The airport makes two changes to the plan:

- every wall is drawn with a thicker line
- one extra doorway is added

Describe how the vector graphic file is changed to make these two changes.

Use the terms **drawing list**, **drawing object** and **property** in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Line thickness is a property of a drawing object, so the value stored for that property is changed. **[1]**

The change is made to the wall drawing objects only, and every other drawing object in the drawing list is left unchanged. **[1]**

A new drawing object for the doorway is added to the drawing list. **[1]**

The properties of that new drawing object are then stored, for example its position in the image, its dimensions and its line colour. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for identifying line thickness / line weight as a property of a drawing object
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the value of this property is changed for the wall drawing objects, and that the other drawing objects in the drawing list are unchanged
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that a new drawing object for the doorway is added to the drawing list
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the properties of the new drawing object are stored, with at least one example such as position, coordinates, dimensions, line colour or fill colour
> 
> Accept "attribute" in place of "property"
> 
> Accept "shape" or "component" in place of "drawing object"
> 
> Do not accept "the pixels making up the walls are recoloured", because a vector graphic stores no pixels
> 
> Do not accept "the whole image is redrawn", because only the objects that change need to be edited

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question tests whether you know which of the three terms holds what. The drawing list holds the drawing objects, and each drawing object holds its properties. Students who swap those around, for example by saying the doorway is added as a new property, lose marks they knew the content well enough to earn.
> 
> The 400 objects in the stem are there for a reason. Say clearly that only the wall objects change, because being able to edit one component without touching the rest is a real benefit of storing an image this way.

parts.problemMd:
A design company must choose a file format for each of four images.

Complete the table by writing either **bitmap image** or **vector graphic** in each empty cell, to show the more suitable format for each image.

| Image | More suitable format |
|---|---|
| A photograph of a mountain for a news website |   |
| A company logo printed on both a pen and a large poster |   |
| A circuit diagram that users zoom into on screen |   |
| A scan of a painting for an online art gallery |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Image | More suitable format |
|---|---|
| A photograph of a mountain for a news website | **Bitmap image** |
| A company logo printed on both a pen and a large poster | **Vector graphic** |
| A circuit diagram that users zoom into on screen | **Vector graphic** |
| A scan of a painting for an online art gallery | **Bitmap image** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **2 marks** for all four rows correct
> 
> **1 mark** for two or three rows correct
> 
> Correct answers, in order: bitmap image, vector graphic, vector graphic, bitmap image
> 
> Accept "bitmap" for "bitmap image" and "vector" for "vector graphic"
> 
> Do not accept a named file extension such as .jpg or .svg in place of the format, because the question asks for the format
> 
> Do not award any mark where a row is left blank or names both formats

> **[exam-tip]**
> The rule that decides every row is what the image is made of, not how good each format is. A photograph and a scan of a painting both contain continuous variation in colour that cannot be described as shapes, so they have to be bitmap images. The logo and the circuit diagram are built from simple shapes and lines, so they can be drawing objects in a vector graphic.
> 
> Students who answer "vector graphic" in all four rows have learned that vector scales better and stopped there. Read what the image actually shows before you decide.

parts.problemMd:
A museum is designing a new sign for the entrance to each of its rooms.

Each sign shows the name of the room and a simple arrow.

The same design will be printed at three sizes: on a small card, on a wall panel and on a large banner outside the building.

Justify the use of a vector graphic rather than a bitmap image for the sign design.
parts.solutionMd:
The sign is made only of text and a simple arrow, so it can be described as a small number of drawing objects with properties. **[1]**

A vector graphic can be enlarged to any size without pixelation, because each drawing object is redrawn from its equation at the new size. **[1]**

One vector file can therefore be used for the card, the wall panel and the banner, whereas a bitmap image enlarged to banner size would look pixelated. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for stating that the sign is made of simple shapes and text, so it can be stored as drawing objects
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that a vector graphic can be enlarged without pixelation / without loss of quality, because each object is redrawn from its equation at the new size
> 
> **1 mark** for linking this to the situation: one file serves all three sizes // a bitmap image would pixelate at banner size // a separate bitmap file would be needed for each size
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the vector file is generally smaller than an equivalent bitmap image of the sign
> 
> Maximum 3 marks
> 
> Accept "scaled up" or "resized" in place of "enlarged"
> 
> Do not accept "a vector graphic has a higher resolution", because a vector graphic has no image resolution
> 
> Do not accept "vector graphics are always better", because the format chosen depends on what the image shows

> **[exam-tip]**
> Justify means you must tie the reason to this situation, not list general facts about vector graphics. The three print sizes in the stem are the whole point, so say that one file can serve all three.
> 
> A frequent error is to claim the sign will have a higher resolution as a vector graphic. Resolution belongs to bitmap images only. Say instead that the sign is redrawn from its equations at whatever size is needed, so nothing is stretched.

parts.problemMd:
A wildlife charity is creating a new website.

The website will use two types of image:

- photographs of animals taken with a camera
- the charity logo, which appears as a small icon in the corner of every page and as a large image on the home page

Compare the use of bitmap images and vector graphics for storing these two types of image.
parts.solutionMd:
A bitmap image stores a binary code for the colour of every pixel, whereas a vector graphic stores a drawing list of drawing objects and their properties. **[1]**

The photographs contain continuous variation in colour and fine detail that cannot be described as shapes, so they must be stored as bitmap images. **[1]**

Storing a photograph as a vector graphic would need an impractical number of drawing objects and would still not look realistic. **[1]**

The logo is made of simple shapes, so it can be stored as a vector graphic and enlarged for the home page without pixelation, because each object is redrawn from its equation. **[1]**

If the logo were a bitmap image, enlarging it would pixelate it, so a separate bitmap file would be needed for the icon and for the home page image. **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for stating the difference in what is stored: a bitmap image stores a binary colour code for every pixel, a vector graphic stores a drawing list of drawing objects and their properties
> 
> Points about the photographs, maximum 3 marks:
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that photographs contain continuous variation in colour and fine detail that cannot be described as shapes / drawing objects
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the photographs must therefore be stored as bitmap images
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that a vector version would need an impractical number of drawing objects // would not look realistic
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that a bitmap photograph has a large file size, which increases page loading time // may need compression
> 
> Points about the logo, maximum 3 marks:
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the logo is made of simple shapes, so it can be stored as drawing objects in a vector graphic
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the vector logo can be enlarged for the home page without pixelation, because each object is redrawn from its equation at the new size
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that a bitmap logo would pixelate when enlarged, so a separate bitmap file would be needed at each size
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the vector logo generally has a smaller file size than the equivalent bitmap logo
> 
> Maximum 5 marks overall, and at least one marking point must be about each type of image
> 
> Accept "attribute" in place of "property"
> 
> Do not accept "vector graphics are better than bitmap images", because the photographs cannot be stored as vector graphics
> 
> Do not accept "bitmap images have a higher resolution than vector graphics", because a vector graphic has no image resolution

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error on this topic is treating vector as the winner in every situation. Vector is not simply better. Scaling favours a vector graphic, but only when the image is built from shapes. A photograph has no shapes to describe, so a bitmap image is the only realistic choice for it.
> 
> Compare means both formats must appear in your answer, and here both types of image must appear too. An answer that only explains why the logo should be a vector graphic gives away the marks available for the photographs.

parts.problemMd:
A digital camera stores each photograph it takes as a bitmap image.

State what is meant by each of the following terms.

(i) Pixel

(1)

(ii) Image resolution

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
(i) A pixel is the smallest element of a bitmap image, and it holds a single colour. **[1]**

(ii) The image resolution is the number of pixels that make up the image, found by multiplying the width in pixels by the height in pixels. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a pixel described as the smallest element / smallest addressable element of a bitmap image // a single square of one colour
> 
> **1 mark** for image resolution described as the number of pixels in the image // the width in pixels multiplied by the height in pixels
> 
> Accept "the total number of pixels that make up the image" for image resolution
> 
> Do not accept "the quality of the image" for image resolution, because that names an effect rather than the quantity being measured
> 
> Do not accept "a dot on the screen" on its own for a pixel, because it does not say that a pixel is the smallest element or that it holds one colour

> **[exam-tip]**
> Image resolution and screen resolution are two different things and CIE mark schemes keep them apart. Image resolution belongs to the image file. Screen resolution belongs to the display device. If you answer this with "the number of pixels across a monitor", you are describing screen resolution and you will not earn the mark.

parts.problemMd:
A student records their voice using a microphone. The recording is stored as a digital sound file.

State what is meant by sampling rate and what is meant by sampling resolution.
parts.solutionMd:
Sampling rate is the number of samples taken per second from the sound wave. **[1]**

Sampling resolution is the number of bits used to store each sample. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for sampling rate being the number of samples taken each second // how many times per second the amplitude is measured
> 
> **1 mark** for sampling resolution being the number of bits used to store each sample
> 
> Accept "measured in hertz" as part of the sampling rate answer, but not on its own
> 
> Accept "bit depth" as an alternative name for sampling resolution
> 
> Do not accept "the number of samples" for sampling rate without "per second", because that describes the whole file rather than the rate
> 
> Do not accept "how good the sound is" for either term, because that is the effect of the setting, not its meaning
> 
> Do not accept an answer that defines sampling resolution using the word "second", because that is the definition of sampling rate

> **[exam-tip]**
> These two terms are swapped more often than any other pair in this topic. Separate them by the unit each one uses. Sampling rate is counted in hertz, which is a number per second. Sampling resolution is counted in bits, which is a number per sample. If the word "second" appears in your answer for sampling resolution, you have written the wrong definition.

parts.problemMd:
A company logo is stored as a bitmap image. The logo uses exactly 40 different colours.

(i) Calculate the minimum colour depth, in bits per pixel, that can be used to store the logo.

Show your working.

(2)

(ii) State how many further different colours could be added to the logo at this colour depth, without increasing the colour depth.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
(i) 5 bits per pixel give 2<sup>5</sup> = 32 different codes, which is fewer than the 40 colours needed. **[1]**

6 bits per pixel give 2<sup>6</sup> = 64 different codes, which is enough, so the minimum colour depth is 6 bits per pixel. **[1]**

(ii) 64 - 40 = 24 further colours. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for working that shows 2<sup>5</sup> = 32 is fewer than 40 // that shows 2<sup>6</sup> = 64 is the first power of 2 to reach 40
> 
> **1 mark** for the answer 6 bits per pixel
> 
> **1 mark** for 24
> 
> Accept 6 bits, 6 bpp or 6 for the second mark
> 
> Accept 64 - 40 shown as working for the third mark
> 
> Do not accept 5 bits, which comes from stopping at the largest power of 2 below 40 instead of the smallest power of 2 that reaches it
> 
> Do not accept 40 bits, which confuses the number of colours with the number of bits per pixel

> **[exam-tip]**
> The colour depth is the number of bits stored for each pixel, not the number of colours. Work up through the powers of 2 until you reach or pass the number of colours needed: 2<sup>5</sup> = 32 is not enough for 40 colours, so 6 bits is the smallest that works. Rounding down to 5 is the usual mistake and it leaves eight of the colours with no code.

parts.problemMd:
A musician records a song using a microphone connected to a computer. The song is stored on the hard disk of the computer as a digital sound file.

Describe how the analogue sound wave is converted into the digital data that is stored.
parts.solutionMd:
The amplitude of the analogue sound wave is measured at regular intervals, a set number of times each second. **[1]**

Each measurement is called a sample, and each sample is given a binary value. **[1]**

The binary values are stored in sequence on the hard disk, and this sequence is the digital version of the sound wave. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the amplitude being measured at regular intervals // a set number of times per second
> 
> **1 mark** for each sample being given, or converted to, a binary value
> 
> **1 mark** for the binary values being stored in sequence
> 
> Accept "loudness" in place of "amplitude"
> 
> Accept "height of the wave" in place of "amplitude"
> 
> Do not accept "the sound is turned into binary" on its own, because it names no step of the process
> 
> Do not accept naming the process as analogue to digital conversion as a marking point, because the question asks how the conversion is carried out
> 
> Do not accept "the wave is stored" for the third mark without the idea of order or sequence

> **[exam-tip]**
> A three-mark describe question wants three separate steps, not one idea written three ways. Plan them as measure, convert, store, then write one sentence for each. Students who open with "the microphone converts the sound into binary" have jumped straight to the end of the process and can only reach one of the three marks. The order matters for the third mark too: the samples are only useful because they are kept in the order they were taken.

parts.problemMd:
A microscope is connected to a computer. Each image captured by the microscope is saved as an uncompressed bitmap file.

Explain how the data for the image is encoded in the file, **and** why the file header is needed when the file is opened again.
parts.solutionMd:
The image is divided into pixels, and each pixel holds one colour. **[1]**

Each colour is given a unique binary code, and the code for each pixel is stored in sequence. **[1]**

The file header stores data about the image, including the image resolution and the colour depth. **[1]**

Without the header the software would not know how many bits belong to each pixel or where each row of pixels ends, so it could not rebuild the image correctly. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each, to a maximum of 4:
> 
> **1 mark** for the image being divided into pixels, each holding one colour
> 
> **1 mark** for each colour being represented by a unique binary code
> 
> **1 mark** for the codes being stored in sequence / one after another
> 
> **1 mark** for the file header storing data about the image, with at least one example such as the image resolution, the colour depth or the file type
> 
> **1 mark** for a consequence: without the colour depth the software cannot tell how many bits belong to each pixel // without the image resolution the software cannot tell where each row of pixels ends
> 
> Accept "bit depth" in place of "colour depth" throughout
> 
> Accept "metadata" for "data about the image" only where at least one example is also given
> 
> Do not accept "the header stores the image", because the header stores data about the image, not the pixel data
> 
> Do not accept "the header compresses the file", because the file in this question is uncompressed

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question has two halves and needs both. A very common answer describes the pixels and the binary codes well, then stops, which caps you at two marks. Say what the header holds and say what would go wrong without it. A useful test: if the header were deleted, could the software still work out where the second row of pixels starts?

parts.problemMd:
A device records sound using a sampling resolution of 3 bits.

The amplitude of the sound wave is measured on a scale from 0 to 8 units.

The device divides this scale into 8 equal levels, numbered 0 to 7:

- level 0 stores any amplitude from 0 up to but not including 1
- level 1 stores any amplitude from 1 up to but not including 2
- this pattern continues up to level 7, which stores any amplitude from 7 up to 8

The level number is then stored as a 3-bit binary value.

Complete the table for the four samples shown.

| Measured amplitude | Level number | 3-bit value stored |
|---|---|---|
| 2.4 |   |   |
| 5.9 |   |   |
| 7.2 |   |   |
| 0.7 |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Measured amplitude | Level number | 3-bit value stored |
|---|---|---|
| 2.4 | **2** | **010** |
| 5.9 | **5** | **101** |
| 7.2 | **7** | **111** |
| 0.7 | **0** | **000** |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for level `2` and the stored value `010`
> 
> **1 mark** for level `5` and the stored value `101`
> 
> **1 mark** for level `7` and the stored value `111`
> 
> **1 mark** for level `0` and the stored value `000`
> 
> Accept the stored value written with spaces between the bits, such as `0 1 0`
> 
> Do not accept a stored value shorter than 3 bits, such as `10` for level 2 or `0` for level 0, because the sampling resolution fixes every sample at exactly 3 bits
> 
> Do not accept level 3 for the amplitude 2.4, or level 6 for the amplitude 5.9, which come from rounding to the nearest level instead of using the level the amplitude falls inside
> 
> Do not accept level 8 for the amplitude 7.2, because 8 cannot be stored in 3 bits and the highest level is 7

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two errors take most of the marks here. The first is rounding to the nearest level: the rule in the question stores the level the amplitude falls inside, so 2.4 gives level 2 and not level 3. Read the rule you are given rather than assuming the one you are used to. The second is dropping the leading zeros. A sampling resolution of 3 bits means every sample occupies exactly 3 bits, so level 2 is stored as `010` and never as `10`. The difference between the real amplitude of 2.4 and the level that stores it is called quantisation error, and reducing that error is exactly why a higher sampling resolution gives a more accurate recording.

parts.problemMd:
A bitmap image has an image resolution of 320 pixels wide by 256 pixels high.

The colour depth is 4 bits per pixel.

Calculate an estimate for the file size of the image. Give your answer in **kibibytes**.

Ignore the size of the file header.

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
320 × 256 = 81 920 pixels

81 920 × 4 = 327 680 bits

327 680 ÷ 8 = 40 960 bytes **[1]**

40 960 ÷ 1024 = 40 kibibytes **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for working that reaches 40 960 bytes, for example `(320 × 256 × 4) ÷ 8`
> 
> **1 mark** for the answer 40 kibibytes
> 
> Accept the whole calculation shown as one expression, `(320 × 256 × 4) ÷ (8 × 1024)`
> 
> Accept 40 KiB
> 
> Do not accept 40 960 on its own, because the question asks for the answer in kibibytes, not bytes
> 
> Do not accept 40.96, which comes from dividing the bytes by 1000 instead of by 1024
> 
> Do not accept 327 680, which is the size in bits

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work in bits first, divide by 8 once to reach bytes, then divide by 1024 for each step up the binary prefixes. A kibibyte is 1024 bytes, not 1000 bytes, and dividing by 1000 here gives 40.96 and loses the answer mark. Write the unit next to your final number so the examiner can see which conversion you stopped at.

parts.problemMd:
A voice message is recorded and saved as a digital sound file.

Tick (✓) one box in each row to identify the effect of each change on the size of the sound file.

| Change | File size increases | File size decreases | File size does not change |
|---|---|---|---|
| The sampling rate is changed from 44.1 kHz to 22.05 kHz. |   |   |   |
| The sampling resolution is changed from 8 bits to 16 bits. |   |   |   |
| The volume of the speaker used to play the saved file is increased. |   |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Change | File size increases | File size decreases | File size does not change |
|---|---|---|---|
| The sampling rate is changed from 44.1 kHz to 22.05 kHz. |   | **✓** |   |
| The sampling resolution is changed from 8 bits to 16 bits. | **✓** |   |   |
| The volume of the speaker used to play the saved file is increased. |   |   | **✓** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for one or two rows ticked correctly
> 
> **1 mark** for all three rows ticked correctly, giving 2 marks in total
> 
> Accept a cross, or any other single clear mark, in place of a tick
> 
> Do not accept a row with more than one box marked; that row scores nothing
> 
> Do not accept "file size increases" for the third row, because the volume of a speaker is set during playback and no extra data is stored in the file

> **[exam-tip]**
> The third row catches students out every year. Anything done after the file has been saved, such as turning the speaker up or using headphones, cannot change the size of the file. Only the settings used while the sound is being recorded, which are the sampling rate, the sampling resolution and the length of the recording, decide how many bits are stored. Check the direction of each change as well: 44.1 kHz to 22.05 kHz is a decrease, even though 22.05 kHz is still a large number.

parts.problemMd:
A camera saves each photograph as an uncompressed bitmap file.

Each photograph has an image resolution of 1024 pixels wide by 768 pixels high, and a colour depth of 24 bits per pixel.

Calculate an estimate for the file size of one photograph. Give your answer in **mebibytes**.

Ignore the size of the file header.

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
1024 × 768 = 786 432 pixels **[1]**

786 432 × 24 = 18 874 368 bits

18 874 368 ÷ 8 = 2 359 296 bytes **[1]**

2 359 296 ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024 = 2.25 mebibytes **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for 786 432 pixels // for multiplying the width by the height
> 
> **1 mark** for 2 359 296 bytes // for `(1024 × 768 × 24) ÷ 8`
> 
> **1 mark** for the answer 2.25 mebibytes
> 
> Accept 2.25 MiB
> 
> Accept the route that converts the colour depth first: 24 bits = 3 bytes, then `1024 × 768 × 3 = 2 359 296 bytes`
> 
> Do not accept 18, which comes from dividing the total in bits by 1024 twice without ever dividing by 8
> 
> Do not accept 2.36, which comes from dividing the bytes by 1 000 000 instead of by 1024 × 1024

> **[exam-tip]**
> The colour depth here is given in bits, so you must divide by 8 exactly once. If you forget that step, you get 18 mebibytes, which is eight times too large and is the single most common wrong answer on this style of question. If you lose track of that division, convert 24 bits to 3 bytes at the very start and then never divide by 8 at all.

parts.problemMd:
A sound file is recorded using:

- a sampling rate of 40 kHz
- a sampling resolution of 16 bits
- a length of 5 minutes

Calculate the size of the sound file. Give your answer in megabytes and show your working.

Use 1 kilobyte = 1000 bytes and 1 megabyte = 1000 kilobytes.
parts.solutionMd:
Length of the recording = 5 × 60 = 300 seconds

Number of bits = 40 000 × 300 × 16 = 192 000 000 bits **[1]**

Number of bytes = 192 000 000 ÷ 8 = 24 000 000 bytes **[1]**

Number of megabytes = 24 000 000 ÷ 1 000 000 = 24 **[1]**

The file size is **24 megabytes**.

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for 192 000 000 bits, from 40 000 × 300 × 16
> 
> **1 mark** for dividing by 8 to give 24 000 000 bytes
> 
> **1 mark** for the final answer of 24 megabytes
> 
> Accept the working carried out in a different order, for example 40 000 × 16 = 640 000 bits per second, then × 300
> 
> Accept 24 MB as the final answer
> 
> Accept 24 000 kilobytes shown as an intermediate step
> 
> Do not accept 24 000 000 as the final answer, because the question asks for megabytes and not bytes
> 
> Do not accept an answer built on 5 seconds or on 300 minutes; the sampling rate is per second, so the length must be converted to 300 seconds
> 
> Do not accept 22.89, which comes from dividing by 1 048 576; that would give mebibytes and the question asks for megabytes

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of this calculation never changes: sampling rate × sampling resolution × time in seconds gives the number of bits, divide by 8 for bytes, then divide by 1000 for each step up the units. The two marks most often lost are the time conversion, because the sampling rate is per second while the recording is given in minutes, and the final unit, because students stop at bytes. Write the unit beside every line of working so you can always see which one you are in. Watch the word used in the question as well: a megabyte is 1 000 000 bytes but a mebibyte is 1 048 576 bytes, and this paper uses both.

parts.problemMd:
A wildlife camera saves each photograph as an uncompressed bitmap file.

Each file contains:

- pixel data for an image with an image resolution of 1024 pixels wide by 1024 pixels high
- a colour depth of 8 bits per pixel
- a file header of 1024 bytes

(i) Calculate the total size of one file, including the file header. Give your answer in **kibibytes**.

Show your working.

(2)

(ii) The camera has 20 mebibytes of storage available for photographs.

Calculate the largest number of complete files the camera can store.

Show your working.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Pixel data: 1024 × 1024 × 8 = 8 388 608 bits, and 8 388 608 ÷ 8 = 1 048 576 bytes, which is 1 048 576 ÷ 1024 = 1024 kibibytes. **[1]**

File header: 1024 ÷ 1024 = 1 kibibyte, so the total size of one file is 1024 + 1 = 1025 kibibytes. **[1]**

(ii) 20 mebibytes = 20 × 1024 = 20 480 kibibytes. **[1]**

20 files would need 20 × 1025 = 20 500 kibibytes, which is more than 20 480, so only 19 complete files can be stored. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for 1024 kibibytes of pixel data // for `(1024 × 1024 × 8) ÷ (8 × 1024)`
> 
> **1 mark** for the total 1025 kibibytes
> 
> **1 mark** for converting the storage to 20 480 kibibytes // to 20 971 520 bytes
> 
> **1 mark** for the answer 19
> 
> Accept part (i) worked entirely in bytes, 1 048 576 + 1024 = 1 049 600 bytes, provided 1025 kibibytes is then given
> 
> Accept 19 supported by `20 480 ÷ 1025 = 19.98` as well as by the comparison shown above
> 
> Do not accept 20, which is what you get when the file header is left out of the file size
> 
> Do not accept 19.98 or any other decimal, because the question asks for the number of complete files

> **[exam-tip]**
> The file header is the whole point of this question. Leave it out and you get exactly 20 files, which looks like a tidy answer and is wrong. Choose one unit, kibibytes is easiest here, and convert everything into it before you divide. Then check that the last file really fits: 20 files need 20 500 kibibytes and only 20 480 are available, so the twentieth file does not fit.

parts.problemMd:
A student records a voice message that is 2 minutes long. The recording uses a sampling rate of 44.1 kHz and a sampling resolution of 16 bits.

The student wants to copy the file to a memory stick that has 6 megabytes of free space.

Calculate the size of the sound file in megabytes and state whether the file will fit in the free space.

Then give one change to the sampling settings that would make the file fit, showing the new file size, and describe the effect that your change would have on the accuracy of the recording.

Use 1 megabyte = 1 000 000 bytes.
parts.solutionMd:
Length of the recording = 2 × 60 = 120 seconds

Number of bits = 44 100 × 120 × 16 = 84 672 000 bits **[1]**

Number of bytes = 84 672 000 ÷ 8 = 10 584 000 bytes, which is 10.584 megabytes **[1]**

10.584 megabytes is greater than the 6 megabytes available, so the file will not fit. **[1]**

Reducing the sampling resolution from 16 bits to 8 bits halves the file size to 5.292 megabytes, which does fit. **[1]**

Each sample is then stored in fewer bits, so fewer different amplitude values can be recorded, the quantisation errors are larger and the digital waveform is further from the original analogue waveform. **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for 84 672 000 bits, from 44 100 × 120 × 16
> 
> **1 mark** for a file size of 10 584 000 bytes // 10.584 megabytes
> 
> **1 mark** for stating the file will not fit, because 10.584 megabytes is greater than the 6 megabytes available
> 
> **1 mark** for one change to the sampling settings that brings the file to 6 megabytes or less, with the new size shown: sampling resolution reduced from 16 bits to 8 bits, or sampling rate reduced from 44.1 kHz to 22.05 kHz, either giving 5.292 megabytes
> 
> **1 mark** for the matching effect on accuracy: for a lower sampling resolution, fewer amplitude values can be stored so the quantisation errors are larger; for a lower sampling rate, the amplitude is measured less often so the gaps between samples are wider. Either way the digital waveform is further from the analogue waveform
> 
> Accept 10.6 megabytes for the second mark, provided 10.584 or 10 584 000 appears in the working
> 
> Accept any change to the sampling rate or the sampling resolution for the fourth mark, provided the file size is recalculated for the new setting and is 6 megabytes or less. A new size of exactly 6 megabytes (for example a sampling rate of 25 kHz) fits, because the question gives exactly 6 megabytes of free space and defines 1 megabyte as 1 000 000 bytes
> 
> Accept the fifth mark for a correct effect of your own change, even where the fourth mark was not earned
> 
> Do not accept "record for a shorter time" for the fourth mark. It does make the file smaller, but the length of a recording is not a sampling setting
> 
> Do not accept "use compression" or "use a different file format" for the fourth mark, for the same reason
> 
> Do not accept a change given with no new file size, because the question asks for a change that makes the file fit
> 
> Do not accept an effect that belongs to the other setting, such as "fewer samples per second" for a change to the sampling resolution

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question hides a decision inside a calculation, and the marks for the decision are the ones most often left blank. Once you reach 10.584 megabytes, write in words whether it fits, because an examiner cannot award that mark for a number on its own. When you choose which setting to change, remember that sampling rate and sampling resolution sit in the same multiplication, so halving either one halves the file size. They do not damage the recording in the same way, though: halving the sampling resolution means fewer amplitude values for each sample, while halving the sampling rate means fewer samples taken each second. Describing the effect of the setting you did not change is the commonest way to lose the final mark.

parts.problemMd:
A bitmap image is saved with a colour depth of 4 bits per pixel.

The colour depth is then changed to 8 bits per pixel. The image resolution does not change.

State the effect of this change on each of the following.

(i) The number of different colours that can be used in the image

(1)

(ii) The file size of the image

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The number of different colours increases from 16 (2<sup>4</sup>) to 256 (2<sup>8</sup>). **[1]**

(ii) The file size doubles, because twice as many bits are now stored for every pixel. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the number of colours increasing // increasing from 16 to 256 // increasing from 2<sup>4</sup> to 2<sup>8</sup>
> 
> **1 mark** for the file size increasing // doubling
> 
> Accept "the file size doubles" and "the file size increases" equally
> 
> Accept 2<sup>4</sup> and 2<sup>8</sup> written as 16 and 256
> 
> Do not accept "the image quality improves" for part (i), because the question asks about the number of colours, not the quality
> 
> Do not accept "the file size increases by 4 bits", which confuses the extra bits stored per pixel with the change to the whole file

> **[exam-tip]**
> Colour depth is measured per pixel, so doubling it doubles the size of the whole file, not just one pixel. Note that the number of colours does not double. The number of colours is 2 raised to the power of the colour depth, so it goes from 16 to 256, which is 16 times more.

parts.problemMd:
A photograph is scanned to produce a bitmap image.

The same photograph is then scanned a second time. For the second scan, the width in pixels and the height in pixels are both doubled. The colour depth is not changed.

(i) Describe the effect of this change on the quality of the second image.

(1)

(ii) Describe the effect of this change on the file size of the second image. Include how many times larger the file size becomes.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
(i) More pixels are used to store the same photograph, so more detail is captured and the image is sharper and less pixelated. **[1]**

(ii) Doubling the width and doubling the height gives 2 × 2 = 4 times as many pixels. **[1]**

The colour depth per pixel has not changed, so the file size becomes 4 times larger. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the image quality improving, with a reason: more pixels are stored for the same photograph // more detail is captured // the image is sharper // the image is less pixelated
> 
> **1 mark** for identifying that there are 4 times as many pixels
> 
> **1 mark** for the file size becoming 4 times larger
> 
> Accept "four times bigger" and "quadruples" for the factor
> 
> Accept the reason for the file size given as "the number of bits per pixel is unchanged"
> 
> Do not accept "the file size doubles", which is the most common error here; the width and the height were both doubled, not just one of them
> 
> Do not accept "the file size increases" on its own for the third mark, because the question asks how many times larger it becomes

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read exactly which measurement has been doubled. Doubling only the width doubles the file size, but doubling the width and the height multiplies the number of pixels by 4. Work out the change in the number of pixels first, then apply it to the file size, because the colour depth is unchanged and so the number of bits per pixel is unchanged.

parts.problemMd:
A travel website shows one photograph of each hotel.

Each photograph is stored on the web server as an uncompressed bitmap image with an image resolution of 3000 pixels wide by 2000 pixels high.

Every photograph is displayed on the web page inside an area that is 600 pixels wide by 400 pixels high.

The website owner decides to store each photograph at an image resolution of 600 pixels wide by 400 pixels high instead.

Explain why this decision is suitable for the website, **and** give **one** situation in which the original photographs would still be needed.
parts.solutionMd:
The display area is only 600 by 400 pixels, so no more than 240 000 pixels of the photograph can ever be shown on the page. **[1]**

The extra pixels in the stored image are discarded when the photograph is displayed, so the image quality seen by the visitor does not fall. **[1]**

The stored image now holds 25 times fewer pixels, so each file is 25 times smaller, which uses less storage on the server, uses less bandwidth and makes the page load faster. **[1]**

The original photographs would still be needed if one is to be printed or enlarged, because the detail removed by reducing the image resolution cannot be recovered. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the display area being only 600 × 400 pixels, so no more detail than that can be seen on the page
> 
> **1 mark** for the quality seen by the visitor being unchanged // the extra pixels not being visible on the page
> 
> **1 mark** for a consequence of the smaller file: less storage used on the server // less bandwidth used // the page loads faster for the visitor
> 
> **1 mark** for a situation that still needs the original, with a reason: printing // enlarging or zooming into the photograph // reusing it in a larger design, because the removed detail cannot be recovered
> 
> Accept "25 times fewer pixels" or "one twenty-fifth of the file size" as an alternative wording of the third marking point
> 
> Accept "6 000 000 pixels reduced to 240 000 pixels" as working for the third marking point
> 
> Do not accept "the photograph will look better", because reducing the image resolution never improves quality

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reducing the image resolution throws detail away permanently, so the removed pixels can never be recovered. The last mark depends on naming a real use for the original, such as printing, where 600 by 400 pixels would look blocky. Writing "you might need it one day" earns nothing.

> **1 mark** for each advantage and **1 mark** for valid corresponding expansion
> 
> - Star topology is more resilient to faults
> - …because there is no single cable, leading to less disruption to teaching
> - Higher performance as there are fewer collisions
> - …because each device in the classroom is only connected to the switch
> - Easier to add new nodes
> - …because each device in the classroom connects directly to the switch
> - Easier to fault find compared to a bus topology

parts.problemMd:
A Local Area Network (LAN) contains four devices:

- a router
- two laptop computers
- a server.

The server has the IP address 192.168.3.2

Explain why this is **not **an IPv6 address.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 2**)
> 
> - Only has four groups of digits // IPv6 has eight groups
> - Uses dotted notation instead of colons
> - Because it is a 32 bit / 4 byte address // IPv6 is 128 bits / 16 bytes

parts.problemMd:
(i) The LAN is set up as a star topology.

Draw a diagram of the topology of the LAN.

(2)

(ii) Explain how data is transmitted between the two laptops in the LAN.

(2)

(iii) Subnetting can be used to separate a network into logical segments.

Describe **two other** reasons why subnetting is used in a network.

(4)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i)** 1 mark** for server only connected to router
> 
> **1 mark** for two laptop computers connected only to router
> 
> ![Diagram shows a server connected to a router, which links to two laptops, labelled 'Laptop 1' and 'Laptop 2', forming a network hierarchy.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-computer-science-19/2-communication-/networks-and-the-internet/assets/001-diagram-shows-a-server-connected-to-a-router-whi.png)
> 
> (ii) **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 2**)
> 
> - The data from the sending laptop is transmitted to the router
> - The data includes the address of the recipient
> - The router determines the recipient’s destination address
> - …by using a routing table
> - The router transmits the data directly / only to the recipient
> 
> (iii) **1 mark** for each use (**max 2**) and** 1 mark** for corresponding expansion (**max 2**)
> 
> - To improve the security of the LAN
> - …so that devices do not receive unintended data

> - …because data sent between devices on the same subnet stays within the subnet

parts.problemMd: State **three **tasks performed by devices to deal with collisions when using the Carrier Sense Multiple Access /Collision Detection (CSMA/CD) protocol in a network.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 3**)
> 
> - To monitor the communications channel
> - To send data only when there is no data being transmitted / the line is quiet / idle
> - **To detect a collision** and then stop transmissions of further data // transmit a **jamming **signal
> - To calculate a **random **wait time / back-off time
> - ... then retransmit the data after that random wait time
> - Increase **random **time if multiple collisions

parts.problemMd:
A company sells online Computer Science courses to students in different countries. The courses are stored on a public cloud.

(i) Explain why the company uses a public cloud to store these courses.

(2)

(ii) Describe **two **disadvantages of storing data on a public cloud compared to storing data on a server in a Local Area Network (LAN).

(4)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i)** 1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 2**).
> 
> - Courses must be available to anyone who wishes to follow them
> - Courses must be available on the internet
> - Company is willing to share infrastructure with other companies (public)
> - …which is more economic for the company
> 
> (ii) **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 2** for each disadvantage).
> 
> - There could be a possible loss of control unlike the LAN
> - …because the data is stored on a remote infrastructure / someone else’s infrastructure
> - …reliance on external agency to complete tasks, e.g. backups, security

parts.problemMd:
An office connects its computers together using cables to form a Local Area Network (LAN). The LAN uses Ethernet.

State **two** features of Ethernet.
parts.solutionMd:
Ethernet is a protocol, which is a set of rules for transmitting data. **[1]**

Data is transmitted in frames. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each for any two of the following
> 
> **1 mark** for Ethernet is a protocol // a set of rules for transmitting data
> 
> **1 mark** for it is used for data transmission over wired / cabled network connections
> 
> **1 mark** for data is transmitted in frames
> 
> **1 mark** for each frame carries a source address and a destination address
> 
> **1 mark** for each frame carries error checking data
> 
> **1 mark** for it uses `CSMA/CD` to detect and avoid collisions
> 
> Accept "a wired networking standard used in a LAN" for the second marking point
> 
> Do not accept "Ethernet is a cable" or "Ethernet is a port", because those are hardware and Ethernet is the protocol that the hardware follows
> 
> Do not accept "Ethernet connects a computer to the internet", which describes the job of a router

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most students who drop marks here describe the cable instead of the protocol. The socket on the back of a computer is a connector; Ethernet itself is the set of rules that says how the bits travel along that cable and how they are packaged. Open your answer with the word "protocol" and the first mark is safe.

parts.problemMd:
Data sent using Ethernet is transmitted in frames. Each frame is made up of several parts.

The table shows three parts of an Ethernet frame. Three cells are incomplete.

| Part of the frame | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Destination address | 1 .............................. |
| 2 .............................. | Identifies the device that sent the frame |
| Frame check sequence | 3 .............................. |

Complete the table.
parts.solutionMd:
| Part of the frame | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Destination address | **1 Identifies the device the frame is being sent to** **[1]** |
| **2 Source address** **[1]** | Identifies the device that sent the frame |
| Frame check sequence | **3 Allows the receiving device to check whether the data was damaged during transmission** **[1]** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for row 1: identifies the device that the frame is being sent to // the address of the receiving device // where the frame must be delivered
> 
> **1 mark** for row 2: source address // sender address
> 
> **1 mark** for row 3: error checking // allows the receiving device to check the data has not been damaged // allows a damaged frame to be detected so it can be sent again
> 
> Accept "MAC address" or "IP address" as part of an answer in rows 1 and 2
> 
> Do not accept "the address" alone in row 2, because the frame carries two addresses and the answer must say which one
> 
> Do not accept "corrects any errors" in row 3, because the frame check sequence detects an error, it does not repair it

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read which column is empty before you write. Students often describe the purpose in a cell that asked for a name, or copy the words already printed in the other column. In row 3, "checks for errors" is enough for the mark, but "corrects errors" is wrong: a damaged frame is discarded and transmitted again, not repaired.

parts.problemMd:
A school library has one powerful computer that stores all of the library's files and manages access to them. The other computers in the library connect to that computer to use the files.

The library network uses a client-server model.

State two characteristics of a client-server network.
parts.solutionMd:
One or more dedicated servers control the network. **[1]**

The files and other resources are stored and managed centrally on the server. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each characteristic, to a maximum of 2
> 
> **1 mark** for one or more dedicated servers control the network
> 
> **1 mark** for the files / resources are stored and managed centrally on the server
> 
> **1 mark** for the clients send requests to the server
> 
> **1 mark** for the server processes each request and returns the result to the client
> 
> **1 mark** for security, user accounts or backup are managed centrally on the server
> 
> **1 mark** for the computers do not have equal status
> 
> Accept "the server provides services to the clients" for the second marking point.
> 
> Do not accept "there is a server", which names a device rather than describing a characteristic of the model.
> 
> Do not accept a description of a network topology, which is a separate idea from the network model.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two marks means two separate characteristics, not one characteristic written twice. "The server stores the files" and "all the files are in one place" are the same marking point, so together they earn one mark, not two.
> 
> Cambridge marks this model on who does what. Write one point about what the server does and one point about what the client does, and you will nearly always land both marks.

parts.problemMd:
A school stores the addresses of the devices on its network.

One server on the network has the IPv6 address `2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329`

Complete the table by writing the two missing values.

| Feature | IPv4 address | IPv6 address |
|---|---|---|
| Total number of bits in the address |   | 128 |
| Number of groups in the address | 4 |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Feature | IPv4 address | IPv6 address |
|---|---|---|
| Total number of bits in the address | **32** **[1]** | 128 |
| Number of groups in the address | 4 | **8** **[1]** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `32` as the total number of bits in an IPv4 address
> 
> **1 mark** for `8` as the number of groups in an IPv6 address
> 
> Accept `4 bytes` for the IPv4 answer and `eight` written as a word for the IPv6 answer
> 
> Do not accept `8` for the IPv4 total. 8 is the number of bits in one group of an IPv4 address, not in the whole address
> 
> Do not accept `16` for the number of IPv6 groups. 16 is the number of bits in one group of an IPv6 address
> 
> Do not accept `128 bits` for IPv4 or `32 bits` for IPv6. The two totals must not be swapped

> **[exam-tip]**
> Learn the two numbers for each address as a pair. An IPv4 address is 4 groups of 8 bits, giving 32 bits in total. An IPv6 address is 8 groups of 16 bits, giving 128 bits in total.
> 
> The mark most often lost here is writing 8 for IPv4, because the student has remembered the size of a single group instead of the size of the whole address. Check whether the question is asking about one group or about the complete address before you write the number down.

parts.problemMd:
A company has 40 computers in one building. They are connected by cables in a Local Area Network (LAN) that uses Ethernet.

One computer sends a document to a printer on the same LAN.

Explain how the Ethernet protocol makes sure that the data reaches the correct device and arrives without errors.
parts.solutionMd:
The data is divided into frames before it is transmitted. **[1]**

Each frame carries the destination address of the printer, so only the printer accepts that frame. **[1]**

Any other device that receives the frame compares the destination address with its own address and discards the frame, because the two do not match. **[1]**

Each frame also carries error checking data, so the printer can test whether the frame was damaged on the way. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each for any four of the following
> 
> **1 mark** for the data is divided into frames before transmission
> 
> **1 mark** for each frame carries a destination address
> 
> **1 mark** for only the device whose address matches accepts the frame // every other device discards it // a switch forwards the frame only to the device with that destination address
> 
> **1 mark** for each frame carries a source address, so the printer knows which computer sent the data
> 
> **1 mark** for each frame carries error checking data
> 
> **1 mark** for the receiving device uses that data to test whether the frame was damaged during transmission
> 
> **1 mark** for a damaged frame is discarded and transmitted again
> 
> Accept `MAC address` or `IP address` wherever an address is named
> 
> Do not accept "Ethernet checks the data is correct" on its own, because it names no mechanism

> **[exam-tip]**
> The command word is "explain", so each point needs a consequence attached to it. "The frame has a destination address" is a statement; "the frame has a destination address, so only the printer accepts it" is an explanation and earns the mark. Whichever way the frame travels across the LAN, it is the destination address that decides which device keeps it, so always name the address and say what it is compared with.

parts.problemMd:
A student uses a tablet computer at home. The tablet connects to the home network using a wireless connection.

Give **two** advantages of using a wireless connection instead of a wired connection for this tablet.
parts.solutionMd:
The tablet can be carried around the home and still stay connected to the network. **[1]**

No cable has to be bought or fitted for the tablet, so the connection is cheaper to set up. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each advantage given, to a maximum of **2 marks**
> 
> Freedom of movement: the tablet stays connected while it is carried from room to room
> 
> No physical connection is needed for the tablet
> 
> Less cabling is needed, so the network costs less to set up
> 
> A new device is easy to add, because no extra cable has to be run to it
> 
> Most devices are made with a wireless adapter already built in
> 
> Accept "the tablet can be used in any room in the house" for the freedom of movement mark
> 
> Do not accept "wireless is faster", which is the reverse of the truth: a wired connection gives the higher transfer rate
> 
> Do not accept "wireless is more secure", which is also the reverse

> **[exam-tip]**
> The wired list and the wireless list are almost mirror images of each other, and this is where the marks are lost. Wireless wins on movement and on cost. Wired wins on speed, on reliability and on security. If you have written "wireless is faster and safer", you have copied down the wrong column.
> 
> Count your points as well. "Give two" means two different advantages. "You can move around with it" and "you can use it anywhere" are the same advantage written twice, so they earn one mark, not two.

parts.problemMd:
A photography club has six members. Each member owns one laptop and keeps their own photographs on it. The members meet once a week and copy photographs directly from one laptop to another.

No member of the club works in computing and the club has a very small budget.

The club uses a peer-to-peer model.

Explain why a peer-to-peer model is suitable for this club.
parts.solutionMd:
In a peer-to-peer network all the computers have equal status, so no member's laptop has to act as a server for the others. **[1]**

No dedicated server has to be bought or maintained, which suits a club with a very small budget. **[1]**

Files are transferred directly between the laptops, which is exactly what the six members already do at their weekly meetings. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** per marking point, to a maximum of 3
> 
> **1 mark** for all the computers have equal status / there is no central server
> 
> **1 mark** for no dedicated server hardware has to be bought, so the network is cheap to set up
> 
> **1 mark** for no administrator or technical staff is needed, and no member works in computing
> 
> **1 mark** for the data is distributed, so each member stores and is responsible for their own photographs
> 
> **1 mark** for computers can share files directly with each other
> 
> **1 mark** for the network is very small, so the slow performance of a peer-to-peer network is not a problem
> 
> Accept "each member is responsible for the security and backup of their own laptop" for the fourth marking point.
> 
> Do not accept "it is cheap" or "it is easy to set up" on its own, with no reason given.
> 
> Do not accept a reason that applies to any network, such as "the members can share photographs", unless it is linked to there being no server.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Explain means give a reason, not just a fact. Naming a feature of peer-to-peer earns nothing on its own; you have to link it to something in the question, such as the very small budget, the six members, or the fact that nobody works in computing.
> 
> The most common way students lose marks here is by writing three general benefits of peer-to-peer networks and never mentioning the club at all.

parts.problemMd:
A news website sends video to its users over the internet using bit streaming.

Complete the table by writing **Real-time** or **On-demand** in each empty cell, to identify the type of bit streaming used in each situation.

| Situation | Type of bit streaming |
|---|---|
| A user watches a football match while the match is being played. |   |
| A user watches a news programme that was recorded and stored last week. |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Situation | Type of bit streaming |
|---|---|
| A user watches a football match while the match is being played. | **Real-time** **[1]** |
| A user watches a news programme that was recorded and stored last week. | **On-demand** **[1]** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `Real-time` in the first row
> 
> **1 mark** for `On-demand` in the second row
> 
> Accept `real time` and `on demand`, with or without the hyphen.
> 
> Accept `live` for real-time.
> 
> Do not accept `streaming` or `bit streaming` on its own in either row, because it does not identify the type.
> 
> Do not accept both rows filled with the same answer.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Decide each row by asking one question: does the whole video already exist on the media server before the user presses play? If it does, the stream is on-demand. If the video is still being created while the user watches it, the stream is real-time.
> 
> Do not decide from the device or from the name of the website. The same website can offer both types, and it often does.

parts.problemMd:
A Local Area Network (LAN) uses Carrier Sense Multiple Access / Collision Detection (CSMA/CD).

A device on this LAN has data ready to send.

State **two** things the device does before the data is transmitted.
parts.solutionMd:
The device monitors the communication channel. **[1]**

The device transmits the data only when the channel is free. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for monitors / listens to / senses the communication channel
> 
> **1 mark** for transmits only when the channel is free // if the channel is busy the device waits and checks again
> 
> Accept "idle", "quiet" or "not in use" in place of "free"
> 
> Do not accept "the device sends a jamming signal", because that happens after a collision, not before transmission
> 
> Do not accept "the device waits a random amount of time", because the random back-off also happens after a collision, not before the first attempt

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question is about the two letters `CS` in `CSMA/CD`, which stand for Carrier Sense. A common mistake is to write out the collision part of the process instead, because that is the part most students revise. Jamming signals and random waiting come after a collision has already happened. Before transmitting, all the device does is listen and wait its turn.

parts.problemMd:
A company office has a Local Area Network (LAN) with 40 computers.

Each computer on the LAN is given a private IP address. The office network is connected to the internet using one public IP address.

Explain how giving each computer a private IP address helps to keep that computer secure.
parts.solutionMd:
A private IP address is used for communication inside the LAN only. **[1]**

Devices on the internet see only the public IP address, so a computer with a private IP address is not visible outside the LAN. **[1]**

A device outside the LAN therefore cannot send data straight to that computer, which reduces the chance of it being attacked. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each point, to a maximum of 3
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that a private IP address is used for internal LAN communication only
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the computer is not visible, or is not directly accessible, from the internet
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that only the public IP address is seen by devices outside the LAN
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that an external device cannot send data directly to the computer
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that this reduces the chance of the computer being attacked or hacked
> 
> Accept `external network` or `WAN` in place of `the internet`
> 
> Do not accept `the data is encrypted`. A private IP address does not encrypt any data
> 
> Do not accept `a private IP address is unique on the internet`. A private IP address is unique only within its own LAN and may be reused on another LAN
> 
> Do not accept `the computer cannot access the internet`. The computer can still send and receive data

> **[exam-tip]**
> The command word is `explain`, so a definition on its own is not enough. Many students write only that a private IP address is used inside the LAN and stop there. That is one mark. The other two marks come from saying what this stops an outside device from doing.
> 
> Also be careful not to claim that a private IP address hides or protects the data itself. It hides the computer, not the contents of the messages.

parts.problemMd:
A photography studio has a desktop computer that uploads very large image files to a server in the same building.

The studio connects this computer to the network using a cable instead of using a wireless connection.

Explain why a wired connection is more suitable than a wireless connection for this computer.
parts.solutionMd:
A wired connection gives a faster transfer rate than a wireless connection. **[1]**

The very large image files are therefore uploaded to the server in less time. **[1]**

A wired connection is also more reliable, because the signal is not weakened by walls or by interference from other equipment. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each point, to a maximum of **3 marks**
> 
> A wired connection has a faster transfer rate / a higher bandwidth
> 
> ... so the very large image files take less time to upload / there is less waiting
> 
> A wired connection is more reliable / more stable
> 
> ... because it is not weakened by distance, by walls or by interference
> 
> A wired connection is more secure, because the data is not transmitted through the air where it could be intercepted
> 
> The computer is a desktop that stays in one place, so the freedom of movement that wireless gives is of no use here
> 
> Accept "less latency" or "fewer delays" for the transfer rate point
> 
> Do not accept "a cable is cheaper", which is not true here: adding a cable for a device costs more than using the wireless connection that is already there
> 
> Do not accept "wireless does not work", which states no property of either connection

> **[exam-tip]**
> The marks on an "explain" question come in pairs: the property and what it does for the studio. "Wired is faster" on its own is one mark. Adding "so the large image files upload in less time" earns the second, because it uses the detail given in the question.
> 
> The last point is the one you are most likely to miss. A desktop computer does not move, so the main advantage of wireless is worth nothing here. Saying why the alternative does not help this particular scenario is a valid way to earn a mark.

parts.problemMd:
A courier company has 10 computers in one office. They are connected as a peer-to-peer network and each employee stores their own delivery records on their own computer.

The company will grow to 150 computers in the same office. Every employee will need to use the same set of delivery records, and the company must make one backup of all the delivery records every night.

Explain why the company should change to a client-server model.
parts.solutionMd:
In a peer-to-peer network each computer is responsible for its own backup, so there is no way to back up all the delivery records in one operation. **[1]**

In a client-server model the delivery records are stored on the server, so backing up the server backs up every record. **[1]**

A record held on one employee's computer can only be reached while that computer is switched on, but a server is always available, so all 150 employees can reach the shared records at any time. **[1]**

The server manages user accounts and access rights centrally, which is far easier than setting security separately on 150 computers. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** per marking point, to a maximum of 4
> 
> **1 mark** for peer-to-peer has no central management of backup / each computer backs up its own data
> 
> **1 mark** for storing the records on the server allows one central backup of all the records
> 
> **1 mark** for data on a peer is only available while that computer is switched on
> 
> **1 mark** for the server is always available, so the shared records can be accessed at any time
> 
> **1 mark** for peer-to-peer has no central management of security or access rights
> 
> **1 mark** for the server can control access rights for all users centrally
> 
> **1 mark** for the performance of an individual computer falls while other computers are accessing it
> 
> **1 mark** for peer-to-peer is not suitable for a large network, but a dedicated server is built to handle many requests
> 
> Accept "each computer is only as secure as the employee who uses it" for the fifth marking point.
> 
> Do not accept "client-server is better" with no reason given.
> 
> Do not accept an answer about network topology or cabling, which is not part of the choice of network model.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The question hands you two facts to use: the growth to 150 computers and the nightly backup. Each fact earns marks only if your answer says what peer-to-peer cannot do and what a client-server model does instead. Answers that list the good points of client-server without that contrast usually score about half the marks.
> 
> "Client-server is more secure" is not a marking point by itself. Say why: in peer-to-peer each user manages their own machine, so the network is only as secure as its weakest computer, while a server controls access rights for everyone from one place.

parts.problemMd:
A news website streams a press conference in real-time while it is happening.

The website also stores a recording of the press conference on its media server, so that users can watch it on demand at any time afterwards.

Compare the real-time bit stream with the on-demand bit stream.
parts.solutionMd:
The real-time stream is sent from the source as the press conference happens, whereas the on-demand stream is sent from a file that is already stored in full on the media server. **[1]**

The real-time stream must be watched while the press conference is taking place, whereas the on-demand stream can be watched at a time chosen by the user. **[1]**

The real-time stream cannot be paused or rewound, whereas the on-demand stream can be paused, rewound and watched again. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each comparison, to a maximum of 3. Each comparison must state something about both streams.
> 
> **1 mark** for source of the data: real-time comes direct from the source as the event happens, on-demand comes from a file already stored on the media server
> 
> **1 mark** for timing: real-time is streamed and watched at the same time, on-demand is watched at a time the user chooses
> 
> **1 mark** for playback control: real-time cannot be paused or rewound, on-demand can be paused, rewound or skipped
> 
> **1 mark** for connection: real-time needs a steady connection and a low delay, on-demand can hold more data in the buffer ahead of the playback point so a short delay does not matter
> 
> Accept a comparison written as two separate sentences, one about each stream.
> 
> Do not accept a point about only one of the two streams, such as "on-demand can be paused", with no statement about the other.
> 
> Accept "real-time comes direct from the source, whereas on-demand is pre-recorded / downloaded to view later" for the source-of-data mark. Do not accept "on-demand is downloaded and real-time is streamed" with no statement of when the data is created, because both are bit streams

> **[exam-tip]**
> The command word is Compare, so every mark needs both sides. A list of three things on-demand streaming can do earns nothing, however correct each one is. Join the two halves with "whereas" and the mark is safe.
> 
> Do not write only "on-demand is a download". Say when the data was created: real-time comes direct from the source as it happens, whereas on-demand was pre-recorded and is downloaded to view later.

parts.problemMd:
The table shows the steps that devices on a Local Area Network (LAN) follow when they use Carrier Sense Multiple Access / Collision Detection (CSMA/CD).

Three steps are missing.

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1 | A device with data to send monitors the communication channel. |
| 2 | .............................. |
| 3 | Two devices begin to transmit at the same time, so a collision occurs. |
| 4 | .............................. |
| 5 | .............................. |

Complete the table.
parts.solutionMd:
| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1 | A device with data to send monitors the communication channel. |
| 2 | **The device transmits the data only when the channel is free. If the channel is busy it waits.** **[1]** |
| 3 | Two devices begin to transmit at the same time, so a collision occurs. |
| 4 | **The devices detect the collision, abort the transmission and send a jamming signal.** **[1]** |
| 5 | **Each device waits a random amount of time, called the back-off time, and then tries to send the data again.** **[1]** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for step 2: data is transmitted only when the channel is free // if the channel is busy the device waits
> 
> **1 mark** for step 4: the transmission is aborted // a jamming signal is transmitted (either alone is enough)
> 
> **1 mark** for step 5: each device waits a random amount of time / a random back-off time before trying to send again
> 
> Accept in step 5 the addition that the wait time is increased if further collisions occur
> 
> Do not accept "the devices wait and then try again" in step 5 without the word random or back-off, because a fixed wait would produce the same collision again
> 
> Do not accept steps written in a different order from the one shown

> **[exam-tip]**
> Step 5 is where most marks are lost. Students write "the devices wait and then resend", which is not enough. The wait has to be random, because two devices that wait for the same length of time will collide all over again. Learn the word "random", or the mark-scheme term "back-off time", and put it in every answer about what follows a collision.

parts.problemMd:
A LAN is divided into subnets.

On this LAN, the first three groups of an IPv4 address are the network ID and the last group is the host ID.

Four devices on the LAN have the IPv4 addresses shown in the table.

| Device | IPv4 address |
|---|---|
| A | 192.168.10.4 |
| B | 192.168.10.37 |
| C | 192.168.25.4 |
| D | 192.168.10.9 |

Explain which of the devices B, C and D are on the same subnet as device A.

Use the terms network ID and host ID in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Devices B and D are on the same subnet as device A. Device C is not. **[1]**

Devices A, B and D all have the network ID `192.168.10`, and every device on the same subnet has the same network ID. **[1]**

Device C has the network ID `192.168.25`, which is different, so device C is on a different subnet. **[1]**

The host IDs of A, B and D are 4, 37 and 9. They are all different, so each device is identified uniquely within the subnet. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for identifying B and D, and only B and D
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that A, B and D share the network ID `192.168.10`, and that devices on the same subnet have the same network ID
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that C has a different network ID, `192.168.25`, so it is on a different subnet
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the host ID is different for every device within a subnet, so it identifies one device inside that subnet
> 
> Accept the network ID written as `192.168.10.0`, or described as the first three groups of the address
> 
> Accept `192.168.25.0` for device C's network ID
> 
> Do not accept device C. Device C has the same host ID as device A, `4`, but the host ID does not decide the subnet
> 
> Do not award the second, third or fourth mark for an answer that lists the devices without naming the network ID or the host ID

> **[exam-tip]**
> The trap in this question is device C. Its address ends in `.4`, exactly like device A, so a student who compares the last group picks C and loses three marks. The subnet is decided by the network ID at the front of the address. The host ID at the end only tells the devices inside one subnet apart.
> 
> Do not assume the split is always three groups to one either. The question tells you where the network ID ends, and a different question can put the boundary somewhere else, so read the stem before you split the address.

parts.problemMd:
A public library is being refitted. Two groups of computers will use the same network:

- 30 desktop computers that are fixed to study desks and are used to search a shared catalogue
- laptops and tablets that visitors bring with them and use anywhere in the building

The library will connect the desktop computers with cables. Visitors will connect their own devices wirelessly.

Explain why each group is given this type of connection.
parts.solutionMd:
The desktop computers are fixed to the study desks and never move, so nothing is lost by tying them to a cable. **[1]**

A wired connection also gives them a faster and more reliable link to the shared catalogue. **[1]**

The visitors carry their devices around the building, so their connection must keep working as the device moves. **[1]**

The library cannot run a cable to every seat, and it cannot fit a cable to a device that it does not own. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each point, to a maximum of **2 marks** for the desktop computers and **2 marks** for the visitors' devices
> 
> Desktop computers, wired:
> 
> The computers are in fixed positions and do not move, so freedom of movement is not needed
> 
> A wired connection has a faster transfer rate / a higher bandwidth for reaching the shared catalogue
> 
> A wired connection is more reliable / more stable
> 
> A wired connection is more secure, so the library's own records are harder to intercept
> 
> Visitors' devices, wireless:
> 
> The devices are carried around the building and must stay connected as they move
> 
> A cable cannot be run to every seat in the building
> 
> Visitors can join and leave the network without any change to the cabling
> 
> The library does not own the visitors' devices, but almost every such device already has a wireless adapter built in
> 
> Accept "the desktops are static" or "the desktops stay in one place" for the fixed position mark
> 
> Do not accept a bare statement of the choice, such as "the desktops use a cable". The choice is given in the question, so only the reason earns a mark
> 
> Do not accept the same reason offered for both groups

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question has two halves and four marks, so it wants two reasons about the desktop computers and two about the visitors' devices. The most common way to lose marks here is to write four good reasons for the cabled computers and nothing at all about the wireless ones, which caps you at two.
> 
> Repeating the choice earns nothing. The question already tells you which group gets which connection, so start every sentence with "because" and then check that what follows is a property of the connection rather than a restatement of it.

parts.problemMd:
A company uses two types of client device.
