> The one shared cable is what defines this topology and it is also its weakness. When a question describes damage to a bus network, the examiner wants you to say that the whole network stops, and to give the reason, not just to name the machines closest to the damage.

parts.problemMd:
Complete the description of a star topology by writing the missing word in each space.

In a star topology, every device on the network has its own cable connecting it to one ............................ device.

On a modern local area network this device is usually a ............................ , which reads the destination address of a packet and sends the packet only to the device it is addressed to.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **central, switch**

In a star topology, every device on the network has its own cable connecting it to one **central** device. **[1]**

On a modern local area network this device is usually a **switch**, which reads the destination address of a packet and sends the packet only to the device it is addressed to. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for central
> 
> **1 mark** for switch
> 
> Accept router for the second space
> 
> Do not accept hub for the second space. A hub sends every packet to every device on the network, so it does not match the description given in the sentence

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hub and switch are not interchangeable in this syllabus. A hub forwards a packet to every device and each device then decides whether to keep it. A switch reads the destination address and forwards the packet to that one device only. Any wording such as "only to the intended device" is describing a switch.

parts.problemMd:
A design company keeps all of its project files on cloud storage. An employee uses a laptop to open one of these files, makes a change to it, and then saves it.

Describe what happens to the file when the employee opens it and when the employee saves it.
parts.solutionMd:
When the file is opened, the laptop sends a request over the internet to the cloud provider's remote server. **[1]**

The server locates the file and transmits a copy of it back to the laptop, where the employee can work on it. **[1]**

When the file is saved, the changed version is transmitted back over the internet and stored on the remote server, so the copy held by the provider becomes the up-to-date one. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the laptop sends a request over the internet to the provider's remote server
> 
> **1 mark** for a copy of the file is transmitted from the remote server to the laptop
> 
> **1 mark** for the edited file is transmitted back and stored on the remote server // the version held on the remote server is updated
> 
> Accept "downloaded" for transmitted to the laptop and "uploaded" for transmitted back
> 
> Accept "the file is opened in a browser and edited there" for the second mark
> 
> Do not accept "the file is saved on the laptop's hard disk", because the stored copy is held on the provider's remote server
> 
> Do not accept "the file moves to the cloud", because it does not describe a transmission over the internet

> **[exam-tip]**
> The command word is "describe", so the marks are for the steps, not for a general statement that the file is "in the cloud". Write the journey: request out, copy back, edited copy returned.
> 
> Students often answer only the first half and lose the third mark. If a question names two actions, opening and saving, there is at least one mark attached to each of them.

parts.problemMd:
A design studio has twelve computers connected in a star topology.

Explain the effect on the network of each of the following:

- the cable between one computer and the central device being damaged
- the central device failing.
parts.solutionMd:
If one cable is damaged, only the computer on that cable loses its connection. **[1]**

The other eleven computers can still communicate, because each of them has its own separate cable to the central device. **[1]**

If the central device fails, no computer can communicate with any other, because every packet on a star network has to pass through the central device. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each, to a maximum of 3
> 
> **1 mark** for only the one computer being disconnected when its cable is damaged
> 
> **1 mark** for the rest of the network being unaffected, because each device has its own separate cable to the central device
> 
> **1 mark** for no device being able to communicate when the central device fails
> 
> **1 mark** for the reason that every packet has to pass through the central device // the central device is a single point of failure
> 
> Accept "the switch" or "the router" in place of "the central device"
> 
> Do not accept "the whole network stops working" as the effect of the damaged cable, which is the behaviour of a bus topology

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two failures, two different answers. That is exactly what this question tests, and students who have learned "a star topology is reliable" as one fixed sentence tend to give the same answer twice.
> 
> Say which devices are affected and give the reason. "The network still works" on its own earns one mark at most. The second mark comes from saying that each device has its own separate cable to the centre.

parts.problemMd:
An online game stores each player's saved progress using cloud computing.

A player begins a game on a computer at home. The player stops playing, and later continues the same game from the same point on a different computer in another city.

Explain how cloud computing makes this possible.
parts.solutionMd:
The saved progress is stored on the game provider's remote servers rather than on either of the two computers. **[1]**

When the player stops playing, the progress is transmitted over the internet from the first computer and stored on those servers. **[1]**

The player signs in on the second computer with the same credentials, so the servers can identify which player's saved progress to send. **[1]**

The second computer has an internet connection, so it can request that saved progress from the same servers and the game continues from the point that was saved. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the saved progress being held on the provider's remote server, not on the player's own computer
> 
> **1 mark** for the progress being uploaded over the internet from the first computer when the player stops
> 
> **1 mark** for the player signing in with the same account or credentials, so the correct saved data is identified
> 
> **1 mark** for the second computer downloading that saved progress over the internet, so play continues from the same point
> 
> Accept "the same user account" for credentials
> 
> Accept "any device with an internet connection can reach the same server" for the fourth mark
> 
> Do not accept "the progress is copied from the first computer to the second computer", because the two computers never communicate directly
> 
> Do not accept "the game saves automatically" on its own, because it does not say where the data is stored

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mistake to avoid is describing a transfer between the two computers. Nothing passes directly between them. Every step goes through the provider's remote server, and an answer that leaves the server out cannot reach full marks.
> 
> Do not overlook the sign-in step either. The remote server holds saved progress for very many players, so something has to tell it whose data to send back. Naming the account or the credentials is worth a mark on its own.

parts.problemMd:
A library has a star topology local area network with fifteen computers connected to one switch.

The library plans to add ten more computers next year. It also wants to be able to find and repair network faults quickly.

Explain how the star topology meets these two requirements, and identify **one** problem the library must plan for.
parts.solutionMd:
A new computer is added by running one new cable from it to the switch. **[1]**

The rest of the network keeps running while this is done, because no existing device shares that cable. **[1]**

A fault on one cable stops only the device on that cable, so the faulty cable is found quickly by seeing which computer has lost its connection. **[1]**

The problem to plan for is that the switch is a single point of failure. If it fails, all twenty-five computers lose their connection. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each, to a maximum of 4
> 
> **1 mark** for a new device being added by connecting one new cable to the switch
> 
> **1 mark** for the existing devices being unaffected while the new device is added
> 
> **1 mark** for a fault affecting only the device on the faulty cable, which makes the fault quick to locate
> 
> **1 mark** for identifying the switch as a single point of failure // for the switch needing enough free ports for twenty-five devices
> 
> Accept "the whole network stops if the switch fails" for the fourth point
> 
> Do not accept "the network is faster" as an answer to either requirement, because speed is not one of the two requirements given in the stem

> **[exam-tip]**
> The command word is "explain", so every advantage needs a reason attached. "It is easy to add a computer" is half a marking point. "It is easy to add a computer, because only one new cable to the switch is needed and no other device is disconnected" is the whole of it.
> 
> The final sentence of the stem asks for a problem, so do not leave it out. A star topology answer that never mentions the central device as a single point of failure is incomplete, and that is the mark most often dropped on this topic.

parts.problemMd:
A student stores school files using cloud computing instead of on a memory stick.

Give one benefit and one drawback of storing the files in this way.
parts.solutionMd:
Benefit: the student can open the files from any computer that has an internet connection, so a memory stick left at home no longer matters. **[1]**

Drawback: the files cannot be opened at all when there is no internet connection. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a correct benefit, from: can be accessed from anywhere with an internet connection // the provider carries out the backups so the student does not have to // storage capacity can be increased easily // files can be shared with other students // small amounts of storage are often free // no separate storage device has to be bought
> 
> **1 mark** for a correct drawback, from: cannot be accessed without an internet connection // the student has no control over the provider's security // the student has no control over whether backups are taken // access is lost if the provider's server fails // free storage is limited and extra capacity must be paid for // uploading and downloading large files can be slow
> 
> Accept "a third party" for "the provider"
> 
> Do not accept "it is cheaper" on its own as a benefit, because the cost depends on how much storage is used; "small amounts of storage are often free" is credited
> 
> Accept "the provider's security may be weaker / the files could be hacked on the provider's server" as a drawback

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read the number of marks and match it to the number of points asked for. This question wants one of each, so a page of benefits with no drawback still scores only one mark.
> 
> Answers such as "it is safer" or "it is faster" are too vague to credit. Name the thing that actually changes: where the files are held, who looks after the backups, or what happens when the connection drops.

parts.problemMd:
Five computers in a research laboratory are connected using a mesh topology.

Identify **two** characteristics of a mesh topology.
parts.solutionMd:
Every computer is connected directly to at least one other computer, and in a full mesh to every other computer. **[1]**

There is more than one route between any two computers. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each, to a maximum of 2
> 
> **1 mark** for all devices being connected directly to at least one other device // for every device being connected to every other device in a full mesh
> 
> **1 mark** for there being multiple routes between any two devices
> 
> **1 mark** for the devices acting as relays, passing packets on towards the final destination
> 
> **1 mark** for there being no central device
> 
> Do not accept "all devices are connected to a central cable", which describes a bus topology
> 
> Do not accept "it is reliable" on its own, which is an advantage rather than a characteristic of the layout

> **[exam-tip]**
> A characteristic describes how the network is laid out or how data moves through it. An advantage says why that is useful. Questions on this topic ask for one or the other, and an advantage written where a characteristic is asked for scores nothing. Check which word the stem uses before you write.

parts.problemMd:
A charity has volunteers working in five different countries. All of the volunteers need to read and update the same set of documents.

Describe three benefits to the charity of storing these documents using cloud computing.
parts.solutionMd:
The documents are held on the provider's remote servers, so a volunteer in any of the five countries can open them from any device with an internet connection. **[1]**

Every volunteer works on the same stored copy, so an update made by one volunteer is seen by the others and the charity does not have to send files from country to country. **[1]**

The provider carries out the backups, so the charity does not have to buy backup hardware or pay someone to manage it. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each, to a maximum of 3, from the following.
> 
> **1 mark** for the documents can be accessed from anywhere with an internet connection
> 
> **1 mark** for the volunteers share one stored copy, so several people can work on the same document and see each other's changes
> 
> **1 mark** for the provider performs the backups, so the charity needs no backup hardware or staff of its own
> 
> **1 mark** for the provider manages the security, so the charity does not have to install and maintain it
> 
> **1 mark** for storage capacity can be increased on demand as the number of documents grows, without buying storage devices
> 
> Accept "small amounts of storage are often free" as a cost benefit
> 
> Do not accept "it is faster", because the transfer speed depends on each volunteer's internet connection and may be slower than local storage
> 
> Do not accept two wordings of the same benefit, for example "accessible anywhere" and "accessible from any country", as two separate points

> **[exam-tip]**
> Three marks means three different benefits. The most common way to lose a mark here is to write one benefit twice, once as "it can be used anywhere" and once as "volunteers in other countries can use it". Those are one point, not two.
> 
> Tie each benefit to the charity in the question. An examiner reading "you can access it anywhere" learns nothing about five countries; "a volunteer in any of the five countries can open the same document" clearly answers what was asked.

parts.problemMd:
A company is building a full mesh network to connect eight servers. Each connection joins exactly two servers.

Calculate the number of connections needed.

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **28 connections**

Each server must be connected to the other 7 servers. **[1]**

8 servers x 7 connections each = 56 **[1]**

Each connection has been counted twice, once at each end, so 56 / 2 = 28 **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each server needing 7 connections // for stating that each server connects to every other server
> 
> **1 mark** for 8 x 7 = 56 // for using n(n - 1) / 2 with n = 8
> 
> **1 mark** for the final answer of 28
> 
> Accept 28 with correct working set out in any order
> 
> Accept a correct count taken from a labelled diagram
> 
> Do not accept 56, which counts every connection twice, once at each end
> 
> Do not accept 64, which comes from 8 x 8 and connects each server to itself

> **[exam-tip]**
> The trap here is doubling. Every connection has two ends, so multiplying the number of devices by the number of connections each device needs counts every connection twice. Always halve at the end.
> 
> This calculation is the reason a full mesh is rarely used for a large network. Eight servers need 28 connections, but sixteen servers need 120. The amount of cabling grows far faster than the number of devices.

parts.problemMd:
A hospital uses a full mesh topology to connect the six computers that control its patient monitoring equipment. The monitoring must keep working even if part of the network fails.

Explain why a full mesh topology is a suitable choice for these six computers.

Explain **one** problem the hospital would have if it later used a full mesh topology for all twenty computers in the department.
parts.solutionMd:
Each of the six computers has a direct connection to every other computer, so there is more than one route between any two of them. **[1]**

If one connection fails, the data takes an alternative route, and the computers act as relays to pass packets on towards the destination, so the monitoring keeps working. **[1]**

For twenty computers the number of connections rises from 15 to 190. **[1]**

That means far more cable and far more network ports on every computer, so the cost rises steeply and the network becomes difficult to install and to expand. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for every computer having a direct connection to every other computer, giving multiple routes between any two
> 
> **1 mark** for the data taking an alternative route if one connection fails, so the monitoring keeps working // for the devices acting as relays
> 
> **1 mark** for the number of connections growing very quickly, from 15 for six computers to 190 for twenty
> 
> **1 mark** for a consequence of that growth: much more cabling and hardware, a higher cost, or a network that is difficult to install and expand
> 
> Accept "there is no single point of failure" for the first point
> 
> Accept the third mark without the figures 15 and 190 if you state clearly that the number of connections grows far faster than the number of computers
> 
> Do not accept "the central switch would be overloaded", because a mesh topology has no central switch

> **[exam-tip]**
> When the stem gives you a requirement, such as "the monitoring must keep working even if part of the network fails", your answer has to use it. Marks for justifying a topology are given for linking a feature of that topology to the requirement in the stem, not for listing advantages you have memorised.
> 
> The second half of this question is where mesh answers usually lose marks. Do not write "it costs more" and stop. Say why it costs more: the number of connections grows much faster than the number of devices.

parts.problemMd:
A publishing company must decide where to store its manuscripts. It can use cloud computing, or it can use storage devices that the company buys and keeps inside its own building.

Describe two drawbacks of choosing cloud computing.
parts.solutionMd:
Drawback 1: the company loses direct control over its manuscripts. **[1]**

The files are held on a provider's remote infrastructure, so the company has to rely on that provider to keep them secure and to take backups, and cannot check those arrangements for itself. **[1]**

Drawback 2: the company has to keep paying for the service. **[1]**

The provider's charges recur for as long as the manuscripts are stored, while storage devices bought for the building are paid for once, so over several years the cloud can cost more. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> A maximum of 2 marks for each drawback, to a maximum of 4.
> 
> **1 mark** for loss of control over the data, and **1 mark** for the development that it is held on someone else's remote infrastructure and the company depends on the provider for security and backups
> 
> **1 mark** for increased recurring cost, and **1 mark** for the development that the provider's charges must be paid repeatedly while the company's own devices are paid for once
> 
> **1 mark** for a reliable internet connection is required, and **1 mark** for the development that the manuscripts cannot be reached at all if the connection or the provider's server fails
> 
> **1 mark** for uploading and downloading is slow for large files, and **1 mark** for the development that the transfer speed is limited by the company's internet connection rather than by its own devices
> 
> Accept "a third party" for "the provider"
> 
> Accept "the provider's security may be weaker" or "it may be less secure" as the first mark of a security drawback; the second mark needs the development that the company relies on the provider for its security and cannot check it
> 
> Do not accept two wordings of one drawback, for example "it needs the internet" and "it cannot be used offline", as two separate drawbacks

> **[exam-tip]**
> Four marks for two drawbacks means each one is worth two, so each needs a point and then a development. "It costs money" is the point; "and the charge is paid every month for as long as the files are stored" is the development that earns the second mark.
> 
> Do not turn this into an argument that cloud computing is simply worse. The examiner is testing whether you can state a real weakness, so keep to the ones the syllabus supports: dependence on an internet connection, charges that recur, and giving up direct control of the data.

parts.problemMd: State what is meant by a **hybrid topology** and give **one** example of a hybrid topology.
parts.solutionMd:
A hybrid topology is a network made by combining two or more different topologies. **[1]**

For example, a star network in one building joined to a mesh network in another building. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a network that combines // joins together two or more different topologies
> 
> **1 mark** for a valid example that names two different topologies, for example star and bus, star and mesh, or bus and mesh
> 
> Do not accept an example that names only one topology, such as "several star networks joined together", because no second topology has been named
> 
> Do not accept "a mixture of wired and wireless connections", which is not a combination of topologies

> **[exam-tip]**
> The example must name two different topologies. Writing "a mixture of topologies" only repeats the definition and cannot earn the second mark.
> 
> The command word is "state", so one clear sentence is enough for the first mark. Listing the advantages of a hybrid topology earns nothing here.

parts.problemMd:
The table gives two descriptions.

Complete the table by writing whether each description refers to a public cloud or a private cloud.

| Description | Type of cloud |
|---|---|
| Computing services are offered by a third-party provider over the internet and are available to anyone with the appropriate equipment and credentials. |   |
| Computing services are dedicated to one organisation, and only that organisation's users may access them. |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Description | Type of cloud |
|---|---|
| Computing services are offered by a third-party provider over the internet and are available to anyone with the appropriate equipment and credentials. | **Public cloud** **[1]** |
| Computing services are dedicated to one organisation, and only that organisation's users may access them. | **Private cloud** **[1]** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `Public` in the first row
> 
> **1 mark** for `Private` in the second row
> 
> Accept "public cloud" and "private cloud" written in full
> 
> Do not accept "shared cloud" or "open cloud" for the first row, and do not accept "personal cloud" or "internal cloud" for the second row, because these are not the terms used in the syllabus

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word that decides the first answer is "anyone". A public cloud shares the provider's infrastructure between many customers, so anyone who pays for it can use it. A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation, so the answer turns on who is allowed in, not on where the servers stand.
> 
> Students often assume that a private cloud must sit inside the organisation's own building. It does not have to. A provider can run a private cloud over the internet and it is still private, because it is reserved for that one organisation.

parts.problemMd:
A company's network is described in the table.

| Part of the network | How the devices are connected |
|---|---|
| Building A | Twelve computers, each with its own cable to a single switch |
| Building B | Five computers, each with a direct connection to every other computer |
| Link between the buildings | One cable from the switch in Building A to one computer in Building B |

(i) Identify the topology used in Building A.

(1)

(ii) Identify the topology used in Building B.

(1)

(iii) Identify the topology of the network as a whole.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Star topology **[1]**

(ii) Full mesh topology **[1]**

(iii) Hybrid topology **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i) **1 mark** for star
> 
> (ii) **1 mark** for mesh
> 
> Accept full mesh for part (ii)
> 
> (iii) **1 mark** for hybrid
> 
> Do not accept star for part (ii). Every computer in Building B connects directly to every other computer and there is no central device
> 
> Do not accept star or mesh for part (iii), because the network as a whole combines two different topologies

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read the description of the connections, not the number of devices. "Each with its own cable to a single switch" is a star every time, and "a direct connection to every other computer" is a mesh every time.
> 
> Part (iii) is the one that is left blank. When one network is built from parts that use different topologies, the network as a whole is a hybrid topology. That word is on the syllabus and it is what the examiner is waiting for.

parts.problemMd:
A bank stores its customer account records using a private cloud rather than a public cloud.

Explain why the bank has chosen a private cloud.
parts.solutionMd:
A private cloud is dedicated to the bank alone, so the infrastructure holding the account records is not shared with other organisations. **[1]**

This gives the bank greater control over the security and privacy of the records, instead of relying on a provider that is serving many other customers at the same time. **[1]**

Access can be limited to the bank's own selected users rather than being open to anyone on the internet, which reduces the risk of unauthorised access to customer data. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each, to a maximum of 3, from the following.
> 
> **1 mark** for the service is dedicated to the bank and is not shared with other organisations
> 
> **1 mark** for the bank keeps greater control over the security or the privacy of the records
> 
> **1 mark** for access is restricted to selected users rather than the general public, reducing unauthorised access
> 
> **1 mark** for the bank controls when and how backups are taken
> 
> **1 mark** for the storage can be tailored to the bank's own requirements
> 
> Accept "bespoke" for "tailored"
> 
> Do not accept "it is more secure" on its own, because the mark is for the control the bank keeps rather than for an unsupported claim
> 
> Do not accept "it is cheaper", because a private cloud is normally more expensive than a public cloud of the same capacity

> **[exam-tip]**
> Answers here usually say "a private cloud is safer" and stop. That is a conclusion, not an explanation. The marks are for the reasons behind it: the infrastructure is not shared, the bank sets the security, and only chosen users are let in.
> 
> Watch the direction of the cost argument. A private cloud usually costs more, because the bank is paying for infrastructure reserved for itself alone. Low cost is a reason to pick a public cloud, so it cannot be used to justify this choice.

parts.problemMd:
A transport company is designing the network for a new site. The site has two areas:

- an open-plan office with thirty computers used for email and word processing. Staff join and leave the company often, so computers are added and removed regularly
- a control room with four computers that track vehicles in real time. These four computers must still be able to communicate with each other if one connection fails.

The two areas will be joined together to form a hybrid topology.

Justify the choice of a suitable topology for each area.
parts.solutionMd:
Office: a star topology. **[1]**

Each computer has its own cable to a central switch, so a computer is added or removed without disconnecting any of the others, which suits an office where staff join and leave often. **[1]**

A fault on one cable stops only the computer on that cable, so the other twenty-nine computers keep working. **[1]**

Control room: a mesh topology. **[1]**

Every one of the four computers has a direct connection to each of the other three, so there is more than one route between any two of them and they still communicate if one connection fails. **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each, to a maximum of 5
> 
> **1 mark** for choosing a star topology for the office
> 
> **1 mark** for a computer being added or removed without disconnecting the other computers, because each has its own cable to the central switch
> 
> **1 mark** for a cable fault affecting only one computer, so the other twenty-nine keep working
> 
> **1 mark** for choosing a mesh topology for the control room
> 
> **1 mark** for every computer having a direct connection to every other, so there is more than one route between any two
> 
> **1 mark** for the four computers still being able to communicate when one connection fails, which is the requirement given in the stem
> 
> **1 mark** for a mesh being affordable for four computers, which need only 6 connections, whereas thirty computers would need 435
> 
> Accept "full mesh" in place of "mesh"
> 
> Accept a bus topology for the office only where you justify it by low cost and accept that a single cable fault stops the whole office
> 
> Do not accept a mesh for the office without a justification, because thirty computers would need 435 connections
> 
> Do not accept a star topology for the control room, because the central device would be a single point of failure and the stem requires communication to continue when a connection fails

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Justify" means give the choice and the reason together, and the reason has to come from the stem. Two details are placed there deliberately: staff join and leave often, and the control room must keep working if a connection fails. Each of those points to a different topology.
> 
> Do not choose the same topology for both areas. The question tells you the site uses a hybrid topology, which means the two areas are meant to be different. An answer that puts a star in both places has missed what the question is asking.

parts.problemMd:
A company runs two separate systems.

- System A holds product brochures that the company wants any member of the public to be able to download.
- System B holds the salary records of the company's employees.

The company will store one system on a public cloud and the other on a private cloud.

Explain which type of cloud the company should choose for each system.
parts.solutionMd:
System A should be stored on a public cloud. **[1]**

The brochures are meant to be available to anyone on the internet, and a public cloud shares the provider's infrastructure between many customers, which makes it the cheaper way to serve a large number of downloads. **[1]**

System B should be stored on a private cloud. **[1]**

A private cloud is dedicated to the company, so access to the salary records can be restricted to selected employees and the company keeps control over the security of the data. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for System A on a public cloud
> 
> **1 mark** for a supporting reason, from: the brochures are intended to be available to anyone on the internet // the infrastructure is shared with other organisations, so it is cheaper // capacity can be increased when many people download at the same time
> 
> **1 mark** for System B on a private cloud
> 
> **1 mark** for a supporting reason, from: the service is dedicated to the company only // access can be restricted to selected employees rather than the general public // the company keeps control over the security of the salary records // the company controls how the records are backed up
> 
> Accept a reason for System B that names the confidential nature of salary data as the cause of the restriction
> 
> Do not award the reason mark in either half if the type of cloud named in that half is wrong, because the reason has to support the choice made
> 
> Do not accept "salary records are private so use a private cloud", because it repeats the name of the cloud instead of giving a reason

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two systems and four marks means one mark for each choice and one mark for each reason. Naming both clouds correctly and giving no reasons throws away half the question.
> 
> The reason for the public cloud is the part students miss. It is easy to explain why salary data must be locked down. The examiner also wants to know why the brochures do not need that, and why sharing a provider's infrastructure with other organisations is an advantage when the material is meant to be public anyway.

parts.problemMd:
A computer system has a dual-core Central Processing Unit (CPU).

Identify **two **disadvantages of using Dynamic RAM (DRAM) instead of Static RAM (SRAM) in a computer system.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 2**)
> 
> e.g.
> 
> - DRAM requires constant refresh cycles unlike SRAM
> - DRAM has lower access speed than SRAM

parts.problemMd:
The computer system is used to store data received from a temperature sensor every five seconds. The data is stored on an optical disc using an optical disc reader/writer.

(i) Describe the principal operation of an optical disc reader/writer

(4)

(ii) The computer uses a buffer when writing data to the optical disc.

Explain the use of a buffer when writing data to the optical disc.

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i) **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 4**)
> 
> - The disc is spun at high speed
> - A laser is shone onto the disc to read or write
> - … using an optical head to move it into position
> - … it follows the spiral track from the centre outwards
> - When writing, the laser burns pits to represent the data
> - When reading, the laser reflects from pits and lands
> - The reflection from a pit and a land is different
> - … the differences are interpreted as 1s or 0s
> 
> (ii)** 1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 3**)
> 
> - The computer and optical disc reader/writer send and receive at different speeds
> - A buffer allows temporary storage of the data
> - … so that the computer can transfer data to the buffer at the higher speed
> - … and is not held up waiting for data to transfer // so the computer can carry on with other tasks
> - … so the optical disc reader/writer is not overloaded
> - … and so that data is transferred to the optical disc reader/writer from the buffer at the slower rate

parts.problemMd:
A security system has both a floodlight (very bright light) and an audio alarm.

The data from multiple sensors is analysed and used to:

- turn on the floodlight
- sound the audio alarm.

Sensors can be used to detect:

- if doors are open
- the external daylight level
- if people are detected within a set distance.

Complete the table to identify the most appropriate type of sensor for each scenario.

| Scenario | Type of sensor |
|---|---|
| A door is open. |   |
| The external daylight level is below a set amount. |   |
| A person is detected within 2 metres. |   |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for all 3 appropriate sensors
> 
> | Scenario | Type of sensor |
> |---|---|
> | A door is open. | Pressure sensor // Infra-red |
> | The external daylight level is below a set amount. | Light sensor |
> | A person is detected within 2 metres. | Infra-red |

parts.problemMd: Explain whether the security system is an example of a monitoring system or a control system.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 3**) for a correct justification No marks for the identification of the system
> 
> **Monitoring system**
> 
> - There is no use of feedback // The light and the alarm are just warnings
> - The output of the floodlight or the audio alarm does not affect the input of data from the sensors
> - The system does not have any actuators

parts.problemMd:
Embedded systems are used in many electronic devices.

Describe the drawbacks of embedded systems.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 3**)
> 
> e.g.
> 
> - It is difficult to change / update the firmware by the user
> - Errors cannot be fixed easily // Troubleshooting / fault-finding / repairing is a specialist task / expensive
> - Functionality cannot be changed/extended easily // Cannot be easily adapted for another task
> - Faulty / outdated devices are often thrown away rather than repaired
> - … leading to e-waste

parts.problemMd:
Data is often transferred between two devices that work at different speeds.

Define the term **buffer**.
parts.solutionMd:
A buffer is an area of memory that is used for the temporary storage of data. **[1]**

It holds the data while the data is being transferred between two devices, or two processes, that work at different speeds. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for stating that a buffer is temporary storage, or an area of memory that holds data temporarily
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that it holds data being transferred between two devices, or two processes, that work at different speeds
> 
> Accept "temporary store", "temporary memory", or "holds data until the receiving device is ready" for the first mark.
> 
> Accept "so that the faster device does not have to wait for the slower device" for the second mark.
> 
> Do not accept "permanent storage" or "secondary storage". A buffer is volatile temporary storage, not a place where data is kept.
> 
> Do not accept "a buffer stores data" on its own, because it does not say that the storage is temporary.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word "temporary" is doing most of the work in this definition and it is the word most often left out. Writing that a buffer "stores data" is true of every kind of memory, so it earns nothing.
> 
> The second mark is for the reason the buffer exists, so always name the difference in speed between the two devices. A definition that stops at "an area of memory" is only half an answer.

parts.problemMd:
A musician uses a microphone that is connected to a computer to record sound.

The microphone captures sound continuously, but the processor is not always free to accept the sound data.

The recording system uses a buffer.

Explain how the buffer is used when sound data is transferred from the microphone to the computer.
parts.solutionMd:
The microphone and the processor work at different speeds, because the microphone produces sound data continuously while the processor accepts that data only when it is free. **[1]**

The sound data is written into the buffer as it is captured, and the buffer holds it temporarily. **[1]**

The processor reads the sound data out of the buffer when it is ready, so the microphone is not held up and no sound data is lost. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for identifying that the microphone and the computer, or processor, work at different speeds
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the captured sound data is written into the buffer and held there temporarily
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the processor reads the data out of the buffer when it is ready, so that no data is lost, or so that the microphone is not held up
> 
> Accept "the microphone sends data faster than the processor can accept it" or "the processor is busy with other tasks" for the first mark.
> 
> Accept "the buffer fills while the processor is busy and empties when the processor reads it" for the third mark.
> 
> Do not accept "the buffer speeds up the microphone" or "the buffer makes the transfer faster". A buffer does not change the speed of either device.
> 
> Do not accept "the buffer stores the whole recording", because a buffer holds only a small amount of data at a time.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most textbook buffer examples send data out of the computer to a printer, so students who have learned only that example often describe the flow the wrong way round here. Decide which device is producing the data and which one is consuming it before you write anything.
> 
> The marks are for the mechanism, not for the benefit. Writing "it stops the sound from lagging" gives a result without saying what the buffer actually does with the data.

parts.problemMd:
A coffee machine is controlled by an embedded system.

State **two** benefits of using an embedded system in the coffee machine.
parts.solutionMd:
- The embedded system runs only the coffee making program, so a low power processor and a small amount of memory are enough, which makes the coffee machine cheaper to manufacture. **[1]**

- The embedded system uses very little electricity, so the coffee machine costs less to run. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - Cheaper to manufacture, because only a small dedicated processor and a small amount of memory are needed
> - Uses less electricity // lower power consumption
> - Small enough to fit inside the coffee machine
> - Starts up and responds quickly, because there is no general purpose operating system to load and only one program to run
> - More reliable, because no other software is running that could interfere with the coffee making program
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept a benefit written from the manufacturer's point of view or the user's point of view.
> 
> Accept "faster response" or "real time response" for the fourth point.
> 
> Do not accept "it is dedicated to one task" or "it is built into the machine" on their own. Those are features of an embedded system, not benefits of using one.
> 
> Do not accept "it is small" with no link to fitting inside the coffee machine.
> 
> Do not accept "it is easy to upgrade". The opposite is true, and this is a standard drawback.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benefits and features are not the same thing, and this is where most marks are lost. "Dedicated to one task" and "built into the device" describe what an embedded system is. Neither of them earns a benefit mark by itself.
> 
> Turn each feature into what it gains. Because the system runs only one program, it needs a smaller processor, so the machine costs less to build. That second half of the sentence is the mark.

parts.problemMd:
A designer sends a large 3D model file from a computer to a 3D printer.

The computer can send the data much faster than the 3D printer can print the model. Printing the whole model takes several hours.

The 3D printer has a buffer.

Explain how the buffer and interrupts are used while the model is being printed.
parts.solutionMd:
The computer sends the model data into the buffer at high speed, while the 3D printer takes data out of the buffer at the much slower speed at which it prints. **[1]**

The buffer stores that data temporarily until the 3D printer is ready to use it. **[1]**

The computer is therefore not held up waiting for the 3D printer, so the processor can carry on with other tasks. **[1]**

When the buffer is full, an interrupt is sent to the computer so that it stops sending any more data. **[1]**

When the buffer is empty, or nearly empty, an interrupt is sent to the computer to request more data, and the computer then sends the next block of data into the buffer. **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any five from:**
> 
> - The computer sends data much faster than the 3D printer can print it, so the two work at different speeds
> - The buffer stores the data temporarily until the 3D printer is ready to use it
> - Data is transferred out of the buffer to the 3D printer at the slower printing speed
> - The computer is not held up waiting for the 3D printer, so the processor can carry on with other tasks
> - When the buffer is full, an interrupt is sent to the computer to stop it sending more data
> - When the buffer is empty, or nearly empty, an interrupt is sent to the computer to request more data
> - The computer responds by sending the next block of data into the buffer
> - This repeats until all of the data for the model has been sent
> 
> **[5 marks]**
> 
> Accept "the interrupt is sent by the 3D printer" or "the interrupt is sent by the device" for either interrupt mark.
> 
> Do not accept an answer that says the computer sends an interrupt to the 3D printer to ask for more data. The interrupt travels from the device that owns the buffer to the computer.
> 
> Do not accept "the buffer stores the whole model file". The buffer is small, which is the reason the interrupts are needed at all.
> 
> Do not accept a description of the fetch-execute cycle. No marks are available for how the processor handles the interrupt once it arrives.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The direction of the interrupt is the mark most often thrown away. The interrupt is a signal from the printer to the computer saying that its buffer needs more data, or that its buffer is full and the computer should stop. Students who write that the computer interrupts the printer have it backwards.
> 
> You do not need to explain what the processor does after it receives the interrupt. The marks here are for what the state of the buffer is signalling, so keep every sentence about the buffer filling and emptying.

parts.problemMd:
A smartphone contains a processor, primary memory, secondary storage and input and output devices. It is small enough to be held in one hand.

Explain why a smartphone is **not** an embedded system.
parts.solutionMd:
- A smartphone is not dedicated to a single task. It performs many different tasks that are not related to each other. **[1]**

- The user can install and remove any software they choose, so the set of functions a smartphone performs is not fixed when it is manufactured. **[1]**

- A smartphone runs a full general purpose operating system, rather than firmware written to control one device. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - A smartphone is not dedicated to one task // it carries out many unrelated tasks // it is a general purpose computer
> - The user can install, remove and change the software, so the functions are not fixed
> - A smartphone runs a full operating system rather than firmware written for one function
> - A smartphone is not built into a larger device // it is not integrated into a larger system
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept "apps" for software.
> 
> Accept a comparison with a named embedded system, for example a washing machine controller, provided the point being made is one credited in this mark scheme.
> 
> Do not accept "a smartphone is too big" or "a smartphone is too small". Physical size does not decide whether a system is embedded. A large industrial machine controller is an embedded system.
> 
> Accept "a smartphone needs a powerful general purpose processor to run many apps, whereas an embedded system needs only limited processing power". Do not accept "a smartphone has too much memory" on its own.
> 
> Accept "a smartphone is not built into / integrated into a larger system". Do not accept "a smartphone is not built into anything" with no reference to a larger system or device.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Size is the trap in this question. Students often decide whether something is an embedded system by how small it is, and a smartphone is small, so they say yes. The controller inside a factory machine is an embedded system and it is not small.
> 
> The test Cambridge marks is whether the system is dedicated to one fixed task set by the manufacturer, or whether the user can choose what software it runs. Write about the task and the software, not the size.

parts.problemMd:
A company manufactures self-service ticket machines for a railway station. Each machine has a touchscreen, a card reader and a printer.

The company must choose between two designs:

- **Design A** uses an embedded system that is built into the machine.
- **Design B** uses a general purpose computer that runs ticket selling software.

Explain **two** benefits and **two** drawbacks of choosing Design A.
parts.solutionMd:
**Benefits of Design A**

- The machine only ever has to run the ticket selling program, so a small processor and a small amount of memory are enough, which makes each machine cheaper to manufacture. **[1]**

- A customer cannot install or run any other software on the machine, so it cannot be used for anything except selling tickets. **[1]**

**Drawbacks of Design A**

- The firmware is difficult to change, so adding a new function such as selling a new type of ticket is far harder than installing new software on a general purpose computer. **[1]**

- Fault finding and repair are specialist tasks, so the company cannot use an ordinary technician and repairs cost more. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two marks for benefits and two marks for drawbacks. A third correct benefit does not earn a drawback mark.
> 
> Each point must be applied to the ticket machine.
> 
> **Benefits, any two from:**
> 
> - Only the ticket selling program has to run, so a smaller processor and less memory are needed and each machine is cheaper to manufacture
> - The machine starts up and responds faster, because there is no general purpose operating system to load
> - The machine is more reliable, because no other program can be installed that could interfere with or crash the ticket selling program
> - A customer cannot install or run other software on the machine, so it cannot be misused
> - Lower power consumption, so the running cost of a station full of machines is lower
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> **Drawbacks, any two from:**
> 
> - The firmware is difficult to update, so adding a new function such as a new ticket type is much harder than installing software on a general purpose computer
> - Fault finding, repair and upgrading are specialist tasks, so repairs cost the company more
> - The machine cannot be adapted to a different task, so it has no other use if the company stops selling tickets this way
> - An out of date machine is likely to be replaced and thrown away rather than upgraded, which adds to e-waste
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept "cheaper" only where the reason is given.
> 
> Do not accept "it is smaller" as a benefit. A ticket machine is a large cabinet and has room for either design.
> 
> Do not accept "it is dedicated to one task" as a benefit without saying what that gains the company here. Accept "it cannot be adapted for another task" as a drawback when applied to the ticket machine.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read the tariff split before you write. Four marks for two benefits and two drawbacks means exactly one mark each, so four sentences about embedded systems in general will not reach four marks. Two of them have to be drawbacks.
> 
> Every point has to touch this ticket machine. "It is cheaper" scores nothing on its own. "It is cheaper because the machine only ever runs the ticket program, so a small processor is enough" scores the mark. The words after "because" are what the examiner is looking for.

parts.problemMd:
A computer system contains input devices and output devices.

Describe the role of an input device and the role of an output device in a computer system.
parts.solutionMd:
An input device allows data or instructions from outside the computer to be entered into the system, so that the processor has something to work on. **[1]**

An output device takes the results the computer has produced and presents them in a form a person can understand or use. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the input role: allows data or instructions to be entered into the computer system // converts data from outside the system into a form the computer can process
> 
> **1 mark** for the output role: presents or communicates the results of processing to the user // converts processed data into a form a person can understand or use
> 
> Accept "sends data to the processor" for the input mark and "receives data from the processor" for the output mark.
> 
> Do not accept a list of device names such as "keyboard" or "monitor" on its own. The question asks for the role a device plays, not for an example of one.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most students lose this mark by naming devices instead of describing what they are for. A list of five input devices scores nothing here. Write one sentence that says what the device lets the system do, then add an example only if you have room.

parts.problemMd:
A student says:

"A computer only needs a processor and memory. Input devices and output devices are optional extras."

Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.solutionMd:
Without an input device there is no way for data or instructions to enter the system, so the processor has nothing to process. **[1]**

Without an output device the results of processing stay inside the computer, so nobody can use them. **[1]**

Input and output are what connect the computer to the world outside it, so a machine with only a processor and memory cannot carry out a useful task. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - Without an input device, no data or instructions can enter the system
> - ... so the processor has nothing to process // the user cannot tell the system what to do
> - Without an output device, the results of processing cannot leave the system
> - ... so the user cannot see or use those results
> - Input and output are how the computer communicates with the world outside it
> - A system with no input and no output cannot perform a useful task for a user
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept "the computer would be useless" only when it is joined to a reason, for example "useless because the user could never see the result"
> 
> Do not accept "the computer would not switch on" or "the computer would break". Both are untrue, and neither answers the question

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question quotes a wrong statement and asks you to explain why it is wrong, you must attack the statement itself. Answers that simply describe what a keyboard and a monitor do never engage with the claim that they are optional. Deal with input and output separately, and in each case say what the system would be unable to do without it.

parts.problemMd:
A laptop computer has a built-in microphone. A student uses it to record their voice during an online lesson.

Describe the principal operation of the microphone.
parts.solutionMd:
The microphone detects sound waves travelling through the air. **[1]**

It converts those sound waves into an electrical signal that the computer can process. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the microphone detecting sound waves // vibrations in the air
> 
> **1 mark** for converting the sound waves into an electrical signal // an analogue signal
> 
> Accept "the electrical signal is then sampled and stored as digital data" for the second mark
> 
> Do not accept "the microphone records the user's voice", which states what the device is used for rather than the operation it carries out

> **[exam-tip]**
> The command word is describe, so the answer has to say what the device physically does, not what it is for. "It lets the user talk to the computer" earns nothing. For a microphone, always name both ends of the conversion: sound waves in, electrical signal out. Students who only write "it turns sound into data" miss the mark because they have skipped the electrical signal.

parts.problemMd:
A hotel installs a self-service check-in kiosk in its reception area. A guest uses the kiosk to check in, and the kiosk then gives the guest a printed room card.

Explain the need for input devices and output devices in this kiosk.
parts.solutionMd:
The kiosk needs an input device so that the guest can enter their booking details into the system. **[1]**

Without one, the processor would have no data to work on and the system could not identify which booking to check in. **[1]**

The kiosk needs an output device so that the results of that processing can leave the system. **[1]**

Without one, the guest could not be told the room number and could not be given the printed room card, so the check-in could never be completed. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for stating that an input device lets the guest supply data to the kiosk, for example a booking reference, a name or payment details
> 
> **1 mark** for the consequence of having no input: the processor has no data to process // the system cannot identify which booking belongs to this guest
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that an output device lets the results of processing leave the system and reach the guest
> 
> **1 mark** for the consequence of having no output: the guest is never told the room number, or never receives the room card, so the check-in cannot be completed
> 
> Accept "the kiosk could not confirm the booking to the guest" for the fourth mark.
> 
> Do not accept a description of how a touchscreen or a printer works internally. This question asks why the kiosk needs input and output at all, not how a named device operates.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The four marks here are two pairs, and the second mark of each pair is the one students miss. Naming an input and an output only gets you halfway. Each time you name one, add "so that ..." or "without it ..." and say what the system would be unable to do. Notice also that a touchscreen counts as both an input device and an output device, so it can earn a mark on either side, but not on both for the same point.

parts.problemMd:
A tablet computer has a capacitive touchscreen. The user taps an icon on the screen to open an application.

Describe the principal operation of a capacitive touchscreen.
parts.solutionMd:
The top layer of a capacitive touchscreen holds an electrical charge. **[1]**

A finger is conductive, so touching the screen changes the electrical charge, or current, at the point of contact. **[1]**

A microprocessor uses that change to calculate the horizontal and vertical coordinates of the point of contact, and passes them to the software. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the screen holding an electrical charge // having an electric field across it
> 
> **1 mark** for the touch of a conductive object changing the charge or the current at that point
> 
> **1 mark** for a microprocessor calculating the coordinates of the point of contact from that change
> 
> Accept "increase in current" or "decrease in current" for the second mark
> 
> Accept "the coordinates are sent to the software as an input" as the third mark
> 
> Do not accept "the two layers touch and complete a circuit", which is the operation of a resistive touchscreen, not a capacitive one

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two types of touchscreen are marked separately, so decide which one the question names before you start writing. Layers touching and a circuit being completed belongs to a resistive screen; a change in electrical charge belongs to a capacitive screen. Mixing them loses the mark even though both sentences are true of some touchscreen. Also remember the final step: something has to work out where on the screen the touch happened, and that is the microprocessor calculating the coordinates.

parts.problemMd: Describe the role of primary memory in a computer system.
parts.solutionMd:
Primary memory holds the data and the instructions that are currently in use while the computer is running. **[1]**

The processor can read from it and write to it directly, and its access times are much faster than those of secondary storage. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - Holds the data and instructions currently in use // holds the program that is running
> - Is directly accessible by the processor // the processor reads from it and writes to it directly
> - Has much faster access times than secondary storage
> - Acts as the short-term or working store while the computer is switched on
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept "Immediate Access Store" as another name for primary memory
> 
> Do not accept "stores data permanently" or "stores files the user has saved". That is the role of secondary storage

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word that earns the mark is "directly". Plenty of answers say primary memory is fast, which is true but is only half the point. What makes it primary is that the processor reaches it without going through anything else. Say that, and the speed mark usually follows.

parts.problemMd:
A cold storage warehouse is fitting a computer terminal that the workers will use to record the goods they move.

The workers wear thick gloves at all times because of the low temperature.

The designer must choose between a capacitive touchscreen and a resistive touchscreen for the terminal.

Explain, using the principal operation of each type of touchscreen, which type should be chosen.
parts.solutionMd:
A capacitive touchscreen works by detecting a change in the electrical charge in its top layer when the screen is touched. **[1]**

The object touching the screen has to be conductive, so a thick glove would not change the charge and the touch would not be registered. **[1]**

A resistive touchscreen has two conductive layers separated by a small gap. Pressing the screen pushes the layers together and completes a circuit at that point. **[1]**

Any object can apply that pressure, including a gloved finger, so the resistive touchscreen should be chosen. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for stating that a capacitive screen detects a change in electrical charge or current
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that a capacitive screen needs a conductive object, so a gloved finger would not be detected
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that a resistive screen has two layers that are pushed together by pressure to complete a circuit
> 
> **1 mark** for choosing the resistive screen because pressure can be applied through a glove
> 
> Accept "the layers touch and the space between them is removed" for the third mark
> 
> Accept a correct answer written the other way round, for example ruling the capacitive screen out first and then recommending the resistive screen
> 
> Do not accept "resistive screens are cheaper" or "resistive screens are more durable", which are not based on the principal operation of the device and are not asked for here
> 
> Do not award the fourth mark if the capacitive screen is recommended, however good the reasoning

> **[exam-tip]**
> A question like this gives marks for the mechanism, not for the choice on its own, so writing "resistive" and stopping scores zero. Work through the operation of each screen and then let the operation decide the answer. The detail examiners look for is that a capacitive screen relies on the conductivity of a bare finger, which is exactly what a glove removes, while a resistive screen only needs pressure and does not care what is doing the pressing.

parts.problemMd:
A photo editing program is stored on a computer's secondary storage. When the user starts the program, it is first copied into primary memory.

Explain why the program must be copied into primary memory before it can run.
parts.solutionMd:
The processor fetches each instruction from an address in primary memory, so a program can only be executed once its instructions are held there. **[1]**

The processor cannot fetch instructions directly from secondary storage. **[1]**

Primary memory also has much faster access times than secondary storage, so the program runs at a speed the user will accept. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for: the processor fetches instructions directly from primary memory // an instruction has to be in primary memory before it can be fetched and executed
> 
> **1 mark** for: the processor cannot access secondary storage directly // secondary storage is not directly addressable by the processor
> 
> **1 mark** for: primary memory has much faster access times, so the program runs at a usable speed // running straight from secondary storage would be far too slow
> 
> Accept a correct reference to the fetch stage of the fetch-execute cycle for the first mark.
> 
> Do not accept "primary memory is bigger than secondary storage". It is normally very much smaller.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Speed is the answer students reach for first, and it is worth only one of the three marks. The other two are about access: the processor can only reach primary memory directly, so an instruction sitting on a hard disk simply cannot be fetched. Make that point before you write anything about speed.

parts.problemMd:
A smart display in a hotel lobby uses speakers to give spoken directions to guests.

Describe the principal operation of a speaker.
parts.solutionMd:
The speaker is sent an electrical signal by the computer. **[1]**

The speaker converts that electrical signal into sound waves that travel through the air to the listener. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the speaker receiving an electrical signal // an analogue signal from the computer
> 
> **1 mark** for converting the electrical signal into sound waves
> 
> Accept "the signal makes part of the speaker vibrate and the vibration produces the sound waves" for the second mark
> 
> Accept a reference to the digital data being converted to an analogue signal before it reaches the speaker, for the first mark
> 
> Do not accept "the speaker plays the sound", which repeats the question instead of describing the operation

> **[exam-tip]**
> A speaker is the exact reverse of a microphone, so learn the two as a pair: a microphone turns sound waves into an electrical signal, and a speaker turns an electrical signal back into sound waves. The common mistake is writing only about what the guest hears. Marks are given for the conversion the device performs, so both the electrical signal and the sound waves have to be named.

parts.problemMd:
A tablet computer has a small amount of primary memory. A user opens several large applications at the same time. The tablet becomes much slower, even though the processor and the secondary storage have not been changed.

Explain why having too little primary memory makes the system slower.
parts.solutionMd:
Only a limited amount of data and instructions can be held in primary memory at any one time. **[1]**

Anything that does not fit has to remain in secondary storage. **[1]**

Before the processor can use it, it must be transferred into primary memory, and other data must be transferred out again to make room. **[1]**

Secondary storage has much slower access times than primary memory, so the tablet spends a large part of its time moving data instead of processing it. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for: primary memory can hold only a limited amount of data and instructions at any one time
> 
> **1 mark** for: the data and instructions that do not fit stay in, or are written back to, secondary storage
> 
> **1 mark** for: data must be transferred into primary memory before the processor can use it, and transferred out again to free space
> 
> **1 mark** for: secondary storage has much slower access times, so the repeated transfers slow the whole system down
> 
> Accept a correct reference to virtual memory or to paging, but neither term is needed for full marks.
> 
> Do not accept "the processor is too slow" or "the tablet needs a better processor". The stem states that the processor has not changed.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The stem rules out two of the three obvious answers on purpose: the processor and the secondary storage are both unchanged, so neither can be the cause. That leaves you to build a chain, and a chain is what the four marks are for. Not enough room, so data stays on the drive, so it has to be shuffled in and out, so the slow drive sets the pace. Write the chain in that order and each link earns a mark.

parts.problemMd:
A desktop computer contains both Random Access Memory (RAM) and Read Only Memory (ROM).

Complete the table by writing **RAM** or **ROM** next to each statement.

| Statement | RAM or ROM |
|---|---|
| The contents are lost when the power to the computer is switched off. |   |
| This memory holds the instructions that the computer needs in order to start up. |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Statement | RAM or ROM |
|---|---|
| The contents are lost when the power to the computer is switched off. | **RAM** **[1]** |
| This memory holds the instructions that the computer needs in order to start up. | **ROM** **[1]** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for RAM against the first statement
> 
> **1 mark** for ROM against the second statement
> 
> Accept the names written in full: Random Access Memory for RAM, Read Only Memory for ROM
> 
> Do not accept ROM for the first statement. ROM is non-volatile, so its contents are still there after the power is switched off
> 
> Do not accept RAM for the second statement. RAM is volatile, so start-up instructions held there would be lost every time the computer was switched off

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word volatile is worth learning precisely. Volatile means the contents are lost when the power is removed, so RAM is volatile and ROM is non-volatile. A very common error is to swap these two round because ROM sounds like the smaller and weaker chip.
> 
> Also be careful not to describe RAM as "permanent storage". RAM is fast working memory, not storage that survives a power cut.

parts.problemMd:
A pilot training centre uses a virtual reality (VR) headset to train pilots.

When a trainee turns their head, the view of the cockpit that they can see changes to match.

Explain how the principal operations of the VR headset produce this effect.
parts.solutionMd:
A sensor in the headset, such as a gyroscope or an accelerometer, detects the movement of the trainee's head. **[1]**

The sensor data is transmitted to a microprocessor, which analyses it to identify the direction and the speed of the movement. **[1]**

The images shown on the headset's two displays are updated to match the new position of the head, so the view of the cockpit changes. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a sensor detecting the head movement, named as a gyroscope or an accelerometer
> 
> **1 mark** for the data being transmitted to a microprocessor that analyses it to identify the direction or speed of movement
> 
> **1 mark** for the images on the displays, screens or lenses being updated to match
> 
> Accept "digital cameras record the user's eye movements for analysis" as an additional operation, but only in place of the first marking point, not as well as it
> 
> Do not accept "the headset knows where the trainee is looking" with no sensor or processing named
> 
> Do not accept "the headset outputs surround sound through its speakers", which is a different output of the headset and does not change the view

> **[exam-tip]**
> Explain questions on a virtual reality headset need the full chain: sensor, then microprocessor, then display. Most lost marks come from stopping after the sensor. Name the sensor as a gyroscope or an accelerometer rather than writing "a movement sensor", because the mark scheme lists the specific components, and remember that the headset has two displays or lenses, one for each eye, which is what creates the three-dimensional effect.

parts.problemMd: State **two** reasons why a computer system needs secondary storage.
parts.solutionMd:
Secondary storage keeps data when the computer is switched off, so saved files are not lost. **[1]**

Secondary storage provides a much larger capacity than primary memory, so far more data can be kept. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - Data is retained when the power is switched off // it is non-volatile // it stores data permanently
> - It has a much larger capacity than primary memory
> - It costs much less per gigabyte, so large amounts of data can be stored affordably
> - Removable secondary storage allows data to be carried between computers or taken off site
> - It holds programs and files that are not currently in use, ready to be loaded when they are needed
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept "long-term storage" or "permanent storage" for the first bullet
> 
> Do not accept "it is faster than primary memory". Secondary storage is very much slower

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two reasons means two different reasons. "It saves your files" and "it stores your work permanently" are the same reason written twice, and they score one mark between them. Pick one point about keeping data without power and one about capacity or cost, and you have two clearly separate marks.

parts.problemMd:
A self-service ticket machine at a railway station has both Read Only Memory (ROM) and Random Access Memory (RAM).

A customer uses the machine to choose a journey and to pay for a ticket.

Explain why the ticket machine needs both types of memory.
parts.solutionMd:
ROM is non-volatile, so the instructions that start the machine are still present each time it is switched on. **[1]**

ROM is read only, so those start-up instructions cannot be overwritten while the machine is in use. **[1]**

RAM can be written to as well as read, so it can hold the journey and payment details entered by the customer while the sale is taking place. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - ROM is non-volatile, so its contents remain when the machine has no power
> - ... so the start-up / boot-up instructions are available every time the machine is switched on
> - ROM is read only, so its contents cannot be changed or overwritten by the running program
> - RAM is read and write, so data can be written into it while the machine is being used
> - RAM holds the data and instructions currently in use, for example the journey selected or the payment being processed
> - RAM is volatile, so the customer's details are cleared when the machine is switched off
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept "temporary" for volatile and "permanent" for non-volatile only where you also state that the contents are lost or kept when the power is removed
> 
> Do not accept "RAM is faster than ROM" on its own. Speed is a difference between the two, but it does not explain why the machine needs both

> **[exam-tip]**
> The command word is explain, so every point needs a because. Writing "ROM is non-volatile and RAM is volatile" lists two facts and earns very little. Turn each fact into a consequence for this machine: non-volatile means the start-up instructions survive being switched off overnight.
> 
> You can also lose marks by describing what RAM and ROM are in general instead of saying what each one does in the ticket machine. Tie every point back to the device in the question.

parts.problemMd:
A research team works at a remote site that has no network connection. At the end of each week they copy their data onto a removable secondary storage device and carry it back to the main office.

Explain why removable secondary storage is suitable for this task.
parts.solutionMd:
The storage is non-volatile, so the data is still there after the device has been disconnected and carried to the office. **[1]**

The device can be physically disconnected from one computer and connected to another, so data can be moved between two machines that are not linked by a network. **[1]**

It has a large enough capacity, at a low cost per gigabyte, to hold a whole week of research data. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - The storage is non-volatile, so data is retained with no power supply while it is being carried
> - The device can be disconnected from one computer and connected to another
> - ... so data can be transferred with no network connection between the two sites
> - Capacity is large enough to hold a week of data // cost per gigabyte is low enough for the amount of data involved
> - The device is small and light enough to be carried by a person
> - The copy also acts as a backup held away from the original site
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept a named example of removable secondary storage, such as a USB flash drive, an external hard disk drive or an optical disc, provided a reason is also given
> 
> Do not accept "it is faster than sending the data over the network". The stem states that there is no network connection at the site

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read the scenario for the constraint before you start writing. The words "no network connection" are there to tell you which property matters, and answers that suggest uploading to the cloud have ignored them. The mark for portability is the one most often missed: say that the device can be unplugged and carried, not just that it is small.

parts.problemMd:
An office uses a laser printer to print documents.

Describe the principal operations of the laser printer, from the point at which the print data reaches the printer to the point at which the printed page leaves the printer.
parts.solutionMd:
The printing drum is given an electrical charge across its whole surface. **[1]**

A laser beam is scanned across the drum and draws the image of the page, changing the charge on the parts of the drum that the laser strikes. **[1]**

Toner is attracted to the parts of the drum that the laser has written on, so the toner takes the shape of the text and images. **[1]**

The paper is passed against the drum and the toner is transferred from the drum onto the paper. **[1]**

The paper then passes through heated rollers, which melt the toner so that it is fixed permanently to the paper. **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the drum being charged
> 
> **1 mark** for a laser scanning across the drum and changing the charge to draw the image of the page
> 
> **1 mark** for toner being attracted to the areas of the drum written by the laser
> 
> **1 mark** for the toner being transferred from the drum onto the paper
> 
> **1 mark** for heated rollers melting the toner so that it is fixed to the paper
> 
> Accept "photosensitive drum" or "photoreceptor drum" for the drum
> 
> Accept "the fuser" for the heated rollers
> 
> Accept "the laser reverses the charge where it strikes the drum" for the second marking point
> 
> Do not accept "ink is sprayed onto the paper", which is the operation of an inkjet printer
> 
> Do not accept "the printer stores the page in a buffer first", which describes the use of a buffer rather than the printing operation

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a sequence, and the marks follow the order of the sequence, so write it as numbered steps rather than as one long sentence.
