The processor can access the Immediate Access Store directly, but it cannot fetch an instruction straight from the hard disk drive. **[1]**

Access times for the Immediate Access Store are much faster than access times for a hard disk drive. **[1]**

This means the processor is not left waiting for each instruction to arrive from the hard disk drive. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the Immediate Access Store (IAS) holding the instructions and data currently in use
> 
> **1 mark** for the processor accessing the Immediate Access Store directly / not being able to fetch an instruction straight from the hard disk drive
> 
> **1 mark** for the Immediate Access Store having much faster access times than the hard disk drive
> 
> **1 mark** for the consequence: the processor is not kept waiting between instructions
> 
> Accept "the hard disk drive is much slower than the Immediate Access Store" for the third mark
> 
> Do not accept "the hard disk drive is not big enough" or "the program will not fit", because storage capacity is not the reason the instructions are copied
> 
> Do not accept "the Immediate Access Store is volatile", because volatility explains why its contents are lost when the power is switched off, not why the instructions must be copied there in order to run

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a question about speed and direct access, not about capacity. Two answers appear again and again and neither of them answers the question: "the hard disk drive is too small", and "because the Immediate Access Store is volatile".
> 
> Build the answer in the order of the marks: what the Immediate Access Store holds, that the processor reaches it directly, that it is much faster than the drive, and what that means for the processor.

parts.problemMd:
A shop sells two computers. Processor P has a higher clock speed than Processor Q. The two processors have different architectures.

A customer buys the computer with Processor P because it has the higher clock speed. The computer with Processor Q runs the customer's programs faster.

Explain why a higher clock speed does not always mean better performance.
parts.solutionMd:
Clock speed only states how many cycles happen each second. It does not state how much work the processor does in each cycle. **[1]**

Processors with different architectures need different numbers of clock cycles to carry out the same instruction, so Processor Q may complete an instruction in fewer cycles than Processor P. **[1]**

Clock speed is therefore only a fair comparison between processors of the same architecture. **[1]**

Processor Q may also have more cores, more cache memory or a wider data bus, and any of these can make it faster in use than Processor P. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each point, to a maximum of 4:
> 
> **1 mark** for clock speed measuring cycles per second, not the amount of work done in each cycle
> 
> **1 mark** for processors of different architectures needing different numbers of clock cycles for the same instruction
> 
> **1 mark** for the conclusion: clock speed can only be compared meaningfully between processors of the same architecture
> 
> **1 mark** for Processor Q having more cores, so more instructions are carried out at the same time
> 
> **1 mark** for Processor Q having more cache memory, so less time is spent waiting for data from RAM
> 
> **1 mark** for Processor Q having a wider data bus, so more data is transferred in each transfer
> 
> Accept "the two processors have different instruction sets" for the second point.
> 
> Do not accept "clock speed does not matter". Clock speed does affect performance; the point is that it cannot be compared on its own across two different architectures.
> 
> Do not accept "Processor Q is a better processor", which gives no reason.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Clock speed is a fair comparison only between two processors built to the same architecture. Across different designs one processor may finish an instruction in fewer clock cycles than the other, so the processor with the lower clock speed can still do more work each second.
> 
> To reach full marks you have to leave clock speed behind and name at least one other factor from this topic. Cores, cache memory and bus width are the three the syllabus expects.

parts.problemMd:
A processor uses cache memory.

State **two** features of cache memory.
parts.solutionMd:
Cache memory is fast-access memory, which is faster to access than RAM. **[1]**

It stores the data and instructions that are used most frequently. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - Cache memory is fast-access memory // it is faster to access than RAM
> - It is located inside or very close to the CPU
> - It stores frequently used data and instructions
> - It holds copies of data and instructions that have recently been used
> - It has a much smaller capacity than RAM
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept "cache is built into each processor core" for the location point
> 
> Do not accept "cache is where the computer stores files it is not using". That describes secondary storage, not cache memory
> 
> Do not accept "cache stores web pages you have visited". That is a browser cache, which is a different thing

> **[exam-tip]**
> A lot of students answer this question about a web browser cache, because that is the meaning of the word they meet outside the classroom. In this topic cache memory means the small, fast memory inside the processor that holds frequently used instructions and data.
> 
> Two features means two separate points. "It is fast and it is quick to get to" counts as one.

parts.problemMd:
A computer is upgraded so that its processor has a larger amount of cache memory.

Explain how this can improve the performance of the computer.
parts.solutionMd:
A larger cache can hold more of the frequently used instructions and data. **[1]**

More of what the processor needs is therefore found in the cache, instead of having to be fetched from RAM. **[1]**

Cache is faster to access than RAM, so the processor spends less time waiting for data and is less likely to be left idle. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a larger cache storing more frequently used instructions / data
> 
> **1 mark** for more of the data needed being found in the cache instead of being fetched from RAM // fewer transfers being needed between RAM and the cache
> 
> **1 mark** for the consequence: cache is faster to access than RAM, so the processor spends less time waiting // the processor is less likely to be idle
> 
> Accept "the CPU can continue working without waiting for data" for the third mark.
> 
> Do not accept "the computer can store more files". Cache memory does not increase the storage capacity of the computer.
> 
> Accept "cache is fast access memory, close to the CPU" for the third mark. Do not accept "the computer is faster" with no reference to cache access or RAM.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most of the marks are for what changes, not for the word "faster". Say what extra thing the bigger cache now holds, say where that data would otherwise have come from, and only then say why that saves time.
> 
> The comparison the examiner is looking for is cache against RAM. If RAM is never mentioned in your answer, you have almost certainly lost a mark.

parts.problemMd:
A computer runs two programs.

Program A repeatedly carries out the same short set of instructions on a small amount of data.

Program B reads every record in a very large data file once, and does not read any record a second time.

The amount of cache memory in the computer is increased.

Explain why the performance of Program A is likely to improve more than the performance of Program B.
parts.solutionMd:
Cache memory stores the data and instructions that are used most frequently. **[1]**

Program A uses the same instructions and data over and over, so after the first use they are already held in the cache. **[1]**

They are then read at the faster cache access speed rather than from the slower RAM, and that time is saved on every repeat. **[1]**

Program B reads each record only once, so a record is not already in the cache when it is needed and must still be fetched from RAM, which means the extra cache brings little benefit. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each point, to a maximum of 4:
> 
> **1 mark** for cache storing the data and instructions that are used most frequently
> 
> **1 mark** for Program A reusing the same instructions / data, so they are already in the cache after the first use
> 
> **1 mark** for the consequence for Program A: they are read from cache rather than from the slower RAM, saving time on each repeat
> 
> **1 mark** for Program B reading each record only once, so a record is not in the cache when it is first needed
> 
> **1 mark** for the consequence for Program B: the record must still be fetched from RAM, so the extra cache is little used
> 
> **1 mark** for the general point: a larger cache only improves performance if the data that is needed is found in it
> 
> Accept "Program A's set of instructions is small enough to fit inside the cache".
> 
> Credit "cache is faster than RAM" as part of the consequence mark for Program A when it is linked to Program A's data being found in the cache. On its own it does not explain why the two programs are affected differently.
> 
> Do not accept "Program B's file is too large so the computer will run out of memory". The records are still read from RAM in the normal way.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The benefit of cache comes from data being found there, not from the cache existing. Data that is used once gains nothing from a bigger cache, because the slow fetch from RAM still has to happen the first time.
> 
> Before you claim an improvement, look in the stem for evidence of repeated use. Here the words "repeatedly" and "does not read any record a second time" are the whole question.

parts.problemMd:
A computer has a data bus that is 32 bits wide.

(i) State what is meant by a data bus that is 32 bits wide.

(1)

(ii) State the effect on data transfer of increasing the width of the data bus to 64 bits.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
(i) 32 bits of data can be carried by the bus at the same time, in a single transfer. **[1]**

(ii) 64 bits can now be transferred at a time, so twice as much data is moved in each transfer and fewer transfers are needed. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i) **1 mark** for 32 bits being transferred / carried at the same time // in one transfer
> 
> (ii) **1 mark** for more data being transferred at a time // 64 bits instead of 32 bits per transfer // fewer transfers being needed for the same amount of data
> 
> Accept in (i) "the bus has 32 parallel lines, one for each bit"
> 
> Do not accept in (ii) "the computer can store more data". Bus width affects how much data is transferred at once, not how much can be stored
> 
> Do not accept in (ii) "the computer becomes twice as fast". Only the transfer of data on that bus is affected, not the whole system

> **[exam-tip]**
> Bus width is measured in bits and it describes how much data moves in one transfer. It says nothing about how much data the computer can store.
> 
> Keep the data bus and the address bus apart in your head. The width of the data bus controls how much data moves at once; the width of the address bus controls how many memory locations can be reached.

parts.problemMd:
The table shows information about two of the buses in a computer.

Complete the table.

| Bus | What the bus carries | Effect of increasing the width of this bus |
|---|---|---|
| Data bus | Data being transferred between the processor and memory |   |
| Address bus |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Bus | What the bus carries | Effect of increasing the width of this bus |
|---|---|---|
| Data bus | Data being transferred between the processor and memory | **More bits of data can be transferred at the same time, so fewer transfers are needed and data transfer is faster** **[1]** |
| Address bus | **The address of the memory location that is to be read from or written to** **[1]** | **More memory locations can be directly addressed, so a larger amount of memory can be used** **[1]** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the effect of a wider data bus: more bits of data transferred at the same time // fewer transfers needed for the same amount of data
> 
> **1 mark** for what the address bus carries: the address of the memory location that is to be read from or written to
> 
> **1 mark** for the effect of a wider address bus: more memory locations can be directly addressed // a larger amount of memory can be used
> 
> Accept for the address bus row "the address held in the Memory Address Register (MAR) is carried to memory"
> 
> Do not accept "the address bus carries data". The address bus carries addresses only, and it carries them in one direction, from the processor to memory
> 
> Do not accept "a wider address bus transfers more data at a time". That is the effect of a wider data bus

> **[exam-tip]**
> The commonest error in this whole topic is treating the two buses as one. A wider data bus moves more data in each transfer. A wider address bus moves no extra data at all; it simply lets the processor reach more memory locations.
> 
> If a question asks about "bus width" without telling you which bus, say which one you are writing about before you describe the effect.

parts.problemMd:
A computer has an address bus that is 20 bits wide and a data bus that is 16 bits wide.

Each memory location stores one byte.

(i) Calculate the number of memory locations that can be directly addressed.

Show your working.

(2)

(ii) Calculate the total size of the memory that can be directly addressed.

Give your answer in mebibytes. Show your working.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Number of locations = 2 to the power of 20 **[1]**

= 1 048 576 memory locations **[1]**

(ii) 1 048 576 bytes / 1024 = 1024 kibibytes, and 1024 kibibytes / 1024 = 1 **[1]**

= 1 mebibyte **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i) **1 mark** for the working: 2^20 // 2 to the power of 20
> 
> **1 mark** for the answer: 1 048 576 locations
> 
> (ii) **1 mark** for the working: 1 048 576 / 1024 / 1024
> 
> **1 mark** for the answer: 1 mebibyte
> 
> Accept 1 048 576 written as 1048576 or 1,048,576.
> 
> Do not accept 65 536 in (i). That is 2 to the power of 16 and uses the width of the data bus. It is the width of the address bus that decides how many locations can be addressed.
> 
> Do not accept 1.048576 in (ii). That is the answer in megabytes. The question asks for mebibytes, so divide by 1024 twice, not by 1000 twice.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read carefully which bus each number belongs to. The number of addressable locations comes from the address bus width alone. The data bus width tells you how much data moves in one transfer and does not appear anywhere in this calculation, so it is there to catch you out.
> 
> Then check the unit word. A mebibyte uses a binary prefix, so you divide by 1024 twice. A megabyte uses a decimal prefix and would need division by 1000 twice, which gives a different answer.

parts.problemMd:
A student uses a laptop to write a program that is saved as a text file.

The program code is written using an Integrated Development Environment (IDE).

(i) One presentation feature found in a typical IDE is prettyprint.

Identify **and **describe **one other** presentation feature found in a typical IDE.

(2)

(ii) One debugging feature found in a typical IDE is single stepping.

Identify **and **describe **one other **debugging feature found in a typical IDE.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i)** 1 mark** for correct name, **1 mark **for matching description
> 
> - Expand/collapse code blocks…
> - … sections of source code that are part of the same block can be expanded to see the content or collapsed so that the overall code is seen
> - Auto-indentation // auto-formatting...
> - ... automatically indents/formats code as the user types so that the structure is clear // aids readability
> 
> (ii) **1 mark** for correct name, **1 mark **for matching description
> 
> - Breakpoints …
> - … stops the code running on a set line to view the current status/variable contents/program flow
> - Report window // variable watch window …
> - … shows the values in variables/data structures and how they change when each line is run

parts.problemMd:
A program is written in a high-level language by a team of three programmers using an Integrated Development Environment (IDE).

Describe how the programmers can use the debugging features of a typical IDE during the development of the program.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 4**)
> 
> e.g.
> 
> - Single stepping
> - Run the program one line at a time
> - … and check the variable contents / program flow // show the effect of each line of code
> - Set breakpoints
> - … run the code up to a set line
> - ... and then check the status
> - Variable/report watch window
> - … view how the data changes as the program is running

parts.problemMd:
A program has been developed and released for general use. After a few months of use an error is detected where under certain circumstances it outputs an unexpected value.

The program contains a function `Lookup()`. After investigation, it is found that this is the function that sometimes returns an incorrect value.

An Integrated Development Environment (IDE) is used to help locate the error.

The IDE features of watch window, single stepping and breakpoint will be used.

Explain these features including the order that they will be used in to locate the error in `Lookup()`.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> For example:
> 
> - Set a breakpoint at the start of / within Lookup, to stop execution at a given statement
> - then use single stepping to execute one statement / instruction at a time
> - to display the value of variables using a watch window
> 
> One mark for each:
> 
> **MP1 **Order starting with a breakpoint **and **an explanation – ‘stop execution <u>at this statement / line’</u>
> 
> **MP2 **Explanation of single stepping – execute ‘line by line’ / statements
> 
> **MP3 **Explanation of watch window – displaying the value of <u>variable(s)</u>

parts.problemMd:
To solve the error a programmer decides to create a new module.

The design of the new module has been completed and the module is being coded.

Identify **two** features of an IDE that will help during the coding of this new module.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Features include:
> 
> **MP1 **Editor
> 
> **MP2 **<u>Auto</u>- (syntax) complete / <u>auto </u>correction // identify undeclared variables(s)
> 
> **MP3 **Prettyprint / <u>auto</u>-indentation / <u>auto</u> (structure) highlighter
> 
> **MP4 **<u>Dynamic</u> syntax checking
> 
> **MP5 **Expand / collapse code blocks
> 
> **MP6 **Context sensitive prompts
> 
> **Max 2 marks**

parts.problemMd:
A software developer is writing a computer program.

The developer uses an interpreter while writing the program code because it is easier for debugging.

Explain **one **reason why it is easier to debug the program code using an interpreter instead of a compiler.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each to **max 2**:
> 
> - The interpreter will stop when an error is found
> - ... so the error can be corrected in real-time, and the result of changes seen immediately
> - Only one error is displayed at a time
> - … so fewer errors to correct simultaneously and no dependent errors

parts.problemMd:
The program is ready to be sold to customers.

The developer uses a compiler because it creates an executable file.

Explain the reasons why the need to create an executable file makes the complier the appropriate choice when the program is complete.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark **each to **max 3**:
> 
> - Program can be distributed without source code
> - ... so it cannot be edited/stolen/plagiarised
> - Users do not require the translator to run the program
> - … so time is not spent retranslating by user

parts.problemMd:
A programmer uses an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) to write a computer program. The IDE has both a compiler and an interpreter as built-in translators.

The programmer decides to use the compiler when testing the final program.

Describe the benefits of using the compiler during testing.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each to **max 2**:
> 
> - Creates an executable file
> - … so the code can be tested multiple times without having to recompile
> - … so** repeated testing** takes less time

parts.problemMd:
IDEs have many features other than built-in translators.

Complete the table by identifying **one other **common IDE feature that can be used for each purpose. Describe how each feature helps the user during program development.

Each feature must be different. Do **not **give translator as one of your features.

| **Purpose** | IDE feature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **for coding** |   |   |
| **for presentation** |   |   |
| **for debugging** |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for identification of each feature and **1 mark** for matching description:
> 
> e.g.
> 
> *For coding:*
> 
> | IDE feature | Description |
> |---|---|
> | Context-sensitive prompts | **Gives suggestions** for code as the user types instead of having to write/remember the code |
> | **Auto**-correct | Corrects spelling mistakes so that user has fewer errors to correct |
> 
> *For presentation:*
> 
> | IDE feature | Description |
> |---|---|
> | Pretty-printing | Colour code keywords so the user can identify any errors |
> | Expand/collapse (code) blocks | The user can hide code that they are not currently working on |
> 
> *For debugging:*
> 
> | IDE feature | Description |
> |---|---|
> | Single stepping | Run the code **one line at a time** // shows the effect of each line of code |
> | Breakpoints | Stop the code running at a set point to check the flow/variable contents |

parts.problemMd:
A programmer uses both a compiler and an interpreter to translate a program written in a high-level language.

Describe the advantages of using the interpreter compared to the compiler to translate the program.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark **for each bullet point (**max 4**)
> 
> - easier to debug the program
> - … because it translates line-by-line and stops when an error is found whereas the compiler translates all the program at the same time
> - … only reporting one error at a time
> - … which allows the error to be corrected in real time whereas the program would need to be corrected and recompiled
> - ... and the program can restart at same point when error occurred with a compiler the program needs to be re-run
> - The effect of any changes made by the programmer can be seen immediately with a compiler the effects can only be seen after re-running
> - A partially completed program can be translated / tested on its own a compiler cannot translate a partial program

parts.problemMd: State **one **reason why some high-level languages are partially compiled and partially interpreted.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 2**)
> 
> - Partially compiled programs can be used on different platforms as they are interpreted when run
> - Code is optimised for the CPU as machine code is generated at run time
> - Source code does not need recompiling so more efficient to run

parts.problemMd:
(i) Identify **two **features that support the visual presentation of the code in a typical Integrated Development Environment (IDE).

(2)

(ii) Identify **two **features that support the debugging of the code in a typical IDE.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 2**)
> 
> - Prettyprint
> - Expand/collapse code blocks
> - Auto indentation / formatting
> 
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 2**)
> 
> - Single stepping
> - Breakpoints
> - Report window
> - Variable expressions

parts.problemMd:
A programmer uses an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) to develop a program that monitors air quality.

Describe the following features of a typical IDE.

Context‑sensitive prompts ....................................

Single stepping .......................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 2** for each feature).
> 
> Context-sensitive prompts:
> 
> - As the code is being written
> - …the options to complete the statement are shown
> 
> Single stepping:
> 
> - allows the programmer to execute the program one line at a time
> - …so that the effects of each statement can be seen

parts.problemMd:
A programmer writes a program in a high-level language using an Integrated Development Environment (IDE).

The IDE provides features for initial error detection.

Describe how a dynamic syntax check helps the programmer.
parts.solutionMd:
Each statement is checked against the rules of the programming language as the code is being typed. **[1]**

Any statement that does not follow the rules is underlined or highlighted, so the programmer sees the error before the program is run. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the check happening while the code is entered, e.g. each statement is checked against the rules (syntax) of the language as it is typed
> 
> **1 mark** for how the error is shown, e.g. the statement that breaks the rules is underlined / highlighted / coloured, so the error is seen before the program is run
> 
> Accept "the grammar of the language" or "the rules of the language" in place of syntax
> 
> Accept "flags", "marks" or "displays an error message beside the line" in place of underlines or highlights
> 
> Do not accept "it produces a list of all the errors at the end of translation", which describes a compiler's error report and not a dynamic check
> 
> Do not accept "it finds logic errors", because a syntax check only tests the rules of the language
> 
> Do not accept "it corrects the error", because the IDE shows the error and the programmer repairs it

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mark that goes missing here is the one hidden in the word "dynamic". The examiner wants to see that the checking happens as you type, not when you press run. Put "as the code is being entered" somewhere in your answer and that mark is safe.
> 
> Keep syntax errors and logic errors apart. A dynamic syntax check cannot tell you that you have written a plus sign where you needed a minus sign, because that statement still obeys the rules of the language.

parts.problemMd:
A programmer is working on a program that contains several thousand lines of code.

The Integrated Development Environment (IDE) displays the code using prettyprint.

Explain how prettyprint helps the programmer while the program is being written.
parts.solutionMd:
Keywords are displayed in a different colour from the rest of the code. **[1]**

Strings, comments and identifiers are each given their own colour, so the separate parts of a statement can be told apart. **[1]**

A keyword that has been typed incorrectly is not coloured, so the programmer notices the mistake as it is made. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - Keywords are displayed in a different colour / font / style from the rest of the code
> - Strings, comments, identifiers and other parts of the code are shown in different colours so they can be told apart
> - A keyword typed incorrectly is not coloured or highlighted, so the mistake is noticed as it is made
> - The code is easier to read, so the programmer can find their way around a long program more quickly
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept "syntax highlighting" as an alternative name, but write prettyprint, which is the term used in the syllabus
> 
> Do not accept "it corrects the spelling of a keyword", because prettyprint changes how the code is displayed and never changes the code itself
> 
> Do not accept "it checks the code against the rules of the language", which is a dynamic syntax check and not prettyprint

> **[exam-tip]**
> "It makes the code look nice" earns nothing. Say what prettyprint does to the code on the screen, which is colour, and then say what the programmer gains from it.
> 
> Keep prettyprint apart from a dynamic syntax check. Prettyprint is a presentation feature, so it changes how correct code is displayed. It does not test a statement against the rules of the language.

parts.problemMd:
A programmer is developing a program using an Integrated Development Environment (IDE).

The table describes five problems the programmer has while developing the program.

Complete the table by naming the feature of a typical IDE that solves each problem.

| Problem | IDE feature |
|---|---|
| The programmer types a keyword incorrectly and wants the mistake to be shown on the screen straight away, before the program is run. |   |
| The programmer cannot remember the exact name of a built-in function and wants the IDE to offer the possible names while the name is being typed. |   |
| The program is now several thousand lines long and the programmer wants to hide the sections of code that they are not working on. |   |
| A variable holds the wrong value, and the programmer wants the program to stop running at a chosen line so that the value can be checked at that point. |   |
| The programmer wants the current values of several variables to be displayed on the screen while the program runs. |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Problem | IDE feature |
|---|---|
| The programmer types a keyword incorrectly and wants the mistake to be shown on the screen straight away, before the program is run. | **Dynamic syntax check** **[1]** |
| The programmer cannot remember the exact name of a built-in function and wants the IDE to offer the possible names while the name is being typed. | **Context-sensitive prompt** **[1]** |
| The program is now several thousand lines long and the programmer wants to hide the sections of code that they are not working on. | **Expand and collapse code blocks** **[1]** |
| A variable holds the wrong value, and the programmer wants the program to stop running at a chosen line so that the value can be checked at that point. | **Breakpoint** **[1]** |
| The programmer wants the current values of several variables to be displayed on the screen while the program runs. | **Report window** **[1]** |

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for row 1: dynamic syntax check. Accept "syntax check as the code is typed" or "dynamic syntax checking". Accept "prettyprint", because Cambridge credits pretty-printing as colour-coding keywords "so the user can identify any errors"
> 
> **1 mark** for row 2: context-sensitive prompt. Accept "auto-complete" or "auto-completion"
> 
> **1 mark** for row 3: expand and collapse code blocks. Accept "collapse code blocks" or "expand/collapse blocks". Do not accept "comments", because commenting out a block removes it from the program instead of hiding it on the screen
> 
> **1 mark** for row 4: breakpoint. Do not accept "single stepping", because single stepping runs the program one statement at a time from the start rather than stopping it at a line the programmer chooses
> 
> **1 mark** for row 5: report window. Accept "watch window", "variable watch window" or "variable window". Do not accept "breakpoint", because a breakpoint halts the program and it is the report window that displays the values

> **[exam-tip]**
> Rows 4 and 5 are where marks are lost, because the three debugging features get mixed up. A breakpoint decides where the program stops, single stepping decides how fast it moves, and the report window is the only one of the three that actually displays the contents of the variables. Learn them as three different jobs, not as three names for debugging.
> 
> The syllabus groups IDE features under four purposes: coding, initial error detection, presentation and debugging. When a question describes a problem, decide which of those four purposes it belongs to first. That narrows five possible answers down to one or two.

parts.problemMd:
A software company writes several programs. Each program must be translated before a computer can run it.

Identify the translator needed in each of the following situations.

(i) A program written in assembly language must be translated into machine code.

(1)

(ii) A finished program written in a high-level language must be translated into an executable file that a customer can run without a translator being installed.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Assembler **[1]**

(ii) Compiler **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for assembler
> 
> **1 mark** for compiler
> 
> Accept "assembler software" for (i)
> 
> Do not accept compiler or interpreter for (i). Only an assembler translates a program written in assembly language
> 
> Do not accept interpreter for (ii). An interpreter does not produce an executable file, and it must be present every time the program is run

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error here is writing "compiler" for the assembly language program. A compiler and an interpreter both take a high-level language as their input. Assembly language is a low-level language, and the assembler is the only translator that handles it.
> 
> Read part (ii) for the words "executable file". Those two words rule the interpreter out on their own.

parts.problemMd:
A programmer writes the control program for a washing machine in assembly language.

Explain why an assembler is needed before the washing machine can run this program.
parts.solutionMd:
The processor in the washing machine can only execute instructions that are in machine code. **[1]**

Assembly language is a low-level language written in a text form, so the processor cannot execute it directly. **[1]**

The assembler translates the assembly language program into machine code, which is then loaded and run by the washing machine. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each point, **max 3**:
> 
> - The processor can only execute machine code
> - Assembly language cannot be executed by the processor directly
> - The assembler translates the assembly language program into machine code
> - ... so the translated program can be loaded and run by the washing machine
> 
> Accept "object code" in place of "machine code".
> 
> Accept "each assembly language instruction is translated into one machine code instruction" for the third point.
> 
> Do not accept "so the computer can understand it" on its own. The answer must name machine code.
> 
> Do not accept a description of the first pass and second pass of the assembler. That is not what this question asks for.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two answers lose marks here every year. The first is "so the computer can understand it", which is too vague to credit. Name machine code and say that this is the only form the processor can execute.
> 
> The second is a description of the two passes of a two-pass assembler. That is a different question. This one asks why the assembler is needed at all, so keep your answer on what the processor can and cannot run.

parts.problemMd:
A company is working on three programs.

- **Program 1** is written in assembly language and controls a robot arm in a factory.
- **Program 2** is written in a high-level language. A programmer is still writing and testing it.
- **Program 3** is a finished high-level language program that will be sold to customers on a memory stick.

Complete the table by naming the most appropriate translator for each program and giving **one** reason for each choice.

| Program | Translator | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Program 1 |   |   |
| Program 2 |   |   |
| Program 3 |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Program | Translator | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Program 1 | **Assembler** **[1]** | **It is the only translator that converts an assembly language program into machine code.** **[1]** |
| Program 2 | **Interpreter** **[1]** | **It translates and executes one statement at a time and stops at the first error, so the programmer can correct the error and see the effect immediately.** **[1]** |
| Program 3 | **Compiler** **[1]** | **It produces an executable file, so the customer can run the program without having a translator installed.** **[1]** |

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each correct translator and **1 mark** for a matching reason.
> 
> Accept for the Program 1 reason: the program is not written in a high-level language, so a compiler or an interpreter cannot be used // it translates the assembly language program into machine code that the robot arm controller can execute
> 
> Accept for the Program 2 reason: only one error is reported at a time, so there are no dependent errors to sort out // a partially written program can be translated and tested
> 
> Accept for the Program 3 reason: the source code is not supplied, so the customer cannot read or change it // the program is translated once rather than every time the customer runs it
> 
> A reason mark can only be awarded if the translator named in the same row is correct.
> 
> Do not accept "it is faster" on its own for any row.
> 
> Do not accept "an interpreter is slower" as the reason for Program 3, because a reason must say what the compiler gives the customer.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each reason must fit the program described in that row, not translators in general. "A compiler is better" earns nothing. "It produces an executable file so the customer does not need a translator installed" earns the mark because it uses the detail in the question, that the program is sold to customers.
> 
> Program 1 catches students out because they are thinking about compilers and interpreters. Look at the language first. Assembly language means assembler, whatever the program is for.

parts.problemMd:
A finished program written in a high-level language is supplied to customers.

State **two** drawbacks of supplying this program so that it is run by an interpreter, instead of supplying a compiled version.
parts.solutionMd:
The customer must have the interpreter installed, otherwise the program will not run. **[1]**

The program is translated every time it is run, so translation takes time on every run. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - The customer must have the interpreter installed in order to run the program
> - The program has to be translated every time it is run // it is not translated once and then reused
> - ... so the program takes longer to run than a compiled executable file
> - The source code has to be supplied to the customer
> - ... so the customer can read, change or copy the program code
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Do not accept "the interpreter reports only one error at a time" or "errors can be corrected in real time". Those describe an interpreter during development, and neither is a drawback of supplying a finished program.
> 
> Do not accept "an interpreter is slower" without saying why it is slower.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students revise the list of interpreter advantages and then write the same points here with the word "not" added. That does not work. The advantages of an interpreter, stopping at the first error and letting you correct it immediately, belong to the programmer writing the code. This question is about the customer running a finished program.
> 
> If you write that the program is slower, add the reason: it is translated again every time it is run.

parts.problemMd:
A program is written in a high-level language.

Compare the way a compiler translates the program with the way an interpreter translates the program.
parts.solutionMd:
A compiler translates the whole program in one go, before any of it is run, and produces an executable file. **[1]**

An interpreter translates one statement at a time and executes each statement immediately after translating it. **[1]**

The executable file produced by the compiler can be run without the compiler being present, but the interpreter has to translate the program again every time it is run, so the interpreter must be present each time. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Max 3 marks**, with at least **1 mark** from each list.
> 
> Compiler:
> 
> - Translates the whole program in one go // translates all of the source code before any of it is run
> - Produces an executable file // produces object code that is saved
> - The program is translated once, and the executable file can then be run many times
> - The compiler is not needed when the program is run
> - Produces a full error report after translating
> 
> Interpreter:
> 
> - Translates one statement at a time
> - Executes each statement immediately after translating it
> - The program is translated again every time it is run
> - The interpreter must be present whenever the program is run
> - Stops at the first error and reports it
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Do not accept "a compiler is faster" without saying what is faster and why.
> 
> Do not accept "an interpreter translates line by line" on its own for both marks. The interpreter mark also needs the execution point, that each statement is executed as it is translated.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A "compare" question needs both sides. Answers that describe only the compiler cannot reach full marks, however detailed they are. Write a point about the compiler, then the matching point about the interpreter.
> 
> The point students most often leave out is that an interpreter executes each statement as well as translating it. A compiler only translates. That single difference explains why the compiler produces a file you can run later and the interpreter does not.

parts.problemMd:
A company has finished writing a program that controls the lighting in a large office building.

The program will be installed on 200 identical control units. Each control unit has a small amount of memory and has no translator software installed on it.

The company does not want its customers to be able to read or change the program code.

Identify whether a compiler or an interpreter should be used to prepare the program for the control units, and justify your choice.
parts.solutionMd:
A compiler should be used.

A compiler produces an executable file, **[1]** so each control unit can run the program even though it has no translator software installed. **[1]**

The program is translated once, before it is installed, so no translation takes place while the program is running. **[1]**

Only the executable file is installed on the control units, not the source code, **[1]** so customers cannot read or change the program code. **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> No mark is given for the choice. **1 mark** for each justification point, **max 5**:
> 
> - A compiler produces an executable file
> - ... so the control unit can run the program without any translator installed
> - ... whereas an interpreter would have to be installed on all 200 control units
> - The program is translated once, before it is installed
> - ... so no translation takes place while the program is running
> - ... so the program does not need memory for a translator while it runs
> - Only the executable file is installed, not the source code
> - ... so the customer cannot read, change or copy the program code
> - The program is complete, so the real-time error correction an interpreter offers is no longer needed
> - The compiler produces a full error report, so all errors can be found before the program is installed on 200 units
> 
> Marks are only available for a justification of the compiler. A justification of the interpreter earns 0.
> 
> Do not accept "compiled code always runs faster" on its own. It must be linked to a reason, for example that the program is translated once before it is run so no translating happens while it runs.
> 
> Do not accept "it is easier to debug" as a justification here. The program is already finished.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The marks in a "justify" question are in the justification, not in the choice, so never stop at "a compiler". Work through the facts you were given, one at a time: no translator installed, small memory, and code that must stay hidden. Each of those gives you a separate justification point.
> 
> "Compiled code runs faster" is the answer examiners see most and credit least. Add the reason and it becomes a mark: the whole program is translated before it is run, so no time is spent translating while it is running.

parts.problemMd:
Some programs written in a high-level language are partially compiled and partially interpreted. Java (console mode) is one example.

Describe what happens when a program is partially compiled and partially interpreted.
parts.solutionMd:
The source code is first compiled into a form that is not the machine code of any one processor. **[1]**

That compiled code is then interpreted when the program is run, so the machine code is generated at run time. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - The source code is compiled first
> - ... into a form that is not the machine code of one particular processor
> - The compiled code is then interpreted when the program is run
> - ... so the machine code is generated at run time
> - Translation is therefore completed in two stages, one before the program is run and one while it runs
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Do not accept "the whole program is compiled into machine code and then run". If the program were fully compiled there would be nothing left to interpret.
> 
> Do not accept an answer that only gives a benefit, such as "it can be used on different platforms". The question asks what happens, not why it is useful.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word students drop is "interpreted". Many answers say the program is compiled and then run, which describes ordinary compilation and earns one mark at most. Say clearly that the compiled code is interpreted while the program runs.
> 
> Two stages, two marks. Write one sentence about the compiling stage and one about the interpreting stage and you have the answer.

parts.problemMd:
A company writes one program and supplies exactly the same partially compiled file to customers who use three different types of computer.

Explain how partial compilation allows the same file to run on all three types of computer.
parts.solutionMd:
The compiled file is not the machine code of one particular processor, so it is not tied to a single type of computer. **[1]**

Each type of computer has its own interpreter, which translates the compiled file when the program is run. **[1]**

The machine code is therefore generated at run time for whichever processor the program is running on, so the company does not need to produce a separately compiled version for each type of computer. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each point, **max 3**:
> 
> - The compiled file is not the machine code of one particular processor
> - Each type of computer has its own interpreter for the compiled file
> - The compiled file is interpreted when the program is run
> - ... so the machine code is generated at run time for that processor
> - The company only has to produce and supply one file rather than one for each type of computer
> 
> Accept "platform" in place of "type of computer".
> 
> Do not accept "Java runs on any computer" on its own. The answer must say why.
> 
> Do not accept "the file is compiled for each computer". Nothing is recompiled by the customer.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "It works on any computer" is a statement, not an explanation, and it earns nothing. An "explain" question wants the mechanism, so give the two halves: the compiled file is not machine code for one processor, and an interpreter on each computer finishes the translation while the program runs.
> 
> Be careful with the word compile in your last sentence. The customer's computer interprets the file; it does not compile it again.

parts.problemMd:
A software company must choose between two ways of supplying a new program to its customers, who use three different operating systems.

**Method A:** fully compile the program separately for each of the three operating systems, and supply three different executable files.

**Method B:** partially compile the program once, and supply one file that is interpreted when it is run.

Explain **one** benefit and **one** drawback to the company of choosing Method B.
parts.solutionMd:
Benefit: the company only has to produce and maintain one file, **[1]** because the partially compiled file is interpreted when it is run and so works on all three operating systems. **[1]**

Drawback: every customer's computer must have the interpreting software installed, **[1]** and part of the translation then happens every time the program is run, so the program takes longer to run than a fully compiled executable file. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Max 2 marks** for the benefit and **max 2 marks** for the drawback.
> 
> Benefit, **1 mark** for each point:
> 
> - Only one file has to be produced // only one file has to be maintained and updated
> - ... because the partially compiled file is interpreted when it is run, so it works on all three operating systems
> - A change to the program only has to be made and translated once, not three times
> - The machine code is generated at run time, so the code is optimised for the processor it is running on
> 
> Drawback, **1 mark** for each point:
> 
> - The customer's computer must have the interpreting software installed
> - ... so the program will not run on a computer that does not have it
> - Part of the translation happens every time the program is run
> - ... so the program takes longer to run than a fully compiled executable file
> 
> Do not credit two benefits or two drawbacks. The maximum for each side is 2 marks.
> 
> Do not accept "Method B is easier" without saying what is easier and why.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read the tariff and the wording together. Four marks split as one benefit and one drawback means two marks are available on each side, so develop each point with a "because" rather than writing four separate one-line advantages. Two benefits and no drawback caps you at 2 marks however good they are.
> 
> The drawback students miss is that Method B still needs a translator on the customer's computer. Method A does not. That is the trade the company is really making.

parts.problemMd:
A student uses a laptop to write a program that is saved as a text file.

The laptop has utility software and an Operating System (OS).

(i) Describe the file management tasks carried out by an OS.

(2)

(ii) Explain the need for back-up software.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i)** 1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 2**)
> 
> e.g.
> 
> - Secondary storage space is divided into file allocation units
> - Space on secondary storage is allocated to particular files
> - Maintains/creates directory structures
> - Specifies the logical method of file storage e.g. FAT or NTFS
> - Provides file naming conventions
> - Controls user access // implements access rights // implements password protection // Makes file sharing possible
> - Controls access to the file by other software
> - Specifies tasks that can be performed on a file e.g. open, close, delete, copy, create, move, etc
> - Allows searching for a file
> 
> (ii) **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 2**)
> 
> - To allow data to be retrieved / restored when lost
> - To automatically make a duplicate copy of data…
> - …so the user does not have to remember to backup data
> - To make regular duplicate copies of data

parts.problemMd:
The student used a program library when writing their program.

Explain the benefits to the student of using library files when writing a program.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark **for each bullet point (**max 3**)
> 
> e.g.
> 
> - It saves development time for the student
> - … by using pre-written code
> - There is less testing to do // the routines are more likely to work correctly
> - … because they have already been tested and are error-free
> - It results in a more robust program
> - Subroutines can be used that they do not have the skill to write
> - … which enables a more complex program to be written

parts.problemMd:
The computer has an Operating System (OS). One of the key management tasks of the OS is process management.

Describe the process management tasks performed by an OS.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 4**)
> 
> e.g.
> 
> - It manages the scheduling of processes // Decides which process is to be run next
> - Allows multi-tasking/multi-processing
> - Ensures fair access
> - Handles interrupts
> - Manages / allocates which resources the processes require
> - Facilitates the sharing and exchange of data between processes
> - Prevents interference between processes // conflict resolution

parts.problemMd:
The programmers created a new program library whilst developing the program.

Describe the benefits to the programmers of creating a program library.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for each bullet point (max 3)
> 
> e.g.
> 
> - Subroutines can be shared / reused
> - … between team members who are working independently
> - … without having to rewrite/re-test them which saves the programmers’ time
> - A program library provides continuity between programs/programmers
> - Individual programmers can contribute their specialisms to the library // Individual programmers can use the specialisms of others

parts.problemMd:
A computer has an Operating System (OS).

Memory management and process management are two OS tasks.

Explain how memory management **and** process management support multi-tasking.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each to **max 4**
> 
> **Max 3** marks for each management task:
> 
> *Memory management*: **Max 3 marks**
> 
> - Stores data from all currently running programs concurrently in RAM
> - Stops the data from overwriting each other in RAM/primary storage
> - Decides which processes should be in main memory
> - Makes efficient use of memory
> 
> *Process management:**** *****Max 3 marks**
> 
> - Allows one process to be paused whilst another process can be actioned
> - Decides which process is to be run next
> - Switches between processes to allow them to share the use of the processor
> - Identification/description of scheduling

parts.problemMd:
The programmer uses program libraries when developing the program.

Describe **two **benefits to the programmer of using program libraries.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark **each to **max 2**:
> 
> - Saves programming/testing time as code does not have to be written/rewritten from scratch // code does not have to be tested
> - Code is already tested so it is more robust/likely to work
> - The programmer does not need to maintain the library // library routines are updated automatically
> - Can perform complex calculations that the programmer may be unable to do
> - Makes code more easily readable

parts.problemMd:
Robots are used to serve food and drink to customers at a restaurant.

![Cartoon robot waiter with tray shelves stands near restaurant tables and chairs, prepared to serve or collect dishes.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-computer-science-19/5-system-software-/operating-systems/assets/001-cartoon-robot-waiter-with-tray-shelves-stands-ne.png)

Program libraries were used when writing the robot’s software.

(i) State what is meant by a program library.

(1)

(ii) Some program libraries include Dynamic Link Library (DLL) files.

Describe the benefits of a programmer using a library with DLL files instead of using a library that does not include DLL files.

(4)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i)** 1 mark** for:
> 
> Pre-written code/functions/routines that can be **imported/called** in another program
> 
> (ii) **1 mark** each to** max 4**:
> 
> - Maintenance not needed to be done by the programmer
> - ... because the DLL is separate from program
> - The calling program does not need recompilation by the programmer when a DLL file changes
> - ... because the DLL file can be updated independently of the calling program
> - … updates will apply to all programs that use the DLL file

parts.problemMd:
A computer has an Operating System (OS).

State **one **purpose of the Operating System.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each bullet point (**max 1**)
> 
> - To hide the complexities of the hardware from the user
> - To provide a platform for software to run
> - To provide a user interface

parts.problemMd:
The Operating System has utility software.

The purpose of some utility software is to improve security.

Identify **one **example of utility software that is **not **intended to improve security.

Explain why this software is needed.
parts.solutionMd:
**1 mark** for the name of the utility software

**2 marks **for the explanation

- Defragmentation software
- … because over time saving and deleting of small files fragments the disk
- ... the software makes (individual) files contiguous
- … so access time to the files is improved
- … because head movement is reduced
- Disk contents analysis/disk repair software
- … to identify and mark bad sectors
- ... to restore corrupted files
- ... to recover lost data (due to hardware failure)
- File compression
- … to reduce the size of files
- ... which saves storage and memory space // by example
- ... and reduces transmission time // by example
- Disk formatter
- … to prepare a disk for use // set up the file system
- ... to partition the disc
- ... to delete all the data from the disc

parts.problemMd:
The program makes use of complex statistical functions. The required functions are not built-in to the programming language and are too complicated for the programmer to write.

One solution would be to employ another programmer who has experience of writing these functions, as there is no time to train the existing programmer.

State **one other** way that these functions may be provided for inclusion in the program.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The use of a program <u>library </u>(routines)

parts.problemMd:
An Operating System is supplied with utility software.

Complete the table by writing the name of the utility software that carries out each purpose.

| Purpose | Utility software |
|---|---|
| To prepare a new hard disk for use by setting up the file system |   |
| To reduce the size of a file so that it uses less storage space |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Purpose | Utility software |
|---|---|
| To prepare a new hard disk for use by setting up the file system | **Disk formatter** **[1]** |
| To reduce the size of a file so that it uses less storage space | **File compression software** **[1]** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for disk formatter in the first row
> 
> **1 mark** for file compression software in the second row
> 
> Accept formatter, hard disk formatter or disk formatting software for the first row
> 
> Accept compression software or file compression for the second row
> 
> Do not accept defragmentation software for the first row. Defragmentation rearranges files that are already stored on a disk; it does not set up the file system on a new disk
> 
> Do not accept back-up software for the second row. A back-up makes a copy of a file; it does not make the file smaller

> **[exam-tip]**
> Formatting and defragmenting are not the same job, and swapping them is the most common error on this topic. Formatting prepares a new disk and removes everything on it. Defragmenting rearranges files that are already stored there.
> 
> Cambridge awards no marks for brand names of software packages, so write the type of utility rather than the name of a product you have used.

parts.problemMd:
A computer has been used for two years. During that time many files have been saved to and deleted from its hard disk. Files now take longer to load than they did when the computer was new.

The user runs the defragmentation software supplied with the Operating System.

Explain how defragmentation software reduces the time taken to load a file.
parts.solutionMd:
Saving and deleting files over a long period leaves the blocks of a single file spread across the disk, so the file is no longer stored in one continuous area. **[1]**

The defragmentation software rearranges the blocks so that each file occupies contiguous blocks, and it moves the free space together. **[1]**

The read/write head then has less movement to make, because it does not have to search for the next fragment of the file, so the file is loaded faster. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - The blocks of a file become spread across the disk // the file is fragmented // the file is not stored in contiguous blocks
> - The software rearranges the blocks of individual files so that each file is contiguous // it moves the free space together
> - There is no need to search for the next fragment or block of the file
> - Less read/write head movement is needed
> - So each file can be accessed or loaded faster
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept stored in one continuous area as an alternative to contiguous.
> 
> Do not accept it deletes unwanted files to make space. Defragmentation moves data; it does not delete it.
> 
> Do not accept it makes the files smaller. That is file compression, not defragmentation.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mark scheme here is narrow and vague answers score nothing. "It tidies up the hard disk" and "it makes the computer run faster" both repeat the question instead of explaining it. The two words examiners are looking for are fragmented and contiguous.
> 
> Build the answer in three steps: what the disk looks like before, what the software does to it, and why that saves time. The link to reduced read/write head movement is the mark most students leave out.

parts.problemMd:
A company stores its customer records on a computer. A technician has two tasks to complete.

**Task 1**

One hard disk in the computer is several years old. Some files stored on it can no longer be opened, and the Operating System reports errors when it reads certain areas of the disk. No copy of these files exists anywhere else.

**Task 2**

A folder of large report files must be sent to a client over a slow internet connection.

For each task, name the utility software the technician should use and describe how that software helps.
parts.solutionMd:
Task 1: disk contents analysis and disk repair software. **[1]**

It checks the disk, identifies the damaged areas and marks the bad sectors so they are not used again, and it restores the corrupted files so that the data is recovered. **[1]**

Task 2: file compression software. **[1]**

It reduces the size of the report files, so fewer bytes have to be sent and the transfer takes less time over the slow connection. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for naming disk contents analysis software or disk repair software for Task 1
> 
> **1 mark** for what it does in Task 1: identifies and marks bad sectors // restores corrupted files // recovers the lost data
> 
> **1 mark** for naming file compression software for Task 2
> 
> **1 mark** for what it does in Task 2: reduces the size of the files // so the transmission time is reduced
> 
> Accept disk analysis software or disk repair software on its own for Task 1.
> 
> Accept compression software or file compression for Task 2.
> 
> Do not accept defragmentation software for Task 1. Defragmentation rearranges files that are stored correctly; it does not detect or repair damaged areas of a disk.
> 
> Do not accept back-up software for Task 1. The stem states that no copy of the files exists, so there is nothing to restore from.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This kind of question tests whether you can match a symptom to the right utility, so read each symptom carefully. Errors when reading certain areas of a disk mean damaged sectors, which is a repair job. Slow loading of files that still open normally would mean fragmentation instead. Students who see the word disk and reach straight for defragmentation software lose both marks for that task.
> 
> Naming the utility is only half of each task. A name on its own earns one mark out of two, however correct it is, so always add what the software actually does.

parts.problemMd:
Complete the description of a program library by writing the missing word in each gap.

A program library is a collection of subroutines that have already been written and ........................ , so a developer does not have to check that they work.

A developer can ........................ the library into their own program so that its subroutines can be called.
parts.solutionMd:
A program library is a collection of subroutines that have already been written and **tested**, so a developer does not have to check that they work. **[1]**

A developer can **import** the library into their own program so that its subroutines can be called. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for tested in the first gap
> 
> **1 mark** for import in the second gap
> 
> Accept compiled for the first gap.
> 
> Accept install or reference for the second gap.
> 
> Do not accept copy and paste for the second gap. The program imports or links to the library; the developer does not paste the library code into their own program.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word library makes students think of storage, so a frequent wrong answer is that it is a place where a programmer keeps their finished programs. A program library holds subroutines, meaning procedures and functions, and the point of it is that they are already written and already tested.
> 
> Whenever you are asked what a program library is, get both ideas into the answer: the routines are pre-written, and another program can call them once it has imported the library.

parts.problemMd:
A company installs an Operating System (OS) on each of its new computers.

One purpose of the Operating System is to provide a user interface.

State **two other** purposes of the Operating System.
parts.solutionMd:
To hide the complexities of the hardware from the user. **[1]**

To provide a platform on which application software can run. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for hiding the complexities of the hardware from the user
> 
> **1 mark** for providing a platform for software to run
> 
> Do not accept "to provide a user interface". The stem has already given this purpose, so it cannot be given again.
> 
> Do not accept a bare list of management tasks such as "memory management, file management". Naming a task does not state what the Operating System is for.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The usual mistake here is to answer with the five management tasks, because those are the easiest part of this topic to remember. Cambridge treats a purpose and a management task as two different things. There are only three purposes: the user interface, hiding the complexities of the hardware, and providing a platform for software. Error checking and recovery is one of the management tasks, not a purpose.
> 
> The second mistake is to write down the purpose the stem has already given you. When a question says "state two other", it has taken one answer off the table.

parts.problemMd:
A developer writes a program that uses many routines from a program library.

The developer can either include the library routines in the program when it is compiled, or supply them separately in a Dynamic Link Library (DLL) file.

Explain the benefits of supplying the routines in a DLL file, in terms of the size of the executable file and the use of main memory.
parts.solutionMd:
The executable file of the program is smaller. **[1]**

This is because the executable does not contain the library routines themselves. **[1]**

The amount of main memory the program needs is also reduced, because the DLL is loaded into memory only once, or only when a routine inside it is required. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for stating that the executable file of the program is smaller
> 
> **1 mark** for the reason: the executable does not contain the library routines
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the main memory required is reduced, because the DLL is loaded only once or only when it is required
> 
> Accept the library code is not built into the program for the second marking point.
> 
> Do not accept the DLL compresses the code. A DLL does not compress anything; the routines are simply held outside the executable file.
> 
> Do not accept the program runs faster on its own. Run speed is not what this question credits, and the DLL still has to be loaded before its routines can run.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often write that a DLL "saves space" and stop. That is one idea, not two marks. Say where the space is saved: on secondary storage, because the executable file no longer holds the routines, and in main memory, because the DLL is loaded only when it is needed.
> 
> Do not confuse a DLL with compression or with a back-up. It is the same library code, kept in its own file and linked to the program while the program is running.

parts.problemMd:
A user starts a word processor on a computer. The word processor is application software.

Explain why the word processor needs an Operating System (OS) in order to run.
parts.solutionMd:
The Operating System provides the platform on which application software runs. **[1]**

The word processor asks the Operating System to reach the hardware for it, for example to save a document to secondary storage, instead of containing its own code to control that hardware. **[1]**

The Operating System hides the complexities of the hardware from the program, so the same word processor can be used on computers built from different hardware. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - The Operating System provides a platform for application software to run on
> - The word processor uses the Operating System to reach the hardware, for example to save a file or to send data to a printer
> - ... so the program does not have to contain its own code for controlling that hardware
> - The Operating System hides the complexities of the hardware from the program and from the user
> - ... so the same word processor can run on computers built from different hardware
> - The Operating System allocates the block of RAM that the word processor needs
> - The Operating System decides when the word processor is given the use of the processor
> - The Operating System provides the user interface that the user needs in order to start the program and open a document
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Do not accept "the computer cannot work without an Operating System". This restates the question instead of answering it.
> 
> Do not accept "the Operating System runs the program" on its own. The answer must say what the Operating System provides or does for the program.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most lost marks here come from listing the five management tasks instead of answering the question that was asked. The question is about one program and what that program cannot do for itself.
> 
> Build the answer around two ideas and you will nearly always reach three marks: the Operating System is the platform the program runs on, and the Operating System reaches the hardware on the program's behalf.

parts.problemMd:
A software company writes three different programs. All three programs use the same set of library routines.

The company must choose one of two methods.

**Method A**: the library routines are included in each program when that program is compiled.

**Method B**: the library routines are supplied in one Dynamic Link Library (DLL) file that all three programs use.

Complete the table to describe the result of choosing Method B in each situation.

| Situation | Result of choosing Method B |
|---|---|
| The size of the executable file of each program |   |
| The number of copies of the library routines held in main memory while all three programs are running |   |
| Whether the three programs must be recompiled after an error in a library routine is corrected |   |
| Which of the three programs receive the correction |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Situation | Result of choosing Method B |
|---|---|
| The size of the executable file of each program | **Each executable file is smaller, because it does not contain the library routines** **[1]** |
| The number of copies of the library routines held in main memory while all three programs are running | **One copy only, because the single DLL file is loaded once and is available to all three programs** **[1]** |
| Whether the three programs must be recompiled after an error in a library routine is corrected | **No, because the DLL file is corrected independently of the programs that call it** **[1]** |
| Which of the three programs receive the correction | **All three, because the update applies to every program that uses the DLL file** **[1]** |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for row 1: each executable file is smaller // the executable does not contain the library routines
> 
> **1 mark** for row 2: only one copy is held in main memory // the DLL is loaded once and shared by all three programs
> 
> **1 mark** for row 3: no, they do not need to be recompiled // the DLL is updated independently of the calling programs
> 
> **1 mark** for row 4: all three of them // every program that uses the DLL file
> 
> Accept the library code is stored outside the executable for row 1
> 
> Accept memory use is reduced for row 2 only if it is linked to a single shared copy
> 
> Do not accept each program keeps its own copy in memory for row 2. That is the result of Method A
> 
> Do not accept only the program that is running at the time for row 4

> **[exam-tip]**
> Check which method the table is asking about before you write anything. Most of the marks lost on comparison questions like this go to students who describe Method A in the Method B column.
> 
> The recompilation point is the one Cambridge asks for most often and it is easy to state backwards. With a DLL, the library file is the thing that changes; the programs that call it do not, so they do not need to be recompiled.

parts.problemMd:
A company makes two products.

**Product A** is a tablet computer. The user can install and run many different applications on it, and can store photographs and documents on it. Product A has an Operating System (OS).

**Product B** is a temperature controller. It is an embedded system. It reads a temperature sensor and switches a fan on or off. Its single program is stored in ROM. Product B does not have an Operating System.

Explain why Product A needs an Operating System but Product B does not.
parts.solutionMd:
Product A runs many different programs that the user chooses, installs and may run at the same time, so an Operating System is needed to share the processor, the memory and the peripherals between them. **[1]**

Product A stores many photographs and documents, so an Operating System is needed to organise them into files and directories and to find them again. **[1]**

Product A has a human user who gives commands to it, so an Operating System is needed to provide the user interface. **[1]**

Product B is dedicated to one task and runs a single fixed program on hardware that never changes, so that program can control the sensor and the fan directly and no Operating System is needed. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each point below, to a maximum of 4. **Maximum 3 marks** for points about Product A and **maximum 3 marks** for points about Product B.
> 
> **Product A:**
> 
> - Runs many different programs, which the user can choose and install
> - ... so the Operating System must share the processor and the memory between them
> - Stores many files that must be organised and found again, which needs file management
> - Has a human user, so it needs a user interface
> - Has many different peripherals, so it needs the Operating System to manage them
> - The applications are written by other people and need a platform to run on
> 
> **Product B:**
> 
> - Is dedicated to a single task
> - Runs one fixed program held in ROM, which is not changed by the user
> - ... so that program can control its known, fixed hardware directly
> - Has no user interface and no user to interact with
> - Stores little or no data, so there are no files to manage
> - Has too little memory or processing power to run an Operating System // an Operating System would add cost for no benefit
> 
> Do not accept "Product B is too small". Size on its own is not a reason; the answer must say that the task is fixed, or that the hardware is known, or that there is no user.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Questions that compare two products are marked on both sides, and students almost always write four points about the tablet and nothing about the embedded system. Cambridge caps each side, so half of your marks are sitting in the product you skipped. Write at least one sentence about each.
> 
> Note also that "it is an embedded system so it does not need an Operating System" earns nothing. That is the fact the question gave you. The mark is for the reason behind it: one fixed task, one fixed program, and hardware that never changes.

parts.problemMd:
The table describes three key management tasks carried out by an Operating System (OS).

Complete the table by writing the name of the missing management task in each empty cell.

| Description of the task | Name of the management task |
|---|---|
| Divides secondary storage into file allocation units and maintains the directory structure. | File management |
| Allocates a block of RAM to each running program and stops one program from overwriting the data of another. |   |
| Checks the user name and the password before access to the computer is allowed. |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Description of the task | Name of the management task |
|---|---|
| Divides secondary storage into file allocation units and maintains the directory structure. | File management |
| Allocates a block of RAM to each running program and stops one program from overwriting the data of another. | **Memory management** **[1]** |
| Checks the user name and the password before access to the computer is allowed. | **Security management** **[1]** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for "Memory management" in the second row
> 
> **1 mark** for "Security management" in the third row
> 
> Accept "memory" and "security" without the word "management"
> 
> Do not accept "process management" in the second row. Process management decides which program runs next; deciding where in RAM a program is placed is memory management
> 
> Do not accept "data security" or "encryption" in the third row. The task carried out by the Operating System is called security management

> **[exam-tip]**
> Row two is the row that catches students out, because "running program" makes them reach for process management. Look at the resource in the description instead. If the sentence is about RAM being given out or protected, the answer is memory management.
>
