> Learn the five names in Cambridge's own words: memory management, file management, security management, hardware management and process management. A mark scheme will not credit an invented name such as "storage management".

parts.problemMd:
A computer in a public library is used by many different people. Each person has their own account on the computer.

Describe the security management tasks carried out by the Operating System (OS) on this computer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Operating System creates a separate account and password for each person who uses the computer. **[1]**

It checks the user name and password when a person signs in, so that it can confirm who they are before access is given. **[1]**

It applies access rights to files, so that one person cannot open or change the documents that belong to another person. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - Creates user accounts and passwords
> - Checks the user name and password // authenticates the user before access is given
> - Applies access rights or permissions to files and folders
> - ... so one user cannot read, change or delete another user's data
> - Allows a password to be changed, or forces it to be changed after a set time
> - Keeps a log or record of which user signed in and what they did
> - Provides or updates a firewall or anti-malware software
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept "authentication" as an alternative to checking the user name and password.
> 
> Do not accept "it keeps the computer safe" or "it stops hackers". These are too vague to credit; the answer must name a task the Operating System actually carries out.
> 
> Do not accept "it backs up the data". Backing up protects against loss, not against unauthorised access.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Security management is the task students describe most vaguely. "It protects the computer" is a restatement, not a description, and it earns nothing. Every mark here comes from naming a concrete action: create an account, check a password, set an access right.
> 
> A useful habit is to give the reason as well as the action. "Applies access rights" is one mark; "applies access rights so that one user cannot open another user's files" gives the examiner two things to credit.

parts.problemMd:
A computer has an Operating System (OS). A user reports three faults with the computer.

Complete the table. For each fault, write the name of the key management task that is not working correctly, and explain how the fault shows that this task has failed.

| Fault | Management task | Explanation |
|---|---|---|
| A document that the user saved yesterday cannot be found anywhere on the hard disk. |   |   |
| A different person used the computer and opened the user's private documents. No user name or password was asked for. |   |   |
| When a second program is started, the data of the first program becomes corrupted and the first program stops responding. |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Fault | Management task | Explanation |
|---|---|---|
| A document that the user saved yesterday cannot be found anywhere on the hard disk. | **File management** **[1]** | **The Operating System records where each file is stored on secondary storage and maintains the directory structure, so a saved file can be found again by its name.** **[1]** |
| A different person used the computer and opened the user's private documents. No user name or password was asked for. | **Security management** **[1]** | **The Operating System creates accounts and passwords and checks them before access is given, and it applies access rights so that one user cannot open another user's files.** **[1]** |
| When a second program is started, the data of the first program becomes corrupted and the first program stops responding. | **Memory management** **[1]** | **The Operating System allocates a separate block of RAM to each program and prevents one program from writing into the area of RAM that another program is using.** **[1]** |

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for "File management" in row one
> 
> **1 mark** for explaining that the Operating System records where a file is stored, or maintains the directory structure, so that a file can be found again
> 
> **1 mark** for "Security management" in row two
> 
> **1 mark** for explaining that the Operating System creates accounts and passwords and checks them before access is given, or that it applies access rights so one user cannot open another user's files
> 
> **1 mark** for "Memory management" in row three
> 
> **1 mark** for explaining that the Operating System gives each program its own block of RAM and stops one program from overwriting the data of another
> 
> An explanation mark can still be awarded when the named task is wrong, as long as the explanation correctly describes the task that would cause that fault.
> 
> Do not accept "hardware management" in row one. The disk itself is working; it is the record of where the file was placed that has failed
> 
> Do not accept "process management" in row three. Process management decides which program runs next. Two programs being given the same area of RAM is a failure of memory management

> **[exam-tip]**
> Fault diagnosis is worth practising because it is the only place this topic is tested as reasoning rather than recall. Work from the symptom to the resource: a lost file points to secondary storage and therefore file management, an unlocked computer points to accounts and therefore security management, and two programs interfering with each other points to RAM and therefore memory management.
> 
> Row three is the one most often answered "process management". Ask yourself what was shared badly. If two programs were given the same space, memory was shared badly. If one program never got a turn on the processor, that would be process management.

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
A bank allows customers to access their accounts using an application that they can download onto a device such as a smartphone.

The bank wants to protect the integrity of its data while transferring the data to other banks. Parity check is one example of data verification.

Complete the description of parity check when Computer A is transmitting data to Computer B.

Computer A and Computer B agree on whether to use ............................... parity. Computer A divides the data into groups of ............................ . The number of 1s in each group is counted. If the agreed parity is ....................... and the group has an even number of 1s, a parity bit of 1 is appended, otherwise a parity bit of 0 is appended.

In a parity ............................ check the bytes are grouped together, for example in a grid. The number of 1s in each column (bit position) is counted. A bit is assigned to each column to make the column match the parity. These parity bits are transmitted with the data as a parity ................................. .
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each correctly completed term:
> 
> - odd or even
> - 7-bits
> - odd
> - block
> - byte
> 
> Computer A and Computer B agree on whether to use **odd or even** parity. Computer A divides the data into groups of **7-bits**. The number of 1s in each group is counted. If the agreed parity is **odd** and the group has an even number of 1s a parity bit of 1 is appended, otherwise a parity bit of 0 is appended.
> 
> In a parity **block **check the bytes are grouped together, for example in a grid. The number of 1s in each column (bit position) is counted. A bit is assigned to each column to make the column match the parity. These parity bits are transmitted with the data as a parity **byte**.

parts.problemMd:
Robots are used to serve food and drink to customers at a restaurant.

![A humanoid robot with shelves stands in a modern café, surrounded by tables and chairs, indicating a futuristic dining setting.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-computer-science-19/6-security-privacy-and-data-integrity-/data-integrity/assets/001-a-humanoid-robot-with-shelves-stands-in-a-modern.png)

The data from the robots is transmitted to a central computer using a wireless connection.

Complete the table by identifying **and **describing **two **methods of data verification that can be used during data transfer.

|   | Method | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 1 |   |   |
| 2 |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each correct method and
> 
> **1 mark** for corresponding description to **max 4**:
> 
> | Method | Description |
> |---|---|
> | Parity byte | An additional bit is added to make the number of 1s in the byte odd or even to match the parity. If a byte with an odd number of 1 bits is received when even parity is used, there is an error. |
> | Parity block | Parity is calculated horizontally and vertically. A parity byte is created from the bits produced by the vertical parity check. This is sent with the data. The parity is re-checked when received and the position of an incorrect bit can be determined. |
> | Checksum | A calculation is made from the data and the result transmitted with the data. The receiver repeats the calculation and compares the result with the value received. If the two are different, there is an error. |

parts.problemMd:
A company stores customer data in a database.

Define the term **data validation** and the term **data verification**.
parts.solutionMd:
Data validation is an automatic check carried out by the software to test whether the data entered is reasonable and follows the rules set for that field. **[1]**

Data verification is a check that the data entered, or the data received, matches the original source data and has not been changed. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for validation: a check made by the computer or the software that the data entered is reasonable // sensible // within the accepted bounds // follows the rules set for the field
> 
> **1 mark** for verification: a check that the data matches the original // matches the source document // has not been changed during entry or during transfer
> 
> Accept "checks the data is sensible" for validation
> 
> Accept "checks the data is the same as the original" for verification
> 
> Do not accept "validation checks that the data is correct" or "validation checks that the data is accurate". Validation cannot test accuracy, only reasonableness
> 
> Do not accept "verification checks that the data is accurate" on its own. Verification compares a copy with the source; it cannot show that the source itself was right

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word "correct" is what loses this mark. Validation asks "could this be right?"; verification asks "is this the same as what I was given?". Neither asks "is this true?".
> 
> Write your two definitions so that the word "reasonable" appears in the validation one and the word "matches" appears in the verification one. Those are the words the mark scheme is built around.

parts.problemMd:
A delivery company stores a telephone number for each customer.

When a clerk adds a new customer, the software carries out a format check and a length check on the telephone number.

A clerk enters a telephone number that is a real telephone number, but it belongs to a different customer. The software accepts it.

Explain why the two validation checks did not detect this error, and state one method of data verification that would.
parts.solutionMd:
Validation only tests whether the data entered is reasonable and follows the rules set for the field. **[1]**

The number the clerk typed has the pattern of characters the format check expects and the number of characters the length check expects, so it is accepted even though it is the wrong number for this customer. **[1]**

A visual check would detect the error, because the clerk compares the number shown on the screen with the number on the original document and confirms that the two match. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for stating that validation only checks that the data is reasonable // of the correct form // within the rules set for the field
> 
> **1 mark** for explaining that the number entered satisfies both the format rule and the length rule, so it is accepted even though it is the wrong number for this customer
> 
> **1 mark** for one verification method, named and with what it compares:
> 
> visual check, the clerk compares the number on the screen with the number on the original document
> 
> OR double entry, the number is typed a second time and the software compares the two entries
> 
> Accept "the data entered is never compared with the source document" as an alternative route to the first mark.
> 
> Do not accept a range check, a presence check, an existence check or a check digit for the third mark. All of these are validation, not verification.
> 
> Do not accept "the clerk should be more careful" or "use a stricter validation rule". No validation rule can separate this number from the right one.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most students answer this by inventing a tighter validation rule. There is no rule that helps, because the data entered is a genuine telephone number in the expected format. The only way to catch the error is to go back to the source document, and that is verification.
> 
> When you name a verification method, always say what is compared with what. "Double entry" written on its own is two words and no marks; "the number is typed twice and the software compares the two entries" earns the mark.

parts.problemMd:
A courier company has depots in several countries. At each depot, a member of staff types a parcel tracking number into a terminal. The terminal carries out a presence check, a length check and a format check on every tracking number.

The tracking numbers are then transmitted over a network to a central server, where they are stored.

Explain why the tracking numbers stored on the central server may still be incorrect.
parts.solutionMd:
Validation only tests whether a tracking number is reasonable and follows the rules set for the field, so it cannot tell whether the number is the right one for that parcel. **[1]**

The tracking number of a different parcel has the same length and the same pattern of characters, so it passes all three checks and is stored. **[1]**

The terminal never compares what was typed with the number printed on the parcel, so a verification method such as a visual check or double entry is also needed during data entry. **[1]**

Bits can also be changed by interference while the data travels over the network, and the three checks are not repeated after transmission, so a verification method such as a parity check or a checksum is needed during data transfer. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any four from:**
> 
> - validation only tests whether the data is reasonable // of the correct form // within the rules set for the field
> - a tracking number belonging to a different parcel has the same length and the same format, so it passes all three checks
> - the terminal does not compare the number typed with the number printed on the parcel, so validation cannot detect a wrong entry
> - a verification method during data entry, named as a visual check or double entry, is needed to compare the entry with the source
> - bits can be changed by interference while the data is transmitted over the network
> - the three validation checks are not repeated after transmission, so an error introduced in transit is not detected
> - a verification method during data transfer, named as a parity check or a checksum, is needed to detect a transmission error
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> Accept "the data could be corrupted on its way to the server" for the transmission point.
> 
> Do not accept answers about hacking, malware or unauthorised access. This question is about data integrity, not data security.
> 
> Do not accept "the validation was not strong enough" unless you also say what validation cannot do.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question has two separate stages in it, and it is easy to answer only one. Marks are available for what can go wrong when the number is typed in, and for what can go wrong while it travels to the server. Deal with both stages and name a verification method for each.
> 
> Watch the boundary with data security. Firewalls, encryption and passwords earn nothing here, because nobody has attacked the system. The data is wrong, not stolen.

parts.problemMd:
The table describes four validation checks that can be carried out on data entered into a system.

Complete the table by writing the name of the missing validation check in each empty cell.

| Description | Validation check |
|---|---|
| Checks that data has been entered and that the field has not been left empty | Presence check |
| Checks that a value falls between a stated lower boundary and a stated upper boundary |   |
| Checks that the data entered contains the correct number of characters | Length check |
| Checks that the data entered follows a stated pattern of letters and digits |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Description | Validation check |
|---|---|
| Checks that data has been entered and that the field has not been left empty | Presence check |
| Checks that a value falls between a stated lower boundary and a stated upper boundary | **Range check** **[1]** |
| Checks that the data entered contains the correct number of characters | Length check |
| Checks that the data entered follows a stated pattern of letters and digits | **Format check** **[1]** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for Range check in the second row
> 
> **1 mark** for Format check in the fourth row
> 
> Accept "range" and "format" written without the word "check"
> 
> Do not accept "limit check" in the second row. A limit check tests a single boundary, and the description gives both a lower and an upper boundary
> 
> Do not accept "type check" in the fourth row. A type check tests the data type, not the pattern of characters

> **[exam-tip]**
> Range check and limit check are the pair students mix up. A range check has two boundaries, one at each end. A limit check has only one, so it is the right answer for "no more than 5 items per customer" and the wrong answer for "between 0 and 100".
> 
> Format check and type check are the other pair. "Must be three letters followed by four digits" is a format check. "Must be a whole number" is a type check.

parts.problemMd:
An online college booking system asks a user to type a course code when making a booking.

The system carries out a presence check and an existence check on the course code.

Describe the difference between these two validation checks on this field.
parts.solutionMd:
A presence check tests only that something has been typed into the course code field, so that the booking cannot be submitted with the field left empty. **[1]**

An existence check tests that the course code that was typed is actually held by the system, by comparing it with the course codes already stored. **[1]**

So a course code such as ZZ99 passes the presence check, because characters were entered, but fails the existence check, because no course is stored with that code. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for presence check: tests that data has been entered // that the field is not left blank or empty
> 
> **1 mark** for existence check: tests that the value entered is held by the system // matches a course code already stored // is one of the values on the stored list
> 
> **1 mark** for an example that separates the two, such as a course code that is not blank but is not stored, passing the presence check and failing the existence check
> 
> Accept "look-up check" as an alternative name for the existence check.
> 
> Do not accept "an existence check makes sure the field is filled in". That is the presence check, and this is the confusion the question is testing.
> 
> Do not accept "a presence check makes sure the course code is valid". A presence check tests nothing about the value that was entered.

> **[exam-tip]**
> These two names sound alike and students swap them constantly. Separate them by what each one looks at: a presence check looks at the box, an existence check looks at the stored data. A presence check never reads the value; it only asks whether the box is empty.
> 
> Give an example that fails one check and passes the other. An example that fails both, such as leaving the field blank, does not show the examiner that you know the difference.

parts.problemMd:
A publisher gives every book an eight-digit code. The first seven digits identify the book. The eighth digit is a check digit.

The check digit is calculated from the first seven digits as follows.

1. Multiply each of the seven digits by a weight. The left-hand digit has a weight of 8, the next digit a weight of 7, and so on down to a weight of 2 for the seventh digit.
2. Add the seven products together to give a total.
3. Divide the total by 11 and take the remainder. The remainder is the amount left over after integer division, so for example 30 divided by 11 leaves a remainder of 8.
4. Subtract the remainder from 11. The result is the check digit. If the result is 10 the check digit is written as X. If the result is 11 the check digit is 0.

The first seven digits of a new book code are 3140268.

Calculate the check digit for this code.

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
Multiply each digit by its weight:

| Digit | 3 | 1 | 4 | 0 | 2 | 6 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weight | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
| Product | **24** | **7** | **24** | **0** | **8** | **18** | **16** |

All seven products correct **[1]**

Add the products: 24 + 7 + 24 + 0 + 8 + 18 + 16 = **97** **[1]**

Divide by 11 and take the remainder: 97 divided by 11 is 8 remainder **9** **[1]**

Subtract the remainder from 11: 11 - 9 = **2** **[1]**

The check digit is **2**, so the complete book code is **31402682**.

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the seven products 24, 7, 24, 0, 8, 18, 16
> 
> **1 mark** for the total 97
> 
> **1 mark** for the remainder 9
> 
> **1 mark** for the check digit 2
> 
> Accept follow-through: if the total is wrong but steps 3 and 4 are then carried out correctly on that wrong total, award the last two marks.
> 
> Accept the answer written as the full code 31402682 provided the working is shown.
> 
> Do not accept 9 as the check digit. That is the remainder from step 3, and step 4 has not been carried out.
> 
> Do not accept a check digit worked out with the weights applied from the right-hand end. The stem states that the left-hand digit has the weight of 8.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two errors cost almost all the marks here. The first is stopping at the remainder and writing 9; step 4 is part of the algorithm, so always carry it out. The second is applying the weights the wrong way round, so read the stem again and write the weights above the digits before you multiply anything.
> 
> Set your working out as a row of digits with a row of weights underneath. Examiners award the products mark from that layout even when the arithmetic that follows goes wrong, so it is worth the thirty seconds.

parts.problemMd:
A hotel receptionist types a guest's passport number into a booking system, reading the number from the guest's passport.

Describe **two** methods of data verification that can be used when the passport number is entered.
parts.solutionMd:
Visual check: the receptionist compares the passport number shown on the screen with the number printed in the passport and confirms that the two are the same. **[1]**

Double entry: the passport number is typed in a second time and the software compares the two entries, showing an error message if they do not match. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for visual check, described as manually comparing the number entered, or shown on the screen, with the number on the source document
> 
> **1 mark** for double entry, described as entering the number twice and the computer comparing the two entries
> 
> Accept "double entry check", and accept the second entry being made by a second person.
> 
> Do not accept a parity check or a checksum. Both are methods of verification during data transfer, and here the number is being typed in.
> 
> Do not accept any validation check, such as a length check, a format check or a check digit.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The syllabus splits verification into two groups and the question tells you which group it wants. "When the passport number is entered" means data entry, so only a visual check and double entry can score. Parity and checksum belong to data transfer.
> 
> Naming a method is not describing it. Add what is compared with what, and one word becomes one mark.

parts.problemMd:
A computer sends a block of five bytes to a printer. A checksum is transmitted with the block so that the printer can detect an error.

The checksum is calculated as follows.

1. Add together the denary values of the five bytes.
2. Divide the total by 256 and take the remainder. The remainder is the amount left over after integer division.
3. The remainder is the checksum.

The five bytes have the denary values 214, 97, 180, 63 and 145.

Calculate the checksum that is transmitted with this block, and state how the printer uses it.
parts.solutionMd:
Add the five values: 214 + 97 + 180 + 63 + 145 = **699** **[1]**

Divide by 256 and take the remainder: 699 divided by 256 is 2 remainder **187**, so the checksum is **187**. **[1]**

The printer adds the denary values of the five bytes it receives, works out the remainder after division by 256 in the same way, and compares its result with the checksum it received. If the two values are different, an error has occurred during transmission. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the total 699
> 
> **1 mark** for the checksum 187
> 
> **1 mark** for the receiver repeating the same calculation on the data it received and comparing the two values, with the conclusion that different values mean an error has occurred
> 
> Accept "if the two values are the same, no error has been detected" as the conclusion
> 
> Accept the working written on one line as 699 MOD 256 = 187
> 
> Do not accept 699 as the checksum. Step 2 of the algorithm has not been carried out
> 
> Do not accept "the checksum tells the printer which bit is wrong". A checksum shows only that the data has changed, not where

> **[exam-tip]**
> The third mark is lost by students who stop at "the printer checks the checksum". The printer cannot check anything until it has recalculated the checksum from the data it actually received, so say that the calculation is repeated and then the two values are compared.
> 
> Do not claim that a checksum locates the error. That is what a parity block does. A checksum, like a single parity check, tells you only that something has changed.

parts.problemMd:
Two computers use a parity block check with **even parity** to detect errors during data transfer.

The sender divides the data into groups of seven bits. It counts the number of 1s in each group and appends a parity bit to the right of the group, so that each byte contains an even number of 1s.

Four bytes are then arranged in a grid, one byte per row. The columns are numbered 1 to 8 from the left, so column 8 holds the parity bits. The sender counts the number of 1s in each column and creates a parity byte in which each bit makes its column contain an even number of 1s. The parity byte is transmitted with the four data bytes.

The receiver receives the grid shown. Exactly one bit was changed during transmission.

|   | Column 1 | Column 2 | Column 3 | Column 4 | Column 5 | Column 6 | Column 7 | Column 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Byte 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| Byte 2 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Byte 3 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Byte 4 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| Parity byte | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

Identify the position of the bit that was changed and write byte 3 as it should have been received.

Show how you worked out the position.
parts.solutionMd:
Byte 3 contains seven 1s. Seven is odd, so byte 3 does not match the agreed even parity and the error is in this row. Every other row contains four 1s and is correct. **[1]**

Column 5 contains three 1s. Three is odd, so column 5 does not match the agreed even parity and the error is in this column. Every other column contains an even number of 1s and is correct. **[1]**

The bit that was changed is where the failing row and the failing column cross, so it is the bit in byte 3, column 5. **[1]**

That bit was received as 1 and should be 0. **[1]**

Byte 3 should have been received as **11100111**. **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for identifying byte 3 as the row whose parity is wrong, supported by the count of seven 1s being odd
> 
> **1 mark** for identifying column 5 as the column whose parity is wrong, supported by the count of three 1s being odd
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the changed bit lies at the intersection of that row and that column
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the bit was received as 1 and should be 0
> 
> **1 mark** for the corrected byte 11100111
> 
> Accept "the fifth bit from the left" in place of "column 5"
> 
> Accept the corrected byte written with the bits spaced out, as 1 1 1 0 0 1 1 1
> 
> Do not accept an answer that identifies only the row or only the column. A single parity check on one byte shows that an error has occurred but cannot locate it; the block check needs both directions
> 
> Do not accept 11101110 or 11100110. Only one bit was changed, and the parity bit in column 8 is correct as received

> **[exam-tip]**
> Count the 1s in every row first and write the count beside each row, then do the same underneath every column. Do not try to spot the error by eye. With even parity you are looking for the one row and the one column whose count is odd, and the answer is where they cross.
> 
> A common mistake is to change the parity bit instead of the data bit. The parity bit in column 8 of byte 3 is part of the failing row, but it is not in the failing column, so it is not the bit that flipped. Only the cell that fails in both directions can be the error.

parts.problemMd:
An assessment board scans exam papers and stores the digitised papers on a server. Exam markers download the digitised papers to mark. The exam markers then upload the mark for each paper.

The assessment board needs to make sure the data stored on the server is secure.

(i) Authentication methods can help to protect the server against hackers.

Identify **one** **other** security measure that helps to protect the server from hackers.

Describe how the security measure works.

(3)

(ii) Identify **one **security measure that helps to protect the data when it is being transmitted to its destination. Describe how the security measure works.

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for security measure
> 
> **1 mark** each to max 2 for how the chosen measure works:
> 
> - Firewall
> - Checks incoming connections
> - ... against criteria
> - Blocks data from entering specific ports
> - Blocks data that does not meet whitelist that meets blacklist
> - Proxy server
> - Prevents devices accessing the web server directly
> - Intercepts any requests
> - Forwards the request using its own IP address
> - Screens returning data before sending it to the user

Robots are used to serve food and drink to customers at a restaurant.

Explain how encryption can protect the security of data during transmission.
parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
Authentication is one method a Database Management System (DBMS) can use to improve the security of a database.

Describe **other **methods that a DBMS can use to improve the security of a database.

> 
> **Max 2 **if no descriptions

parts.problemMd: State the meaning of **privacy of data**.
parts.solutionMd:

> Either
> 
> - Ensuring data can only be accessed by / disclosed to authorised persons

parts.problemMd:

Phishing email

>

>

parts.problemMd: State **one **difference and **one **similarity between pharming and phishing.

> 
> Difference:

parts.problemMd: Explain how the data security risks of malware can be restricted.

parts.problemMd:
A hospital stores the medical records of its patients on a computer system.

Each statement below describes **one** of these three terms: **security** of data, **privacy** of data, **integrity** of data.

**Statement 1:** The hospital makes sure that a patient's record can only be read by the doctor who is treating that patient.

**Statement 2:** The hospital makes sure that a blood test result is stored in the record without any change to its value.

Identify the term that each statement describes.
parts.solutionMd:
Statement 1 describes the **privacy** of data. **[1]**

Statement 2 describes the **integrity** of data. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for Statement 1: privacy (of data)
> 
> **1 mark** for Statement 2: integrity (of data)
> 
> Accept "data privacy" for privacy and "data integrity" for integrity.
> 
> Do not accept security for either statement. Security of data is the protection of data from loss, damage and unauthorised access, which is the general idea behind both statements and so identifies neither of them.
> 
> Do not accept "accuracy" alone for Statement 2 unless the word integrity is given, because the question asks for one of the three named terms.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most students who lose marks here write security for both statements, because both statements are about keeping data safe. Look at what each statement actually controls. If it controls who is allowed to see the data, the answer is privacy. If it controls whether the stored value is correct and complete, the answer is integrity.

parts.problemMd:
An online shop stores the names, addresses and payment card details of its customers.

Explain the difference between the **security** of data, the **privacy** of data and the **integrity** of data for the shop's customer records.
parts.solutionMd:
Security of data means that the customer records are protected from loss, damage and unauthorised access, so they cannot be stolen, deleted or damaged. **[1]**

Privacy of data means that the shop controls who is allowed to see each customer record and what the data may be used for, so a customer's address and card details are only shown to people who are authorised to see them. **[1]**

Integrity of data means that the customer records are accurate, complete and up to date, and have not been changed by mistake during entry, processing or transfer. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for security: the data is protected from loss, damage or unauthorised access // the records cannot be stolen, deleted or damaged
> 
> **1 mark** for privacy: the shop decides who is allowed to see the data and how it may be used // only authorised people may see a customer's address or card details
> 
> **1 mark** for integrity: the data is accurate, complete, consistent and up to date // the data has not been changed by mistake during entry, processing or transfer
> 
> Accept "the data is not disclosed to unauthorised people" for privacy.
> 
> Accept "the data is not corrupted" for integrity.
> 
> Do not accept an answer that defines one of the three terms using another of them, for example "privacy means the data is kept secure", "security means the data has integrity" or "integrity means the data is safe". Each term must be described in its own words.
> 
> Do not accept "integrity means the data is protected from hackers", which describes security.
> 
> Do not accept "privacy means the data is encrypted". Encryption is a measure used to protect data, not a definition of privacy.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The commonest way to lose all three marks here is to answer with the other two words. "Privacy means keeping data secure and private" earns nothing, because it has not said anything the examiner did not already give you in the question. Write each one without using either of the other two words: who may see it is privacy, whether it is correct is integrity, and whether it is protected from loss or attack is security.

parts.problemMd:
A company gives each of its sales managers a laptop. The customer records stored on each laptop are encrypted.

One of the laptops is stolen.

Describe how encryption protects the customer records held on the stolen laptop.
parts.solutionMd:
Encryption has converted the customer records into cipher text. **[1]**

The thief cannot understand the records without the decryption key. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the records being encoded / scrambled / turned into cipher text
> 
> **1 mark** for the records being impossible to understand without the decryption key
> 
> Accept "scrambled", "encoded", "converted into an alternative form" and "ciphertext" written as one word for the first mark.
> 
> Accept "the key is needed to decode the data" or "the algorithm is needed to decode the data" for the second mark.
> 
> Do not accept "the thief cannot open the file". Encryption does not stop the file being opened, only understood.
> 
> Do not accept "the data is hidden" or "the data is deleted". Encrypted data is still there and is still readable as characters; it is the meaning that is protected.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students very often write that encryption "stops the data being stolen". It does not. The thief still has the file. Encryption changes what the stolen file is worth, so always finish the sentence with what the thief cannot do: understand it without the key.
> 
> Two marks means two separate ideas here. Saying only "the data is encrypted so it is safe" repeats the question and scores nothing.

parts.problemMd:
A delivery company stores its delivery records on a server. All the records on the server are encrypted.

A power failure happens while the server is writing a group of new delivery records. When the server restarts, some of the delivery records contain only part of the data that should have been written.

The company manager says:

"Our records are encrypted, so our data is safe. Nothing else needs to be done."

Explain why the manager is wrong. Use the terms **security** of data and **integrity** of data in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Encryption protects the security of the data. If the records are copied or intercepted, they cannot be understood without the decryption key. **[1]**

Encryption does nothing to protect the integrity of the data, because it does not check that the values stored are accurate or complete. **[1]**

The part-written records are incomplete, so the value stored is not the value that should have been stored. This is a loss of data integrity, not a loss of data security. **[1]**

The incomplete records are still encrypted, so they will decrypt to incorrect delivery data and the company will use them as though they were correct. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any four from:**
> 
> - encryption protects the security of the data: data that is intercepted or copied cannot be understood without the decryption key
> - encryption does not check that the values stored are accurate or complete, so it does not protect integrity
> - the part-written records are incomplete, so this is a loss of data integrity, not a loss of data security
> - the incomplete records are still encrypted, so they decrypt normally and the wrong data is used as though it were correct
> - a separate measure is needed to protect integrity, for example restoring the affected records from a backup, or verifying the written records against the original data
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> Accept "encoded" or "turned into cipher text" for encrypted.
> 
> Do not accept "encryption keeps the data safe so the manager is right". The question asks why the manager is wrong.
> 
> Do not accept "the data was not encrypted properly" or "the encryption key was lost in the power failure". Neither is stated in the question and neither is the reason the records are wrong.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question is testing whether you can keep security and integrity apart under pressure. Encryption is an answer to the question "can someone else read this?", not to the question "is this the right value?". A record that is wrong and encrypted is still wrong. When a question describes data being lost, cut short or corrupted, reach for integrity measures such as backups and verification, not for encryption.

parts.problemMd:
A travel company stores a file of ticket prices on its file server. The company uses access rights to control how this file can be used.

The table shows three groups of user accounts and what each group must be able to do with the file.

| User group | What the group must be able to do | Access right |
|---|---|---|
| Sales assistants | Look at the current prices while serving a customer, but never change them |   |
| Pricing team | Change the prices in the file and delete prices that are no longer offered |   |
| Warehouse staff | Must not be able to open the file at all |   |

Complete the table by writing the access right that should be given to each group.
parts.solutionMd:
| User group | Access right |
|---|---|
| Sales assistants | **Read-only access** **[1]** |
| Pricing team | **Full access** **[1]** |
| Warehouse staff | **No access** **[1]** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for sales assistants: read-only access
> 
> **1 mark** for pricing team: full access
> 
> **1 mark** for warehouse staff: no access
> 
> Accept "read only" or "view only" for the sales assistants.
> 
> Accept "read and write", "read/write" or "read, write and delete" for the pricing team.
> 
> Accept "access denied" for the warehouse staff.
> 
> Do not accept "restricted access" or "limited access" on their own in any row. They do not say which actions are allowed.
> 
> Do not accept "write only" for the pricing team. A user who edits a price must be able to read it first.

> **[exam-tip]**
> There are only three answers the mark scheme wants here: full access, read-only access and no access. Learn those three terms.
> 
> The row students lose is the last one. They write "restricted access" for the warehouse staff, which is true of the sales assistants as well, so it does not identify anything. If a group must not open the file at all, the answer is no access.

parts.problemMd:
A student uses a stand-alone PC at home. The PC is not connected to any other computer.

Anti-virus software is installed on the PC.

Describe how the anti-virus software helps to protect the PC.
parts.solutionMd:
The anti-virus software scans the files on the PC and compares them against a stored database of known viruses. **[1]**

Any file that matches is deleted or quarantined, so the virus cannot run on the PC. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - scans the files on the computer // checks files as they are downloaded or opened
> - compares the files against a stored database of known viruses
> - any virus found is deleted or quarantined // the download is stopped before it completes
> - the database of virus definitions must be updated regularly so that new viruses are recognised
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept anti-malware software in place of anti-virus software.
> 
> Do not accept "it removes all viruses from the PC". Anti-virus software only recognises viruses that are already in its database.
> 
> Do not accept "it stops hackers getting into the PC" or "it blocks traffic that does not meet set rules". That describes a firewall.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two marks means two separate steps, so do not write one long sentence saying the software "protects the PC from viruses". Say what it looks at and say what it does when it finds something. Students also mix up the three measures: anti-virus scans files, anti-spyware looks for software that records what the user does, and a firewall checks traffic entering and leaving the computer.

parts.problemMd:
An online bookshop keeps its customer records in one file on a server.

At present:

- every member of staff signs in with the same user account
- that account has full access to every file on the server
- the customer records file is not encrypted

A security consultant makes two recommendations:

- give every member of staff their own user account, with access rights that match their job
- encrypt the customer records file

Explain why the bookshop needs both of these recommendations, rather than only one of them.
parts.solutionMd:
Access rights control which members of staff can open the customer records file and what they are allowed to do with it, such as read-only access or full access. **[1]**

This means each member of staff can reach only the data their job needs, and staff who do not need the customer records cannot open the file at all. **[1]**

Access rights on their own are not enough, because they are applied by the system to a user account. If a copy of the file is taken from the server, the customer records can still be read. **[1]**

Encryption turns the contents of the file into cipher text, so a copy of the file cannot be understood without the decryption key. **[1]**

Encryption on its own is not enough either, because it does not decide who is allowed to open the file. A member of staff who has the decryption key still sees the customer records in full. **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for saying what access rights do: control which users can open the file, and which actions they may perform on it
> 
> **1 mark** for the effect of that: different users are given different permissions, so a user sees only what their job needs
> 
> **1 mark** for the limit of access rights: they are enforced on a user account, so a copy of the file taken from the server, or intercepted in transmission, can still be read
> 
> **1 mark** for saying what encryption does: the file contents are turned into cipher text, which cannot be understood without the decryption key
> 
> **1 mark** for the limit of encryption: it does not control who may open the file, so a user who holds the decryption key still reads the records
> 
> Accept "read/write, read only, full access" as the description of what access rights set.
> 
> Accept "encoded" or "scrambled" in place of "turned into cipher text".
> 
> Accept a stolen backup, a stolen hard disk or a copied file as the example that defeats access rights alone.
> 
> Do not accept an answer that only describes the two methods one after the other with no statement of what each one fails to protect against. Maximum 3 marks in that case.
> 
> Do not accept "encryption stops unauthorised people accessing the data". Encrypted data can still be accessed and copied; what it cannot be is understood.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The marks in this question are in the word "both". Many students describe access rights, then describe encryption, and stop. That answer earns about half the marks because it never says why one of them alone would leave the bookshop exposed.
> 
> Use a simple pairing as you write: one sentence for what the method does, one sentence for what it does not do. Access rights are checked when a user signs in, so they do nothing once a copy of the file has left the server. Encryption is undone by the key, so it does nothing about a member of staff who is entitled to hold that key. The two methods cover each other's gap, which is exactly why the consultant asked for both.

parts.problemMd:
A design company protects each office computer with a user account and a password.

The company decides to replace the passwords with a fingerprint scanner. Each employee will log in to their computer by placing a finger on the scanner.

Explain why a fingerprint scanner gives better protection against unauthorised access than a password.
parts.solutionMd:
A password can be guessed, or found by trying a very large number of combinations, but a fingerprint cannot be guessed in this way. **[1]**

A password can be written down, shared or seen by another person, who can then use it. A fingerprint cannot be handed to somebody else. **[1]**

The employee has to be physically present for the fingerprint to be scanned, so knowing a stolen detail is not enough to get in. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - a password can be guessed, or found by trying many combinations, while a fingerprint cannot be guessed
> - a password can be written down, shared or watched as it is typed, so another person can use it, while a fingerprint cannot be passed on in this way
> - the user must be physically present for the scan, so a stolen detail on its own does not give access
> - every user's fingerprint is different, so the system identifies the individual person rather than anybody who knows the password
> - a user cannot forget a fingerprint, so they do not need a short or reused password that is easier to break
> - spyware that records keystrokes cannot capture a fingerprint
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept "biometric data is unique to each user" for the uniqueness point.
> 
> Do not accept "a fingerprint cannot be copied" or "biometrics can never be broken". Both are too strong to credit.
> 
> Do not accept "it is faster to scan a finger than to type a password" or "the employee does not have to remember anything". Those are advantages of convenience, not of protection against unauthorised access.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Biometrics was added to this part of the syllabus, so it is worth having three separate points ready rather than one. The mark is lost most often by writing about convenience: "it is quicker" and "you cannot forget it" do not answer a question about protection unless you go on to say why that makes unauthorised access harder. Compare the fingerprint with the password at every point, because the question asks which gives better protection, not what a fingerprint scanner is.

parts.problemMd:
A school has 20 computers in one room. At the moment each computer is a stand-alone PC. It is not connected to any other computer and it has no connection to the internet. Each PC is protected by a user account with a password, and by anti-virus software.

The school will now connect all 20 computers together in a network, and will give the network a connection to the internet.

Explain why the school will need additional security measures once the computers are networked. Name each measure and give the reason it is now needed.
parts.solutionMd:
Once the computers have a connection to the internet, a person outside the school can try to reach any of the 20 computers, which was impossible while they were stand-alone. A firewall is needed. **[1]**

The firewall monitors all traffic entering and leaving the network and compares it against set criteria, such as a whitelist or a blacklist of addresses. **[1]**

It blocks any traffic that does not meet the criteria, and it can block the ports that the school does not use. **[1]**

Users can now download files from the internet, so anti-spyware software is needed to detect any software that is installed without the user's knowledge. **[1]**

Data sent from one computer to another can now be intercepted on the network, so it should be encrypted, which means it cannot be understood without the decryption key. **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any five from:**
> 
> - an attacker outside the school can now attempt to reach any computer through the internet connection, so a firewall is needed
> - the firewall monitors all incoming and outgoing traffic
> - ... and compares it against set criteria, a whitelist or a blacklist
> - the firewall blocks any traffic that does not meet the criteria, and can block unused ports
> - malware on one computer can now spread to the other computers across the network
> - ... so the anti-virus definitions on every computer must now be updated regularly
> - users can now download files from the internet, so anti-spyware software is needed to detect software installed without the user's knowledge
> - data sent between the computers can now be intercepted, so it should be encrypted
> - ... so that intercepted data cannot be understood without the decryption key
> 
> **[5 marks]**
> 
> Accept a proxy server in place of a firewall, if it is described: it stops devices reaching the school's computers directly, intercepts requests and screens the data that is returned.
> 
> Do not accept "the school should use stronger passwords" on its own. Each computer already has a user account and a password, so a mark needs a measure the network adds.
> 
> Do not accept "install anti-virus software" or "buy better anti-virus software". Anti-virus software is already installed on every computer, so it is not an additional measure. Only keeping its definitions up to date is credited.
> 
> Do not accept "the internet is dangerous" or any similar statement with no measure attached.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The syllabus asks you to describe security measures ranging from the stand-alone PC to a network of computers, and this is exactly that question. Do not simply list measures. For each one, say what changed when the computers were connected, because the marks are for the link between the new risk and the measure. A firewall on a machine with no network connection protects nothing, which is why the school did not need one before.

parts.problemMd:
Viruses and spyware are two types of malware.

Malware is one of the threats to data that is posed by networks and the internet.

State **one** feature of a virus that spyware does not have.

State **one** feature of spyware that a virus does not have.
parts.solutionMd:
Feature of a virus: it replicates itself, so copies of it spread to other programs or files on the computer. **[1]**

Feature of spyware: it secretly records what the user does on the computer, such as the keys they press, and sends that record to a third party. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a feature of a virus only: it replicates itself // it makes copies of itself // it spreads to other programs or files on the computer
> 
> **1 mark** for a feature of spyware only: it records the user's actions or keystrokes // it sends the data it has gathered to a third party
> 
> Accept "self-replicating" for replicates itself
> 
> Accept "records the keys the user presses" or "records keystrokes" for the recording
> 
> Accept "it can corrupt, damage or delete data" as the feature of a virus
> 
> Accept "it is downloaded without the user's knowledge" for spyware
> 
> Do not accept "it is malicious software" for either, because both are malware and the question asks what separates them

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students call every piece of malware a virus. Cambridge names only two types in this part of the syllabus, and the clearest way to separate them is one thing each: a virus **replicates**, spyware **records and reports**. Learn the pair that way and the mark is easy.
> 
> Be precise about what a virus does. "It can corrupt or delete data" is credited, but replication is the safest answer because it is the feature that makes a program a virus. For spyware, "it spies on you" is worth nothing on its own; say that it records what the user types, or that it sends the record to a third party.

parts.problemMd:
Two customers of an online bank each lose their account details to a criminal.

**Customer A** types the correct web address of the bank into a web browser. The browser opens a website that looks like the bank's website but is not owned by the bank. Customer A enters their username and password. A later security check finds malicious code on Customer A's computer.

**Customer B** receives an email that appears to come from the bank. The email asks Customer B to click a link and confirm their username and password. Customer B clicks the link and enters the details.

Identify the threat experienced by each customer.

Give **one** difference between the two threats that is shown by the scenarios.
parts.solutionMd:
Customer A experienced pharming. **[1]**

Customer B experienced phishing. **[1]**

Difference: the malicious code redirected Customer A to the fake website automatically, even though the correct web address was typed, while Customer B had to take action by clicking a link in an email. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for pharming as the threat experienced by Customer A
> 
> **1 mark** for phishing as the threat experienced by Customer B
> 
> **1 mark** for one difference shown by the scenarios: pharming redirects the user automatically while phishing requires the user to act // pharming uses malicious code on the computer while phishing uses a fraudulent email
> 
> Accept "pharming attack" and "phishing email"
> 
> Do not accept phishing for Customer A. Customer A received no message and typed the correct web address, so nothing lured them to the fake site
> 
> Do not accept a difference in which Customer A clicks a link, because pharming redirects the browser without the user doing anything
> 
> Do not accept spyware or a virus for Customer A. Spyware records and sends what the user types and a virus replicates itself; neither redirects a browser to a fake website
> 
> Do not accept "both use a fake website" as the difference, because that is a similarity between the two threats, not a difference

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students describe pharming as "phishing but on a website", and lose the mark every time. Both threats end at a fake website, so the website is never the difference. Ask instead: **who acted?** If the victim had to open a message or click a link, it is phishing. If the browser reached the fake site on its own from a correct address, it is pharming.
> 
> The phrase "types the correct web address" is put in a stem deliberately. It rules out phishing, because a fraudulent message would have sent the user somewhere else. When you see it, write pharming.

parts.problemMd:
An online shop stores the names, addresses and payment card details of its customers on a server. The server is connected to the internet.

Complete the table by identifying **two different** threats to the customers' data that are posed by networks and the internet. Choose each threat from: hacker, virus, spyware.

Describe each threat.

Identify **one** measure that restricts the risk posed by each threat. The two measures must be different.

| Threat | Description | Measure that restricts the risk |
|---|---|---|
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Threat | Description | Measure that restricts the risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Hacker** **[1]** | **A person gains unauthorised access to the server over the internet in order to read, change or delete the customer records.** **[1]** | **A firewall** **[1]** |
| **Virus** **[1]** | **Malicious software replicates itself on the server and corrupts or deletes the customer records.** **[1]** | **Anti-virus software** **[1]** |

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each correctly identified threat, to a maximum of 2
> 
> **1 mark** for each description that matches the threat identified, to a maximum of 2
> 
> **1 mark** for each measure that restricts the threat identified, to a maximum of 2
> 
> The two threats must be different and the two measures must be different.
> 
> Accept any two of the following rows.
> 
> Hacker: gains unauthorised access to the server over the internet // accesses the customer data without permission, with the intention of reading, changing or deleting it. Measure: firewall // strong password // biometric authentication // access rights
> 
> Virus: malicious software that replicates itself and can corrupt or delete the customer data. Measure: anti-virus software // anti-malware software // firewall
> 
> Spyware: malware installed without the user's knowledge that records the keystrokes of a member of staff, such as the server password, and sends them to a third party. Measure: anti-spyware software // anti-malware software // a virtual or on-screen keyboard
> 
> Do not accept a description that only repeats the name of the threat, such as "a hacker hacks the server" or "a virus infects the server"
> 
> Do not accept a description that gives only the consequence, such as "the customers lose money", with no statement of how the threat reaches the data
> 
> Do not accept encryption as the measure against a virus, because encryption does not stop a virus corrupting or deleting a file; it only stops the contents being understood

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two marks go missing here for the same two reasons. The first is giving the same threat twice. Hacker, virus and spyware are three different threats, so any two of them can score, as long as the two measures are also different.
> 
> The second is the description. Writing "a hacker hacks the server" repeats the name and earns nothing. The mark is for the mechanism, so say how the threat reaches the data: unauthorised access over the internet, or software that replicates itself. Finally, check that your measure would really stop your threat. Encryption, for example, does not stop a virus deleting a file, so it will not be credited against a virus.

parts.problemMd: State **two **benefits to a programmer of distributing a program using a shareware licence.
parts.solutionMd:
