parts.problemMd:
A college library uses a relational database to store data about its members and the books they borrow.

The database design includes these tables:

`MEMBER(MemberID, FirstName, LastName, YearGroup)`

`MEMBER_CARD(CardNumber, MemberID, DateIssued)`

`LOAN(LoanID, MemberID, BookCopyID, DateBorrowed)`

Each member is given exactly one library card. Each library card belongs to exactly one member.

A member can make many loans. Each loan is made by one member.

Complete the entity-relationship (E-R) table by writing the degree of each relationship.

| First entity | Relationship | Degree of relationship | Second entity |
|---|---|---|---|
| MEMBER | is given | ................................ | MEMBER_CARD |
| MEMBER | makes | ................................ | LOAN |
parts.solutionMd:
| First entity | Relationship | Degree of relationship | Second entity |
|---|---|---|---|
| MEMBER | is given | **one-to-one** | MEMBER_CARD |
| MEMBER | makes | **one-to-many** | LOAN |

One member is given one card, and one card belongs to one member, so the first relationship is one-to-one. **[1]**

One member can make many loans, but each loan belongs to one member only, so the second relationship is one-to-many. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `MEMBER` to `MEMBER_CARD` is one-to-one
> 
> **1 mark** for `MEMBER` to `LOAN` is one-to-many
> 
> Accept `1:1` and `1 to 1` for one-to-one
> 
> Accept `1:M`, `1:many` and `1 to many` for one-to-many
> 
> Do not accept one-to-many for `MEMBER` to `MEMBER_CARD`. Each member is given exactly one card, so only one row of `MEMBER_CARD` can ever match a member
> 
> Do not accept many-to-many for `MEMBER` to `LOAN`. Each loan is made by one member only

> **[exam-tip]**
> Check every relationship in both directions before you write anything down. For the first row, ask "how many cards does one member have?" and then ask "how many members does one card belong to?" The relationship is only one-to-one when both answers are one.
> 
> Do not decide the answer from the table definitions alone. `MemberID` appears as a foreign key in `MEMBER_CARD` and in `LOAN`, so the two tables look the same in the definitions, yet the two relationships have different degrees. The sentences in the question are what tell you which is which.

parts.problemMd:
A sports centre uses a relational database to store data about its coaches, its members and the fitness classes that it runs.

- Each fitness class is led by one coach. A coach can lead many fitness classes.
- Each coach has one set of login details for the computer system at the centre. Each set of login details belongs to one coach.
- A member can book many fitness classes. A fitness class can be booked by many members.

Complete the entity-relationship (E-R) table by writing the degree of each relationship.

| First entity | Relationship | Degree of relationship | Second entity |
|---|---|---|---|
| COACH | leads | ................................ | CLASS |
| COACH | has | ................................ | COACH_LOGIN |
| MEMBER | books | ................................ | CLASS |
parts.solutionMd:
| First entity | Relationship | Degree of relationship | Second entity |
|---|---|---|---|
| COACH | leads | **one-to-many** | CLASS |
| COACH | has | **one-to-one** | COACH_LOGIN |
| MEMBER | books | **many-to-many** | CLASS |

A coach leads many classes, but each class has only one coach, so `COACH` to `CLASS` is one-to-many. **[1]**

A coach has one set of login details and a set of login details belongs to one coach, so `COACH` to `COACH_LOGIN` is one-to-one. **[1]**

A member books many classes and a class is booked by many members, so `MEMBER` to `CLASS` is many-to-many. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `COACH` to `CLASS` is one-to-many
> 
> **1 mark** for `COACH` to `COACH_LOGIN` is one-to-one
> 
> **1 mark** for `MEMBER` to `CLASS` is many-to-many
> 
> Accept `1:M`, `1:many` and `1 to many` for one-to-many
> 
> Accept `1:1` and `1 to 1` for one-to-one
> 
> Accept `M:M`, `M:N` and `many to many` for many-to-many
> 
> Do not accept one-to-many for `MEMBER` to `CLASS`. Both directions are many, because one class is booked by many members as well as one member booking many classes
> 
> Do not accept many-to-one for `COACH` to `CLASS`. Each row is read from left to right, and one coach leads many classes

> **[exam-tip]**
> The many-to-many is the row students lose. Reading only "a member books many classes" gives one-to-many, and the answer looks finished. You have to read the second sentence as well: a class is also booked by many members, and it is the two answers together that make the relationship many-to-many.
> 
> Watch the direction as well. Each row is read from left to right, so `COACH` to `CLASS` is one-to-many, not many-to-one. Writing the two halves in the wrong order describes a different relationship and does not earn the mark.

parts.problemMd:
A conference organiser uses a relational database to store data about the speakers, the sessions and the delegates who attend the conference.

- Each session is given by one speaker. A speaker can give many sessions.
- Each session takes place in one room. A room is used for many sessions.
- A delegate can attend many sessions. A session can be attended by many delegates.

The organiser wants a design in which **no** relationship is many-to-many, so one extra entity must be added.

Complete the entity-relationship (E-R) table for this design.

Read each row from left to right. Choose a suitable name for the entity that you add and write that same name in **both** empty entity cells.

| First entity | Relationship | Degree of relationship | Second entity |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPEAKER | gives | ................................ | SESSION |
| ROOM | is used for | ................................ | SESSION |
| DELEGATE | makes | ................................ | ................................ |
| ................................ | is for | ................................ | SESSION |
parts.solutionMd:
| First entity | Relationship | Degree of relationship | Second entity |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPEAKER | gives | **one-to-many** | SESSION |
| ROOM | is used for | **one-to-many** | SESSION |
| DELEGATE | makes | **one-to-many** | **ATTENDANCE** |
| **ATTENDANCE** | is for | **many-to-one** | SESSION |

One speaker gives many sessions and each session has one speaker, so `SPEAKER` to `SESSION` is one-to-many. **[1]**

One room is used for many sessions and each session uses one room, so `ROOM` to `SESSION` is one-to-many. **[1]**

The many-to-many between `DELEGATE` and `SESSION` is replaced by a linking entity, `ATTENDANCE`, which holds one row for each session that a delegate attends. **[1]**

One delegate makes many `ATTENDANCE` rows, so that row is one-to-many, and many `ATTENDANCE` rows are for the same session, so read from left to right the last row is many-to-one. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `SPEAKER` to `SESSION` is one-to-many
> 
> **1 mark** for `ROOM` to `SESSION` is one-to-many
> 
> **1 mark** for the same suitably named linking entity written in both empty entity cells
> 
> **1 mark** for `DELEGATE` to the linking entity being one-to-many **and** the linking entity to `SESSION` being many-to-one
> 
> Accept any suitable name for the linking entity, for example `ATTENDANCE`, `BOOKING`, `SESSION_DELEGATE` or `DELEGATE_SESSION`
> 
> Accept `1:M` and `1 to many` for one-to-many, and `M:1` and `many to 1` for many-to-one
> 
> Do not accept many-to-many anywhere in the completed table. The design must not contain one, which is the reason the extra entity is added
> 
> Do not accept two different names in the two empty entity cells. Both cells name the same entity
> 
> Do not accept one-to-many in the final row. Many rows of the linking entity are for the same session, so from left to right the degree is many-to-one

> **[exam-tip]**
> A many-to-many relationship is not left in a finished design. It is replaced by a linking entity that sits between the two original entities, and it becomes two relationships: one-to-many from the first entity into the linking entity, and many-to-one from the linking entity into the second.
> 
> Two marks are commonly lost here. The first goes to students who invent two names, such as `BOOKING` in one cell and `ATTENDANCE` in the other, which describes six entities rather than five. The second goes to students who write one-to-many in the last row out of habit. Check the direction of every row by asking which side of it can appear many times.

parts.problemMd:
A driving school stores its data using a file-based approach.

The office keeps a file of learner details, including each learner's name and telephone number.

Each instructor keeps a separate file of the lessons they have taught. This file also holds each learner's name and telephone number.

Identify **two** limitations of storing the data in this way.

1 .............................................................................................................................

2 .............................................................................................................................
parts.solutionMd:
Data redundancy: a learner's name and telephone number are stored in the office file and again in each instructor's file. **[1]**

Data inconsistency: if a learner changes telephone number and only one file is updated, the files no longer agree. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - Data redundancy // data duplication // the same data is stored more than once
> - Data inconsistency // poor data integrity // data changed in one file is not changed in the others
> - Program-data dependence // a change to the structure of a file means the programs that read it must be re-written
> - Complex queries are difficult // a new program has to be written for each new search
> - Lack of privacy // user views cannot easily be provided
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept `data duplication` for data redundancy, and `the same data is stored many times`.
> 
> Do not accept `data redundancy` and `data duplication` given as two separate answers. They are the same point written twice and earn one mark, not two.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two answers that mean the same thing earn one mark between them. `Data redundancy` and `data duplication` are one point, and so are `data inconsistency` and `the files do not match`. Choose two limitations from different lines of the list.
> 
> It also pays to say where the duplicated data actually is in the scenario. A limitation written with the learner's telephone number in it is easier to credit than one copied straight from a textbook.

parts.problemMd:
A medical clinic stores its data using a file-based approach.

- The reception desk keeps an appointments file. It holds each patient's name, telephone number and appointment time.
- The nursing team keeps a separate treatments file. It also holds each patient's name and telephone number.

A patient tells the reception desk that they have a new telephone number. The receptionist changes the number in the appointments file.

Explain why the file-based approach has now caused data inconsistency.
parts.solutionMd:
The patient's telephone number is stored in two separate files, so the same data item is held more than once. **[1]**

The receptionist has changed the number in the appointments file only, so the treatments file still holds the old number. **[1]**

The two files now give different values for the same patient, so the clinic cannot tell which number is correct and the data can no longer be relied on. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the telephone number being stored in more than one file // data redundancy // data duplication
> 
> **1 mark** for the change being made in one file only, so the other file keeps the old value
> 
> **1 mark** for the two files now holding different values for the same patient // the data is no longer accurate // data integrity is lost
> 
> Accept "a nurse would ring the old number" for the third mark, because it states the consequence of the two files disagreeing.
> 
> Accept "cannot be trusted" for "cannot be relied on".
> 
> Do not accept "the receptionist made a mistake". The receptionist did exactly what was asked. The fault is the file-based design that holds the same number twice.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most answers stop at "the data is duplicated". Duplication on its own is redundancy, not inconsistency. Inconsistency is what happens next: one copy is changed, the other is not, and the two copies now disagree.
> 
> Write all three steps every time. Stored twice, changed once, now different. An answer that skips the middle step almost always loses a mark.

parts.problemMd:
A bus company stores data about its journeys using a file-based approach. Each journey is held in a data file as a record with a fixed structure. A separate program is used to produce each of the reports the company needs.

The company now wants to do both of the following:

- add a new data item to each journey record, to store the number of passengers carried
- answer a one-off question about how many journeys ran late on one particular day

Explain **two** further limitations of the file-based approach that these two requirements show.

Give the limitation and explain it in each case.
parts.solutionMd:
There is program-data dependence. **[1]**

Adding the passenger count changes the structure of the journey record, so every program that reads the file has to be re-written before it will work again. **[1]**

Complex queries are difficult to carry out. **[1]**

No existing program answers the question about late journeys, so a new program has to be written for this one-off search. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for naming program-data dependence // the programs depend on the structure of the data
> 
> **1 mark** for: a change to the record structure means the programs that access the file must be re-written
> 
> **1 mark** for naming that complex queries or searches are difficult
> 
> **1 mark** for: a new program has to be written for each new search or report
> 
> Accept `the software has to be changed whenever the file layout changes` for the second mark.
> 
> Accept `ad hoc query` or `one-off query` as a way of naming the third mark.
> 
> Do not accept `the file would get too big` or `the data would be lost`. Neither follows from adding a field or from running a one-off search.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each pair of marks depends on the naming mark being about the right thing. Program-data dependence is about the **structure** of the file, not about the values in it. The programs break because the record layout changed, not because a number changed.
> 
> The query limitation is also easy to overstate. The one-off search is not impossible. The point is that somebody has to write a whole new program to do it, which is slow and expensive.

(i) A flat file database stores all of its data in a single table, with no links to any other table. **[1]**

(ii) The same data is stored many times, which is data redundancy. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for: all of the data is held in one single table // there is only one table, so no tables are linked
> 
> **1 mark** for any one problem: data redundancy // data duplication; data inconsistency // poor data integrity; program-data dependence; complex queries are difficult; user views cannot easily be provided
> 
> Accept "one big table" for the first mark.
> 
> Do not accept "a database saved as a text file" for the first mark. The word flat describes the single-table structure, not the type of file the data is saved in.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Flat describes the shape of the data, not the file format. A flat file database can be a spreadsheet, a text file or one table inside database software. What makes it flat is that there is one table and nothing is linked to anything else.
> 
> Write "one single table" and the first mark is safe. Answers that only say "it is simple" or "it is stored in one place" are too vague to credit.

parts.problemMd:
The table gives three statements about databases.

Complete the table by placing **one** tick in each row to show whether the statement is true of a flat file database or of a relational database.

| Statement | Flat file database | Relational database |
|---|---|---|
| All of the data is stored in a single table. |   |   |
| Data is split between several tables that are linked by a foreign key. |   |   |
| A user can be given a view that shows only some of the data. |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Statement | Flat file database | Relational database |
|---|---|---|
| All of the data is stored in a single table. | **✓** |   |
| Data is split between several tables that are linked by a foreign key. |   | **✓** |
| A user can be given a view that shows only some of the data. |   | **✓** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a tick in the Flat file database column for `All of the data is stored in a single table.`
> 
> **1 mark** for a tick in the Relational database column for `Data is split between several tables that are linked by a foreign key.`
> 
> **1 mark** for a tick in the Relational database column for `A user can be given a view that shows only some of the data.`
> 
> Do not award a mark for a row that has a tick in both columns.
> 
> Do not accept a cross or a written `yes` in place of a tick, unless you have marked no other box in that row.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The third row is the one that is missed. Views are a relational feature: because the data sits in linked tables, a user can be shown one table, or only a few fields, and nothing else. In a flat file there is a single table, so limiting what somebody sees is far harder.
> 
> One tick per row. A row ticked twice earns nothing, even when one of the two ticks is right.

parts.problemMd:
A sports club stores data about its members and the events it organises.

Two tables in the club's database are:

`MEMBER(MemberID, FirstName, LastName, DateJoined)`

`EVENT(EventID, EventName, EventDate)`

A member can enter many events. An event can be entered by many members. The club also records the position each member finished in each event.

Give the definition of the one additional table that is needed so that the design is normalised.

Use the format `TableName(PrimaryKey, Field1, Field2, ...)` and state the primary key and any foreign keys of your table.
parts.solutionMd:
`MEMBER_EVENT(MemberID, EventID, Position)` **[1]**

The primary key is the composite key `MemberID` and `EventID`. `MemberID` is a foreign key that links to `MEMBER` and `EventID` is a foreign key that links to `EVENT`. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a linking table with a suitable name that contains `MemberID` and `EventID`
> 
> **1 mark** for placing `Position` in that linking table and identifying the composite primary key `MemberID` and `EventID`
> 
> Accept any sensible table name, for example `ENTRY`, `RESULT` or `EVENT_MEMBER`
> 
> Accept a new single attribute such as `EntryID` as the primary key, provided `MemberID` and `EventID` are both still present as foreign keys
> 
> Do not accept `Position` placed in `MEMBER` or in `EVENT`, because a member has a different position in each event
> 
> Do not accept a design that adds `EventID` to `MEMBER`, because a member enters more than one event

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students usually remember to create the linking table but then leave `Position` out of it, or park it in `MEMBER`. Ask yourself which key the attribute actually depends on. `Position` is only meaningful once you know both the member and the event, so it belongs in the table whose primary key is both of them.

parts.problemMd:
A swimming club stores all of its data in one flat file table, `MEMBER`.

| MemberID | MemberName | CoachName | CoachPhone |
|---|---|---|---|
| M101 | Amina Diallo | Ravi Menon | 555 0192 |
| M102 | Chen Wei | Sofia Marek | 555 0140 |
| M103 | Tomas Silva | Ravi Menon | 555 0192 |
| M104 | Priya Nair | Ravi Menon | 555 0134 |

The club replaces the flat file with a relational database that has these two tables:

`COACH(CoachID, CoachName, CoachPhone)`

`MEMBER(MemberID, MemberName, CoachID)`

Identify the fault in the flat file table **and** explain how the relational design prevents this type of fault.
parts.solutionMd:
Ravi Menon is given two different telephone numbers: `555 0192` for members `M101` and `M103`, but `555 0134` for member `M104`. **[1]**

The coach's telephone number is stored once for every member the coach trains, so it is stored many times. One copy has been changed and the others have not, so the table is now inconsistent. **[1]**

In the relational design the coach's name and telephone number are stored only once, in the table `COACH`. **[1]**

The table `MEMBER` holds only `CoachID`, a foreign key that links to `COACH`, so there is a single telephone number for each coach and it cannot be entered differently for two members. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for identifying that Ravi Menon is given two different telephone numbers in the table
> 
> **1 mark** for: the coach's telephone number is stored more than once (data redundancy), so changing one copy leaves the others holding the old value
> 
> **1 mark** for: in the relational design each coach's details are stored once only, in the table `COACH`
> 
> **1 mark** for: `MEMBER` stores `CoachID` as a foreign key that links to `COACH`, so there is only one copy of the telephone number to change
> 
> Accept naming the row `M104`, or quoting the value `555 0134`, as identification of the fault.
> 
> Accept `data inconsistency` for the first mark only where the two differing values are also identified.
> 
> Do not accept `the telephone number is wrong`. The table does not say which of the two numbers is correct. The fault is that the table gives two different values for one coach.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read the data before writing anything. The first mark is for naming the two values that disagree, not for writing the word inconsistency.
> 
> Keep the second half of the answer about **structure**. The relational design wins because the telephone number exists in exactly one place, so there is nothing to change twice. An answer that says a relational database is `better organised` or `more professional` earns nothing.

parts.problemMd:
A driving school stores data about its instructors and the lessons it gives.

- Each instructor has an instructor number, a first name, a last name and one mobile number.
- Each lesson has a lesson number, a date and a start time.
- Each lesson is given by exactly one instructor. An instructor gives many lessons.

Write a normalised database design for this data.

Use the format `TableName(PrimaryKey, Field1, Field2, ...)` and state the primary key and any foreign keys in each table.
parts.solutionMd:
`INSTRUCTOR(InstructorNumber, FirstName, LastName, MobileNumber)` **[1]**

`LESSON(LessonNumber, LessonDate, StartTime, InstructorNumber)` **[1]**

The primary key of `INSTRUCTOR` is `InstructorNumber` and the primary key of `LESSON` is `LessonNumber`. In `LESSON`, `InstructorNumber` is a foreign key that links to `INSTRUCTOR`. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for an instructor table with `InstructorNumber` as the primary key, containing `FirstName`, `LastName` and `MobileNumber`
> 
> **1 mark** for a lesson table with `LessonNumber` as the primary key, containing `LessonDate` and `StartTime`
> 
> **1 mark** for `InstructorNumber` appearing in the lesson table as a foreign key
> 
> Accept any sensible table names
> 
> Accept `TelephoneNumber` or `Mobile` in place of `MobileNumber`
> 
> Do not accept the instructor's name or mobile number repeated inside the lesson table, because that data would then be stored more than once
> 
> Do not accept `LessonNumber` placed in the instructor table, because an instructor gives many lessons

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error here is putting the foreign key at the wrong end of a one-to-many relationship. The foreign key always goes in the table on the many side, so `InstructorNumber` goes into `LESSON`. If you put `LessonNumber` into `INSTRUCTOR` you can only ever record one lesson per instructor.

Secondary key: an additional key, used as well as the primary key, to locate specific data. It is a candidate key that has not been chosen as the primary key. **[1]**

Foreign key: a field in one table that is linked to the primary key in another table. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for secondary key: an additional or alternative key used as well as the primary key to locate specific data // a candidate key that has not been chosen as the primary key
> 
> **1 mark** for foreign key: a field in one table that is linked to a primary key in another table
> 
> Accept `used to search or sort the table on a field other than the primary key` for the secondary key mark.
> 
> Accept `attribute` for `field` throughout.
> 
> Do not accept `a key in another table` on its own for foreign key. The answer must say that it links to a primary key.

> **[exam-tip]**
> These are the two keys you are most likely to swap. A foreign key points **out** of its table, at the primary key of another table, and is how two tables are joined. A secondary key stays **inside** its own table and is there so the table can be searched quickly on a field that is not the primary key.
> 
> Use that as a check. If your answer for secondary key mentions a second table, you have described a foreign key and the mark is gone.

parts.problemMd:
A language school wants a database to store data about its students, its courses and its enrolments.

- Each student has a student number, a first name, a last name and one email address.
- Each course has a course code, a language, a level and a fee. Two courses that teach the same language at the same level can have different fees.
- A student can enrol on many courses. A course can have many students.
- For each enrolment the school stores the date the student enrolled and the final grade.

Write a database design for this data. All tables must be in Third Normal Form (3NF).

Use the format `TableName(PrimaryKey, Field1, Field2, ...)` and state the primary key and any foreign keys in each table.
parts.solutionMd:
`STUDENT(StudentNumber, FirstName, LastName, EmailAddress)` **[1]**

`COURSE(CourseCode, Language, Level, Fee)` **[1]**

`ENROLMENT(StudentNumber, CourseCode, EnrolDate, Grade)` **[1]**

The primary key of `STUDENT` is `StudentNumber` and the primary key of `COURSE` is `CourseCode`. **[1]**

The primary key of `ENROLMENT` is the composite key `StudentNumber` and `CourseCode`. Both of these are also foreign keys, linking to `STUDENT` and to `COURSE`. **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any five from:**
> 
> - A student table with `StudentNumber` as the primary key
> - ... containing `FirstName`, `LastName` and `EmailAddress`
> - A course table with `CourseCode` as the primary key
> - ... containing `Language`, `Level` and `Fee`
> - A linking table with a suitable name for the enrolments
> - ... containing `EnrolDate` and `Grade`
> - ... with a composite primary key of `StudentNumber` and `CourseCode`, or a new single primary key such as `EnrolmentID`
> - ... with `StudentNumber` and `CourseCode` both present as foreign keys
> 
> **[5 marks]**
> 
> Accept any sensible table names, for example `ENROLMENT`, `STUDENT_COURSE` or `REGISTRATION`
> 
> Do not accept `Grade` or `EnrolDate` stored in `STUDENT` or in `COURSE`, because both depend on the student and the course together
> 
> Do not accept a separate fee table keyed on `Level`, because the question states that two courses at the same level can have different fees, so `Fee` depends on `CourseCode` alone

> **[exam-tip]**
> Watch for the sentence that rules out a dependency you were about to invent. Students see `Level` and `Fee` in the same table and split the fee out into a table of its own, which loses a mark because the question says two courses at the same level can charge different fees. Read every line of the scenario before you decide what depends on what.

parts.problemMd:
A college is designing a table `STUDENT` to store data about its students. The table has these fields:

`STUDENT(StudentID, NationalIDNumber, EmailAddress, FirstName, LastName, DateOfBirth)`

The college has **not** yet chosen a primary key for this table.

- Every student is given a `StudentID` that no other student has.
- Every student has a `NationalIDNumber` that no other person has.
- Every student has an `EmailAddress` that no other student has.
- Two students may share a `FirstName`, a `LastName` or a `DateOfBirth`.

Identify **two** candidate keys in the table `STUDENT` **and** explain the difference between a candidate key and a primary key.
parts.solutionMd:
Two candidate keys are `StudentID` and `NationalIDNumber`. **[1]**

A candidate key is an attribute, or the smallest set of attributes, whose value is different for every record, so it could be used as the primary key. A table can have several candidate keys. **[1]**

The primary key is the one candidate key that the designer chooses to identify each record. A table has exactly one primary key. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for naming any two of: `StudentID`, `NationalIDNumber`, `EmailAddress`
> 
> **1 mark** for: a candidate key is a field or attribute, or the smallest set of fields, whose value is different for every record // no two tuples have the same value // it could be a primary key
> 
> **1 mark** for: the primary key is the candidate key that is chosen // a table can have several candidate keys but only one primary key
> 
> Accept `a field that could be a primary key but is not` for the second mark.
> 
> Accept `unique` for `different for every record`.
> 
> Do not accept `FirstName`, `LastName` or `DateOfBirth` as candidate keys. The question states that two students may share any of them, so none of them identifies a record uniquely.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Answers often say a candidate key is `a key that is not the primary key`. That is close, but it leaves out the part that earns the mark: its value must be different for every record, which is exactly what makes it a candidate in the first place.
> 
> Before naming any candidate key, find the sentence in the question that tells you which fields are unique. A field is only a candidate key when no two records can share its value, which is why a name never qualifies.

parts.problemMd: State what is meant by a database table being in First Normal Form (1NF).
parts.solutionMd:
The table contains no repeating groups of attributes, so every attribute in every record holds one single value. **[1]**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for either of the following
> 
> - There are no repeating groups of attributes
> - Every attribute contains a single value // all data is atomic
> 
> Accept "each field holds only one item of data"
> 
> Do not accept "there are no duplicate records", because 1NF is about repeating groups within a record, not about repeated rows
> 
> Do not accept "there are no partial dependencies", which is the condition for 2NF

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three normal forms are easy to mix up because the wording is similar. Tie each one to a single phrase and keep them separate: 1NF is repeating groups, 2NF is partial dependencies, 3NF is non-key dependencies. Writing the 2NF answer for a 1NF question is the most common way to lose this mark.

parts.problemMd:
A delivery company stores data in the following table. The table is not normalised.

| CustomerID | CustomerName | DeliveryDates |
|---|---|---|
| C101 | Ana Silva | 04/03/2025, 11/03/2025 |
| C102 | Wei Zhang | 06/03/2025 |
| C103 | Priya Nair | 05/03/2025, 12/03/2025, 19/03/2025 |

Explain how this table should be modified so that it is in First Normal Form (1NF).
parts.solutionMd:
`DeliveryDates` is a repeating group because one record holds more than one delivery date. **[1]**

The repeating group must be removed by storing one delivery date per record, so `CustomerID` and the customer's name are repeated on each of that customer's records. **[1]**

`CustomerName` is not atomic, so it should be split into `FirstName` and `LastName`. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - Identify the repeating group ...
> - ... `DeliveryDates` holds more than one value in a single record
> - Remove the repeating group by storing one delivery date per record
> - Ensure every attribute is atomic ...
> - ... `CustomerName` should be split into `FirstName` and `LastName`
> - Identify a primary key for the table, which must now be the composite key `CustomerID` and `DeliveryDate`
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept `DeliveryDates` renamed to `DeliveryDate` once it holds a single value
> 
> Do not accept "delete the extra dates", because no data may be lost during normalisation
> 
> Do not accept "move the dates into a new table", because that step is not needed to reach 1NF and the question asks only about this table

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often jump straight to a full 3NF design and start creating new tables. This question stops at 1NF, so stay in one table: repeat the customer data down the rows and give each delivery date its own record. Also check the name column. An examiner will look for the point that `CustomerName` holds two items of data and is therefore not atomic.

parts.problemMd:
A sports league uses a relational database with these two tables:

`TEAM(TeamID, TeamName, HomeGround)`

`PLAYER(PlayerID, PlayerName, TeamID)`

`TeamID` in the table `PLAYER` is a foreign key that links to the primary key of the table `TEAM`.

The database enforces referential integrity.

A user attempts each of these two operations:

- add a new row to `PLAYER` with a `TeamID` of `T99`, when no row in `TEAM` has that `TeamID`
- delete the row in `TEAM` with a `TeamID` of `T04`, when rows in `PLAYER` still have a `TeamID` of `T04`

Explain what referential integrity means **and** how it deals with each of these two operations.
parts.solutionMd:
Referential integrity means that every value of a foreign key must match an existing primary key value in the related table. **[1]**

The first operation is refused, because there is no row in `TEAM` with a `TeamID` of `T99`, so the foreign key would point at data that does not exist. **[1]**

The second operation is refused while rows in `PLAYER` still hold a `TeamID` of `T04`. **[1]**

If the delete were allowed, those `PLAYER` rows would refer to a team that is no longer in the database. A cascade delete may be used instead, which removes the matching `PLAYER` rows at the same time. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for: every foreign key value must match a primary key value in the related table // data that does not exist cannot be referenced
> 
> **1 mark** for: the new `PLAYER` row is rejected because `T99` is not a `TeamID` in `TEAM`
> 
> **1 mark** for: the delete is rejected while `PLAYER` rows still reference `T04`
> 
> **1 mark** for: otherwise those `PLAYER` rows would reference a team that does not exist // a cascade delete removes the matching `PLAYER` rows instead
> 
> Accept `cascading update/delete` (a change or deletion in one table is reflected in all related rows) as part of the meaning of referential integrity for the first mark.
> 
> Accept `cascading delete` as the credited outcome of the second operation, provided you say which rows are removed.
> 
> Accept `record` or `tuple` for `row`.
> 
> Do not accept `the database checks that the data is correct`. Referential integrity checks only that a foreign key value exists as a primary key value. Checking that a name or a date is sensible is validation, not referential integrity.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Referential integrity is a rule about **links**, not about values being sensible. It never checks that a player's name is spelled correctly. That is validation, and mixing the two is the commonest way to lose the first mark here.
> 
> Say the words `foreign key` and `primary key` in the same sentence every time you write about it, because that pairing is what the mark scheme looks for. Note too that the delete case has two credited outcomes: the delete is refused, or it cascades and takes the linked rows with it. Either earns the mark as long as you say which one you mean.

| OrderID | OrderDate | ItemCode | Quantity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **5001** | **04/03/2025** | **K12** | **2** |
| **5001** | **04/03/2025** | **K19** | **1** |
| **5002** | **06/03/2025** | **K12** | **5** |
| **5003** | **07/03/2025** | **K07** | **1** |
| **5003** | **07/03/2025** | **K12** | **1** |
| **5003** | **07/03/2025** | **K19** | **3** |

Order 5001 becomes two records, with quantity 2 for `K12` and quantity 1 for `K19`. **[1]**

Order 5003 becomes three records, with quantity 1 for `K07`, quantity 1 for `K12` and quantity 3 for `K19`. **[1]**

`OrderDate` is repeated on every record that belongs to the same order. **[1]**

The primary key is the composite key `OrderID` and `ItemCode`. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for order 5001 split into two records, `K12` with quantity 2 and `K19` with quantity 1
> 
> **1 mark** for order 5003 split into three records, `K07` with quantity 1, `K12` with quantity 1 and `K19` with quantity 3
> 
> **1 mark** for `OrderDate` correctly repeated on every record belonging to the same order
> 
> **1 mark** for a composite primary key of `OrderID` and `ItemCode`
> 
> Accept the six records written in any order
> 
> Do not accept `OrderID` alone as the primary key, because 5001 and 5003 now each appear on more than one record
> 
> Do not accept a quantity matched to the wrong item code

> **[exam-tip]**
> The trap here is the `Quantity` column. It is a second repeating group and it must stay lined up with `ItemCode`, so `K19` on order 5003 takes quantity 3, not 1. Split both columns together, one pair per record. Then remember that once `OrderID` repeats down the rows it can no longer be the primary key on its own.

parts.problemMd: State the two conditions that a database table must meet to be in Second Normal Form (2NF).
parts.solutionMd:
The table is already in First Normal Form (1NF). **[1]**

Every non-key attribute is fully dependent on the whole primary key, so there are no partial dependencies. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the table being in 1NF // there are no repeating groups // all data is atomic
> 
> **1 mark** for every attribute being fully dependent on the whole primary key // there are no partial dependencies
> 
> Accept "no attribute depends on only part of a composite primary key"
> 
> Do not accept "there are no transitive dependencies", which is the extra condition for 3NF

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each normal form builds on the one before it, so a 2NF answer that never mentions 1NF is only half an answer. State the previous form first, then add the new condition. The second mark needs the words full dependency or partial dependency, not just "the fields depend on the key".

parts.problemMd:
A hotel database contains the following table, which is in First Normal Form (1NF).

`ROOM_STAY(RoomNumber, StayDate, RoomType, GuestID)`

The primary key is the composite key `RoomNumber` and `StayDate`.

Some sample data is shown.

| RoomNumber | StayDate | RoomType | GuestID |
|---|---|---|---|
| 101 | 12/05/2025 | Double | G88 |
| 101 | 13/05/2025 | Double | G88 |
| 205 | 12/05/2025 | Single | G91 |

Explain why the table `ROOM_STAY` is not in Second Normal Form (2NF).
parts.solutionMd:
The primary key is a composite key made up of `RoomNumber` and `StayDate`. **[1]**

`RoomType` depends only on `RoomNumber`, because room 101 is a Double room whatever the date is. **[1]**

`RoomType` therefore depends on only part of the primary key. This is a partial dependency, which is not allowed in 2NF. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for identifying that the primary key is a composite key of `RoomNumber` and `StayDate`
> 
> **1 mark** for `RoomType` depending only on `RoomNumber` // `RoomType` does not depend on `StayDate`
> 
> **1 mark** for naming this as a partial dependency, which 2NF does not allow
> 
> Accept the sample data used as evidence, for example that room 101 is Double on both dates
> 
> Do not accept `GuestID` given as the faulty attribute, because which guest is in a room does depend on both the room number and the date
> 
> Do not accept "`RoomType` is repeated" on its own, because repetition is the symptom and the partial dependency is the reason

> **[exam-tip]**
> Marks are given for the reason, not the symptom. Many students write only that Double appears twice, which earns nothing on its own. You must name the attribute, name the part of the key it depends on, and use the term partial dependency.

parts.problemMd:
A logistics company uses a database that contains the following two tables. Both tables are in First Normal Form (1NF).

`DELIVERY(DeliveryID, DriverID, DriverName, DeliveryDate)`

The primary key of `DELIVERY` is `DeliveryID`.

`STOCK(WarehouseID, PartID, QuantityHeld, WarehouseCity)`

The primary key of `STOCK` is the composite key `WarehouseID` and `PartID`. `WarehouseCity` is the city in which the warehouse is located.

Explain, for each table, whether it is in Second Normal Form (2NF).
parts.solutionMd:
`DELIVERY` is in 2NF. **[1]**

Its primary key is the single attribute `DeliveryID`, so the key has no separate parts and no attribute can depend on only part of it. A partial dependency is only possible when the primary key is a composite key. **[1]**

`STOCK` is not in 2NF. **[1]**

`WarehouseCity` depends only on `WarehouseID`, which is part of the composite primary key. This is a partial dependency. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for stating that `DELIVERY` is in 2NF
> 
> **1 mark** for the reason: its primary key is a single attribute, so there is no part of the key for an attribute to depend on // a partial dependency requires a composite primary key
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that `STOCK` is not in 2NF
> 
> **1 mark** for the reason: `WarehouseCity` depends on `WarehouseID` only, which is part of the composite primary key, so this is a partial dependency
> 
> Accept "a table in 1NF whose primary key is a single attribute is automatically in 2NF"
> 
> Do not accept `DELIVERY` judged as not in 2NF because `DriverName` depends on `DriverID`. That is a transitive dependency, so it breaks 3NF, not 2NF
> 
> Do not accept `QuantityHeld` given as the faulty attribute in `STOCK`, because it depends on both `WarehouseID` and `PartID`

> **[exam-tip]**
> `DELIVERY` is designed to tempt you. `DriverName` really does sit in the wrong table, but the fault is a transitive dependency and this question asks about 2NF. Check the primary key first. If it is a single attribute and the table is in 1NF, it is in 2NF, and you can say so in one line.

parts.problemMd:
A college stores data about its students and courses in a relational database. The database designer says that every table in the database is now in Third Normal Form (3NF).

Describe **two** characteristics that each of these tables must have.
parts.solutionMd:
The table is in Second Normal Form (2NF), so there are no repeating groups and no partial dependencies. **[1]**

Every attribute depends only on the primary key and not on any other non-key attribute, so there are no transitive dependencies. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - No repeating groups of attributes // all data is atomic
> - No partial key dependencies // every attribute is fully dependent on the whole primary key
> - No non-key dependencies // no transitive dependencies // no attribute depends on another non-key attribute
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept "the table is in 2NF" for one mark
> 
> Accept "all attributes are fully dependent on the primary key and on no other attribute" for the non-key dependencies point

> **[exam-tip]**
> Say "and on no other attribute". Students write "every attribute depends on the primary key" and stop, which is also true of a 2NF table, so it does not separate 3NF from 2NF. Make sure that extra clause is in your answer, because it is the only point that belongs to 3NF alone.

parts.problemMd:
A college database contains the following table, which is in Second Normal Form (2NF).

`STUDENT_RECORD(StudentID, FirstName, LastName, TutorID, TutorRoom)`

The primary key is `StudentID`. `TutorRoom` is the room in which a student's tutor teaches.

Explain why the table `STUDENT_RECORD` is not in Third Normal Form (3NF).
parts.solutionMd:
`TutorRoom` depends on `TutorID`, because the room is decided by which tutor the student has. **[1]**

`TutorID` is not the primary key. It is a non-key attribute. **[1]**

`TutorRoom` therefore depends on another non-key attribute rather than only on `StudentID`. This is a transitive dependency, which is not allowed in 3NF. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for identifying that `TutorRoom` depends on `TutorID`
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that `TutorID` is a non-key attribute // `TutorID` is not the primary key
> 
> **1 mark** for naming this as a transitive dependency // a non-key dependency, which 3NF does not allow
> 
> Accept the dependency written as a chain, `StudentID` to `TutorID` to `TutorRoom`
> 
> Do not accept "`TutorRoom` is repeated for students who have the same tutor" on its own, because that is the symptom rather than the reason
> 
> Do not accept "there is a partial dependency", because the primary key is a single attribute so a partial dependency is impossible

> **[exam-tip]**
> The examined wording is "explain why", so a bare statement that the table is not in 3NF earns nothing. Trace the chain out loud: the primary key gives you the tutor, and the tutor gives you the room. Any time you can say A gives you B and B gives you C, and B is not a key, you have found a transitive dependency.

parts.problemMd:
A cinema uses a database that contains the following two tables. Both tables are in Second Normal Form (2NF).

`SCREENING(ScreeningID, FilmID, FilmTitle, ScreenNumber, StartTime)`

`TICKET(TicketID, ScreeningID, SeatCode, PricePaid)`

The primary key of `SCREENING` is `ScreeningID` and the primary key of `TICKET` is `TicketID`. The price paid is recorded separately for every ticket sold.

Explain which one of these tables is not in Third Normal Form (3NF), and write a corrected design so that the whole database is in 3NF.
parts.solutionMd:
`SCREENING` is not in 3NF. **[1]**

`FilmTitle` depends on `FilmID`, and `FilmID` is a non-key attribute, so this is a transitive dependency. **[1]**

The film data should be moved into a table of its own. **[1]**

`FILM(FilmID, FilmTitle)` with `FilmID` as the primary key **[1]**

`SCREENING(ScreeningID, FilmID, ScreenNumber, StartTime)` with `ScreeningID` as the primary key and `FilmID` kept as a foreign key that links to `FILM` **[1]**

`TICKET` does not change, because every attribute in it depends only on `TicketID`.

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for identifying `SCREENING` as the table that is not in 3NF
> 
> **1 mark** for `FilmTitle` depending on the non-key attribute `FilmID` // naming this as a transitive dependency or a non-key dependency
> 
> **1 mark** for creating a separate film table with a suitable name
> 
> **1 mark** for `FILM(FilmID, FilmTitle)` with `FilmID` as the primary key
> 
> **1 mark** for `FilmTitle` removed from `SCREENING` and `FilmID` retained there as a foreign key
> 
> Accept any sensible name for the new table
> 
> Do not accept `FilmID` also removed from `SCREENING`, because the link between a screening and its film would then be lost
> 
> Do not accept `TICKET` named as the faulty table. `SeatCode` and `PricePaid` are recorded for each individual ticket, so both depend only on `TicketID`

> **[exam-tip]**
> When you split a transitive dependency out, the determining attribute stays behind as the foreign key and only the attributes it determines move. Here `FilmID` appears in both tables and `FilmTitle` appears in only one. Students who delete `FilmID` from `SCREENING` break the link and lose the last mark.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark **each to **max 2** for data dictionary and **max 2** for logical schema:
> 
> Data dictionary:
> 
> - Data about the data in the database // metadata
> - Identifies the characteristics of the data that will be stored
> - Appropriate example e.g. field names, table name, validation rules, data types, primary / foreign keys, relationships etc.
> 
> Logical schema:
> 
> - Conceptual design
> - Platform/database independent overview of the database
> - Is used to design the physical structure
> - Appropriate example e.g. Design of entities / E-R diagram / views

parts.problemMd:
A shipping company stores its data in a relational database. The database is created and managed using a Database Management System (DBMS).

One of the features provided by the DBMS is data security.

State **two** ways in which the DBMS provides data security.
parts.solutionMd:
The DBMS carries out backup procedures, so a copy of the data is kept and the database can be restored if data is lost or damaged. **[1]**

The DBMS gives access rights to individual users or to groups of users, so a user can only see or change the data that user is allowed to. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for backup procedures // the DBMS takes backup copies of the data // the database can be restored from a backup
> 
> **1 mark** for access rights given to individuals or to groups of users // different users are given different levels of access, for example read-only or read and write
> 
> Accept "permissions" or "privileges" for access rights.
> 
> Accept "recovery" only where it is linked to a backup copy, for example "the data can be recovered from the backup".
> 
> Accept views, where the answer says that different users are shown different parts of the database. This is credited in the published mark scheme for this content even though the syllabus does not name it.
> 
> Accept encryption, where the answer says the stored data is encoded so it cannot be understood without the key.
> 
> Do not accept "a password" on its own. A password identifies the user; it is the access rights attached to that user that then control what the user may do.
> 
> Do not accept "a firewall" or "anti-virus software". Both protect the computer system rather than the data held in the database, and neither is provided by the DBMS.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often answer this with general computer security points such as firewalls, anti-virus software or strong passwords. The question is about what the DBMS itself provides, so answer with the things the DBMS controls: backups, access rights, and the views each user is shown.
> 
> Make sure your access rights point says what the rights actually do. "The DBMS has access rights" simply repeats the question. "Each group of users is given read-only or read and write access" earns the mark.

parts.problemMd:
A college stores information about its students in a relational database. Part of the table STUDENT is shown with some sample data.

| StudentID | FamilyName | DateOfBirth |
|---|---|---|
| S1041 | Okonkwo | 02/09/2008 |
| S1042 | Haddad | 17/01/2009 |

The Database Management System (DBMS) maintains a data dictionary for this database.

Complete the table by giving **three** different items of data that the data dictionary stores about the field FamilyName.

| Number | Item of data the data dictionary stores about the field FamilyName |
|---|---|
| 1 |   |
| 2 |   |
| 3 |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Number | Item of data the data dictionary stores about the field FamilyName |
|---|---|
| 1 | **The name of the field** **[1]** |
| 2 | **The data type of the field** **[1]** |
| 3 | **The validation rule applied to the field** **[1]** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - The name of the field
> - The data type of the field
> - The size, or maximum length, of the field
> - The validation rule applied to the field
> - Whether the field is a primary key, a foreign key or an indexed field
> - The name of the table that the field belongs to
> - A description of what the field holds
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept a correctly named example alongside an item, for example "data type: text of up to 30 characters".
> 
> Do not accept the data values themselves, such as "Okonkwo" or "Haddad". A data dictionary stores data about the data, never the data.
> 
> Do not accept the same item written twice in different words, for example "field size" and "maximum number of characters". Award one mark only.
> 
> Do not accept "metadata" on its own. It is the correct heading for all of these items, but the question asks for three specific items.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The commonest mistake here is to write down the contents of the table instead of the description of the table. The data dictionary does not know that one student is called Okonkwo. It knows that there is a field called FamilyName, that it holds text, and how long that text may be.
> 
> A quick test before you write an answer: could the data dictionary hold this item before a single student had been added to the database? If it could, it belongs in your answer.

parts.problemMd:
A chain of language schools operates in six countries. The chain asks a designer to produce one new database that all six countries will use.

Before any tables are created, the designer produces a logical schema for the database.

Explain why the designer produces a logical schema before the database is built.
parts.solutionMd:
The logical schema is the design of the whole database. It sets out the tables, the fields in each table and how the tables link together. **[1]**

The logical schema is not tied to one particular DBMS, so the same design can be built using whichever DBMS each of the six countries runs. **[1]**

The design can be checked, and any errors put right, before any data is stored or any programs are written. Correcting a design on paper is far cheaper than correcting a database that is already in use. **[1]**

The logical schema is then used to design the physical structure, so the developers have one agreed design to build from. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any four from:**
> 
> - The logical schema is the conceptual design, or overall design, of the database
> - It sets out the tables, the fields in each table and how the tables are linked
> - It is independent of any particular DBMS or platform
> - ... so the same design can be implemented on whichever DBMS a country uses
> - The design can be checked and corrected before any data is entered
> - Changing the design later, once data is stored and programs have been written, costs far more
> - It is used to design the physical structure of the database
> - It gives every developer one agreed design to work from
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> Accept "views" as an example of something the logical schema defines.
> 
> Do not accept "it holds data about the data" or "it holds the field names and data types". That describes the data dictionary, which is a different DBMS feature.
> 
> Do not accept a description of how the data is stored on the disk, or which file organisation is used. The logical schema deliberately leaves the physical storage out.
> 
> Do not accept "so the database works faster". The logical schema is a design document and has no direct effect on performance.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Data dictionary and logical schema are the two DBMS features that students most often mix up, and an answer that describes the wrong one scores nothing. Hold on to the difference: the logical schema is the design of the structure, the data dictionary is the record of what is in that structure once it exists.
> 
> The word "logical" is doing real work in the name. It means the design says what the database contains and how the parts relate, and says nothing about how the data is physically stored. Any answer that mentions disks, files or storage devices has drifted away from the mark scheme.

parts.problemMd:
A Database Management System (DBMS) contains a software tool called the query processor.

State the purpose of the query processor.
parts.solutionMd:
The query processor allows the user to enter the criteria for a search, or to write a query in Structured Query Language (SQL). **[1]**

It then processes the query, finds the data that matches the criteria and returns the result to the user. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the user enters the criteria for a search // the user writes a query, for example in SQL
> 
> **1 mark** for the query processor processes or executes the query and returns the matching data // it finds and returns the appropriate result
> 
> Accept "runs", "carries out" or "executes" for "processes".
> 
> Accept "searches the database and displays the records that match".
> 
> Do not accept "it stores the queries" or "it stores data about the database". That is the data dictionary.
> 
> Do not accept "it allows the user to create tables, forms and reports". That is the developer interface.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two software tools in a DBMS get swapped in a great many answers. The query processor finds data that is already in the database. The developer interface creates the things that hold and present that data. If your answer contains the word "create", check that you have not described the wrong tool.
> 
> Two marks means two ideas, not one idea written twice. The user supplies the criteria is the first idea; the tool returns the matching records is the second.

parts.problemMd:
A travel company uses a Database Management System (DBMS) to hold data about its bookings.

A member of staff at the company uses the developer interface of the DBMS.

Describe **three** tasks that the member of staff can carry out using the developer interface.
parts.solutionMd:
The member of staff can create a new table and define the fields that the table will hold. **[1]**

The member of staff can create a form, so that other staff can type in the details of a booking without working directly on the table. **[1]**

The member of staff can create a report, which presents selected data from the database in a chosen layout, for example a list of all bookings for one month. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - Create a table and define the fields it will hold
> - Change an existing table definition, for example by adding a field
> - Create a form that other users use to enter or edit data
> - Create a report that presents or prints selected data in a chosen layout
> - Create and save a query that other users can run
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept "design" or "set up" for "create".
> 
> Do not accept "type in the details of a booking". Entering data through a finished form is using the database, not using the developer interface.
> 
> Do not accept "search for a customer" or "run a query". Running a search is the query processor.
> 
> Do not accept two answers that are the same task in different words, for example "create a form" and "make a data entry screen". Award one mark only.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Notice the words "the use and purpose of" in this part of the syllabus. Naming the tool is not enough here, because the question already names it. Each of your three answers has to be a task, so it needs a verb: create a table, create a form, create a report.
> 
> A very common lost mark is describing what an ordinary user does with the finished database. The developer interface is used to build the tables, forms and reports; it is not used to fill them in.

parts.problemMd:
An online bookshop uses a Database Management System (DBMS).

Two members of staff work with the database on the same day.

- Anika is a database developer. She needs to add a new table to the database and build a screen that other staff will use to type in new stock.
- Ben works in the warehouse. He needs a list of every order that was placed in March.

For **each** member of staff, identify the DBMS software tool they use and explain why that tool is the correct one.
parts.solutionMd:
Anika uses the developer interface. **[1]**

The developer interface is the tool that allows a user to create items such as tables, forms and reports, which is exactly what Anika needs in order to add the new table and build the data entry screen. **[1]**

Ben uses the query processor. **[1]**

Ben does not need to change the structure of the database. He enters the criteria, in this case the month March, and the query processor finds and returns the orders that match. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for Anika uses the developer interface
> 
> **1 mark** for a reason linked to building the database, for example it allows the user to create tables, forms and reports // it is the tool used to create or change the structure of the database
> 
> **1 mark** for Ben uses the query processor
> 
> **1 mark** for a reason linked to retrieving data, for example the user enters the criteria and the tool returns the records that match // it processes and executes the query without changing the structure of the database
> 
> Accept the two members of staff in either order, provided each reason is clearly attached to the person it belongs to.
> 
> Do not accept "the developer interface, because Anika is a developer". The reason must say what the tool does, not repeat the person's job title.
> 
> Do not award a reason mark where the tool named for that person is the wrong one. The reason has to justify the tool that was actually named.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Half the marks in a question shaped like this sit in the reasons, and students routinely name both tools correctly and then stop writing. Add a second sentence for each person that says what the tool does for them.
> 
> The clue that separates the two tools is whether the structure of the database is changing. Anika is changing it, so she needs the developer interface. Ben is only reading data that is already stored, so he needs the query processor.

parts.problemMd:
An algorithm will output the **last** three lines from a text file `Result.txt`

The lines need to be output in the same order as they appear in the file.

Assume:

- Three variables` LineX`, `LineY` and `LineZ` will store the three lines. These are of type string and all three variables have been initialised to an empty string.
- The file exists and contains **at least** three lines.

The algorithm to output the lines is expressed in eight steps.

Complete the steps.

1. Open the file ...........................................................................

2. Loop until ...........................................................................

3. ........................................................................... and store in `ThisLine `

4. Assign `LineY `to `LineX`

5. Assign `LineZ` to `LineY`

6. Assign `ThisLine` to `LineZ`

7. After the loop, ...........................................................................

8. Output `LineX, LineY, LineZ`

Explain the purpose of steps 4, 5 and 6 in the algorithm from part **(a)**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Example answer:
> 
> So that the last three lines of the file are output in the correct **order **
> 
> A mark for mentioning one of:
> 
> - (Ensuring) the lines are **output in correct order**

parts.problemMd:
A global integer variable `Tick` is always incremented every millisecond (1000 times per second) regardless of the other programs running.

The value of `Tick` can be read by any program but the value should not be changed.

Assume that the value of `Tick` does not overflow.

As an example, the following pseudocode algorithm would output `"Goodbye" `40 seconds after outputting `"Hello"`.

`    DECLARE Start : INTEGER `

`    OUTPUT "Hello" `
`    Start Tick `

`    REPEAT `
`      //do nothing `
`    UNTIL Tick = Start + 40000 `

`    OUTPUT "Goodbye" `

A program is needed to help a user to time an event such as boiling an egg.

The time taken for the event is known as the elapsed time.

The program contains a procedure `Timer() `which will:

- take two integer values representing an elapsed time in minutes and seconds
- use the value of variable `Tick` to calculate the elapsed time
- output a warning message 30 seconds before the elapsed time is up
- output a final message when the total time has elapsed

For example, to set an alarm for 5 minutes and 45 seconds the program makes the following call:

`    CALL Timer(5, 45) `

When 5 minutes and 15 seconds have elapsed, the program will output:

`    "30 seconds to go" `

When 5 minutes and 45 seconds have elapsed, the program will output:

`    "The time is up!"`

Write pseudocode for the procedure `Timer()`.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Example solution:
> 
> `PROCEDURE Timer(Mins, Secs : INTEGER) `
> `   DECLARE WarningTick, EndTick : INTEGER `
> 
> `   EndTick `$\leftarrow$` Tick + 1000 * ((Mins * 60) + Secs) `
> `   WarningTick `$\leftarrow$` EndTick - (30 * 1000) `
> 
> `   REPEAT `
> `      //do nothing `
> `   UNTIL Tick = WarningTick `
> `   OUTPUT "30 seconds to go" `
> 
> `   REPEAT `
> `     //do nothing `
> `   UNTIL Tick = EndTick `
> 
> `   OUTPUT "The time is up!" `
> 
> `ENDPROCEDURE `
> 
> Mark as follows: 
> **MP1** Procedure heading **and** parameters **and** ending 
> **MP2** ‘Attempt’ to calculate ‘total time’/`EndTick` // ‘elapsed time’ // `WarningTick `
> **MP3** Correct calculation of `EndTick` **and** `WarningTick`
> 
> **MP4** **(Design mark) **
> 
> - Two separate loops – checking warning time then the final time, **OR** …
> - Single loop checking the final time with an IF statement to check for warning time, **OR** …
> - Single loop with two IF statements checking the warning time and final time
> 
> **MP5** Completely correct MP4 
> **MP6** Output both messages (must be meaningful and follow successful MP4)

parts.problemMd:
A shop sells sandwiches and snacks. The owner chooses a ‘daily special’ sandwich which is displayed on a board outside the shop. Each ‘daily special’ has two different fillings and is made with one type of bread.

The owner wants a program to randomly choose the ‘daily special’ sandwich.

The program designer decides to store the possible sandwich fillings in a 1D array of type string.

The array is declared in pseudocode as follows:

`   DECLARE Filling : ARRAY [1:35] OF STRING `

Each element contains the name of one filling.

An example of the first five elements is as follows:

| **Index** | **Element value** |
|---|---|
| 1 | `"Cheese"` |
| 2 | `"Onion"` |
| 3 | `"Salmon"` |
| 4 | `"Anchovies"` |
| 5 | `"Peanut Butter"` |

A second 1D array stores the possible bread used:

`     DECLARE Bread : ARRAY [1:10] OF STRING `

Each element contains the name of one type of bread.

An example of the first three elements is as follows:

| **Index ** | **Element value** |
|---|---|
| 1 | `"White"` |
| 2 | `"Brown"` |
| 3 | `"Pitta"` |

Both arrays may contain unused elements. The value of these will be an empty string and they may occur anywhere in each array.

A procedure `Special() `will output a message giving the ‘daily special’ sandwich made from **two** randomly selected different fillings and **one** randomly selected bread.

Unused array elements must** not** be used when creating the ‘daily special’ sandwich.

Using the above examples, the output could be:

`     "The daily special is Cheese and Onion on Brown bread."`

Complete the pseudocode for the procedure `Special()`.

Assume that both arrays are global.

`PROCEDURE Special()`
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Example solution:
> 
> `PROCEDURE Special() `
> `   DECLARE Index : INTEGER `
> `   DECLARE Filling1, Filling2 : STRING `
> 
> `   REPEAT `
> `      Index `$\leftarrow$` INT(RAND(35)) + 1 `
> `   UNTIL Filling[Index] <> "" `
> 
> `   Filling1 `$\leftarrow$` Filling[Index] `
> 
> `   REPEAT `
> `      Index `$\leftarrow$` INT(RAND(35)) + 1 `
> `   UNTIL Filling[Index] <> "" AND Filling1 <> Filling[Index] `
> 
> `   Filling2 `$\leftarrow$` Filling[Index] `
> 
> `   REPEAT `
> `      Index`$\leftarrow$` INT(RAND(10) + 1) `
> `   UNTIL Bread[Index] <> "" `
> 
> `   OUTPUT "The daily special is ", Filling1, " and ", __ Filling2, "   on ", Bread[Index], " bread." `
> 
> `ENDPROCEDURE `
> 
> Mark as follows: 
> **MP1**   Loop for Filling 1, avoiding unused elements 
> **MP2**  Loop for Filling 2 avoiding unused elements 
> **MP3**  Check Filling 2 is different from Filling 1 – could correctly compare either the indices or the array contents
> 
> **MP4**   Loop for Bread, avoiding unused elements
> 
> **MP5**   Using `RAND(10)` /` RAND(35)` 
> **MP6**   Completely correct use of RAND() - including `INT()`and +1 in all cases
> 
> **MP7**   Correct output -** once only** – following a reasonable attempt at selection of filings and bread

parts.problemMd:
The owner decides that some combinations of fillings do not go well together. For example, anchovies and peanut butter.

Describe how the design could be changed to prevent certain combinations being selected.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Answers include:
> 
> **MP1**    For each filling, create a list of <u>acceptable</u> / <u>incompatible</u> fillings/indexes 
> **MP2**   When selecting the second filling, (as well as checking for an unused element) <u>check</u> that the filling / index is / is not on the list
> 
> ALTERNATIVE: 
> **MP1**    Create a list of ‘good’ combinations 
> **MP2**   <u>Randomly select</u> from this list

parts.problemMd:
An algorithm will:

1. prompt and input a sequence of 100 integer values, one at a time
2. sum the positive integers
3. output the result of the sum.

Write pseudocode for the algorithm.

Assume the value zero is neither positive nor negative.

You must declare all variables used in the algorithm.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> `DECLARE Count, Total, NextNumber : INTEGER `
> 
> `Total `$\leftarrow$` 0 `
> `FOR  Count `$\leftarrow$` 1 TO 100 `
> `    OUTPUT "Input an integer value"`
> `    INPUT NextNumber `
> `    IF NextNumber > 0 THEN `
> `       Total `$\leftarrow$` Total + NextNumber `
> `    END IF `
> `NEXT Count `
> 
> `OUTPUT Total `
> 
> Mark as follows: 
> **MP1**     Declarations of all variables used 
> **MP2**    Loop for 100 iterations 
> **MP3**    Prompt **and** input a value **in a loop and **
> **MP4**    Test for value > 0 // >=1 **in a loop **
> **MP5**    Sum the Total **in a loop** 
> **MP6**    Output of Total after the **loop**
> 
> **Max 5 marks**

parts.problemMd:
An examination paper has a maximum of 75 marks. One of five pass grades (A to E) is assigned, depending on the mark obtained. The lowest mark for a given grade is known as the grade boundary.

A program is being written to process examination marks.

The five grade boundaries are stored in a global 1D array `GB` of type `INTEGER`, for example:

| **Index** | **Value** | **Comment** |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `65` | The minimum mark for an A grade. |
| 2 | `57` | The minimum mark for a B grade. |
| 3 | `43` | The minimum mark for a C grade. |
| 4 | `35` | The minimum mark for a D grade. |
| 5 | `27` | The minimum mark for an E grade. |

Any paper that achieves a mark within 2 marks of a grade boundary must be checked. Using the given table, a paper with 45 marks would need to be checked.

The pseudocode algorithm to determine whether a paper should be checked is as shown. The mark for the paper is stored in variable `Mark`. Global variables Mark, Index, Upper and Lower are declared as integers.

Complete the pseudocode.

`FOR Index `$\leftarrow$` 1 TO ........................................... `

`    Lower `$\leftarrow$` GB[Index] - 2 `

`    Upper `$\leftarrow$` ....................................................... `

`    IF Mark ........................................... AND Mark ........................................... THEN `

`       OUTPUT "Check this paper" `

`    ENDIF `

` NEXT Index`
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One mark per highlighted part:
> 
> `FOR Index `$\leftarrow$ `1 TO` <u>**5**</u> 
>         `Lower `$\leftarrow$` GB[Index] - 2 `
>         `Upper `$\leftarrow$ <u>**GB[Index] + 2**</u> `// `<u>**Lower + 4**</u> 
>         `IF Mark` <u>**>= Lower**</u> `AND Mark` <u>**<= Upper**</u> `THEN` 
>  `//IF Mark` <u>**<= Upper **</u>`AND Mark` <u>**>= Lower**</u> `THEN `
>              `OUTPUT "Check this paper" `
> `   ENDIF `
> `NEXT Index`

parts.problemMd:
In some countries, on the third Sunday in March, daylight saving time begins when clocks move forward by one hour.

A module `AdjustClock()` will take an integer parameter representing a year. The module will return an integer value representing the number of the day in March on which the clocks move forward.

For example, the following line of pseudocode would assign `DayNumber `the value 20:

`DayNumber`$\leftarrow$`AdjustClock(2022) `

Write pseudocode for the function `AdjustClock()`.

Date functions from the **insert** should be used in your solution.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Loop Solution 
> Example solution:
> 
> `FUNCTION AdjustClock(ThisYear : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER`
> `   DECLARE ThisDayNumber, SundayCount : INTEGER `
> `   DECLARE ThisDate : DATE `
> 
> `   ThisDayNumber `$\leftarrow$` 0 `
>          `SundayCount `$\leftarrow$` 0 `
>          `REPEAT `
>                  `ThisDayNumber `$\leftarrow$` ThisDayNumber + 1 `
>                  `ThisDate `$\leftarrow$` SETDATE(ThisDayNumber, 3, ThisYear) `

Step 1  Input the number of items.

Step 2  ...................................................................................................

Step 3  Multiply the number of items by the price of one item to give the total cost.

Step 4  Check whether the number of items is 10 or more.

Step 5  If the check is true, reduce the total cost by 5%.

Step 6  ...................................................................................................

Step 2  Input the price of one item. **[1]**

Step 6  Output the total cost. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> 
> **1 mark** for Step 6: output the total cost
> 
> Accept "read", "enter" or "prompt for" in place of "input", and "print", "display" or "show" in place of "output".
> 
> Accept "output the amount the customer must pay" or "output the final cost" for Step 6.
> 
> Do not accept "input the total cost" for Step 2, because the total cost is worked out in Step 3, not input.

- it contains exactly one `@` character
- there is at least one character before the `@`
- its last four characters are `.com`

Stepwise refinement is applied to the algorithm. The first refinement is:

Step 1  Input the email address.

Step 2  Check that the email address is valid.

Step 3  If the email address is valid, store it in the array at the next free index.

Step 4  If the email address is not valid, output an error message.

Step 2 is not yet at a level of detail from which the task may be programmed.

Outline the three steps that Step 2 refines into.

Do **not** use pseudocode statements in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Step 2.1  Check that the email address contains exactly one `@` character. **[1]**

Step 2.2  Check that there is at least one character before the `@` character. **[1]**

Step 2.3  Check that the last four characters of the email address are `.com`. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a step that counts the `@` characters and checks there is exactly one
> 
> **1 mark** for a step that checks at least one character comes before the `@`
> 
> **1 mark** for a step that checks the last four characters are `.com`
> 
> Accept the three steps in any order.
> 
> Accept "check the email address ends with `.com`" for the third step.
> 
> Accept "check the `@` is not the first character" for the second step.
> 
> Do not accept "check that the email address is valid", because it repeats Step 2 and adds no detail.
> 
> Do not accept "check that the email address contains an `@`", because it does not test that there is exactly one.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A refinement step must add detail. Writing the original step again in different words is the most common way to score zero here, so check that each step you write could be coded without any further thinking.
