parts.solutionMd:
| **Assignment statement** | **Error** |
|---|---|
| `Grade ← LEFT(StudentID, 2)` | A string of length 2 is returned, and a string longer than one character cannot be assigned to a CHAR variable **[1]** |
| `StudentID ← Grade` | NO ERROR **[1]** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for stating that `LEFT(StudentID, 2)` returns a `STRING` of length 2, which cannot be assigned to a `CHAR`
> 
> **1 mark** for `NO ERROR`
> 
> Accept for the first mark: the value returned is too long for a `CHAR`, or a `CHAR` can hold only one character.
> 
> Accept for the second mark: valid, correct, or no error.
> 
> Do not accept for the first mark: `LEFT` is the wrong function. The function call itself is properly formed. The error is the data type of the value it returns.
> 
> Do not accept an error for the second statement. The insert states that a `CHAR` may be assigned to a `STRING`.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students throw this mark away by assuming `CHAR` and `STRING` are interchangeable. The insert allows the conversion in one direction only. A `CHAR` may be assigned to a `STRING`, but a `STRING` of more than one character may not be assigned to a `CHAR`.
> 
> `LEFT`, `RIGHT` and `MID` always return a `STRING`. A string of length 1 may be treated as either type, so `LEFT(StudentID, 1)` would be accepted here. Always check the length of the value returned before you decide whether the assignment is legal.

An online service bills its members once a month. The program stores the variable `JoinDate`, which is of data type `DATE` and holds the date on which a member joined.

The billing module needs a new variable, `BillDate`. This must store the **first day of the month** in which the member joined. For example, if `JoinDate` holds 17/04/2026 then `BillDate` must hold 01/04/2026.

Write pseudocode to declare `BillDate` and to assign the correct value to it.
parts.solutionMd:
The declaration earns one mark, calling `SETDATE` with `1` as the day earns one mark, and taking the month and the year from `JoinDate` earns the third. **[3]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `DECLARE BillDate : DATE`
> 
> **1 mark** for an assignment to `BillDate` that calls `SETDATE` with `1` as the day parameter
> 
> **1 mark** for `MONTH(JoinDate)` as the month parameter and `YEAR(JoinDate)` as the year parameter
> 
> Accept the work split across extra statements, for example `ThisMonth ← MONTH(JoinDate)` followed by `BillDate ← SETDATE(1, ThisMonth, YEAR(JoinDate))`.
> 
> Accept `01` in place of `1` for the day parameter.
> 
> Do not accept a declaration of any type other than `DATE`, such as `DECLARE BillDate : STRING`.
> 
> Do not accept a value built as text, for example joining the characters `"01/"` to the month and the year with the `&` operator. That produces a `STRING`, not a `DATE`.
> 
> Do not accept the parameters of `SETDATE` in any other order. The insert defines the order as day, month, year.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The commonest error here is building the date as a string and joining the parts with `&`. It looks right when printed, but the variable then holds a `STRING`, and every date function on the insert expects a value of type `DATE`.
> 
> `DATE` is a single value, not three numbers. To change part of a date you have to pull the parts out with `DAY`, `MONTH` and `YEAR`, which each return an `INTEGER`, and then build a new date with `SETDATE`. Learn the order of the three `SETDATE` parameters, because day, month, year is not the order every country writes dates in.

The loop does visit element 2, but the `IF` statement blocks every line inside it, so nothing about slot 2 changes. Test the `IF` condition separately for each element before you change any value.

parts.problemMd:
A weather station records the total rainfall for each day.

At the end of each day the program adds one new line to the text file `Rainfall.txt`. This file already contains the totals for all the previous days. The totals for the previous days must not be lost.

Explain why the program stores the daily totals in a text file rather than in an array, and why the file is opened in `APPEND` mode rather than `WRITE` mode.
parts.solutionMd:
An array is held in memory while the program is running, so the daily totals would be lost when the program ends or the computer is switched off. A text file stores the totals permanently, so the earlier days are still there the next time the program is run. **[1]**

`WRITE` mode creates a new file, so the totals already in `Rainfall.txt` would be lost. `APPEND` mode adds the new line after the data that is already in the file, so the earlier totals are kept. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the data in an array is lost when the program ends / when the computer is switched off, but a file stores the data permanently
> 
> **1 mark** for `WRITE` mode would create a new file / overwrite the data already in `Rainfall.txt`, while `APPEND` mode adds the new line after the existing data
> 
> Accept for the first mark: "a file is non-volatile storage", or "the totals do not have to be entered again each time the program runs".
> 
> Accept for the second mark: "`APPEND` keeps the existing data" on its own.
> 
> Do not accept "a file can hold more data than an array" for the first mark. Capacity is not the reason the data is stored in a file here; losing the data when the program ends is.
> 
> Do not accept "a file is faster than an array". Reading from a file is slower than reading from memory, so this is not true.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students write only "so the data is saved". That sentence does not say what would be lost, so it rarely earns the mark. Say where an array lives and when it disappears: an array is in memory, and memory contents go when the program stops.
> 
> Learn the three text file modes by what they do to the data that is already in the file. `READ` does not change it, `WRITE` throws it away and starts the file again, and `APPEND` keeps it and adds after it. Any question that says the file already contains data that must not be lost is asking for `APPEND`.

parts.problemMd:
A program writes a message to a log file each time an error occurs.

The text file `ErrorLog.txt` already exists and contains the messages from earlier runs of the program. These messages must not be lost.

The procedure `AddError()` takes one parameter `Message` of type `STRING`. It adds `Message` to `ErrorLog.txt` as a new line, then closes the file.

The first and last lines of the procedure are given.

Complete the procedure by writing the three pseudocode statements that are missing.
parts.solutionMd:
**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `OPENFILE "ErrorLog.txt" FOR APPEND`
> 
> **1 mark** for `WRITEFILE "ErrorLog.txt", Message`
> 
> **1 mark** for `CLOSEFILE "ErrorLog.txt"` written after the `WRITEFILE` statement
> 
> Accept a `STRING` variable holding the file name in place of the literal `"ErrorLog.txt"`, provided the same variable is used in all three statements.
> 
> Do not accept `OPENFILE "ErrorLog.txt" FOR WRITE`. `WRITE` mode creates a new file and the earlier messages would be lost.
> 
> Do not accept `WRITEFILE Message` without the file name. The file name is the first argument of `WRITEFILE`.
> 
> Accept `OPEN` for `OPENFILE`, `WRITE` for `WRITEFILE` and `CLOSE` for `CLOSEFILE`, provided the file name and the mode or the data are correct; Cambridge mark schemes use these short forms in their own model answers and marking points.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The commonest loss here is dropping the file name. `WRITEFILE` and `CLOSEFILE` both need it, because a program may have more than one file open at the same time. Write `WRITEFILE "ErrorLog.txt", Message`, not `WRITEFILE Message`.
> 
> The second commonest loss is forgetting `CLOSEFILE` altogether. A procedure that opens a file and never closes it leaves the file open in `APPEND` mode, so the next part of the program cannot open it for reading.

parts.problemMd:
A weather station stores its temperature readings in the text file `Readings.txt`.

Each line of the file holds one reading as a numeric string, for example `18.4`. The number of readings in the file is not known, and the file may be empty.

Write pseudocode for a function `CountAbove()` that:

- takes one parameter `Limit` of type `REAL`
- opens `Readings.txt` for reading
- reads every line in the file
- counts the readings that are greater than `Limit`
- closes the file
- returns the count as an `INTEGER`, returning 0 if the file is empty.

You may use the built-in functions `EOF()` and STR<u>TO</u>NUM().
parts.solutionMd:
The `WHILE` loop tests for the end of the file before it reads. If `Readings.txt` is empty then `EOF("Readings.txt")` is `TRUE` on the first test, the loop body never runs, and the function returns 0.

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a function header naming the parameter and the return type, `FUNCTION CountAbove(Limit : REAL) RETURNS INTEGER`, with a matching `ENDFUNCTION`
> 
> **1 mark** for a counter set to 0 before the loop
> 
> **1 mark** for `OPENFILE "Readings.txt" FOR READ`
> 
> **1 mark** for a pre-condition loop controlled by the end of the file, `WHILE NOT EOF("Readings.txt")` with `ENDWHILE`
> 
> **1 mark** for `READFILE "Readings.txt", ThisLine` inside the loop, then a test of the form IF STR<u>TO</u>NUM(ThisLine) > Limit THEN, and adding 1 to the counter
> 
> **1 mark** for `CLOSEFILE "Readings.txt"` followed by `RETURN Count`
> 
> Accept a `STRING` variable holding the file name in place of the literal `"Readings.txt"`, used consistently.
> 
> Do not accept `REPEAT ... UNTIL EOF("Readings.txt")`. A post-condition loop reads a line before it tests for the end of the file, so it fails on an empty file and cannot return 0.
> 
> Do not accept a comparison written without a conversion, such as `IF ThisLine > Limit THEN`. `READFILE` stores a `STRING`, and a `STRING` cannot be compared with a `REAL`.
> 
> Do not accept the comparison written with `>=`. A reading equal to `Limit` is not greater than `Limit`.
> 
> Accept `OPEN` for `OPENFILE` and `CLOSE` for `CLOSEFILE`. Do not accept `READ` in place of `READFILE`.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The empty file is what this question is testing, and `REPEAT ... UNTIL EOF()` is the answer that fails it. A post-condition loop always runs its body once, so it calls `READFILE` on a file that has no lines. Use `WHILE NOT EOF(...)` whenever the number of lines is unknown, and keep `REPEAT` for loops that must run at least once.
> 
> `READFILE` always gives you a `STRING`, even when the line looks like a number. Convert it with STR<u>TO</u>NUM() before any numeric comparison or arithmetic. Check the spelling on the Insert. It is STR<u>TO</u>NUM, and there is no `ROUND`, `ABS` or `SPLIT` on this paper.

The table shows the contents of `CityList`. `StartPointer` has the value 2.

| 6 | `Lima` | 1 |

parts.solutionMd:
`StartPointer` is 2, so the first node is at index 2. Each `Pointer` field gives the index of the next node.

`Cairo` (index 2), `Dhaka` (index 4), `Lima` (index 6) **[1]**

`Nairobi` (index 1), `Oslo` (index 5), `Perth` (index 3), whose `Pointer` field is 0, so the linked list ends here **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `Cairo`, `Dhaka`, `Lima` given as the first three names, in that order
> 
> **1 mark** for `Nairobi`, `Oslo`, `Perth` given as the last three names, in that order

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:

- `StartPointer` stores the array index of the first node in the linked list.
- `FreeListPointer` stores the array index of the first node in the free list.
- The value 0 is used as the null pointer.
- A node on the free list has nothing stored in its `Data` field.

`StartPointer` has the value 8 and `FreeListPointer` has the value 4.

| Index | Data | Pointer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 |   | 6 |
| 2 | `BK208` | 7 |
| 3 | `BK115` | 2 |
| 4 |   | 1 |
| 5 | `BK340` | 0 |
| 6 |   | 0 |
| 7 | `BK297` | 5 |
| 8 | `BK061` | 3 |

The node storing `BK208` is deleted from the linked list and returned to the free list. It becomes the first node on the free list.

Complete the table to show the `Pointer` field of every array element, and the values of `StartPointer` and `FreeListPointer`, after this deletion.

| Index | Data | Pointer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 |   |   |
| 2 | `BK208` |   |
| 3 | `BK115` |   |
| 4 |   |   |
| 5 | `BK340` |   |
| 6 |   |   |
| 7 | `BK297` |   |
| 8 | `BK061` |   |

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `StartPointer` |   |
| `FreeListPointer` |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Index | Data | Pointer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 |   | **6** |
| 2 | `BK208` | **4** |
| 3 | `BK115` | **7** |
| 4 |   | **1** |
| 5 | `BK340` | **0** |
| 6 |   | **0** |
| 7 | `BK297` | **5** |
| 8 | `BK061` | **3** |

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `StartPointer` | **8** |
| `FreeListPointer` | **2** |

`StartPointer` is unchanged, because `BK208` was not the first node in the linked list. **[1]**

Index 3 holds `BK115`, the node before the deleted one. Its `Pointer` field is changed from 2 to 7, so `BK115` now points straight to `BK297`. **[1]**

Index 2 is the deleted node. Its `Pointer` field is changed from 7 to 4, the old value of `FreeListPointer`, so it now points to the rest of the free list. **[1]**

`FreeListPointer` is changed from 4 to 2, so the deleted node is now the first node on the free list. **[1]**

The linked list is now `BK061`, `BK115`, `BK297`, `BK340`, and the free list runs 2, 4, 1, 6.

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `StartPointer` still 8
> 
> **1 mark** for the `Pointer` field of index 3 changed to 7
> 
> **1 mark** for the `Pointer` field of index 2 changed to 4
> 
> **1 mark** for `FreeListPointer` changed to 2
> 
> All six other `Pointer` fields must be left at their original values: 6, 1, 0, 0, 5, 3 for indices 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. A response that alters any of these scores a maximum of 3.
> 
> Accept the `Data` field of index 2 either left as `BK208` or shown as empty. The `Data` field of a deleted node does not have to be erased, because the node is only reachable through the free list.
> 
> Do not accept `FreeListPointer` left at 4 with the `Pointer` field of index 2 set to 0. Index 2 is then on neither list and can never be reused.
> 
> Do not accept the `Pointer` field of index 3 set to 0. That would end the linked list at `BK115` and lose `BK297` and `BK340`.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Returning a node to the free list is two assignments and the order matters. Copy the current value of `FreeListPointer` into the `Pointer` field of the deleted node first, then set `FreeListPointer` to the index of the deleted node. Students who do it the other way round overwrite `FreeListPointer` before they have used it, and the rest of the free list is lost.
> 
> Check `StartPointer` before you change it. It only changes when the node you delete is the first node in the linked list.

parts.problemMd:
An online shop stores product codes in a linked list.

The record type `Node` and the array `Product` are declared as follows.

The linked list works as follows.

- `StartPointer` stores the array index of the first node in the linked list.
- The `Pointer` field of a node stores the array index of the next node in the linked list.
- The value 0 is used as the null pointer.
- `StartPointer` has the value 0 when the linked list is empty.

The function `FindNode()` takes a product code as a parameter. It searches the linked list, in order, for that product code.

- If a node in the linked list stores the product code in its `Data` field, the function returns the array index of that node.
- If no node in the linked list stores the product code, the function returns 0.

The function uses a local integer variable `ThisPointer` to store the array index of the node currently being looked at.

Describe the algorithm for `FindNode()` in **six** steps.

Do not use pseudocode statements in your answer.

Step 1 ..............................................................................................

Step 2 ..............................................................................................

Step 3 ..............................................................................................

Step 4 ..............................................................................................

Step 5 ..............................................................................................

Step 6 ..............................................................................................
parts.solutionMd:
Step 1: Assign the value of `StartPointer` to `ThisPointer`, so the search starts at the first node in the linked list. **[1]**

Step 2: Repeat steps 3 to 5 while `ThisPointer` is not 0, so the loop stops when the null pointer is reached. **[1]**

Step 3: Compare the `Data` field of the array element at index `ThisPointer` with the product code. **[1]**

Step 4: If they are the same, return the value of `ThisPointer` and stop. **[1]**

Step 5: If they are not the same, assign the `Pointer` field of the current node to `ThisPointer`, to move to the next node in the linked list. **[1]**

Step 6: If the loop ends because `ThisPointer` is 0, the product code was not found, so return 0. **[1]**

The test in step 2 comes before any array element is read. If the linked list is empty, `StartPointer` is 0, so the loop ends straight away and the function returns 0.

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for assigning `StartPointer` to `ThisPointer` // identifying the first node using `StartPointer`
> 
> **1 mark** for looping until `ThisPointer` is 0 // until the null pointer is reached
> 
> **1 mark** for comparing the `Data` field of the array element at index `ThisPointer` // of the current node with the product code
> 
> **1 mark** for returning `ThisPointer` when the product code is found
> 
> **1 mark** for assigning the `Pointer` field of the current node // array element to `ThisPointer`
> 
> **1 mark** for returning 0 when the loop ends without finding the product code
> 
> Accept "current pointer" for `ThisPointer` and "null pointer" for 0.
> 
> Accept a version that uses a variable such as `Found`: set `Found` to 0 before the loop, set `Found` to `ThisPointer` when the product code is found, stop the loop when `Found` is not 0, and return `Found` after the loop. This version earns the fourth and sixth marks.
> 
> Do not accept "add 1 to `ThisPointer`" or "move to the next array element" for the fifth mark. The next node in the linked list is at the index stored in the `Pointer` field, which is not usually the next array element.
> 
> Do not accept checking every array element from 1 to 50 in turn. Some array elements are not part of the linked list, so this can find a product code in a node that has been deleted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error is moving on by adding 1 to the pointer. In a linked list the next node is wherever the `Pointer` field of the current node says it is, which is almost never the next array element.
> 
> Order matters. Test `ThisPointer` against 0 before you read the array element at that index, otherwise an empty linked list sends you to element 0, which does not exist in an `ARRAY[1:50]`. Students also often forget step 6. A search that only says what happens when the product code is found has not described the whole algorithm.

parts.problemMd:
A program uses a stack to store reference codes. The stack is implemented using a 1D array and one integer variable, declared in pseudocode as follows:

`DECLARE ItemStack : ARRAY[1:50] OF STRING`

`DECLARE TopOfStack : INTEGER`

The stack operates as follows:

- `TopOfStack` holds the index of the array element that contains the last item added to the stack.
- `TopOfStack` holds 0 when the stack is empty.
- The array is filled from the lowest indexed element towards the highest.

A module `Pop()` will remove the item at the top of the stack and return that item to the calling program.

If there are no items on the stack, `Pop()` will output an error message and return an empty string.

Describe the algorithm for module `Pop()` in five steps.

Do not use pseudocode in your answer.

Step 1 ..............................................

Step 2 ..............................................

Step 3 ..............................................

Step 4 ..............................................

Step 5 ..............................................
parts.solutionMd:
Step 1: Check whether the stack is empty by testing whether `TopOfStack` holds 0. **[1]**

Step 2: If the stack is empty, output an error message and return an empty string, taking no further action. **[1]**

Step 3: Otherwise use `TopOfStack` as an index to the array and copy that element into a local variable. **[1]**

Step 4: Decrease `TopOfStack` by 1. **[1]**

Step 5: Return the value held in the local variable to the calling program. **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for testing whether the stack is empty, described as `TopOfStack` = 0 or as the stack holding no items
> 
> **1 mark** for outputting an error message and returning an empty string when the stack is empty
> 
> **1 mark** for using `TopOfStack` as an index to the array to read the item, storing it in a local variable
> 
> **1 mark** for decreasing `TopOfStack` by 1
> 
> **1 mark** for returning the item that was read
> 
> Accept `TopOfStack < 1`, or `TopOfStack` being less than the lower bound of the array, for the empty test.
> 
> Accept `subtract 1 from TopOfStack` or `move TopOfStack down one element` for the fourth mark.
> 
> Do not accept increasing `TopOfStack`. That is the `Push()` operation.
> 
> Do not accept returning `ItemStack[1]`. That is the item at the bottom of the stack, which is the first item that was added.
> 
> Do not accept reading the item after `TopOfStack` has been decreased, because this returns the wrong element.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of steps 3 and 4 is where marks are lost. If you move the pointer first and then read the array, you return the item below the one you were asked for. Read the element, then move the pointer.
> 
> When a question says do not use pseudocode, write plain sentences but keep the real identifier names from the question, such as `TopOfStack` and `ItemStack`. Cambridge credits the identifiers; it is the `IF ... THEN` and `ENDIF` keywords that earn nothing here.

parts.problemMd:
A program uses a queue to store the reference numbers of messages waiting to be sent.

- The `EndOfQueue` pointer holds the index of the last data item added.
- The variable `NumItems` holds the number of data items currently in the queue.

The table shows the current state of the queue. All eight elements have been used at least once.

| Array element | Data |
|---|---|
| 1 | `"M7"` |
| 2 | `"M8"` |
| 3 |   |
| 4 |   |
| 5 |   |
| 6 | `"M4"` |
| 7 | `"M5"` |
| 8 | `"M6"` |

`FrontOfQueue` = 6

`EndOfQueue` = 2

(i) State the number of data items currently in the queue.

[1]

(ii) State the index of the array element that will store the next data item added to the queue.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) 5 **[1]**

(ii) 3 **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for 5 in part (i)
> 
> **1 mark** for 3 in part (ii)

parts.problemMd:
A help desk program stores the reference numbers of customers who are waiting to speak to a support agent. The reference numbers are stored in a queue Abstract Data Type (ADT).

The queue is implemented as a circular queue using a 1D array of eight elements, declared in pseudocode as `DECLARE CustQueue : ARRAY[1:8] OF STRING`.

The queue works as follows.

- The pointer `FrontOfQueue` stores the index of the reference number that will be removed next.
- The pointer `EndOfQueue` stores the index of the reference number added most recently.
- The variable `NumItems` stores how many reference numbers are in the queue.
- When either pointer moves on from element 8, it goes back to element 1.

When a support agent is free, the procedure `TakeNext()` removes the next reference number from the queue and outputs it.

Describe the algorithm for `TakeNext()` in **four** steps.

Do not use pseudocode statements in your answer.

Step 1 ..............................................................................................

Step 2 ..............................................................................................

Step 3 ..............................................................................................

Step 4 ..............................................................................................
parts.solutionMd:
Step 1: Check that the queue is not empty. If `NumItems` is 0, stop. **[1]**

Step 2: Output the reference number stored in the array element at the index stored in `FrontOfQueue`. **[1]**

Step 3: Increment `FrontOfQueue`. If `FrontOfQueue` is now 9, set it to 1. **[1]**

Step 4: Decrement `NumItems`. **[1]**

`EndOfQueue` does not change, because removing a reference number only affects the front of the queue.

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any four from:**
> 
> - checking that the queue is not empty // `NumItems` is not 0, and stopping if it is empty
> - outputting the reference number in the array element at the index stored in `FrontOfQueue`
> - incrementing `FrontOfQueue`
> - setting `FrontOfQueue` to 1 when it goes past 8 // when it becomes 9
> - decrementing `NumItems`
>

Identify the error and suggest a correction.
parts.solutionMd:
Error: the message `"Access denied"` is output every time this pseudocode runs, including when `CardValid` is `TRUE`, because the second `OUTPUT` statement is outside the IF construct. **[1]**

Correction: put the second `OUTPUT` statement in an `ELSE` clause of the same IF construct. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for identifying that `"Access denied"` is output whatever the value of `CardValid` // that both messages are output when `CardValid` is `TRUE` // that the final `OUTPUT` statement is not inside the IF construct
> 
> **1 mark** for a correction that places `OUTPUT "Access denied"` in an `ELSE` clause of the existing IF construct
> 
> Accept a correction that adds a second IF construct testing the opposite condition, for example `IF CardValid = FALSE THEN`, then `OUTPUT "Access denied"`, then `ENDIF`. This gives the same output for both possible values of `CardValid`.
> 
> Accept `IF CardValid THEN` in place of `IF CardValid = TRUE THEN`.
> 
> Do not accept a correction that simply deletes the second `OUTPUT` statement. The program must still report a card that is not valid.
> 
> Do not accept "the indentation is wrong". Indentation does not decide which statements belong to an IF construct in 9618 pseudocode. `ENDIF` does.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Trace a selection construct with every possible value, not only the value the question seems to be about. The fault here shows up when `CardValid` is `TRUE`, which is the case most students check last.
> 
> Look for the `ENDIF`, not for the indentation. In 9618 pseudocode the indentation is there to help you read the code, and it may be left out when line numbers are used. `ENDIF` is what actually closes an IF construct, so anything written after it runs every time.

parts.problemMd:
A weather station has a program that decides whether visitors may enter.

The program has already input two variables:

- `WindSpeed`, of type `INTEGER`, holding the wind speed in kilometres per hour
- `Visibility`, of type `INTEGER`, holding the visibility in metres

The program must output exactly one message, chosen as follows.

- If the wind speed is greater than 80, output `"Station closed"`.
- Otherwise, if the visibility is less than 200, output `"Restricted access"`.
- Otherwise, output `"Station open"`.

Write the pseudocode selection statement for this.

You must use nested IF statements.
parts.solutionMd:
**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for an outer `IF WindSpeed > 80 THEN` that outputs `"Station closed"`
> 
> **1 mark** for an `ELSE` containing a second IF construct that tests `Visibility < 200` and outputs `"Restricted access"`
> 
> **1 mark** for the inner `ELSE` outputting `"Station open"`, with both constructs closed by `ENDIF`
> 
> Accept the outer test written as `IF WindSpeed <= 80 THEN` with the two branches swapped over, provided the nesting still produces exactly one message.
> 
> Accept the messages written with or without a preceding prompt.
> 
> Do not accept `WindSpeed >= 80`. A wind speed of exactly 80 is not greater than 80, so the station is not closed.
> 
> Do not accept `Visibility <= 200`. A visibility of exactly 200 metres is not less than 200, so the station is open.
> 
> Do not accept three separate IF constructs in place of the nesting. The question requires nested IF statements.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each "otherwise" in a specification is an `ELSE`, and every "otherwise" after the first opens a new IF construct inside that `ELSE`. 9618 pseudocode has no `ELSE IF` keyword, so you cannot join the two tests on one line, and each `IF` you write needs its own `ENDIF`. Count your `ENDIF` lines against your `IF` lines before you move on.
> 
> Then check the two boundary values named in the question. A wind speed of 80 and a visibility of 200 must both leave the station open, so the conditions are `> 80` and `< 200`, not `>= 80` and `<= 200`.

A program will:

1. input the mass of the parcel in kilograms and the delivery zone
2. output the message `"Parcel refused"` if the mass is greater than 30, and work out no cost
3. otherwise work out the cost, which is 5.00 for a mass of 10 or less and 9.00 for any greater mass
4. double the cost if the delivery zone is `"International"`
5. output the cost.

The program handles one parcel only.

Write pseudocode for the program.

You must declare all variables used.
parts.solutionMd:
**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for declaring `Mass` and `Cost` as `REAL` and `Zone` as `STRING`
> 
> **1 mark** for inputting a mass and a delivery zone
> 
> **1 mark** for `IF Mass > 30 THEN` outputting `"Parcel refused"`, followed by an `ELSE`
> 
> **1 mark** for a selection inside the `ELSE` that assigns 5.00 when the mass is 10 or less and 9.00 otherwise
> 
> **1 mark** for a further selection inside the `ELSE` that doubles `Cost` when `Zone` is `"International"`
> 
> **1 mark** for outputting `Cost` inside the `ELSE`, with every IF construct closed by `ENDIF`
> 
> Accept two separate IF constructs, `IF Mass > 30 THEN` and then `IF Mass <= 30 THEN`, in place of the `ELSE`. This produces the same output for every mass.
> 
> Accept `Cost ← Cost + Cost` or `Cost ← Cost * 2.0` for the doubling.
> 
> Accept a prompt before each `INPUT` statement, or no prompt at all.
> 
> Accept the cost output with or without a message.
> 
> Do not accept `Mass` declared as `INTEGER`. A mass of 12.4 kilograms could not then be stored.
> 
> Do not accept `Mass >= 30` for the refusal test. A parcel of exactly 30 kilograms is accepted and costs 9.00.
> 
> Do not accept `Mass < 10` for the 5.00 band. A parcel of exactly 10 kilograms costs 5.00.
> 
> Do not accept the doubling or the final output placed after the last `ENDIF`. A refused parcel must not have a cost worked out or output.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The marks most often lost here are about where a statement sits, not about what it says. The doubling and the final output both belong inside the `ELSE`. A student who writes them after the last `ENDIF` prices a parcel the company has already refused, and a program that both refuses a parcel and quotes a price for it cannot gain the final mark.
> 
> Check the two boundary values the question names, 10 and 30, against your conditions before you finish. `>` and `>=` give different answers for exactly those two masses, and the question tells you which one it wants with the wording "greater than 30" and "10 or less".

parts.problemMd:
A program contains the following pseudocode.

Complete the table by writing the answer for each row.

| Statement | Answer |
|---|---|
| The number of times the statement `Total ← Total + Position` is executed |   |
| The last value taken by `Position` inside the loop |   |
| The value that is output |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Statement | Answer |
|---|---|
| The number of times the statement `Total ← Total + Position` is executed | **4** |
| The last value taken by `Position` inside the loop | **11** |
| The value that is output | **26** |

`Position` takes the values 2, 5, 8 and 11, so the loop body runs 4 times. **[1]**

The last of those values is 11, because the next value would be 14, which is past the end value. **[1]**

The total is 2 + 5 + 8 + 11, which is 26. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for 4 in the first row
> 
> **1 mark** for 11 in the second row
> 
> **1 mark** for 26 in the third row
> 
> Accept the list 2, 5, 8, 11 written in the first row in place of the number 4.
> 
> Do not accept 10 in the first row. That is the answer when `STEP 3` is ignored and `Position` is treated as counting up in ones.
> 
> Do not accept 14 in the second row. `Position` reaches 14 only by passing the end value of 11, and the loop stops before the body runs again.
> 
> Do not accept 65 in the third row, which is the total of every whole number from 2 to 11.

> **[exam-tip]**
> `STEP` changes the size of each jump, not the end value. The loop body runs for every value from the start value upwards that has not passed the end value, so here it runs for 2, 5, 8 and 11 and then stops. Write the values out as a list before you count them, because working the number of iterations out in your head from 2, 11 and 3 is where most marks are lost.
> 
> The end value does not have to be reached exactly. If the end value had been 12 instead of 11, `Position` would still take the values 2, 5, 8 and 11, and all three answers would be unchanged.

parts.problemMd:
A college converts an examination mark into an award. Marks are whole numbers from 0 to 100.

| Mark | Award |
|---|---|
| 0 to 49 | Fail |
| 50 to 69 | Pass |
| 70 to 89 | Merit |
| 90 to 100 | Distinction |

Part of the program is written in pseudocode as follows. Two clause values are missing.

Complete the pseudocode by writing the two missing clause values.
parts.solutionMd:
The first missing clause value is `50 TO 69` **[1]** and the second is `70 TO 89` **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `50 TO 69`
> 
> **1 mark** for `70 TO 89`
> 
> Accept each clause value written with or without its colon.
> 
> Accept a comparison in place of a range where it gives the same award for every mark from 0 to 100, for example `<= 69` as the second clause value and `<= 89` as the third. The earlier clauses have already dealt with the lower marks.
> 
> Do not accept `50 TO 70` or `70 TO 90`. A range in a CASE clause includes both of its end values, so these overlap the clause that follows, and the marks 70 and 90 would be given the wrong award.
> 
> Do not accept `50 TO 68` or `70 TO 88`. The marks 69 and 89 would then match no clause at all and `Award` would keep whatever value it already held.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A range in a CASE clause includes both of its end values, so `50 TO 69` and `70 TO 89` must not share a number. Writing `50 TO 70` is the usual slip and it produces no error message at all: the mark 70 simply gets the wrong award, because the clauses are tested in order and the first clause that applies is the one that runs.
> 
> Check your bands against the table by listing the end values, here 49, 50, 69, 70, 89 and 90. Every mark from 0 to 100 should match exactly one clause, with no mark left out and no mark in two clauses.

parts.problemMd:
A hotel stores the number of bookings it took last year. The data is held in a global two-dimensional array that is declared as follows.

The first index is the month number, from 1 to 12. The second index is the room type, from 1 to 4.

For example, `Bookings[3, 2]` holds the number of bookings taken in month 3 for room type 2.

A procedure `MonthTotals()` will output, for each month in turn, the month number followed by the total number of bookings taken in that month across all four room types. The procedure produces 12 lines of output.

Write pseudocode for the procedure `MonthTotals()`.

You must declare all local variables that you use.
parts.solutionMd:
**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the procedure heading `PROCEDURE MonthTotals()` together with the closing `ENDPROCEDURE`
> 
> **1 mark** for declaring every local variable used, as `INTEGER`
> 
> **1 mark** for an outer count-controlled loop running from 1 to 12
> 
> **1 mark** for setting the running total to 0 inside the outer loop, before the inner loop
> 
> **1 mark** for an inner count-controlled loop running from 1 to 4 that adds `Bookings[Month, RoomType]` to the running total
> 
> **1 mark** for outputting the month number and that month's total together, inside the outer loop and after the inner loop
> 
> Accept either loop, or both, written as a conditional loop, provided the control variable is set before the loop and increased inside it. For example:
> 
> Accept any `OUTPUT` statement that gives the month number and that month's total on the same line, with or without a message.
> 
> Do not accept `Total ← 0` placed before the outer loop. The total then carries over from one month to the next, so only the first month's figure is correct.
> 
> Do not accept the `OUTPUT` statement placed inside the inner loop. That produces 48 lines of output instead of 12.
> 
> Do not accept the two loops swapped so that `RoomType` is the outer loop. That gives a total for each room type across the whole year, which is not what the procedure must do.
> 
> Do not accept index ranges of 0 to 11 and 0 to 3. The array is declared `ARRAY[1:12, 1:4]`, so both indices start at 1.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mark lost most often in a nested count-controlled loop is the one for resetting the running total. Ask yourself how many times the total must go back to zero. It must go back to zero once for every month, so it belongs inside the outer loop and above the inner loop, never before the outer loop.
> 
> Decide what one line of output looks like before you write any code, then place the `OUTPUT` statement where exactly that happens once per month. Inside the inner loop it gives four lines per month; after `NEXT Month` it gives a single line for the whole year.

parts.problemMd:
A robot moves along a single track in a warehouse. An operator types one character at a time to control it.

The program stores the character in a variable `Command` of type `CHAR`. Three global variables have already been declared and given values:

- `Position`, of type `INTEGER`
- `Moving`, of type `BOOLEAN`
- `Errors`, of type `INTEGER`

The program must respond to `Command` as follows.

| Command | Action |
|---|---|
| F | add 1 to Position |
| B | subtract 1 from Position |
| H | set Moving to FALSE and set Position to 0 |
| any other character | add 1 to Errors |

Write a CASE structure for this.
parts.solutionMd:
**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `CASE OF Command` with a matching `ENDCASE`, and the `'F'` and `'B'` clauses each written as a character value, a colon and a correct statement
> 
> **1 mark** for the `'H'` clause carrying both of its statements
> 
> **1 mark** for an `OTHERWISE` clause, written last, that adds 1 to `Errors`
> 
> Accept the character values written in double quotes, for example `"F"`.
> 
> Accept the `'F'` and `'B'` clauses in either order.
> 
> Accept `Position ← Position - 1` written as `Position ← Position + (-1)`.
> 
> Do not accept a `BREAK` or `EXIT` statement at the end of a clause. A 9618 CASE clause needs none, and neither keyword exists in this pseudocode.
> 
> Do not accept `OTHERWISE` placed anywhere other than last. An `OTHERWISE` clause runs when no earlier clause applies, so it must be the final clause.
> 
> Do not accept the `'H'` clause written with only one of its two statements.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A CASE clause may carry as many statements as it needs, written one under the next and lined up after the colon. Students who have met other languages often add a break or exit line at the end of every clause, or move the two `'H'` statements into a separate IF construct. Neither is needed here, and neither earns the mark.
> 
> `Command` holds a single character, so each clause value is a character literal in single quotes. Remember that a lower case `f` is a different character from `'F'`, so it would fall through to the `OTHERWISE` clause and be counted as an error.

parts.problemMd:
A warehouse program counts how many full packs of 10 items can be made from a quantity of loose items.

State the value that is output in each of the following two cases.

Case 1: the value 35 is input.

Case 2: the value 7 is input.
parts.solutionMd:
Case 1: the value output is 3 **[1]**

Case 2: the value output is 0 **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for 3 in Case 1
> 
> **1 mark** for 0 in Case 2
> 
> Accept working shown alongside either answer, for example `Stock` taking the values 35, 25, 15 and then 5.
> 
> Do not accept 4 in Case 1. After three subtractions `Stock` holds 5, the condition `Stock >= 10` is FALSE, and the loop stops without a fourth pack.
> 
> Do not accept 1 in Case 2. `WHILE` is a pre-condition loop, so the condition is tested before the first pass. `7 >= 10` is FALSE, the body never runs, and `Packs` keeps the value 0 it was given before the loop.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Case 2 is the one students get wrong, because they assume every loop runs at least once. That is true of a post-condition loop, written `REPEAT ... UNTIL`, and false of a pre-condition loop, written `WHILE ... ENDWHILE`. If this loop were written as `REPEAT ... UNTIL Stock < 10` instead, an input of 7 would output 1 and leave `Stock` holding -3.
> 
> Before tracing any pre-condition loop, test the condition once using the starting values. If it is already FALSE, the answer is simply whatever the variables held before the loop.

parts.problemMd:
A shop gives every product a four-digit code, which is stored in an integer variable `Code`. Every code is in the range 1000 to 9999.

The first digit of the code identifies the department.

| First digit | Department |
|---|---|
| 1 | Books |
| 2 | Music |
| 3 | Films |
| 4 to 9 | Warehouse |

A variable `Dept` of type `STRING` has already been declared.

Write a CASE structure that assigns the correct department name to `Dept`.
parts.solutionMd:
**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a selector that isolates the first digit using integer division, written as `Code DIV 1000`
> 
> **1 mark** for the three clause values `1`, `2` and `3` assigning `"Books"`, `"Music"` and `"Films"` respectively
> 
> **1 mark** for a final clause covering the first digits 4 to 9, for example `4 TO 9`, assigning `"Warehouse"`
> 
> **1 mark** for `CASE OF` closed by `ENDCASE`, with `Dept` assigned a value in every clause
> 
> Accept the selector written with or without the brackets, so `CASE OF Code DIV 1000` is also correct.
> 
> Accept `INT(Code / 1000)` as the selector. `INT()` takes the integer part, which for a code in the range 1000 to 9999 gives the same digit as `DIV`.
> 
> Accept `OTHERWISE : Dept ← "Warehouse"` in place of the `4 TO 9` clause. Every code is in the range 1000 to 9999, so the only first digits that can reach that clause are 4 to 9.
> 
> Accept a selector that takes the first character of the code as a string, with the clause values written as characters and an `OTHERWISE` clause for the rest:
> 
> Do not accept `Code MOD 1000`. `MOD` gives the remainder after division, which is the last three digits, so the code 3456 would give 456 and match no clause.
> 
> Do not accept `Code DIV 100`. That gives 34 for the code 3456, not 3.
> 
> Do not accept clause values written as ranges such as `1000 TO 1999` alongside a selector of `Code DIV 1000`. The selector has already reduced the code to a single digit.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When every clause of a CASE would otherwise be a range of the same width, look for an expression that turns the value into the single number the clause needs. `DIV` is the operator that does this and it is listed on the insert you are given in the exam. The usual error is to reach for `MOD`: `MOD` keeps the digits at the right-hand end of a number and `DIV` keeps the digits at the left-hand end.
> 
> A range clause includes both of its end values, so `4 TO 9` covers the first digits 4 and 9 as well as everything between them.

parts.problemMd:
An operator enters temperature readings into a program. A reading is accepted only if it is a whole number from -40 to 60 inclusive.

The program must:

- prompt the operator and input a reading
- keep asking until an acceptable reading is entered
- count how many readings the operator entered altogether
- output the accepted reading and the number of readings entered.

Complete the pseudocode by writing the missing part at each of the three gaps.
parts.solutionMd:
Gap (i) is `Tries ← 0` **[1]**

Gap (ii) is `Tries ← Tries + 1` **[1]**

Gap (iii) is `Temp >= -40 AND Temp <= 60` **[1]**

The completed post-condition loop is:

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for gap (i) setting the attempt counter to 0 before the loop, as `Tries ← 0`
> 
> **1 mark** for gap (ii) increasing the attempt counter by 1 inside the loop, as `Tries ← Tries + 1`
> 
> **1 mark** for gap (iii) giving a condition that is TRUE only for a reading from -40 to 60 inclusive, as `Temp >= -40 AND Temp <= 60`
> 
> Accept `NOT (Temp < -40 OR Temp > 60)` or `Temp > -41 AND Temp < 61` in gap (iii). For a whole number, all three forms accept exactly the same set of values.
> 
> Do not accept `Temp < -40 OR Temp > 60` in gap (iii). `UNTIL` ends the loop when its condition is TRUE, so that form ends the loop on every reading that should be rejected and repeats for every reading that should be accepted.
> 
> Do not accept `Temp > -40 AND Temp < 60` in gap (iii). The range is inclusive, so -40 and 60 must both be accepted.
> 
> Do not accept gap (i) written inside the loop. `Tries` would return to 0 on every pass and the final output would always be 1.

> **[exam-tip]**
> `UNTIL` states when the loop stops, not when it carries on. Students write the rejection test here out of habit, because `WHILE` takes the opposite condition. Read the line as "keep going until this becomes true", then check it once with an acceptable value and once with an unacceptable value before moving on.
> 
> A post-condition loop suits input validation because the operator has to be asked at least once. A pre-condition loop would test `Temp` before any value had been entered at all.

parts.problemMd:
A biology program models the growth of a colony of cells. The number of cells doubles once every hour.

A function `HoursToReach()` will:

- take two parameters of type INTEGER, the starting number of cells and a target number of cells
- work out how many whole hours pass before the number of cells first becomes greater than the target
- return that number of hours.

If the starting number of cells is already greater than the target, the function returns 0.

Assume the starting number of cells is always 1 or more.

For example, `HoursToReach(1, 10)` returns 4, because the colony grows 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 16 is the first value greater than 10.

Write pseudocode for the function `HoursToReach()`.

You must declare all local variables that you use, and you must use a conditional loop.
parts.solutionMd:
**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the function heading with two `INTEGER` parameters and `RETURNS INTEGER`, together with the closing `ENDFUNCTION`
> 
> **1 mark** for declaring both local variables as `INTEGER`
> 
> **1 mark** for setting the running cell count to the starting value and the hour count to 0 before the loop
> 
> **1 mark** for a conditional loop that continues while the running cell count is not greater than `Target`
> 
> **1 mark** for doubling the running cell count inside the loop
> 
> **1 mark** for increasing the hour count by 1 inside the loop and returning it after the loop
> 
> Accept `WHILE NOT (Cells > Target)` in place of `WHILE Cells <= Target`. The two conditions are logically equivalent.
> 
> Accept `Cells ← Cells + Cells` in place of `Cells ← Cells * 2`.
> 
> Accept the parameter `StartCells` used directly as the running value, with no separate local variable for it.
> 
> Do not accept a post-condition loop such as `REPEAT ... UNTIL Cells > Target`. Its body always runs once, so a colony that already exceeds the target returns 1 rather than 0.
> 
> Do not accept `WHILE Cells < Target`. That stops while the count is still only equal to the target, and equal is not greater. `HoursToReach(5, 10)` then returns 1 instead of 2.
> 
> Do not accept a `FOR` loop. The number of hours is not known before the function runs, so a count-controlled loop cannot be used here.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Test your loop condition against the case where the loop must not run at all. This function has to return 0 when the colony already exceeds the target, and only a pre-condition loop can do that. `REPEAT ... UNTIL` returns 1 in that case and costs two marks, because the body runs before the condition is ever tested.
> 
> The other trap is writing `<` where `<=` is needed. The function counts the hours until the colony becomes greater than the target, so a colony that exactly equals the target has not finished growing and must double once more. Read the wording of the task twice before choosing between the two operators.

[1]

(ii) Describe the benefits of your answer to part **(b)(i)** with reference to this program.

[3]

parts.problemMd:
A program prints address labels for a delivery company.

Two of the values used by the program never change while the program runs:

- the character that is printed in every empty position on a label, which is the asterisk character
- the width of one label in centimetres, which is 4.5

Write a pseudocode statement to declare each of these two values.

Choose a suitable identifier for each one.
parts.solutionMd:
**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a constant declaration of the fill character, in the form `CONSTANT <identifier> = '*'`
> 
> **1 mark** for a constant declaration of the label width, in the form `CONSTANT <identifier> = 4.5`
> 
> Accept any identifier that describes the value it holds and follows the naming rules, so letters, digits and the underscore character only, starting with a letter.
> 
> Accept `"*"` written in double quotes. A string of length 1 may be treated as either `CHAR` or `STRING`.
> 
> Do not accept a declaration that uses the assignment arrow, such as `CONSTANT FillChar ← '*'`. A constant declaration uses `=`.
> 
> Do not accept `DECLARE FillChar : CHAR` followed by a separate assignment statement. That creates a variable, and its value could then be changed while the program runs.
> 
> Do not accept a value that is not a literal, such as `CONSTANT LabelWidth = MaxWidth / 2`. Only a literal may be used as the value of a constant.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A constant is declared in one single statement, and the value is part of that statement. Students very often write the name on one line and the value on the next, the way they would set up a variable, and lose the mark because a value written that way can be changed later.
> 
> Watch the quote marks and the decimal point. One character goes between single quotes, such as `'*'`, and text of more than one character between double quotes, such as `"Label"`. A real number must have at least one digit on each side of the decimal point, so write `4.5`, never `4.` or `.5`.

parts.problemMd:
A program manages the loan of books in a public library.

Complete the identifier table for four of the values that the program stores.

| Example value | Explanation | Variable name | Data type |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Kigali" | The city in which the library branch is located |   |   |
| TRUE | A value that shows whether the book is on loan at the moment |   |   |
| 14/03/2026 | The day on which the book must be returned |   |   |
| 2.75 | The fine in dollars charged for each day a book is returned late |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Example value | Explanation | Variable name | Data type |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Kigali" | The city in which the library branch is located | **BranchCity** | **STRING** |
| TRUE | A value that shows whether the book is on loan at the moment | **OnLoan** | **BOOLEAN** |
| 14/03/2026 | The day on which the book must be returned | **DueDate** | **DATE** |
| 2.75 | The fine in dollars charged for each day a book is returned late | **DailyFine** | **REAL** |

Row 1: a suitable identifier such as `BranchCity`, with data type `STRING`. **[1]**

Row 2: a suitable identifier such as `OnLoan`, with data type `BOOLEAN`. **[1]**

Row 3: a suitable identifier such as `DueDate`, with data type `DATE`. **[1]**

Row 4: a suitable identifier such as `DailyFine`, with data type `REAL`. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for row 1: a suitable identifier together with the data type `STRING`
> 
> **1 mark** for row 2: a suitable identifier together with the data type `BOOLEAN`
> 
> **1 mark** for row 3: a suitable identifier together with the data type `DATE`
> 
> **1 mark** for row 4: a suitable identifier together with the data type `REAL`
> 
> Each mark needs both the identifier and the data type to be correct.
> 
> Accept any identifier that describes the value it holds and follows the naming rules, so letters, digits and the underscore character only, starting with a letter.
> 
> Do not accept `CHAR` for row 1. A `CHAR` holds exactly one character and `"Kigali"` holds six.
> 
> Do not accept `STRING` for row 3. The `DATE` data type exists in this pseudocode, and a date held as a string cannot be used with the date functions on the insert.
> 
> Do not accept `INTEGER` for row 4. The value 2.75 has a fractional part.
> 
> Do not accept a single letter such as `C` as an identifier here. The identifier must describe the value it holds.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two rows lose marks again and again. The date is written as `STRING` because it contains slashes and looks like text, and the fine is written as `INTEGER` because money often is. Ask yourself what the program will need to do with the value: if it has to work out which month a date falls in, it must be a `DATE`, and if a value can end in 75 cents, it must be a `REAL`.
> 
> Give the variable a name that says what it holds. `DueDate` earns the mark, `D` does not, and a name with a space in it such as `Due Date` is not a legal identifier.

parts.problemMd:
A program calculates the cost of the water that a household has used in one month.

The program already contains this declaration:

The identifier `UnitCost` holds the cost in dollars of one unit of water. A water meter always shows a whole number of units.

The program must:

- declare every variable that it uses
- prompt for and input the meter reading taken at the start of the month
- prompt for and input the meter reading taken at the end of the month
- calculate the number of units used, which is the reading at the end minus the reading at the start
- calculate the total cost, which is the number of units used multiplied by the cost of one unit
- output the total cost together with a suitable message.

Write pseudocode for the program.

You do not need to check that the readings are valid. You must not declare `UnitCost` again.
parts.solutionMd:
**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for declaring every variable used, each with a suitable data type
> 
> **1 mark** for a prompt followed by an input of the start reading
> 
> **1 mark** for a prompt followed by an input of the end reading
> 
> **1 mark** for calculating the units used as the end reading minus the start reading
> 
> **1 mark** for calculating the total cost using `UnitCost`, and outputting it with a message
> 
> Accept the declarations written as four separate `DECLARE` statements.
> 
> Accept the two calculations combined into one statement, for example:
> 
> Where the calculations are combined, the variable `UnitsUsed` is not needed and does not have to be declared.
> 
> Accept any sensible identifiers, and any sensible wording for the prompts and the message.
> 
> Do not accept `TotalCost` declared as `INTEGER`. An `INTEGER` multiplied by a `REAL` gives a `REAL`, so a cost such as 38.25 would be lost.
> 
> Do not accept a declaration of `UnitCost`. It is already declared as a constant, and declaring it again as a variable would allow its value to change.
> 
> Do not accept an `INPUT` statement with no `OUTPUT` prompt before it.
> 
> Do not accept `UnitsUsed ← StartReading - EndReading`. That subtraction is the wrong way round and gives a negative number of units.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most expensive mistake here is multiplying a meter reading by the unit cost. A meter reading is a running total of everything the household has ever used, so only the difference between the two readings belongs to this month.
> 
> The other mark that goes missing is the prompt. In this pseudocode `INPUT` takes an identifier and nothing else, so `INPUT "Enter the reading", StartReading` is not valid. Write the prompt as a separate `OUTPUT` statement on the line above.

parts.problemMd:
A program controls the entry barrier at a car park. It uses the `INTEGER` variables `Count` and `Limit`.

Two conditions in the program are written as follows.

Condition 1: `(Count > Limit) OR (Count = Limit)`

Condition 2: `NOT (Count >= Limit)`

Write each condition in its simplest form.

Each answer must use one comparison operator only.
parts.solutionMd:
Condition 1: `Count >= Limit` **[1]**

Condition 2: `Count < Limit` **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `Count >= Limit`
> 
> **1 mark** for `Count < Limit`
> 
> Accept the operands written the other way round, so `Limit <= Count` for condition 1 and `Limit > Count` for condition 2.
> 
> Do not accept `Count > Limit` for condition 1. That answer is `FALSE` when the two values are equal, but the original condition is `TRUE`.
> 
> Do not accept `Count <= Limit` for condition 2. That answer is `TRUE` when the two values are equal, but the original condition is `FALSE`.
> 
> Do not accept an answer that still contains `NOT`, `AND` or `OR`. The question asks for one comparison operator only.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both marks turn on the case where the two values are equal, and that is exactly the case students skip. Test every answer you write three times: once with `Count` below `Limit`, once with the two equal, and once with `Count` above.
> 
> `NOT` in front of a comparison flips it completely, it does not simply relax it. The opposite of `>=` is `<`, never `<=`. Getting this wrong builds an off by one error into the program that shows up on only one value in a million inputs.

parts.problemMd:
A cinema has 200 seats, numbered 1 to 200.

A program stores the number of a seat in the `INTEGER` variable `SeatNum`, and whether that seat has already been booked in the `BOOLEAN` variable `Booked`.

A seat may be reserved only when all three of the following are true:

- the seat number is an even number
- the seat has not already been booked
- the seat number is either less than 50 or greater than 150.

Write a single pseudocode condition that evaluates to `TRUE` only when a seat may be reserved.

Use only the operators given on the insert.
parts.solutionMd:
**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for testing that the seat number is even, using `SeatNum MOD 2 = 0`
> 
> **1 mark** for testing that the seat has not been booked, using `NOT Booked`
> 
> **1 mark** for testing the two ranges with `OR` inside brackets, and joining all three tests with `AND`
> 
> Accept `Booked = FALSE` in place of `NOT Booked`.
> 
> Accept `SeatNum MOD 2 <> 1` in place of `SeatNum MOD 2 = 0`.
> 
> Accept the three tests written in any order, and the whole condition written inside an `IF ... THEN` statement.
> 
> Do not accept `SeatNum MOD 2 = 1`. That is `TRUE` for odd seat numbers.
> 
> Do not accept `(SeatNum < 50) AND (SeatNum > 150)`. No seat number can be both, so the condition would never be `TRUE`.
> 
> Do not accept `Booked` on its own in place of `NOT Booked`.
> 
> The brackets around the `OR` test are part of the third marking point. This pseudocode sets no order of precedence for `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`, so without brackets the condition can be read in two different ways.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word "either" in the third rule means `OR`, and students write `AND` there because the three rules above it are joined by "all three of the following are true". Read carefully: the three rules are joined by `AND`, but the two halves of the third rule are joined by `OR`.
> 
> `MOD` gives the remainder, so an even number is one where `SeatNum MOD 2` gives 0. Write that comparison with 0 out in full. `SeatNum MOD 2` on its own is a number, not a `BOOLEAN`, so it cannot be joined to the rest of the condition with `AND`.

parts.problemMd:
A program calculates the average of a set of test marks. The marks have already been added together.

The program should:

- input the total of all the marks and the number of marks
- calculate the average mark, which may have a fractional part
- set `Valid` to `TRUE` only when the average is 40 or more and 100 or less
- set `Top` to `TRUE` when the average is 90 or more
- build a message that joins the text `"Average mark: "` to the average
- output the message.

The pseudocode below contains four errors. Each error is caused by the incorrect use of an operator. Line numbers are for reference only.

Identify each error and state the correction required.
parts.solutionMd:
Line 08: `DIV` gives only the whole number part of a division, so the fractional part of the average is thrown away. It should be the division operator, giving `Average ← Total / Count`. **[1]**

Line 09: `OR` is the wrong logical operator and makes the condition `TRUE` for every possible average. It should be `Valid ← (Average >= 40) AND (Average <= 100)`. **[1]**

Line 10: `>` leaves out an average of exactly 90, which should count as a top mark. It should be `Top ← Average >= 90`. **[1]**

Line 11: `+` adds two numbers and cannot join two strings. It should be the concatenation operator, giving: **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for line 08: `DIV` should be `/`
> 
> **1 mark** for line 09: `OR` should be `AND`
> 
> **1 mark** for line 10: `>` should be `>=`
> 
> **1 mark** for line 11: `+` should be `&`
> 
> Each mark needs the line to be identified and the correction to be given. Accept the corrected statement written out in full instead of naming the operator on its own.
> 
> Accept "integer division" or "whole number division" as a description of `DIV`.
> 
> Do not accept a correction of line 08 that uses `INT()`. That also throws the fractional part away.
> 
> Do not accept a change to line 02. `Average` is correctly declared as `REAL`, and the fault is the operator used on line 08.
> 
> Do not accept `Top ← Average > 89` as the correction on line 10. `Average` is a `REAL`, so an average of 89.5 would then be treated as a top mark.
> 
> Do not accept a fifth error. Lines 06, 07 and 12 are correct.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work from the list of requirements, not from the code. Each error is only an error because the code does something different from what the list says, and line 09 proves it: `(Average >= 40) OR (Average <= 100)` is perfectly legal pseudocode, it is just always `TRUE`, so `Valid` never becomes `FALSE`.
> 
> Two habits picked up from other languages cost marks here. `+` joins text in many programming languages, but in this pseudocode `+` is arithmetic only and `&` is the operator that joins strings. And `DIV` is not a neater way of writing `/`, it is a different operator that discards the remainder, so 290 `DIV` 7 gives 41 while 290 `/` 7 gives 41.428571.

parts.problemMd:
A program uses three global integer variables` HH, MM` and `SS` to represent the current time in hours, minutes and seconds using the 24-hour clock notation.

Midnight would be represented as 00:00:00 (`HH:MM:SS`). If the variables `HH, MM` and `SS` contained the values 16, 30 and 10 respectively, then the time would be 16:30:10 or just after 4.30 in the afternoon.

A procedure `Tick() `will be called every second. 
The procedure `Tick() `will:

- update the value in `SS` each time it is called
- update the values in `HH` and `MM` as appropriate
- call a procedure `CheckAlarm()` at the start of each minute
- call a procedure `NewDay()` whenever the time reaches midnight.

Complete the pseudocode for procedure `Tick(). `

`PROCEDURE Tick()`
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Example solution:
> 
> `PROCEDURE Tick() `
> `   SS `$\leftarrow$` SS + 1 `
> `   IF SS = 60 THEN `
> `      SS `$\leftarrow$` 0 `
>                  `MM `$\leftarrow$` MM + 1 `
> `      IF MM = 60 THEN `
> `         MM `$\leftarrow$` 0 `
> `         HH `$\leftarrow$` HH + 1`
> `         IF HH = 24 THEN `
> `            HH `$\leftarrow$` 0 `
> `            CALL NewDay() `
> `         ENDIF `
> `      ENDIF `
> `      CALL CheckAlarm() `
> `   ENDIF `
> 
> `ENDPROCEDURE `
> 
> Mark as follows:
> 
> 1. Increment SS anywhere in the code
> 2. Call `CheckAlarm() `when <u>SS is set to zero</u>
> 3. Test if `SS` = 60 anywhere in the code … if so:
> 4. set `SS` to 0
> 5. increment `MM`

parts.problemMd:
A program is being developed to process bank card information.

When a card number is displayed, all the characters except the last four are replaced with the asterisk character '*'.

Card numbers are stored as strings. The strings are between 10 and 20 characters in length.

The function Conceal() will take a string representing a card number and return a modified string.

Example strings:

| **Original string** | **Modified string** |
|---|---|
| "1234567890" | "******7890" |
| "1234567897652" | "*********7652" |
| "1234567890123456" | "************3456" |

The function Conceal() will:

- take a numeric string as a parameter representing the card number
- return a string in which the asterisk character replaces all except the last four characters of the card number parameter.

Write pseudocode for the function Conceal().
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Example ‘loop solution’:
> 
> `FUNCTION Conceal(CardNumber : STRING) RETURNS STRING `
> `   DECLARE MaskedString : STRING `
> `   DECLARE Count : INTEGER `
> `   CONSTANT Asterisk = '*' `
> 
> `   MaskedString `$\leftarrow$` RIGHT(CardNumber, 4) `
> `   FOR Count `$\leftarrow$` 1 TO LENGTH(CardNumber) - 4   `
> `       MaskedString `$\leftarrow$`Asterisk & MaskedString `
> `   NEXT Count `
> 
> `   RETURN MaskedString `
> 
> `ENDFUNCTION `
> 
> Mark as follows: 
> **MP1** Function heading and parameter and ending and return type 
> **MP2** Declaration of all local variables used - including the loop counter 
> **MP3** Calculate number of digits to mask / number of asterisks required 
> **MP4** use of a ‘relevant’ Loop 
> **MP5** Correct number of iterations 
> **MP6** Concatenate asterisk to start/end of `MaskedString `in a loop 
> **MP7** Assign last four characters to `MaskedString //` Concatenate the retained original last four digits 
> **MP8** Return masked string
> 
> **Max 6 marks**
> 
> ALTERNATIVE ‘non loop’ solution:
> 
> `FUNCTION Conceal(CardNumber : STRING) RETURNS STRING `
> `   DECLARE MaskedString : STRING `
> `   DECLARE Count : INTEGER `
> `   CONSTANT Asterisks = "********************" //20 asterisks `
> `   Count `$\leftarrow$`LENGTH(CardNumber) - 4 `
> `   MaskedString `$\leftarrow$` LEFT(Asterisks, Count) & RIGHT(CardNumber, 4) `
> `   RETURN MaskedString `
> 
> `ENDFUNCTION `
> 
> Mark as follows: 
> **MP1** Function heading **and** parameter **and** ending **and** return type 
> **MP2** Declaration of all local variables used 
> **MP3** Calculate number of digits to mask / number of asterisks required
> **MP4** Trim asterisk string to number calculated in **MP3** 
> **MP5** Extract the last four characters 
> **MP6** Concatenate trimmed asterisk string with last four characters of `CardNumber `
> **MP7** Return masked string
> 
> **Max 6 marks**

parts.problemMd:
An alternative algorithm to determine if a paper needs to be checked uses a global 1D array `Check`, containing 76 elements of type `BOOLEAN.` The indices of the array are from 0 to 75 (inclusive), corresponding to the range of possible marks.

An element value in `Check` is `TRUE` if the index is within 2 marks of a grade boundary. For example, in the case where the C grade boundary is 43 the corresponding part of the `Check` array would be as follows:

![Table showing index 40 to 46 with Boolean values. Index 41 marked with “The grade boundary for a C grade,” indicating a threshold.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-computer-science-19/11-programming-/structured-programming/assets/010-table-showing-index-40-to-46-with-boolean-values.png)

A procedure `GBInitialise()` will initialise the `Check` array using values from the `GB` array.

Note it can be assumed that the maximum grade boundary value for A is 70 and the minimum value for E is 15.

Write pseudocode for the procedure.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Example:solution
> 
> `PROCEDURE GBInitialise() `
> `   DECLARE GBIndex, GBMark, ThisIndex : INTEGER `
> 
> `   FOR ThisIndex `$\leftarrow$`0 TO 75 `
> `      Check[ThisIndex] `$\leftarrow$` FALSE // initialise all values `
> `   NEXT ThisIndex `
> 
> `   FOR GBIndex `$\leftarrow$` 1 TO 5 `
> `      GBMark `$\leftarrow$` GB[GBIndex] `
> `      FOR ThisIndex `$\leftarrow$` GBMark - 2 TO GBMark + 2 `
> `         Check[ThisIndex]`$\leftarrow$` TRUE //Set GBMark `$\leftarrow$` 2 to TRUE `
> `     NEXT ThisIndex `
> `   NEXT GBIndex `
> `ENDPROCEDURE`
> 
> Mark as follows: 
> **MP1    **Procedure heading and ending 
> **MP2**   Initialise `Check` array to `FALSE` 
> **MP3**   Loop through `GB` array 
> **MP4   **Extract the `GB` mark 
> **MP5**   Loop for 5 elements across `GBMark` $\leftarrow$ 2 // Check if within `GBMark `$\leftarrow$ 2 
> **MP6**  Assign each element of `Check` array to `TRUE`
> 
> ALTERNATIVE – Example using selection Version 1
> 
> `FOR ThisIndex `$\leftarrow$` 0 TO 75 `
> `   CASE ThisIndex `
> `      GB[1] – 2 TO GB[1] + 2 : Check[ThisIndex] `$\leftarrow$` TRUE `
> `      GB[2] – 2 TO GB[2] + 2 : Check[ThisIndex] `$\leftarrow$` TRUE `
> `      GB[3] – 2 TO GB[3] + 2 : Check[ThisIndex] `$\leftarrow$` TRUE `
> `      GB[4] – 2 TO GB[4] + 2 : Check[ThisIndex] `$\leftarrow$` TRUE `
> `      GB[5] – 2 TO GB[5] + 2 : Check[ThisIndex] `$\leftarrow$` TRUE `
> `  OTHERWISE: Check[ThisIndex] `$\leftarrow$`FALSE `
> `  ENDCASE `
> `NEXT ThisIndex`
> 
> ALTERNATIVE – Example using selection Version 2
> 
> `   DECLARE ThisIndex, GBIndex : INTEGER `
> `   DECLARE Lower, Higher : INTEGER `
> 
> `   FOR ThisIndex  `$\leftarrow$` 0 TO 75 `
> `       For GBIndex  `$\leftarrow$` 1 T0 5 `
> `         Lower  `$\leftarrow$` GB[GBIndex] - 2 `
> `         Higher  `$\leftarrow$` GB[GBIndex] + 2 `
> `         IF ThisIndex >= Lower AND ThisIndex <= Higher THEN `
> `            Check[ThisIndex]  `$\leftarrow$` TRUE `
> `         ELSE `
> `            Check[ThisIndex]  `$\leftarrow$` FALSE `
> `         ENDIF `
> `       NEXT Index `
> `   NEXT ThisIndex `
> 
> Mark as follows: 
> **MP1   **Procedure heading and ending 
> **MP2**   Loop through `Check` array// loop from 0 to 75 
> **MP3**   Attempt at using CASE / Selection structure with five clauses/ **five** checks for range 
> **MP4**   Extract GB grade 
> **MP5**   Compare `ThisIndex` with each element in GB array $\pm$2 
> **MP6**   Assign each element of `Check` array to `TRUE` if in range **or **`FALSE` if not in range

parts.problemMd:
A global 1D array `Data` contains 100 elements of type integer.

A function `Check()` will:

- total the element values in odd index locations (1, 3, 5 ... 97, 99)
- total the element values in even index locations (2, 4, 6 ... 98, 100)
- return one of three strings ‘Odd’, ‘Even’ or ‘Same’ to indicate which total is the greater, or whether the totals are the same.

Write pseudocode for the function `Check().`
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Example:
> 
> `FUNCTION Check() RETURNS STRING `
> `            DECLARE Odd, Even, Index : INTEGER `
> 
> `            Odd `$\leftarrow$` 0 `
> `            Even `$\leftarrow$` 0 `
> 
> `            FOR Index `$\leftarrow$` 1 TO 100 `
> `               IF Index MOD 2 = 0 THEN `
> `                  Even `$\leftarrow$` Even + Data[Index] `
> `               ELSE `
> `                  Odd `$\leftarrow$` Odd + Data[Index] `
> `               ENDIF `
> `            NEXT Index `
> 
> `ENDFUNCTION `
> 
> Mark as follows:
>

parts.problemMd:
Three points on a grid form a triangle with sides of length A, B and C as shown in the example:

![Graph with axes ranging 0 to 10, depicting a triangle with vertices labelled A at (5,3), B at (4,6), and C at (7,5) on a grid.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-computer-science-19/11-programming-/structured-programming/assets/008-graph-with-axes-ranging-0-to-10-depicting-a-tria.png)

A triangle is said to be right-angled if the following test is true (where A is the length of the longest side):

A<sup>2</sup> = B<sup>2</sup> + C<sup>2</sup>

A<sup>2</sup> means A multiplied by A, for example 3<sup>2</sup> means 3 × 3 which evaluates to 9

You can calculate A<sup>2</sup>, B<sup>2</sup> and C<sup>2</sup> by using the coordinates of the endpoints of each line.

For example, B<sup>2</sup> is calculated as follows:

![Graph showing a line from point P1 at (2, 2) to P2 at (6, 5) with labelled coordinates, on a 10x10 grid, x and y axes marked.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-computer-science-19/11-programming-/structured-programming/assets/009-graph-showing-a-straight-line-from-point-p1-at-2.png)

The endpoints, P1 and P2, have the coordinates (3, 2) and (6, 6).

The value B<sup>2</sup> is given by the formula:

B<sup>2</sup> = (x<sup>1</sup> − x<sup>2</sup>) <sup>2</sup> + (y<sup>1</sup> − y<sup>2</sup>) <sup>2</sup>

In this example:

B<sup>2</sup> = (3 − 6)<sup>2</sup> + (2 − 6)<sup>2</sup> 
            B<sup>2</sup> = (–3)<sup>2</sup> + (–4)<sup>2</sup> 
            B<sup>2</sup> = 9 + 16 
            B<sup>2</sup> = 25

A function `IsRA()` will:

- take three sets of integers as parameters representing the coordinates of the three endpoints that form a triangle
- return `TRUE` if the endpoints form a right-angled triangle, otherwise return `FALSE`.

In pseudocode, the operator `‘^’` represents an exponent, which is the number of times a value is multiplied by itself. For example, the expression Value<sup>2</sup> may be written in pseudocode as `Value ^ 2 `

Complete the pseudocode for the function `IsRA().`

`FUNCTION IsRA(x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3 : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN`
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> `FUNCTION IsRA(x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3 : INTEGER) RETURNS `
> `BOOLEAN `
> `   DECLARE Len1, Len2, Len3 : INTEGER `
> 
> `   Len1 `$\leftarrow$` (x1 - x2) ^ 2 + (y1 - y2) ^ 2 `
> `   Len2 `$\leftarrow$` (x1 - x3) ^ 2 + (y1 - y3) ^ 2 `
> `   Len3 `$\leftarrow$` (x2 - x3) ^ 2 + (y2 - y3) ^ 2 `
> 
> `   IF (Len1 = Len2 + Len3) OR__ `
> `      (Len2 = Len1 + Len3) OR__ `
> `      (Len3 = Len1 + Len2) THEN `
> `      RETURN TRUE `
> `   ELSE `
> `      RETURN FALSE `
> `   ENDIF `
> 
> `ENDFUNCTION `
> 
> Mark as follows:
> 
> 1. Calculate the square of the length of at least one side
> 2. Calculation of all three lengths squared correctly
> 3. **One** correct comparison of square of three lengths
> 4. **All three** comparisons…
> 5. combined using logical operators / nested `IF` // completely correct selection
> 6. Return result correctly in both cases

22 **[1]**
