> **1 mark** for stating that a copy of `TotalWeight` is passed to the procedure
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the change made at line 21 is lost when the procedure ends, so `TotalWeight` is still 0
> 
> **1 mark** for changing `BYVAL Total` to `BYREF Total` in the header at line 20
> 
> Accept local copy, separate copy or copy of the argument for the second marking point
> 
> Accept the corrected header written out in full for the fourth marking point
> 
> Accept passed by reference written in words in place of the keyword `BYREF`
> 
> Do not accept the procedure does not return a value on its own. `AddParcel()` is a procedure and is not expected to return one, and this names the symptom rather than the cause
> 
> Do not accept there is a syntax error. The header at line 20 is valid pseudocode, which is why the program compiles

> **[exam-tip]**
> The signal to look for is a procedure that is meant to send a value back to the calling routine but has no `BYREF` in its header. Weak answers say the procedure does not return the value, which just repeats the question. Say what a value parameter actually does: it copies the argument, and the copy dies at `ENDPROCEDURE`.
> 
> The question asks for a change to the header, so `BYREF` is the fix here. Note that the Cambridge pseudocode rules say a parameter should not be passed by reference to a function, so this technique belongs to procedures. When a function needs to send a single value back, use its return value instead.

parts.problemMd:
A weather station program stores temperature readings in a text file.

The procedure `SaveReading()` has already been written. Its header is:

The procedure writes one reading to the file. It does not return a value.

At the station named Delta, a temperature of 21.5 degrees Celsius is recorded at hour 14.

Write the pseudocode statement that calls `SaveReading()` to store this reading.
parts.solutionMd:
The procedure name is followed by brackets holding the three values. **[1]**

The keyword `CALL` is used, and the three values are in the same order and of the same data types as the parameters in the header. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the procedure name `SaveReading` followed by brackets containing at least one of the three values, correct
> 
> **1 mark** for a completely correct statement, which needs the keyword `CALL`, the string `"Delta"` in double quotes, then `14`, then `21.5`
> 
> Accept `21.50` or `21.5` for the temperature
> 
> Do not accept the statement written without `CALL`, because the Pseudocode Guide states that a procedure call is a complete program statement written in the form `CALL Identifier(value1, value2, ...)`
> 
> Do not accept `Result ← SaveReading("Delta", 14, 21.5)`, because a procedure does not return a value, so there is nothing to assign
> 
> Do not accept `"14"` or `"21.5"` written in quotes, because those parameters are an `INTEGER` and a `REAL`, not strings

> **[exam-tip]**
> The header is the only thing that tells you the order and the data types of the values, so read it before you write anything. Swapping `14` and `21.5` costs the second mark even though both numbers are right.
> 
> Students who have just met functions often drop the `CALL` keyword, or try to assign the result to a variable. Remember the split: a procedure call stands alone as a statement and needs `CALL`, while a function call is never written with `CALL` because its returned value has to be used inside an expression.

parts.problemMd:
A stock control program prints a label for each item that is placed on a shelf.

The program uses the procedure `PrintLabel()`. Its header is:

Explain the term procedure interface with reference to `PrintLabel()`.
parts.solutionMd:
The procedure interface is the mechanism that allows the calling program to pass data into `PrintLabel()`. **[1]**

It defines the three parameters `Code`, `Quantity` and `Price`, giving the data type of each one and the order in which the values must be supplied when the procedure is called. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - The interface provides the mechanism that allows the calling program to pass data to the procedure
> - It defines the parameters of `PrintLabel()`, which are `Code`, `Quantity` and `Price`
> - It gives the data type of each parameter, so `Code` is a `STRING`, `Quantity` is an `INTEGER` and `Price` is a `REAL`
> - It fixes the order in which the values must be supplied in the call
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept the three parameters listed by name without their data types for the second point only
> 
> Do not accept an answer that describes only what the procedure does with the data, such as "it prints a label", because that is the purpose of the procedure and not its interface
> 
> Do not accept "it is the first line of the procedure" on its own, with no reference to the parameters

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word interface makes many students think of a screen that a user sees. Here it means something different: the agreed list of what must be handed to the module, and in what order.
> 
> Answer with reference to the named procedure, as the question asks. A general definition of the word scores less well than one that actually names `Code`, `Quantity` and `Price` and states their data types.

parts.problemMd:
A global 1D array of integers contains four elements, which are assigned values as shown:

A procedure `Adjust()` changes the values stored in the array.

The procedure is written in pseudocode as follows:

Complete the trace table by dry running the procedure when it is called as follows:

| Index | Count | Score[1] | Score[2] | Score[3] | Score[4] | OUTPUT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Index | Count | Score[1] | Score[2] | Score[3] | Score[4] | OUTPUT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **0** | **4** | **7** | **2** | **9** |   |
| **2** | **0** | **4** | **7** | **2** | **9** |   |
| **3** | **1** | **4** | **3** | **2** | **9** |   |
| **4** | **1** | **4** | **3** | **2** | **9** |   |
| **5** | **2** | **4** | **3** | **2** | **5** |   |
|   |   | **4** | **3** | **2** | **5** | **2** |

The first row records the state once `Index` and `Count` have been initialised. **[1]**

`Score[1]` holds 4, which is not greater than 4, so nothing changes on the first pass. `Score[2]` holds 7, so it becomes 3 and `Count` becomes 1. **[1]**

`Score[3]` holds 2, so nothing changes. `Score[4]` holds 9, so it becomes 5 and `Count` becomes 2. **[1]**

The loop stops when `Index` reaches 5, and `Count` is output as 2. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the initialisation row: `Index` 1, `Count` 0 and the array holding 4, 7, 2, 9
> 
> **1 mark** for the first two passes: `Index` reaching 3, `Score[2]` changed to 3 and `Count` 1
> 
> **1 mark** for the next two passes: `Index` reaching 5, `Score[4]` changed to 5 and `Count` 2
> 
> **1 mark** for `OUTPUT` 2, with `Score[1]` left at 4 and `Score[3]` left at 2 throughout
> 
> Accept a trace table in which only the values that change are written on each row and the unchanged cells are left blank
> 
> Accept the final row omitted if `OUTPUT` 2 is written on the row where `Index` reaches 5
> 
> Do not accept a final `Score[4]` of 1, which comes from testing 5 against the limit a second time. `Index` has already moved on, so each element is tested once only
> 
> Do not accept a final `Count` of 3, which comes from counting `Score[1]` as a change. 4 is not greater than 4

> **[exam-tip]**
> The trap here is the element that is still above the limit after it has been changed. `Score[4]` starts at 9 and becomes 5, and 5 is still greater than 4, but `Index` has already been increased so the loop never looks at that element again. Follow the order of the statements exactly and never go back.
> 
> The other lost mark is the boundary. `Score[1]` holds 4 and the test is `> Limit`, not `>= Limit`, so 4 is left alone and it is not counted. Write the condition out for each element before you decide.

parts.problemMd:
A library program works out the fee a member owes when a book is returned late.

The function `LateFee()` is written in pseudocode as follows. Two lines are missing.

Complete the pseudocode by writing the two missing lines.
parts.solutionMd:
Line (1) sends 0.00 straight back to the calling expression, and because `RETURN` takes effect immediately the rest of the function is not carried out. **[1]**

Line (2) sends back the fee that has been worked out, after the maximum has been applied. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for line (1) being `RETURN 0.00`
> 
> **1 mark** for line (2) being `RETURN Fee`
> 
> Accept `RETURN 0` or `RETURN 0.0` for line (1)
> 
> Do not accept `OUTPUT 0.00` or `OUTPUT Fee`. `OUTPUT` writes a value to the console and gives the calling expression nothing to use, so the function would not return a value
> 
> Do not accept `Fee ← 0.00` for line (1). Execution would carry on to `Fee ← DaysLate * DailyRate`, which overwrites it, and a `DaysLate` of -3 would then give a fee of -0.75
> 
> Do not accept `ENDFUNCTION`, or `RETURN` with no value after it, for line (2)

> **[exam-tip]**
> `RETURN` and `OUTPUT` are not interchangeable, and mixing them up is the single most common error on function questions. `OUTPUT` shows something on the screen. `RETURN` hands a value back to the point where the function was called, which is the whole reason a function exists.
> 
> Notice why the early `RETURN` on line (1) works. The Pseudocode Guide says that when `RETURN` is executed it takes effect immediately and any later lines are skipped, so a member who is not late never reaches the multiplication at all.

parts.problemMd:
A hotel booking program needs a new module called `StayCost()`.

The module is described as follows:

- it takes one parameter, an integer representing the number of nights of a stay
- it works out the total cost of the stay as a real value
- the total cost is needed inside a larger calculation in four different places in the program

Explain why `StayCost()` must be written as a function and not as a procedure.
parts.solutionMd:
A function returns a single value to the point at which it was called, so `StayCost()` can hand the total cost back to the line that needs it. **[1]**

The value returned replaces the function call inside the expression, so `StayCost(Nights)` can be written directly in each of the four calculations and the expression is then worked out. **[1]**

A procedure returns no value, and a procedure call such as `CALL StayCost(Nights)` is a complete program statement on its own, so it could not form part of a larger calculation. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for stating that a function returns a single value to the point at which it is called
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the returned value replaces the call inside the expression, so the call can be used directly in each of the four calculations
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that a procedure returns no value, so a procedure call is a complete statement and cannot appear inside an expression
> 
> Accept "the total cost is needed in an expression, and only a function call can be part of an expression" for the second mark
> 
> Accept a worked example such as `Total ← StayCost(Nights) * TaxRate` in support of the second mark
> 
> Do not accept answers that give only the general benefits of splitting a program into modules, such as less repeated code, easier testing or easier maintenance. Those are equally true of a procedure and do not explain the choice here
> 
> Do not accept "a function is faster" or "a function uses less memory", because neither follows from the description given

> **[exam-tip]**
> The commonest wrong answer here lists the benefits of modular design. Those benefits are real, but they apply to procedures just as much as to functions, so they cannot explain why this module has to be a function. Keep your answer on the returned value.
> 
> Watch how you write the call as well. The Pseudocode Guide says the keyword `CALL` is never used with a function, because a function call is not a complete statement. Writing `CALL StayCost(Nights)` tells the examiner you have not made the distinction.

A company installs parcel collection lockers in shops. A customer collects a parcel by scanning a code at the locker.

The behaviour of the locker software is documented using a state-transition diagram.

The table shows the inputs, outputs and states for the software:

| Current state | Input | Output | Next state |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Scan-Code | Show-Menu | S2 |
| S2 | Press-Open | Open-Door | S3 |
| S2 | Press-Cancel | none | S1 |
| S2 | Scan-Code | Show-Error | S2 |
| S3 | Close-Door | Lock-Door | S1 |
| S3 | Timeout | Show-Alert | S4 |

Complete the table with reference to the information above.

|   | Answer |
|---|---|
| The number of different inputs |   |
| The final or halting state |   |
parts.solutionMd:
|   | Answer |
|---|---|
| The number of different inputs | **5** |
| The final or halting state | **S4** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the number of different inputs given as 5
> 
> **1 mark** for the final or halting state given as S4
> 
> Accept "five" written in words for the first row
> 
> Do not accept 6 for the first row. There are six transitions, but Scan-Code appears twice, so only five different input values are used
> 
> Do not accept S1 for the second row. S1 is where the software starts, not where it stops

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word "different" is doing the work in the first row. Count the distinct values in the Input column, not the number of rows. Here Scan-Code is used twice, once from S1 and once from S2, so six transitions use only five different inputs.
> 
> To find the halting state, look for a state that appears in the Next state column but never in the Current state column. Once the software reaches S4 there is no row that can take it anywhere else, so it stops there.

parts.problemMd:
The entry gate of a car park is controlled by a program. A driver presses a button to receive a ticket, and the gate opens when the ticket is taken.

The behaviour of the program is documented using a state-transition diagram.

The table shows the inputs, outputs and states for the program:

| Current state | Input | Output | Next state |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Press-Button | Print-Ticket | S2 |
| S2 | Take-Ticket | Open-Gate | S3 |
| S2 | Timeout | none | S1 |
| S3 | Car-Detected | none | S4 |
| S3 | Timeout | Close-Gate | S1 |
| S4 | Car-Gone | Close-Gate | S1 |
| S4 | Timeout | Sound-Alarm | S5 |

The current state is S1. The following inputs occur, in this order:

1. Press-Button
2. Take-Ticket
3. Timeout
4. Press-Button
5. Timeout

Give the number of outputs that are produced, the outputs in the order they are produced, and the current state after the last input.
parts.solutionMd:
Number of outputs: 4 **[1]**

Outputs in order: Print-Ticket, Open-Gate, Close-Gate, Print-Ticket **[1]**

Current state: S1 **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the number of outputs given as 4
> 
> **1 mark** for the four outputs listed in this exact order: Print-Ticket, Open-Gate, Close-Gate, Print-Ticket
> 
> **1 mark** for the current state given as S1
> 
> Accept "four" written in words.
> 
> Accept the outputs separated by commas, by arrows or written on separate lines, provided the order is correct.
> 
> Do not accept 5 for the number of outputs. The fifth input, Timeout from S2, has an output of none, so it produces no output.
> 
> Do not accept S2 as the current state. S2 is the state reached after the fourth input, not after the fifth.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work one input at a time and write the state down after each one. The most common mistake here is counting an output of none as an output, which gives 5 instead of 4. A row with none in the Output column still changes the state, it just produces nothing.
> 
> The second most common mistake is stopping one input early. There are five inputs, so trace all five. The state you must give is the one reached after input 5, even though input 5 produces no output.

parts.problemMd:
An electric vehicle charging point is controlled by a program.

The behaviour of the program is documented using a state-transition diagram.

The table shows the inputs, outputs and states for the program:

| Current state | Input | Output | Next state |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Plug-In | Show-Ready | S2 |
| S2 | Start-Charge | Begin-Power | S3 |
| S2 | Unplug | none | S1 |
| S3 | Stop-Charge | End-Power | S2 |
| S3 | Full-Battery | Show-Full | S4 |
| S3 | Fault-Found | Show-Error | S5 |
| S4 | Unplug | Show-Total | S1 |
| S5 | Reset | none | S1 |

One driver uses the charging point. Complete the table below to show the inputs, outputs and next states.

Assume that the current state for each row is given by the Next state on the previous row. For example, the first Plug-In is made when the program is in state S1.

If there is no output for a given transition, the output cell should contain none.

The first two rows have been completed.

| Input | Output | Next state |
|---|---|---|
|   |   | S1 |
| Plug-In | Show-Ready | S2 |
| Start-Charge |   |   |
|   | End-Power |   |
|   |   | S3 |
| Full-Battery |   |   |
|   |   | S1 |
parts.solutionMd:
| Input | Output | Next state |
|---|---|---|
|   |   | S1 |
| Plug-In | Show-Ready | S2 |
| Start-Charge | **Begin-Power** | **S3** |
| **Stop-Charge** | End-Power | **S2** |
| **Start-Charge** | **Begin-Power** | S3 |
| Full-Battery | **Show-Full** | **S4** |
| **Unplug** | **Show-Total** | S1 |

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> One mark per row, for rows 3 to 7. Every cell in a row must be correct for that row to earn its mark.
> 
> **1 mark** for row 3: Start-Charge, Begin-Power, S3
> 
> **1 mark** for row 4: Stop-Charge, End-Power, S2
> 
> **1 mark** for row 5: Start-Charge, Begin-Power, S3
> 
> **1 mark** for row 6: Full-Battery, Show-Full, S4
> 
> **1 mark** for row 7: Unplug, Show-Total, S1
> 
> Do not accept Full-Battery in row 4. Full-Battery is also an input from S3, but its output is Show-Full, not End-Power
> 
> Do not accept Unplug in row 5. Unplug is an input from S2, but it gives an output of none and a next state of S1, which does not match the S3 already given
> 
> Do not accept Reset in row 7. Reset is an input from S5, and the program is in S4 at the start of row 7

> **[exam-tip]**
> The current state is never written in this table, so you must keep track of it yourself. Before filling a row, look at the Next state in the row above and use that as the current state. Write it in the margin if it helps.
> 
> Rows 4, 5 and 7 are the hard ones because you are given the wrong end of the transition and must work backwards. For row 4 the current state is S3 and the output is End-Power, so find the row of the first table that starts at S3 and outputs End-Power. Students who instead read down the first table in order and copy the next input they see will get row 4 wrong, and then every row after it, because one wrong next state carries all the way down.

parts.problemMd:
A program controls a ticket machine at a railway station. The program is built from four modules. A structure chart has been produced during the design stage. The table summarises the relationship between the modules that the chart shows. Any return values are stated in the description. | Module name | Description | |---|---| | `Sell` | calls `GetZone` followed by `PrintTicket` | | `GetZone` | • has no parameters
• returns an integer value | | `PrintTicket` | • called with parameter `Zone`, of type integer
• repeatedly calls `PrintLine` | | `PrintLine` | • called with parameter `Text`, of type string | (a) Identify the module that would be implemented as a function. (b) The structure chart uses a curved arrow symbol to show iteration. Identify the module that this symbol is applied to.
parts.solutionMd:
(a) `GetZone` **[1]**

(b) `PrintTicket` **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `GetZone` in part (a)
> 
> **1 mark** for `PrintTicket` in part (b)
> 
> Accept the module name written with or without brackets, so `GetZone()` and `PrintTicket()` are both credited.
> 
> Do not accept `PrintLine` in part (b). The iteration arrow is applied to the module that makes the repeated calls, not to the module that is called repeatedly.
> 
> Do not accept `Sell` in part (b). `Sell` calls `GetZone` and `PrintTicket` once each, in sequence, so the line from `Sell` carries no iteration arrow.
> 
> Do not accept `PrintTicket` in part (a). It returns no value, so it is a procedure.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A module is a function only when the description says it returns a value. Changing a parameter, or doing a lot of work, does not make a module a function. `PrintTicket` prints a whole ticket and is still a procedure.
> 
> The words in the description tell you which symbol the chart carries. "Repeatedly calls" gives the curved arrow, and "decided when the program runs" gives the diamond. Both symbols belong to the module doing the calling, so stay on the row where you found the words.

parts.problemMd:
A weather station program is built from three modules. A structure chart has been produced during the design stage. The table summarises the relationship between the modules that the chart shows. Any return values are stated in the description. | Module name | Description | |---|---| | `Record` | • has no parameters
• calls `ReadTemp` followed by `StoreTemp` | | `ReadTemp` | • called with parameter `SensorID`, of type integer
• returns a real value | | `StoreTemp` | • called with parameter `Saved`, of type Boolean
• `Saved` is passed by reference
• does not return a value | Write the pseudocode module headers for `ReadTemp` and `StoreTemp`.
parts.solutionMd:
**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `FUNCTION ReadTemp(SensorID : INTEGER)`, with the parameter name and its data type
> 
> **1 mark** for `RETURNS REAL`
> 
> **1 mark** for `PROCEDURE StoreTemp(BYREF Saved : BOOLEAN)`, with `BYREF` and the data type
> 
> Accept `ENDFUNCTION` and `ENDPROCEDURE` written as well, even though only the headers were asked for.
> 
> Accept any spacing around the colon and the brackets.
> 
> Do not accept `FUNCTION StoreTemp`. `StoreTemp` returns no value, so it is a procedure.
> 
> Do not accept `BYVAL Saved`. A parameter passed by value cannot pass a change back to `Record`.
> 
> Do not accept `PROCEDURE ReadTemp`, or a header with `RETURNS` missing or with the wrong return type.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word FUNCTION or PROCEDURE is decided by one thing only: does the description say a value is returned? Students lose this mark by reasoning that `StoreTemp` "sends something back" because `Saved` is passed by reference. Passing by reference is not the same as returning a value, and a module that does it is still a procedure.
> 
> Write the return type every time. `RETURNS` on its own earns nothing, and a real value returned as `RETURNS INTEGER` is wrong even though the rest of the header is right.

parts.problemMd:
A parcel delivery company uses a program to sort parcels. The program is built from five modules. A structure chart has been produced during the design stage. The table summarises the relationship between the modules that the chart shows. Any return values are stated in the description. | Module name | Description | |---|---| | `Dispatch` | • has no parameters
• calls `CountParcels` once and stores the value returned
• then calls `Weigh` once for each parcel, numbered 1 to the value returned by `CountParcels`
• after each call to `Weigh`, calls either `Express` or `Standard`, decided when the program runs
• calls `Express` when the value returned by `Weigh` is greater than 2000, otherwise calls `Standard`
• does not return a value | | `CountParcels` | • has no parameters
• returns an integer value, which is the number of parcels waiting | | `Weigh` | • called with parameter `ParcelNum`, of type integer
• returns an integer value, which is the mass of that parcel in grams | | `Express` | • called with parameter `ParcelNum`, of type integer
• does not return a value | | `Standard` | • called with parameter `ParcelNum`, of type integer
• does not return a value | Write the equivalent pseudocode for module `Dispatch`. Do not write the pseudocode for the other four modules.
parts.solutionMd:
**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `PROCEDURE Dispatch()` with no parameters, closed with `ENDPROCEDURE`
> 
> **1 mark** for declaring the local variables with correct data types
> 
> **1 mark** for storing the value returned by `CountParcels` in a variable
> 
> **1 mark** for a loop that runs once for each parcel, from 1 to that stored value, correctly closed
> 
> **1 mark** for storing the value returned by `Weigh`, called with the parcel number, inside the loop
> 
> **1 mark** for selection inside the loop that calls `Express` when the mass is greater than 2000 and `Standard` otherwise
> 
> Accept a conditional loop in place of the count-controlled loop, provided its counter is initialised before the loop and incremented inside it, for example `WHILE ParcelNum <= Total`.
> 
> Accept `NEXT` written without the identifier.
> 
> Accept the condition written as `Mass >= 2001`, since the mass is an integer number of grams.
> 
> Accept `IF Weigh(ParcelNum) > 2000 THEN` only where `Weigh` is then not called a second time.
> 
> Do not accept `FUNCTION Dispatch()`. `Dispatch` returns no value.
> 
> Do not accept `CALL CountParcels()` or `CALL Weigh(ParcelNum)`. `CALL` introduces a procedure call, and a function call must appear on the right of an assignment so that its value is kept.
> 
> Do not accept selection placed after the loop. Every parcel is weighed and routed separately, so `ENDIF` must come before `NEXT`.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each phrase in the description maps onto one pseudocode construct. "Calls A followed by B" is sequence, "decided when the program runs" is the diamond and becomes `IF ... ELSE ... ENDIF`, and "once for each parcel" is the curved arrow and becomes `FOR ... NEXT`. Write the empty loop and the empty selection first, then drop the calls inside them.
> 
> The mark most often lost here is the nesting. If you write `NEXT ParcelNum` before `ENDIF`, the program weighs every parcel but routes only the last one. Line up each closing keyword under the keyword that opened it before you move on.
> 
> The other frequent error is `CALL` in front of a function. `Weigh` hands back a value, so it belongs on the right of an arrow: `Mass ← Weigh(ParcelNum)`. Writing `CALL Weigh(ParcelNum)` throws the mass away.

parts.problemMd:
A software developer follows a program development life cycle. The life cycle divides the development process into various stages.

The following table lists some development activities.

Complete the table by writing the name of the life cycle stage for each activity.

| Activity | Name of life cycle stage |
|---|---|
| The walkthrough method is used. |   |
| An algorithm is implemented in a programming language. |   |
| The client is interviewed about problems with the current system. |   |
| The program is modified to run on new hardware. |   |
| Records and file structures are defined. |   |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> | Activity | Name of life cycle stage |
> |---|---|
> | The walkthrough method is used. | **Testing** |
> | An algorithm is implemented in a programming language. | **Coding** |
> | The client is interviewed about problems with the current system. | **Analysis** |
> | The program is modified to run on new hardware. | **Maintenance** |
> | Records and file structures are defined. | **Design** |
> 
> One mark per row

parts.problemMd:
A program has been developed and released for general use. After a few months of use an error is detected where under certain circumstances it outputs an unexpected value.

The error in the program needs to be corrected.

Identify the stage of the program development life cycle that this correction is made in.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> (Corrective) Maintenance

parts.problemMd:
A software developer follows a program development life cycle. The life cycle divides the development process into various stages.

The following table lists some development activities.

Complete the table by writing the name of the life cycle stage for each activity.

| Activity | Name of life cycle stage |
|---|---|
| A compiler is used. |   |
| A program that has been released for general use is modified. |   |
| The dry run method is used. |   |
| The program structure is specified. |   |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> | Activity | Name of life cycle stage |
> |---|---|
> | A compiler is used. | **Coding** |
> | A program that has been released for general use is modified. | **Maintenance** |
> | The dry run method is used. | **Testing** |
> | The program structure is specified. | **Design** |
> 
> One mark per row

parts.problemMd:
A coffee shop owner wants to introduce a computerised loyalty card system.

A programmer discusses the details of the system with the shop owner.

Identify the stage of the program development life cycle that this discussion is part of and give a document that will be produced during this stage.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One mark per answer:
> 
> **MP1 **Analysis
> 
> **MP2 Named **document, examples include:
> 
> - A requirement specification
> - Definition of System Objectives
> - List of problems with existing system
> - Survey results
> - Feasibility study
> - Interview notes
> 
> **Max 2 marks**

parts.problemMd:
A team of developers is building a new online booking program for a chain of hotels.

The team decides to follow a program development life cycle, which divides the work into separate stages.

State one benefit to the team of dividing the work into stages.
parts.solutionMd:
The project is easier to plan and manage, because each stage can be scheduled and costed separately. **[1]**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any one from:**
> 
> - The project is easier to plan / manage / schedule
> - The time and the cost of the work are easier to estimate and control
> - A clear deliverable is produced at the end of each stage, so progress can be checked before the next stage starts
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept an answer phrased around one stage having to be completed, and its output approved, before the next stage begins.
> 
> Do not accept "it is faster" or "it is cheaper" on its own. The benefit must say what dividing the work into stages lets the team do.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The commonest wrong answer here describes what one stage does, for example "you can test the program". That is a benefit of testing, not a benefit of splitting the work into stages. Say what the team gains: it can plan, cost and check the work one stage at a time.
> 
> Read the question carefully. This asks about using a development life cycle at all. It is not asking you to compare waterfall, iterative and RAD, and a comparison of those models earns nothing here.

parts.problemMd:
A company is developing a new module for its online ticket booking program. The module will send a reminder message to a customer two days before an event takes place.

The analysis of the new module is complete and the project has moved on to the design stage. During this stage the algorithms for the module will be designed.

State three other items that will be produced or decided during the design stage.
parts.solutionMd:
The data structures the module will use, recorded in an identifier table. **[1]**

The layout and the content of the reminder message that the customer receives. **[1]**

The programming language and the development environment that will be used to write the module. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - The data structures to be used // an identifier table // a data dictionary
> - The validation rules to be applied to the data
> - A diagram that documents the module, for example a structure chart, a state-transition diagram or a data-flow diagram
> - The user interface // the layout and the content of the reminder message
> - The test plan // the test data to be used and the expected results
> - The programming language and the development environment to be used
> - Any library routines or existing modules that will be reused
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept the name of the design document instead of the item itself, for example "an identifier table" for the data structures.
> 
> Do not accept "the algorithms" or "the pseudocode for the module". The question states that these are already being designed and asks for three other items.
> 
> Do not accept "the program code", which is produced in the coding stage, or "the results of the tests", which are produced in the testing stage.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students lose marks here by naming work that belongs to a later stage. The design stage decides the test plan and the test data; it does not run the tests. It chooses the programming language; it does not write the code.
> 
> A useful check: everything produced in the design stage is a decision or a document about how the program will work, written before any code exists.

parts.problemMd:
A software company is developing a program for a transport company. The development follows a program development life cycle with analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance stages.

The development team is behind schedule. To save time, the team spends only a few hours on the analysis stage before moving on to the design.

Explain two problems that this decision may cause at later stages of the life cycle.
parts.solutionMd:
The requirements specification produced by the analysis stage will be incomplete, **[1]** so the design and the code may solve a different problem from the one the transport company actually has. **[1]**

The testing stage has no complete statement of requirements to test the program against, **[1]** so faults reach the user and a large amount of maintenance is then needed to correct them. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two problems from:** one mark for the problem and one mark for the linked effect on a later stage.
> 
> - The requirements specification is incomplete or wrong, so the design and the coding are based on the wrong requirements and the finished program does not do what the transport company asked for
> - The transport company has not agreed what the program must do, so it asks for changes during the coding stage and work that is already complete has to be done again
> - There is no complete list of requirements, so the testing stage cannot confirm that the program meets them and faults are not detected
> - The size of the problem is not understood, so the time and the cost of the later stages cannot be estimated and the project falls further behind
> - Faults caused by the missing requirements are found only after release, so more maintenance is needed and correcting a fault at that point costs more than correcting it during analysis
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> Accept the problem and its effect given in either order.
> 
> Do not accept "the program will not work" or "the program will contain errors" on its own, with no named later stage and no explanation of why that stage is affected.

> **[exam-tip]**
> An explain question on the life cycle needs two linked ideas, not one. Name the later stage that suffers, then say why it suffers. "The program will be wrong" names no stage and earns nothing.
> 
> Remember what the analysis stage hands on: a requirements specification. Every later stage reads that document, so a thin analysis weakens the design, the coding, the testing and the maintenance in turn.

parts.problemMd:
A software company develops programs using the waterfall model of the program development life cycle.

A new trainee is shown a diagram of this model. Each stage is drawn in its own box, from Analysis in the top box to Maintenance in the bottom box. Every pair of neighbouring stages is joined by two arrows, one pointing down and one pointing up.

The trainee asks what each type of arrow represents.

Explain what a downward arrow represents and what an upward arrow represents in this diagram.
parts.solutionMd:
Downward arrows: the work produced by one stage is passed on and used as the input to the next stage. **[1]**

Upward arrows: more work is needed at an earlier stage before the current stage can be completed, so the team returns to that earlier stage. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the downward arrows: the result produced by one stage is passed to the next stage // the next stage uses the documents or code produced by the stage above it
> 
> **1 mark** for the upward arrows: more work is required at a previous stage in order to complete the current stage // the team returns to an earlier stage to correct or add to the work done there
> 
> Do not accept "the project moves forwards" or "the project goes backwards" on their own. Neither answer says what is passed between the stages, nor why the team would return to an earlier one.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most students who lose marks here write about the direction of travel and stop. The mark is for what travels along the arrow: finished work going down, and a need for rework going up. Say what the next stage receives, and say why a team would ever go back up.

parts.problemMd:
A development team is writing a program for a supermarket company to manage its stock. The team is using the waterfall model of the program development life cycle.

The analysis and design stages are complete and the team is part-way through the coding stage.

The supermarket company now tells the team that the program must also store the country that each product comes from.

Describe what the development team must do to add this new requirement to the program.
parts.solutionMd:
The team must return to the analysis stage and record the new requirement in the requirements specification. **[1]**

The team must then return to the design stage and change the design, for example by adding a new field to the record that stores each product and amending any algorithm that uses that record. **[1]**

The coding stage and the testing stage must then be carried out again for every part of the program that the change affects. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for returning to the analysis stage // amending the requirements specification to include the new requirement
> 
> **1 mark** for returning to the design stage // changing the design, for example the data structure, the identifier table or an algorithm
> 
> **1 mark** for repeating the coding stage and then the testing stage for the affected parts of the program
> 
> **1 mark** for stating that the stages must again be completed in order, so work already finished in a later stage may have to be done again
> 
> Max 3 marks
> 
> Accept named design documents such as a structure chart, a flowchart or an identifier table in place of "the design".
> 
> Accept "requirements document" in place of "requirements specification".
> 
> Do not accept "the team adds the extra code and carries on". In the waterfall model a change cannot be made in a later stage without first changing the stages it depends on.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The common error is to answer as though the change costs one line of code. The question is testing the rule that makes the waterfall model what it is: every stage takes its input from the stage above, so a change in an early stage forces every later stage to be repeated. Work down the stages in order in your answer and you will pick up the marks in sequence.

parts.problemMd:
A software company is writing two programs for a transport authority.

Program A controls the doors on a driverless train. The safety rules that the program must follow are fixed by law and are published in full. Before the program can be used, an inspector must check the finished program against a written design document.

Program B is a smartphone app that shows travellers how busy each train is. The transport authority does not yet know which features travellers will want, and it wants a first version of the app available within two months.

The company will use the waterfall life cycle for one of these two programs and a different life cycle for the other.

Identify the program that should be developed using the waterfall life cycle and justify your answer by referring to both programs.
parts.solutionMd:
Program A. **[1]**

All of the requirements for Program A are known before development starts, because the safety rules are fixed by law and are published in full, so each stage can be completed before the next one begins. **[1]**

The waterfall life cycle produces a written document at the end of each stage, including the design document that the inspector must check the finished program against. **[1]**

Program B is a poor fit because the transport authority does not yet know what the app must do, and the waterfall life cycle is slow and difficult to change once the requirements have been agreed. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for identifying Program A
> 
> Max 3 marks for justification, one mark per point:
> 
> **1 mark** for the requirements of Program A being known and fixed before development starts, so each stage can be completed before the next begins
> 
> **1 mark** for the clear deliverables produced at the end of each stage of the waterfall life cycle, in particular the design document the inspector needs // the project is easier to manage, plan and cost
> 
> **1 mark** for the requirements of Program B being likely to change, and the waterfall life cycle being difficult or slow to cope with changes to the requirements
> 
> **1 mark** for the waterfall life cycle producing no working software until late in the life cycle, so Program B would not have a usable first version within two months
> 
> Accept a justification that names the relevant stage, for example "the analysis stage can be finished completely because nothing is left to decide".
> 
> Do not accept an answer that gives no reason connected to the two programs, such as "Program A is more important" or "Program A is harder".
> 
> No marks for the justification if Program B is identified.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The command word is justify, and the question asks you to refer to both programs. A common answer lists what the waterfall life cycle is like in general and never mentions the trains or the app. Half of the justification marks here sit on Program B: say what the app needs and why the waterfall life cycle cannot give it.

parts.problemMd:
A small team is writing a program that a language school will use to book lessons.

The school is not sure exactly what it wants the program to do. It wants to use a working version of the program from the end of the first month, and it expects to ask for changes once its staff have used that version.

The team has decided not to use the waterfall life cycle.

Give the name of a suitable program development life cycle model for this project and give one reason for your choice.
parts.solutionMd:
Name: the iterative life cycle. **[1]**

Reason: the stages of the life cycle are repeated, so a working version of the program is produced early and the changes the school asks for after using it can be included in the next version. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the name: Iterative
> 
> Accept: Rapid Application Development // RAD
> 
> **1 mark** for one reason, from:
> 
> the stages are repeated, so a working version is available early // small releases are made, each one adding functionality to the last
> 
> the requirements are allowed to change during development
> 
> the client is involved throughout development and their feedback decides what is built next
> 
> Accept "development is quicker // a working version is available sooner" as the reason. Do not accept a reason that is true of every life cycle, such as "it splits the work into stages".

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reason mark is lost far more often than the name mark. A reason such as "it is more modern" or "it is organised" would be just as true of the waterfall life cycle, so it earns nothing. Point at something this model does that the waterfall life cycle does not: repeat the stages, release early, and accept changed requirements.

parts.problemMd:
Two companies are each writing a program that lets customers order food from local restaurants. The two programs will do the same job.

Company A uses the waterfall life cycle. Company B uses an iterative life cycle. Both companies start work on the same day.

Six months later, customers are already using Company B's program. Company A has not yet released anything.

Explain why the iterative life cycle allowed Company B to release a usable program first.
parts.solutionMd:
In the waterfall life cycle every stage must be completed before the next one begins, so there is no working software until late in the life cycle. **[1]**

In an iterative life cycle the stages are repeated, and each repetition produces a working version of the program. **[1]**

The first version does not have to contain every feature, because later repetitions add functionality to it, so Company B could release its program before the program was complete. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the waterfall life cycle producing no working software until late in the life cycle, because each stage must be completed before the next begins
> 
> **1 mark** for the stages being repeated in an iterative life cycle, with each repetition producing a working version of the program
> 
> **1 mark** for a release being possible before the program is complete, because later repetitions add functionality to the version already released
> 
> **1 mark** for feedback from the customers using the early version being available to Company B, so early review shapes the next repetition
> 
> Max 3 marks
> 
> Do not accept "an iterative life cycle is faster", which restates the outcome given in the question instead of explaining it.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Questions like this give you the outcome and ask for the mechanism, so an answer that repeats the outcome scores nothing. Two of the three marks here are for saying what each life cycle has produced at the six month point. Compare what exists, not how good each model is.

parts.problemMd:
A program has been written for a chain of hotels using an iterative life cycle. At the end of the project the hotel chain reports two problems.

Problem 1: the project cost much more, and finished much later, than the figures the development company gave at the start.

Problem 2: a developer who joined the team near the end of the project could find very little written information about how the program works.

Explain how the use of an iterative life cycle could have caused each of these two problems.
parts.solutionMd:
Problem 1: the number of repetitions the project will need is not known when it starts, because the requirements are not fixed at that point. **[1]** After seeing each version the hotel chain could ask for changes and new features, and every change added more work, so the cost and the completion date could not be estimated accurately at the start. **[1]**

Problem 2: this life cycle carries out little detailed planning at the start and documentation is often left out. **[1]** The design changed with every repetition, so any document written for an earlier version would have been out of date, and the team's effort went into producing working software rather than written records. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Max 2 marks for Problem 1, one mark per point:
> 
> **1 mark** for the number of repetitions, or the final set of requirements, not being known when the project starts
> 
> **1 mark** for the client being able to ask for changes or new features after seeing each version, with each change adding work to the project
> 
> **1 mark** for the conclusion that the cost and the time to complete the project are therefore difficult to estimate
> 
> Max 2 marks for Problem 2, one mark per point:
> 
> **1 mark** for minimal or no detailed planning being carried out in this life cycle // documentation often being omitted
> 
> **1 mark** for the design changing with each repetition, so a document written for an earlier version is out of date
> 
> **1 mark** for effort being directed at producing working software rather than at written records
> 
> Max 4 marks in total
> 
> Do not accept "the developers were disorganised" or "the client was difficult". The question asks for a cause that comes from the life cycle itself, not from the people.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both of these are drawbacks of the iterative life cycle, and both follow from the same feature: the requirements are deliberately left open so that they can change. Students often write that the team should simply have estimated better or written more documents. That misses the point being examined, which is that the model itself makes estimating and documenting harder.

parts.problemMd:
A software company has been asked to write a program that a city bus service will use to sell tickets. The company will develop the program using the Rapid Application Development (RAD) life cycle.

State two principles of this life cycle.
parts.solutionMd:
Modules of the program are developed in parallel, as prototypes. **[1]**

Small releases are made during development, each one adding more functionality to the program. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - modules are developed in parallel // modules are developed as prototypes
> - minimal or no detailed planning is carried out // the requirements are allowed to change during development
> - the development process is flexible
> - small incremental releases are made, each one adding functionality
> - the client is involved during all stages of development
> - it is used for time critical development
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Do not accept "it is rapid" or "it is fast", which repeat the name of the model instead of giving a principle of it.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The name of this model tells you its aim, not how it works, so an answer built out of the word "rapid" earns nothing. Learn the principles as a short list and give two that are clearly different from each other: "it is flexible" and "requirements can change" are close enough that an examiner may read them as one point.

parts.problemMd:
A charity needs a program that will register volunteers for a sports event. The event takes place in four months' time and the date cannot be changed. The charity has a general idea of what it needs but has not written down a full list of requirements.

A developer suggests using the Rapid Application Development (RAD) life cycle rather than the waterfall life cycle.

Give two benefits and one drawback of using the RAD life cycle instead of the waterfall life cycle for this program.
parts.solutionMd:
Benefit 1: several modules of the program can be developed at the same time, so the program is finished sooner than it would be if every stage were completed in turn. **[1]**

Benefit 2: a prototype is produced at an early stage, so the charity can review it and ask for changes to the requirements while there is still time to make them. **[1]**

Drawback: the cost and the time needed to complete the project are difficult to estimate, because the requirements are not fixed at the start. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** each for two benefits (max 2), from:
> 
> quicker development is possible, because several modules can be worked on at the same time
> 
> a prototype is produced at an early stage in the process
> 
> requirements are easier to change // usable modules are delivered sooner
> 
> early review is possible // the developer and the charity work closely together
> 
> **1 mark** for one drawback, from:
> 
> it is difficult to estimate the cost or the time to complete the project
> 
> documentation is often omitted
> 
> the charity must be available throughout the life cycle, and it is too easy for a client to keep changing its mind
> 
> Do not accept a benefit that is not a comparison, such as "it uses stages", because the waterfall life cycle uses stages too.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read the tariff split carefully: two benefits and one drawback means three separate points, and a fourth benefit cannot replace the missing drawback. The single most common wasted answer is to repeat the same benefit in two forms, for example "it is quicker" and "it saves time". Give one benefit about speed and one about the client.

parts.problemMd:
A company is writing a program to sell tickets for a music festival. The festival dates are fixed and cannot be moved, so the program must be working on the day tickets go on sale.

The company will use the Rapid Application Development (RAD) life cycle.

The festival organisers have told the company that they are very busy and will not be able to meet the development team often.

Explain how two principles of the RAD life cycle help the company to meet the fixed date, and explain one problem that will be caused by the organisers being unavailable.
parts.solutionMd:
Meeting the fixed date: modules are developed in parallel, so several parts of the ticket program are built at the same time and the total development time is shorter. **[1]** Small releases are made, each adding functionality, so a version that can sell tickets exists on the fixed date even if some features are not finished. **[1]**

The problem: the RAD life cycle needs the client to be involved during all stages of development. **[1]** If the organisers are not available, the prototypes are not reviewed on time, so the team keeps building on requirements that have not been confirmed and that work may have to be done again. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Max 2 marks for the fixed date, one mark per principle applied, from:
> 
> **1 mark** for modules being developed in parallel, so several parts of the program are built at the same time and the elapsed development time is shorter
> 
> **1 mark** for small incremental releases, so a usable ticket program exists on the fixed date even if some functionality is still missing
> 
> **1 mark** for minimal detailed planning, so work on the program starts sooner
> 
> **1 mark** for prototypes being produced early, so problems are found and corrected well before the date
> 
> Max 2 marks for the problem:
> 
> **1 mark** for identifying that the RAD life cycle requires the client to be involved during all stages of development
> 
> **1 mark** for a consequence: prototypes are not reviewed on time, so the team continues to work from requirements that have not been confirmed // work has to be repeated later // the release is delayed
> 
> Max 4 marks in total
> 
> Accept "the development process is flexible" or "RAD is used for time-critical development" as a principle when it is linked to meeting the date, for example requirements can be changed without restarting the project. Do not accept a principle stated with no link to the deadline.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This model asks as much of the client as it does of the developers, and that is what the second half of the question is testing. Students revise the benefits of RAD and forget that they depend on the client turning up. Whenever a question tells you something about how available a client is, expect that detail to carry marks.

parts.problemMd:
Refer to the [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2025/11/33139-9618_w24_in_21.pdf)for the list of pseudocode functions and operators.

Calculations will occur at many places in the program and these involve the use of one of three tax rates.

Tax rate values represent a percentage. For example, a tax rate value of 5.23 represents 5.23%. In this case, the tax payable on an item costing \$100 would be \$5.23.

Tax rate values are used at several places within the program. One example is given in pseudocode as follows:

`HighRate ← FALSE `

`CASE OF ItemCost `

`    <= 50 : TaxRate ← 3.75 // tax rate of 3.75% `

`    <= 200 : TaxRate ← 5.23 // tax rate of 5.23% `

`    > 200 : TaxRate ← 6.25 // tax rate of 6.25% `

`            HighRate ← TRUE `

`ENDCASE`

`TaxPayable ← ItemCost * TaxRate // tax payable`

The pseudocode contains a logical error.

Identify the error **and **suggest a correction.

>

> 
> Correction: TaxPayable  (ItemCost * TaxRate) / 100

parts.problemMd:
A program contains a global 1D array `Data `with 100 elements of type `INTEGER`.

The program contains a function `Process()` expressed in pseudocode as follows:

`FUNCTION Process(Number : INTEGER, Label : STRING) RETURNS STRING`

`    DECLARE Index, Count : INTEGER`

`    DECLARE ReturnValue : STRING`

`    Count INT(100 / Number)`

`    Index Data[Number]`

`    CASE OF (Index MOD 2)`

`        0 : ReturnValue TO_UPPER(RIGHT(Label, Count))`

`        1 : ReturnValue "****"`

`    ENDCASE`

`    RETURN RetVal`

`ENDFUNCTION`

Run-time errors can be generated in different ways. For example, a run-time error will be generated if a function is called with invalid parameters.

The pseudocode contains three statements that could generate a run-time error.

Write the **three **statements **and **explain how each could generate a run-time error
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **MP1**` Count ← INT(100 / Number)`
> Number could be zero (giving a divide by zero)
> 
> **MP2**` Index ← Data[Number]`
> Potential error: Value Number could be outside the range of array indices
> 
> **MP3 **`ReturnValue ← TO_UPPER(RIGHT(Label, Count))`
> Potential Error: Number to extract may be too big / negative / out of range for use in the RIGHT function // Label has insufficient characters
> 
> **MP4**` RETURN RetVal`
> Potential Error: There is no value to be returned // there is no variable named `RetVal`
> 
> Mark as follows:
> 1 mark for each statement <u>**and **</u>description
> **Max 3 marks**

parts.problemMd:
A software developer follows a program development life cycle. The life cycle divides the development process into various stages.

parts.solutionMd:

> **MP2 **The modules `Test_A()`<u> and </u>`Test_B()`are replaced by dummy modules

parts.problemMd:

The pseudocode contains **two **syntax errors and **one** other error.

parts.problemMd:
An algorithm is designed to find the smallest numeric value from an input sequence and count how many numeric values have been input. 
An example of an input sequence is:

23, AB56, 17, 23ZW, 4, 10, END

Numeric input values are all integers and non-numeric input is ignored, except for the string "END" which is used to terminate the sequence.

The algorithm is expressed in pseudocode as shown:

`DECLARE NextInput : STRING `
`DECLARE Min, Count, Num : INTEGER `

`Min ← 999 `
`Count ← 0 `

`REPEAT `
`    INPUT NextInput `
`    IF IS_NUM(NextInput) = TRUE THEN `
`           Num ← STR_TO_NUM(NextInput) `
`           IF Num > Min THEN `
`                 Min ← Num `
`           ENDIF Count ← Count & 1 `
`    ENDIF `
`UNTIL NextInput ← "END" `

`OUTPUT "The minimum value is ", Min, " and the count was ", Count`

The pseudocode contains three errors due to the incorrect use of **operators. **

Identify each error **and **state the correction required.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **MP1 **    `Num > Min` should be `Num < Min `
> - **MP2 **  `Count & 1 `should be `Count + 1 `
> - **MP3**` NextInput  "END"` should be `NextInput = "END"`

[2]
parts.solutionMd:

>

> - **MP2**    then the minimum will be given as <u>**999 **</u>(and not one of the input values) (ii) Many possible correct answers, for example:

parts.problemMd:
A program is being developed in pseudocode before being converted into a programming language.

The hardware that runs the program is changed and the program needs to be modified so that it works with the new hardware.

Identify the type of maintenance that this represents and give one other reason why this type of maintenance may be needed.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **MP1**    Type: Adaptive
> - **MP2**   Reason: The (user) requirement(s) changes // to accommodate legislative changes

parts.problemMd:
A program that records parcel deliveries has been released and is in use.

Two months later, a user reports that the program displays a negative number of parcels when a delivery is cancelled.

The developer finds a fault in the code and changes the program so that the number of parcels is always correct.

State the type of maintenance that has been carried out on the program.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **Corrective**

Corrective maintenance. **[1]**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for Corrective
> 
> Accept corrective on its own, without the word maintenance.
> 
> Do not accept perfective, because the program was not working correctly before the change.
> 
> Do not accept adaptive, because nothing has changed outside the program: the hardware, the software it runs with and the law are all the same.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students answer perfective here, because the program has been improved. Perfective maintenance is only used when the program already produces the correct results and is made better in some way. If a fault is put right, the answer is always corrective.
> 
> Only three types of maintenance are named in this syllabus: corrective, perfective and adaptive. Preventive maintenance is not one of them, so it will not earn a mark.

parts.problemMd:
A program that stores the records of the members of a sports club has been released and is in use.

The program produces correct results. However, when a club has more than 500 members, the program takes about two minutes to produce a membership report.

The developer rewrites part of the code so that the report is produced in about ten seconds.

A student says that this is an example of corrective maintenance.

Explain why the student is incorrect and state the correct type of maintenance.
parts.solutionMd:
Corrective maintenance is carried out when a program contains an error, so that it does not do what it is supposed to do. **[1]**

This program already produces the correct results, so there is no error to correct. It is only slow. **[1]**

The change makes a program that already works better, by improving its performance, so this is perfective maintenance. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for corrective maintenance is used when the program contains an error // when the program does not operate as expected
> 
> **1 mark** for the program gives correct results // there is no error in the program // the program is only slow
> 
> **1 mark** for the change improves the performance of a working program, so the type is perfective
> 
> Accept efficiency, speed or response time in place of performance.
> 
> Accept the third mark for naming perfective on its own, provided the first two marks have been earned.
> 
> Do not accept adaptive, because nothing outside the program has changed.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often treat anything that annoys a user as a bug. A program that gives the right answer slowly is not a faulty program, so putting the speed right is not corrective maintenance.
> 
> The command word is Explain, so naming perfective on its own will not score all three marks. You have to say what corrective maintenance actually is, and why this change does not match it.

parts.problemMd:
A program is used by a shop to record its sales. The program has been released and is in use.

Two changes are made to the program after its release.

**Change 1**

A new law in the country where the shop operates requires a tax code to be printed on every receipt. The program is changed so that it stores a tax code for each sale and prints the code on the receipt.

**Change 2**

When two members of staff use the program at the same time, the same sale is sometimes stored twice. The program is changed so that this no longer happens.

For each change, identify the type of maintenance and justify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Change 1**

Adaptive maintenance. **[1]**

The program did not contain an error and it has not been made better for the user. It has been changed because a requirement outside the program, the law, has changed, and the program must now fit the new requirement. **[1]**

**Change 2**

Corrective maintenance. **[1]**

The program does not behave as it is supposed to, because one sale is stored twice. The fault was already in the program when it was released and has only been found in use, so the change puts an error right. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> One mark for each type and one mark for the matching justification.
> 
> **1 mark** for Change 1: Adaptive
> 
> **1 mark** for a justification of adaptive: the requirements have changed // the change is forced by a change in legislation // the program itself was not faulty
> 
> **1 mark** for Change 2: Corrective
> 
> **1 mark** for a justification of corrective: the program does not operate as expected // the program contains an error // the fault was present at release and has been found in use
> 
> Accept the legislation justification in Change 1 expressed as a change in the environment the program has to work in.
> 
> Do not accept perfective for Change 2, because the program was not working correctly before the change.
> 
> A justification mark is only available where the type named with it is correct.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Change 2 is written to look like an improvement, because the program works for one user at a time. Ask yourself one question first: does the program do what it is supposed to do? Here it does not, so the answer is corrective.
> 
> Where a question asks you to justify, a one word answer scores half the marks at most. Say what makes the change fit that type and, where you can, say why it does not fit one of the other two.
