Shortest job first executes the processes in ascending order of the processor time needed: Q, S, R, P. **[1]**

The short processes Q, S and R are completed first, so more processes are executed in a smaller amount of time, which is an increased throughput. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One mark for each point (max 2) for first come first served:**
> 
> - processes are executed one by one in the order they joined the queue // in the order P, Q, R, S
> - ... so P, the longest process, is executed first // Q, R and S must all wait until P has finished // no process is completed for the first 45 ms
> 
> **One mark for each point (max 2) for shortest job first:**
> 
> - processes are executed in ascending order of the amount of processor / CPU time required // short processes are executed first and followed by longer processes // in the order Q, S, R, P
> - ... which leads to an increased throughput because more processes are executed in a smaller amount of time // Q, S and R are all completed before P would have finished under first come first served
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> The answer must use the processes in the table: a description of the two routines that never refers to P, Q, R or S earns a maximum of 2 marks
> 
> Do not accept "shortest job first completes all four processes sooner": both routines finish all four processes at the same time

> **[exam-tip]**
> Shortest job first does not finish the whole set of processes any sooner, because the processor has the same total amount of work to do. The benefit is that more processes are finished early on, which is what throughput measures.
> 
> Make the table do the work. Name the long process that holds everything up under first come first served, and give the order that shortest job first uses. A general description of the two routines that could apply to any set of processes will not earn full marks.

parts.problemMd:
A computer uses segmentation for memory management.

Identify the **two** values that make up an address in a program's logical address space when segmentation is used.
parts.solutionMd:
Segment number / segment name **[1]**

Offset / offset value **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for segment number / segment name
> 
> **1 mark** for offset / offset value
> 
> Accept the two values in either order
> 
> Do not accept page number, because pages are the fixed-size blocks used in paging, not in segmentation
> 
> Do not accept physical address, because the address the program uses is a logical address that is mapped to a physical address

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students mix up the vocabulary of paging and segmentation and write "page number and offset". In segmentation the blocks are called segments, so the address holds the segment number or segment name together with an offset.
> 
> Do not answer "the physical address". The program works with logical addresses. The operating system uses the segment number as an index in the segment map table, and that table maps the logical address to a physical address.

parts.problemMd:
Paging and segmentation are both used in memory management.

Complete the table to show **one** difference between paging and segmentation for each feature.

| Feature | Paging | Segmentation |
|---|---|---|
| Size of each block of memory |   |   |
| What calculates the size of the blocks |   |   |
| Speed of access |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Feature | Paging | Segmentation |
|---|---|---|
| Size of each block of memory | **Fixed size** | **Variable size** **[1]** |
| What calculates the size of the blocks | **The operating system** | **The compiler** **[1]** |
| Speed of access | **Faster** | **Slower** **[1]** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for paging: fixed size **and** segmentation: variable size
> 
> **1 mark** for paging: the operating system **and** segmentation: the compiler
> 
> **1 mark** for paging: faster **and** segmentation: slower
> 
> Both cells in a row must be correct for the mark
> 
> Accept same size / equal size for fixed size, and varying size / different sizes for variable size
> 
> Accept OS for the operating system
> 
> Accept access times are shorter for paging and longer for segmentation
> 
> Do not accept a row that gives the same answer for paging and segmentation, because the row must show a difference

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error is to describe segments as "bigger" than pages, or as blocks for "different types of data". Neither is the difference that is credited. The key word is size: pages are all a fixed size, but each segment has its own variable size.
> 
> Treat every row as a two-sided comparison. A row with only one column filled in, or with a statement about only one technique, cannot earn the mark.

parts.problemMd:
A computer has 8 GiB of RAM. A user starts a program that needs 12 GiB of memory for its code and data. The operating system uses segmentation and virtual memory.

Explain how segmentation and virtual memory allow this program to run on the computer.
parts.solutionMd:
The logical address space of the program is divided into blocks of varying size called segments **[1]**

The segments are held in virtual memory, which uses secondary storage such as a hard disk to extend the RAM **[1]**

While the program runs, a segment is loaded from virtual memory into physical memory only when it is needed, so only the segments in use are in RAM **[1]**

A segment map table maps the logical addresses in the program to physical addresses in RAM **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any four from:**
> 
> - The logical / virtual address space is divided into variable / varying sized blocks called segments
> - Each segment has a name / number and a size
> - Segments are held in virtual memory / on secondary storage, which is used to extend the RAM available
> - During execution, segments are loaded from virtual memory into physical memory / RAM when they are needed
> - Only the segments in use need to be in RAM, so segments are swapped between RAM and virtual memory as necessary
> - A segment map table maps logical / virtual addresses to physical addresses
> - An address is given as a segment number and an offset, and the segment number is used as an index in the segment map table
> - So the CPU appears to be able to access more memory (12 GiB) than the RAM available (8 GiB)
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> Accept disk / hard disk for secondary storage
> 
> Do not accept "virtual memory adds more RAM", because the RAM stays at 8 GiB and secondary storage only makes more memory appear to be available
> 
> Do not accept segments of fixed size, because fixed-size blocks are pages

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common error is to write that virtual memory increases the RAM. It does not. Secondary storage is used to extend the memory available, so the CPU only appears to have access to more memory than the RAM holds.
> 
> Students also answer about segmentation and virtual memory separately and never connect them. To reach 4 marks, show the link: the segments wait in virtual memory and are loaded into RAM only when they are needed, and the segment map table tells the computer where each segment is in physical memory.

parts.problemMd: Describe what is meant by **virtual memory**.
parts.solutionMd:
Virtual memory is when secondary storage, such as a hard disk, is used to extend the RAM **[1]**

This means the computer appears to be able to access more memory than the RAM it actually has **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - Secondary storage / disk is used to extend the RAM / to simulate additional main memory
> - The CPU appears to be able to access more memory than the RAM available
> - Only the data in use needs to be held in RAM
> - Data / programs not immediately needed are swapped between RAM and virtual memory as necessary
> - Virtual memory is created temporarily
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Do not accept cache memory, because cache is fast memory used by the processor, not secondary storage used to extend RAM
> 
> Do not accept a virtual machine, because a virtual machine is software that emulates a computer, which is a different idea

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not confuse virtual memory with a virtual machine. The names are similar, but a virtual machine emulates a whole computer, while virtual memory is secondary storage being used as if it were extra main memory.
> 
> Avoid writing that virtual memory "is extra RAM". No RAM is added. The mark is for saying that secondary storage is used to extend the memory available.

parts.problemMd:
A computer uses paging and virtual memory. The RAM is full. A running program needs a page that is currently held in virtual memory.

Describe how the operating system replaces a page in RAM so that the program can use the page it needs.
parts.solutionMd:
A page in RAM that is not immediately needed is identified **[1]**

This page is swapped out of RAM and moved to virtual memory on secondary storage, which frees space in RAM **[1]**

The page the program needs is swapped in from virtual memory into the space in RAM **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - A page in RAM that is not immediately needed / not in use is identified
> - This page is moved / swapped out of RAM to virtual memory / secondary storage
> - This frees space in RAM
> - The needed page is moved / swapped in from virtual memory / secondary storage into RAM
> - Pages are swapped between RAM and virtual memory in this way whenever they are needed
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept disk / hard disk for secondary storage
> 
> Do not accept "the program waits until RAM becomes free", because the operating system makes the space itself by swapping a page out

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often describe only half of the swap. They say the needed page is loaded into RAM but never say where the space comes from. The RAM is full, so a page that is not immediately needed must first be swapped out to virtual memory.
> 
> Past mark schemes describe replacement as pages being swapped in and out of virtual memory. They have not asked for a named method of choosing which page to remove, so spend your time describing both directions of the swap clearly.

parts.problemMd:
A computer uses virtual memory stored on a hard disk drive. A technician records how the computer spends its time as more programs are opened.

| Number of programs open | Percentage of time spent processing data | Percentage of time spent swapping pages |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 95 | 5 |
| 4 | 88 | 12 |
| 6 | 70 | 30 |
| 8 | 45 | 55 |
| 10 | 10 | 90 |

(i) Using the table, state the smallest number of programs open at which the computer has reached the thrash point. Give a reason for your answer.

(2)

(ii) Explain why the percentage of time spent swapping pages increases as more programs are opened.

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
**(i)**

8 programs **[1]**

At 8 programs, more time is spent swapping pages (55%) than processing data (45%) **[1]**

**(ii)**

As more programs are opened, the RAM fills up **[1]**

More and more pages need to be swapped in and out of virtual memory **[1]**

This causes a very high rate of hard disk access, and moving the read/write head takes a relatively long time, so swapping uses up more and more of the computer's time **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **(i)**
> 
> **1 mark** for 8 (programs)
> 
> **1 mark** for more time is spent swapping pages than processing data / 55% swapping is greater than 45% processing
> 
> The reason mark can only be awarded with the answer 8
> 
> Do not accept 10, because the thrash point is reached as soon as more time is spent swapping pages than processing data, which first happens at 8 programs
> 
> **(ii)**
> 
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - As more programs are opened, the RAM / main memory fills up
> - More and more pages need to be swapped in and out of virtual memory / secondary storage
> - This leads to a very high rate of hard disk access / excessive disk head movements
> - Moving the hard disk read/write head takes a relatively long time / has a long latency
> 
> **[3 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In (i), a frequent error is to choose 10 programs because the computer has almost stopped processing. The thrash point is not the moment the computer freezes. It is the point at which more time is spent swapping pages than processing data, and at 8 programs swapping (55%) has already overtaken processing (45%).
> 
> In (ii), "the computer slows down" earns nothing on its own. Build the chain of cause and effect: the RAM fills, so pages are swapped in and out more often, and every swap needs slow hard disk access.

parts.problemMd: Explain how an expression stored in RPN can be evaluated.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One** mark per mark point **(Max 3) **
> 
> - MP1    The (RPN) expression is read from left to right, one item at a time
> - MP2    Each element is checked to see if it as operator or a value
> - MP3    Values are pushed onto a stack until an operator is found
> - MP4    The operator is applied to the last two values on the stack and the result is pushed back onto the stack

parts.problemMd: Write this infix expression in Reverse Polish Notation (RPN).
parts.solutionMd:
The bracketed subtraction is divided by r first, which gives `p q - r /` **[1]**

The multiplication has higher precedence than the addition, so s is multiplied by 3 and the addition is applied last, which gives `s 3 * +` **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `p q - r /`
> 
> **1 mark** for `s 3 * +`
> 
> Complete answer:
> 
> Accept the two operands of the addition in the other order, `s 3 * p q - r / +`, or the operands of the multiplication swapped, `3 s *`, because both operators give the same result either way
> 
> Do not accept `p q - r / s + 3 *`, which adds s before multiplying by 3 and ignores operator precedence
> 
> Do not accept `q p - r / s 3 * +`, which calculates q - p instead of p - q

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common mistake is to copy the operators in the order they appear from left to right. That gives `p q - r / s + 3 *`, which works out ((p - q) / r + s) multiplied by 3. Multiplication and division are carried out before addition and subtraction, so add the hidden brackets first: ((p - q) / r) + (s * 3). Then convert one bracket at a time.
> 
> The safest method is to keep the letters and numbers in the same order as they appear in the infix expression. Only the operators move. If your answer has q before p, the subtraction is the wrong way round.

parts.problemMd:
A program written in a high-level language is run using an interpreter.

Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether each statement about how the interpreter executes the program is true or false.

| Statement | True | False |
|---|---|---|
| The interpreter checks each statement for errors before it executes that statement. |   |   |
| The interpreter translates the whole program into an executable file before it executes any statement. |   |   |
| The statements inside a loop are interpreted again on every iteration of the loop. |   |   |
| After the program has been run once, it can be run again without being interpreted again. |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Statement | True | False |
|---|---|---|
| The interpreter checks each statement for errors before it executes that statement. | **✓** |   |
| The interpreter translates the whole program into an executable file before it executes any statement. |   | **✓** |
| The statements inside a loop are interpreted again on every iteration of the loop. | **✓** |   |
| After the program has been run once, it can be run again without being interpreted again. |   | **✓** |

Rows 1 and 3 are true. Rows 2 and 4 are false. **[2]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **2 marks** for all four rows correct
> 
> **1 mark** for two or three rows correct
> 
> A row with both boxes ticked, or with no box ticked, is incorrect.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Row 3 is the row students get wrong most often. They picture an interpreter reading down the program once, from top to bottom. An interpreter keeps nothing it has translated, so each time a loop sends it back to a statement, it must check and execute that statement again.
> 
> Row 2 describes a compiler, not an interpreter. A compiler produces an executable file. An interpreter executes the program without producing a translated version of it.

parts.problemMd:
A program that is run using an interpreter contains this loop.

A student makes this claim:

"The interpreter translates the statement inside the loop once. It stores the translated version and reuses it on each pass of the loop. When the program is run again next week, the stored version is used again."

Explain why the student's claim is wrong.
parts.solutionMd:
An interpreter does not produce a translated version of the program, so there is nothing to store and reuse. **[1]**

It examines one statement at a time, checks it for errors and then executes it. This means the statement inside the loop is interpreted again on each of the 1000 iterations. **[1]**

Nothing is kept after the program finishes, so the whole program has to be interpreted again when it is run next week. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - An interpreter does not produce or store a translated version of the program
> - It examines one statement at a time, checks the statement for errors and then executes it
> - The statement inside the loop is interpreted again on every iteration // it is interpreted 1000 times
> - The program has to be interpreted again every time it is run // next week it is interpreted again from the start
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept "line" in place of "statement".
> 
> Do not accept "an interpreter translates line by line" on its own. It does not explain why the claim about storing and reusing a translation is wrong.
> 
> Do not accept "the interpreter produces an executable file that is used next week". That describes a compiler.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many answers describe an interpreter correctly but never apply it to the loop. The question tells you the loop runs 1000 times, so use that number: the statement inside it is interpreted 1000 times.
> 
> The same fact answers the last part of the claim. No translated version is ever kept, so next week the interpreter starts again from the first statement.

parts.problemMd: Write this Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) expression in infix form.
parts.solutionMd:
b and c are multiplied, and the result is added to a, giving `a + b * c` **[1]**

a is subtracted from d, in that order, giving `(d - a)` **[1]**

The whole of the first term is divided by the whole of the second term, so both terms are in brackets **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `a + b * c` as one term
> 
> **1 mark** for `(d - a)` with the operands in this order
> 
> **1 mark** for the division of the first term by the second, with brackets around both terms
> 
> Complete answer:
> 
> Accept extra brackets that do not change the meaning, for example `(a + (b * c)) / (d - a)`
> 
> Accept the operands of the addition or the multiplication in the other order, for example `(b * c + a) / (d - a)`
> 
> Do not accept `a + b * c / (d - a)`, which divides only b multiplied by c by (d - a) (loses the third mark)
> 
> Do not accept `(a + b) * c / (d - a)`, which adds a and b before multiplying (loses the first mark)
> 
> Do not accept `(a + b * c) / (a - d)`, which reverses the subtraction (loses the second mark)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an operator is reached, it joins the two terms just before it, and the earlier of those two terms goes on the left. Students often write a - d here, because a is the letter nearest to the minus sign. The RPN has d then a, so the answer is d - a.
> 
> The brackets are where most marks are lost. In RPN the division comes last, so it applies to everything before it. Without brackets, precedence would make the division happen before the addition and the subtraction. Check your answer by converting it back to RPN: you should get the expression you started with.

parts.problemMd:
A program is run using an interpreter. The line numbers are for reference only and are not part of the program. Variable declarations are not shown.

Line 07 contains a syntax error. There are no other errors in the program.

Describe what happens when the program is run using the interpreter.
parts.solutionMd:
The interpreter examines the program one statement at a time. It checks each statement for errors before it executes that statement. **[1]**

Lines 01 to 06 contain no errors, so each one is executed as soon as it has been checked. Lines 03 and 04 are checked and executed again on each of the three iterations of the loop. **[1]**

This output is displayed before the interpreter reaches line 07: **[1]**

When line 07 is checked, the syntax error is found and reported, and the interpreter halts. Line 08 is never executed. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any four from:**
> 
> - Each statement is examined and checked for errors before it is executed
> - Lines 01 to 06 are each executed as soon as they have been checked // the program starts to run even though it contains an error
> - Lines 03 and 04 are interpreted again on each iteration of the loop // they are interpreted three times
> - `Pass 1`, `Pass 2`, `Pass 3` and `Total is 6` are output before the error is found
> - The error in line 07 is reported and the interpreter halts
> - Line 08 is never examined or executed
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> For the output point, all four lines of output must be given in the correct order.
> 
> Accept "stops" in place of "halts".
> 
> Do not accept "the error in line 07 is reported before any statement is executed" or "nothing is output". That is how a compiler behaves, because a compiler translates the whole program before any of it can run.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common wrong answer says that nothing is output because the program contains an error. That is true of a compiled program, not an interpreted one. The interpreter does not look at line 07 until it gets there, so lines 01 to 06 have already run and their output is already on the screen.
> 
> Write the output exactly. The loop runs three times, so there are three Pass lines, and the total is 6 because 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

Name the stage of compilation described by each statement.

(i) The source code is converted from a sequence of characters into a sequence of tokens.

(1)

(ii) The program is changed to minimise its execution time and its memory requirement.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Lexical analysis **[1]**

(ii) Optimisation **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for lexical analysis
> 
> **1 mark** for optimisation
> 
> Accept the spelling "optimization".
> 
> Do not accept syntax analysis for (i). Syntax analysis works on the tokens after lexical analysis has produced them.
>

parts.problemMd:
A game uses a short code to unlock each level. The Backus-Naur Form (BNF) for a code is shown.

State whether each of the following codes is valid or invalid for `<code>`. Give a reason for your choice in each case.

`C4%`

`B6@`
parts.solutionMd:
`C4%` is **valid**. It is a letter (C), followed by a digit (4), followed by a symbol (%), so it matches `<letter><digit><symbol>`. **[1]**

`B6@` is **invalid**. The 6 is not a valid digit, because `<digit>` only allows 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `C4%` valid, with a reason: a letter followed by a digit followed by a symbol // it matches `<letter><digit><symbol>`
> 
> **1 mark** for `B6@` invalid, with a reason: 6 is not a valid digit // `<digit>` only allows 1 to 5
> 
> Each mark needs both the decision and a correct reason
> 
> Do not accept that `B6@` is invalid because it ends with a symbol: a code can end with a symbol, and @ is a valid symbol

> **[exam-tip]**
> `B6@` has the right shape: a letter, then a digit, then a symbol. Many students stop there and call it valid. Check every character against its own rule. The rule `<digit>` allows only the values listed after `::=`, and 6 is not one of them.
> 
> When you give a reason, say exactly which character breaks which rule. "It does not follow the rules" does not earn the mark.

parts.problemMd:
A program contains this statement.

The statement contains an error. The program is compiled.

Identify the stage of compilation at which this error is reported, and explain why the error is not reported during lexical analysis.
parts.solutionMd:
The error is reported during syntax analysis. **[1]**

Lexical analysis converts the characters into a sequence of tokens: `Cost`, `←`, `Price`, `+`, `*` and `Quantity`. Every one of these is a valid token, so lexical analysis finds no error. **[1]**

Syntax analysis checks that the sequence of tokens follows the grammar of the language. There is no operand between the operators `+` and `*`, so the rules are broken and a syntax error is reported. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for syntax analysis
> 
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - Lexical analysis only converts the characters into tokens
> - Each token in the statement is valid // `+` and `*` are both valid tokens
> - Syntax analysis checks the sequence of tokens against the grammar / rules of the language
> - Two operators next to each other do not match the rules // an operand is missing between `+` and `*`
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept "parsing" or "the parser" for syntax analysis.
> 
> Do not accept lexical analysis or code generation as the stage.
> 
> Do not accept "run-time error" or "logic error". This error is found during compilation, before the program can be run.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often choose lexical analysis because it is the first stage, and they expect the first stage to find every mistake. Lexical analysis only decides whether each group of characters is a valid token. It does not check the order of the tokens.
> 
> A statement made entirely of valid tokens can still break the rules of the language. Checking the order of the tokens against the grammar is the job of syntax analysis.

parts.problemMd:
A program contains this statement.

The statement contains no errors. The program is compiled.

Describe what happens to this statement at each stage of compilation.
parts.solutionMd:
Lexical analysis: the characters in the statement are converted into a sequence of tokens, `Area`, `←`, `Length`, `*`, `Width`, `+` and `10`. **[1]**

Syntax analysis: the sequence of tokens is checked against the grammar of the language. The statement follows the rules, so no syntax error is reported and a parse tree is produced. **[1]**

Code generation: the intermediate representation of the statement is converted into an executable form, for example object code. **[1]**

Optimisation: the code is changed to minimise the program's execution time and memory requirement. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each stage named with a correct description, **max 4**:
> 
> - Lexical analysis: the characters are converted into a sequence of tokens
> - Syntax analysis: the tokens are checked against the grammar / rules of the language // a parse tree is produced
> - Code generation: the intermediate representation / parse tree is converted into an executable form // object code / machine code is produced
> - Optimisation: the code is changed to minimise execution time // to minimise memory requirement
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> A stage name without a description, or a description without a stage name, earns no mark.
> 
> Accept the stages described in any order.
> 
> Do not accept "the statement is executed" for any stage. A compiler translates the program; no stage of compilation executes it.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A frequent error is to describe code generation as the stage that runs the code. No stage of compilation runs the program. Code generation produces the executable form, and the program is run later.
> 
> Tie each description to what the stage takes in and what it produces: characters into tokens, tokens into a parse tree, intermediate representation into executable form. "It checks the code" is too vague to earn the mark for any stage.

parts.problemMd:
The Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) expression:

is to be evaluated when a = 40, b = 3, c = 2, d = 4 and e = 11.

Show the changing contents of the stack as the RPN expression is evaluated. Complete the table. Each column shows the stack after one more item has been read. Fill each column from the bottom row upwards.

| Item read | `a` | `b` | `c` | `d` | `+` | `*` | `-` | `e` | `/` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
| Bottom of stack |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Item read | `a` | `b` | `c` | `d` | `+` | `*` | `-` | `e` | `/` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|   |   |   |   | **4** |   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   | **2** | **2** | **6** |   |   |   |   |
|   |   | **3** | **3** | **3** | **3** | **18** |   | **11** |   |
| Bottom of stack | **40** | **40** | **40** | **40** | **40** | **40** | **22** | **22** | **2** |

Columns 1 to 3: a, b and c are pushed, giving 40, then 40, 3, then 40, 3, 2 **[1]**

Columns 4 and 5: d is pushed, giving 40, 3, 2, 4, then the addition pops 4 and 2 and pushes 6, giving 40, 3, 6 **[1]**

Columns 6 and 7: the multiplication pops 6 and 3 and pushes 18, then the subtraction pops 18 and 40 and pushes 40 - 18 = 22 **[1]**

Columns 8 and 9: e is pushed, giving 22, 11, then the division pops 11 and 22 and pushes 22 / 11 = 2 **[1]**

The value of the expression is 2.

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for columns 1 to 3: 40; 40, 3; 40, 3, 2
> 
> **1 mark** for columns 4 and 5: 40, 3, 2, 4; 40, 3, 6
> 
> **1 mark** for columns 6 and 7: 40, 18; 22
> 
> **1 mark** for columns 8 and 9: 22, 11; 2
> 
> Values within a column are listed from the bottom of the stack to the top, and semicolons separate the columns.
> 
> Accept the values in each column placed at the top of the column instead of the bottom, provided the most recently pushed value is the highest one in that column
> 
> Do not accept operators written into the stack
> 
> Do not accept -22 in column 7 or -2 in column 9, which come from subtracting 40 from 18 instead of 18 from 40
> 
> Do not accept 0.5 in column 9, which comes from dividing 11 by 22

> **[exam-tip]**
> The first value popped is the right-hand operand, not the left-hand one. When the minus sign is read, 18 is popped first and 40 second, so the calculation is 40 - 18. Students who work out "first pop minus second pop" get -22, and every column after that is wrong too.
> 
> Keep every value that is not popped. After the multiplication, 40 is still at the bottom of the stack, waiting. A column that loses it cannot earn the mark.

parts.problemMd:
A parcel locker is opened with a code. The Backus-Naur Form (BNF) for some parts of the code is shown.

A new syntax rule, `<locker>`, is required. A locker code must begin with two letters, followed by one digit or one symbol, and end with one or two digits.

Write the BNF for `<locker>`.
parts.solutionMd:
One mark for `<locker> ::=` followed by one correct alternative **[1]**

One mark for two more correct alternatives, separated by `|` **[1]**

One mark for all four alternatives correct, with no incorrect alternative **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `<locker> ::=` followed by any one correct alternative
> 
> **1 mark** for two further correct alternatives, each separated by `|`
> 
> **1 mark** for all four alternatives correct and no incorrect alternative
> 
> The alternatives can be written in any order
> 
> Accept this answer, which uses extra rules. Award one mark for each correct rule:
> 
> Any names can be used for the extra rules, as long as each one is defined and used correctly
> 
> Do not accept an attempt such as `<locker> ::= <letter><letter><digit> | <symbol><digit><digit>`: `|` separates whole alternatives, so the second alternative allows a code with no letters

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common error is to put `|` in the middle of an alternative, expecting it to choose only between the two items next to it. In BNF, `|` separates complete alternatives. Anything written before `|` is one whole alternative and anything after it is another.
> 
> Work through the description and list every combination before you write any BNF. Two middle options and two endings give four alternatives. Students often write three and miss a code made of a letter, a letter, a symbol, a digit and a digit, such as `PQ#12`.
> 
> In a syntax diagram, the choice between a digit and a symbol is two parallel paths, and the second end digit is a path that can bypass the box. In BNF, each of these choices becomes an extra alternative.

parts.problemMd:
A weather station sends its temperature readings to a computer as text. The Backus-Naur Form (BNF) for some parts of the text is shown.

The following rules are also needed.

- An integer contains one or more digits.
- A reading is an integer that may have one sign in front of it.
- A message contains one or more readings. When a message has more than one reading, a comma separates each reading from the next one.

For example, `25` and `12,-3,+40` are both valid messages.

Write the BNF for `<integer>`, `<reading>` and `<message>`.
parts.solutionMd:
One mark for `<integer> ::= <digit>` as one alternative **[1]**

One mark for `<integer><digit>` as the second alternative **[1]**

One mark for `<reading> ::= <integer> | <sign><integer>` **[1]**

One mark for `<message> ::= <reading>` as one alternative **[1]**

One mark for `<message>,<reading>` as the second alternative **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `<integer> ::= <digit>` as one alternative
> 
> **1 mark** for a second alternative of `<integer><digit>` // `<digit><integer>`
> 
> **1 mark** for `<reading> ::= <integer> | <sign><integer>`
> 
> **1 mark** for `<message> ::= <reading>` as one alternative
> 
> **1 mark** for a second alternative of `<message>,<reading>` // `<reading>,<message>`
> 
> The alternatives can be written in either order
> 
> Do not accept `<integer> ::= <digit><integer>` with no single `<digit>` alternative: the rule never ends, so it cannot produce any integer
> 
> Do not accept `<message> ::= <reading> | <reading>,<reading>`: this allows only one or two readings, not three or more
> 
> Do not accept `<reading> ::= <integer> | <sign><reading>`: this allows more than one sign, such as `--4`

> **[exam-tip]**
> "One or more" in a question means the rule must refer to itself. Every rule that refers to itself also needs an alternative that does not, such as the single `<digit>` in `<integer>`. Without it, the rule can never finish, so it matches nothing.
> 
> Check where the comma goes. The alternative `<message>,<reading>` always puts a comma between two readings. It can never give a message that starts or ends with a comma, and the question does not allow one.
> 
> In a syntax diagram, "one or more" is drawn as a loop that goes back over the box. In BNF, that loop becomes the rule referring to itself.

parts.problemMd: Describe what is meant by a digital certificate.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One **mark per point (**max 3**)
> 
> MP1 A digital certificate is an electronic/online document.
> 
> MP2 used to authenticate/prove the identity of a website/the online identity of an individual/organisation
> 
> MP3 typically issued by a CA
> 
> MP4 For example: it contains information identifying a website owner/individual and a public key

parts.problemMd: Explain the role of a digital certificate in creating a digital signature.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One **mark per point (**max 2**)
> 
> MP1 The digital certificate **provides the public key **
> 
> MP2 … that can be used to validate the private key associated with the organisation/website/digital signature

parts.problemMd:
Sheila has a customer called Fred. Fred wants to send Sheila a confidential document as part of a transaction.

Explain how Fred uses asymmetric encryption to send his document securely.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One **mark per mark point (**Max 4**)
> 
> MP1 Sheila’s computer uses an algorithm to generate a matching pair of keys private and public
> 
> MP2 Sheila’s computer sends Fred’s computer Sheila’s public key // Fred‘s computer acquires Sheila’s public key
> 
> MP3 Fred’s computer encrypts the document/plain text using Sheila’s public key to create cipher text
> 
> MP4 Fred’s computer sends the cipher text to Sheila’s computer The **cipher text** can only be decrypted using Sheila’s private key // Sheila’s computer uses Sheila’s private key to decrypt the cipher text.

parts.problemMd:
Quantum cryptography can be used to exchange encryption keys securely. However, few organisations use it at present.

State **two** drawbacks of quantum cryptography.
parts.solutionMd:
Quantum cryptography currently only works over relatively short distances. **[1]**

It needs a dedicated fibre optic line and specialist hardware. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - only works over relatively short distances // limited range
> - requires a dedicated fibre optic line and specialist hardware
> - high cost of buying // maintaining the equipment (the dedicated fibre optic line and specialist hardware)
> - the polarisation of light can change during transmission along the fibre optic cable
> - error rates are relatively high because the technology is still being developed
> - lacks features such as digital signatures // certified mail
> - allows criminals and terrorists to hide their communications
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept "the equipment is expensive" for the cost point
> 
> Do not accept a drawback of symmetric encryption, such as "the key has to be shared with the receiver"

> **[exam-tip]**
> Vague answers are the usual way to lose marks here. "It is new technology" does not match a marking point, so say what the newness causes: error rates are still relatively high. In the same way, "it is complicated" is too vague; name what it needs, which is a dedicated fibre optic line and specialist hardware.
> 
> Do not mix this topic up with symmetric and asymmetric encryption. Problems with sharing a key are a reason to use quantum cryptography, not a drawback of it.

parts.problemMd:
A bank exchanges encryption keys between its computers. At present, the security of this key exchange depends on mathematical algorithms. The bank is considering using quantum cryptography for the key exchange instead.

Explain why quantum cryptography can make the key exchange more secure.
parts.solutionMd:
The security of quantum cryptography is based on the laws of physics (the principles of quantum mechanics), not on mathematical algorithms. **[1]**

Any eavesdropping on the key can be detected... **[1]**

...because eavesdropping changes the properties of the photons, so the state of the key is changed. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - security is based on the laws of physics // principles of quantum mechanics // properties of photons, rather than on mathematical algorithms
> - it is virtually unbreakable // virtually unhackable
> - eavesdropping on the key can be detected...
> - ...because the state // properties of the photons will be changed
> - the integrity of the key once transferred can be guaranteed // the key cannot be copied and decrypted at a later date
> - longer // more secure keys can be exchanged
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Award the "because the state is changed" point only together with the point that eavesdropping can be detected
> 
> Do not accept "it uses a public key and a private key": that describes asymmetric cryptography, not quantum cryptography

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students answer this by describing asymmetric encryption, with a public key and a private key. That is a different method and earns nothing here.
> 
> "Eavesdropping can be detected" is only one mark. On a 3-mark explain question, add the reason: the eavesdropping changes the properties of the photons. Then give a separate point, such as the security coming from the laws of physics rather than from mathematical algorithms.

parts.problemMd:
A company uses a digital certificate on its website.

State **two** items of information that the digital certificate contains.
parts.solutionMd:
- The identity details of the owner, for example the name of the company or website owner **[1]**
- The owner's public key **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - information that identifies the owner of the certificate (the company / the website owner / the individual)
> - the owner's public key
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept the name of the Certificate Authority (CA) that issued the certificate, the date the certificate expires, or the digital signature of the CA, as one item each
> 
> Do not accept the owner's private key. A private key is kept secret by its owner and is never sent to anyone, so it cannot be inside a certificate that is shared with the public

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common wrong answer is "the private key". A digital certificate is shared openly, so it can only hold the public key. If the private key were in the certificate, anyone could use it.
> 
> Write "public key" in full. The answer "a key" is not enough, because it does not say which key.

parts.problemMd:
An engineering company is considering using quantum cryptography to exchange encryption keys on two different links.

- **Link A** connects the company's two offices, which are in the same city. The offices are joined by a dedicated fibre optic cable that only the company uses. Secret designs for new machines are sent over this link every day.
- **Link B** connects the company's website to thousands of customers in many different countries. The customers use their own computers and connect to the website over the internet.

Explain why quantum cryptography is suitable for Link A but is **not** suitable for Link B.
parts.solutionMd:
**Link A**

The designs are valuable secrets, and quantum cryptography is virtually unhackable because any eavesdropping on the key can be detected. **[1]**

The two offices are close together and are already joined by a dedicated fibre optic cable, which quantum cryptography needs. **[1]**

**Link B**

The customers are in many different countries, but quantum cryptography only works over relatively short distances. **[1]**

The customers connect over the internet, so each one would need a dedicated fibre optic line and specialist hardware, which would be far too expensive for thousands of customers. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Link A, max 2 from:**
> 
> - the designs are valuable (industrial) secrets, and quantum cryptography is virtually unhackable // eavesdropping can be detected // longer keys can be used
> - the offices are close together, so the link is within the limited range of quantum cryptography
> - the dedicated fibre optic line that quantum cryptography requires is already in place
> 
> **Link B, max 2 from:**
> 
> - the customers are far away // in many different countries, and quantum cryptography only works over relatively short distances // has a limited range
> - the customers connect over the internet and do not have a dedicated fibre optic line and specialist hardware
> - the cost of dedicated fibre optic lines and specialist hardware for thousands of customers is too high
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> If benefits and drawbacks are only listed, with no reference to either link, award a maximum of 2 marks
> 
> Do not accept "the offices have a wired connection" on its own for Link A: the requirement is a dedicated fibre optic line, not any wired connection
> 
> Do not accept that Link B is unsuitable because customer data is not secret: the drawbacks are the distance and the equipment, not the value of the data

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common mistake is to write down two benefits and two drawbacks of quantum cryptography from memory, without saying which link each one applies to. The question gives you the clues: the distance between the sites, the dedicated cable and the number and location of the customers. Use each clue in your answer.
> 
> Notice the word dedicated. The customers are connected by the internet, and the internet is not a dedicated fibre optic line between two points. That is why Link B would need new lines and specialist hardware for every customer.

parts.problemMd:
An online shop sells products to customers in many countries. The shop needs a digital certificate for its website.

Describe how the online shop acquires its digital certificate.
parts.solutionMd:
- The online shop sends a request for a digital certificate to a Certificate Authority (CA) **[1]**
- The shop gives the CA the information it needs to prove the shop's identity **[1]**
- The CA checks / verifies the identity of the shop **[1]**
- If the identity is verified, the CA creates and issues the digital certificate, which includes the shop's public key **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One mark for each point (max 4):**
> 
> - the shop makes a request / enquiry for a certificate to a Certificate Authority (CA)
> - the shop gathers / sends the information the CA needs to prove the shop's identity
> - the shop sends its public key to the CA // the public key is agreed with the CA
> - the CA checks / verifies the shop's identity / details
> - the CA creates / issues the certificate that includes the shop's public key
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> Accept: data sent to or from the CA is encrypted using the CA's public key / private key
> 
> Do not accept the CA sending the shop its private key. The private key belongs to the shop and is never transmitted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many answers say the shop "buys a certificate" or "downloads one" and stop there. That earns nothing. The mark scheme rewards the checking step: the CA must verify the identity of the shop before it issues anything, otherwise anyone could pretend to be the shop.
> 
> Be careful with the keys. The certificate carries the shop's public key. Students often write that the CA gives the shop a private key, which is wrong.

parts.problemMd:
A software company sends an update for one of its programs to customers over the internet.

The company attaches a digital signature to the update. The customer's computer also receives the company's digital certificate.

Explain how the customer's computer uses the digital certificate and the digital signature to check that the update came from the company and has not been altered.
parts.solutionMd:
**Using the digital certificate**

- The digital certificate is issued by a Certificate Authority (CA), so it proves the identity of the company **[1]**
- The certificate provides the company's public key, so the computer knows this public key belongs to the company **[1]**

**Checking the digital signature**

- The digital signature is decrypted using the company's public key to recover the message digest that the company sent **[1]**
- The update that was received is hashed with the same (agreed) hashing algorithm to produce a second message digest **[1]**
- The two message digests are compared **[1]**
- If they are the same, the update came from the company and has not been altered. If they are different, the update has been altered

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Role of the digital certificate (max 2):**
> 
> - the certificate is issued by a CA // authenticates / proves the identity of the company
> - the certificate provides the company's public key
> 
> **Checking the digital signature (max 3):**
> 
> - the digital signature is decrypted with the company's (sender's) public key to recover the message digest sent
> - the received update is hashed with the agreed / same hashing algorithm to produce a message digest of the update received
> - the two message digests are compared
> - if they are the same the update has not been altered / is authentic // if they are different the update has been altered
> 
> **[5 marks]**
> 
> Accept digest for message digest
> 
> Accept for the second certificate point: the public key from the certificate is used to verify / validate the digital signature
> 
> Do not accept the digital signature being decrypted with the company's private key. Only the company holds its private key

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error is using the wrong key. The signature was made with the company's private key, so the customer's computer needs the matching public key, and it gets that key from the digital certificate.
> 
> Many students also skip the second hash. The computer cannot compare anything until it has hashed the update it received. Say that it uses the same hashing algorithm, and say that the two message digests are compared, not the signature and the update.

parts.problemMd:
Data sent between a client and a server across the internet can be protected using SSL/TLS.

State **two** purposes of SSL/TLS.
parts.solutionMd:
To encrypt the data sent between the client and the server, so that the data cannot be understood if it is intercepted **[1]**

To authenticate the server, so that the client knows it is communicating with the genuine website **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - to encrypt data sent between a client and a server // to provide an encrypted connection between the two computers ... so that intercepted data cannot be understood
> - to authenticate the server // to confirm the identity of the website or organisation // to show that the data comes from a trusted source
> - to ensure that the data is not altered during transmission
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept "so that only the intended receiver can understand the data" as part of the encryption point
> 
> Award only **one** mark if both answers describe encryption, for example "it encrypts the data" and "hackers cannot read the data". These are the same point
> 
> Do not accept "to stop data being intercepted". Encryption does not stop interception; it makes intercepted data meaningless
> 
> Do not accept "to protect the computer from viruses" or "to block hackers from the server". These describe anti-virus software and a firewall, not SSL/TLS

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common mistake is to write that SSL/TLS stops data from being intercepted. It does not. Data travelling across the internet can still be intercepted, but because it is encrypted the interceptor cannot understand it. Write "cannot be understood if intercepted".
> 
> The syllabus writes SSL/TLS as one term. Answer about SSL/TLS as a whole, and do not spend time comparing SSL with TLS.

parts.problemMd:
A hospital allows patients to book appointments on its website. A patient uses a web browser to log in with a username and password. The patient then enters their date of birth and a description of their symptoms.

The hospital's web server uses SSL/TLS.

Explain why the use of SSL/TLS is appropriate in this situation.
parts.solutionMd:
The password, date of birth and symptoms are personal, confidential data **[1]**

SSL/TLS encrypts this data while it travels between the patient's browser and the hospital's web server, so if it is intercepted it cannot be understood **[1]**

SSL/TLS authenticates the hospital's web server, so the patient knows they are entering their details on the genuine hospital website **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - the data being sent (password / date of birth / symptoms) is personal / confidential / sensitive
> - the data is encrypted between the browser (client) and the web server ... so it cannot be understood if it is intercepted
> - the web server is authenticated (using its digital certificate) ... so the patient knows the website is genuine / belongs to the hospital
> - SSL/TLS ensures the data is not altered during transmission, for example the booking details are not changed
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Award the first point only if at least one item of data from the scenario is named
> 
> Accept "a hacker who intercepts the password cannot read it" for the encryption point
> 
> Do not accept "SSL/TLS stops hackers intercepting the data". Intercepted data is still intercepted; it is meaningless because it is encrypted
> 
> Do not accept "SSL/TLS keeps the patient records secure on the hospital's server". SSL/TLS protects data while it is transmitted between the client and the server, not data stored on the server

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often write a general answer about encryption that could describe any system. The question says "in this situation", so name the data from the scenario, such as the password or the symptoms, and say why it needs protecting.
> 
> SSL/TLS only protects data while it travels between the browser and the web server. Do not claim that it keeps the records safe once they are stored in the hospital's database. That needs a different security measure.

parts.problemMd:
A company encrypts a message before it sends the message over the internet.

State what is meant by plain text and cipher text.
parts.solutionMd:
Plain text is the original data, before it is encrypted, which can be read and understood **[1]**

Cipher text is the data produced by encryption, which is meaningless and cannot be understood without the key to decrypt it **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for plain text: the original / unencrypted data, which can be understood
> 
> **1 mark** for cipher text: the encrypted / scrambled data, which cannot be understood without the (decryption) key
> 
> Accept "readable" for "can be understood", and "scrambled" or "encoded" for "encrypted"
> 
> Do not accept "text with no formatting" for plain text, because that is a word-processing meaning, not the encryption meaning

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often write that cipher text "cannot be intercepted". Encryption does not stop anyone intercepting the data. It makes the intercepted data meaningless to anyone who does not have the key.
> 
> Plain text does not have to be text. A photo or a spreadsheet is also plain text before it is encrypted.

parts.problemMd:
A customer uses a web browser to connect to an online bank. The browser is the client and the bank's computer is the web server. The connection uses SSL/TLS.

Describe how SSL/TLS is used to set up secure communication between the browser and the web server.
parts.solutionMd:
The web server sends the browser its digital certificate, which contains the server's public key **[1]**

The browser checks that the certificate is valid and was issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA), so it knows the server is the genuine bank **[1]**

A symmetric key is exchanged securely: the browser encrypts it using the server's public key, and only the server's private key can decrypt it **[1]**

All data sent between the browser and the web server is then encrypted using the symmetric key **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any four from:**
> 
> - the browser requests a secure connection // asks the web server to identify itself
> - the web server sends its digital certificate to the browser
> - ... the certificate contains the web server's public key
> - the browser checks that the certificate is valid / was issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) ... so the web server is authenticated / genuine
> - a symmetric key is agreed / exchanged securely // the browser encrypts a symmetric key with the server's public key ... which only the server's private key can decrypt
> - all data sent between the browser and the web server is then encrypted using the symmetric key
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> Accept "session key" for "symmetric key"
> 
> Do not award the final point for "all the data is encrypted using the server's public key". SSL/TLS uses the public key to exchange the symmetric key, and the symmetric key encrypts the data
> 
> Do not accept "the web server sends its private key to the browser". A private key is never transmitted
> 
> No marks for describing how the bank obtained its digital certificate from the CA. The question asks how the certificate is used, not how it is acquired

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common mistake is to mix up the two keys. The server's private key never leaves the server. The browser uses the server's public key, taken from the certificate, so that only the server can read the symmetric key.
> 
> Another mistake is to say that all of the data is encrypted with the public key. Asymmetric encryption is slower, so SSL/TLS uses it only to exchange the symmetric key. The faster symmetric encryption then protects the rest of the communication.

parts.problemMd:
Asymmetric cryptography uses a public key and a private key.

Describe the relationship between the public key and the private key.
parts.solutionMd:
The public key and the private key are generated together, by an algorithm, as a matching pair **[1]**

The private key is kept secret by its owner and is never transmitted **[1]**

Data encrypted with one key of the pair can only be decrypted with the matching key **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - the keys are a matching pair / are generated together (by an algorithm)
> - the public key is available to everyone / is shared / is published
> - the private key is kept secret / is unpublished / is never transmitted
> - data encrypted with one key can only be decrypted with the other, matching key (for example, encrypted with the public key and decrypted with the matching private key)
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Do not accept a description in which the same key both encrypts and decrypts the data, because that is symmetric cryptography
> 
> Do not accept "the private key is sent securely to the receiver", because the private key is never transmitted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students learn "public key encrypts, private key decrypts" as a fixed rule. It only describes sending a private message. The keys work in both directions: data encrypted with the private key can be decrypted with the matching public key. That is how a sender proves a message came from them. Describe the relationship as "one key encrypts, only the matching key decrypts" and you are right in both cases.

parts.problemMd:
A national weather agency publishes storm warnings to the public over the internet. Members of the public need to be sure that a warning really came from the agency, and not from someone pretending to be the agency.

The agency uses asymmetric cryptography.

Explain how the agency's keys are used so that members of the public can verify that a warning came from the agency.
parts.solutionMd:
The agency makes its public key available to everyone **[1]**

The agency encrypts the warning using its own private key **[1]**

A member of the public decrypts the warning using the agency's public key **[1]**

Only the agency holds the matching private key, and it is never transmitted, so a warning that decrypts correctly with the agency's public key must have come from the agency **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any four from:**
> 
> - the agency has / generates a matching pair of keys, a public key and a private key
> - the agency's public key is made available to everyone / the public
> - the warning is encrypted using the agency's (the sender's) private key
> - the public decrypt the warning using the agency's (the sender's) public key
> - only the agency has the private key / the private key is kept secret / is never transmitted
> - so a warning that can be decrypted with the agency's public key must have been encrypted by the agency / is authentic
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> Accept "sender's private key" and "sender's public key"
> 
> Accept the same key steps applied to a digest of the warning (a digital signature)
> 
> Do not accept the warning being encrypted with the public's or the receiver's public key, because there is no single receiver and the agency would not be proving who sent it
> 
> Do not accept "the agency sends its private key to the public", because then anyone could pretend to be the agency

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error is to use the private-message method out of habit and encrypt with the receiver's public key. Ask two questions before you write. Who must be able to read it? Everyone, so the public key decrypts. Who must be the only one able to create it? The agency, so the agency's private key encrypts.
> 
> This method does not keep the warning secret, because anyone with the public key can decrypt it. That is not a weakness here: a public warning is not confidential, and the aim is to prove who sent it.

parts.problemMd:
Data can be encrypted using symmetric cryptography or asymmetric cryptography.

Tick (✓) one box in each row to show whether the statement applies to symmetric cryptography or asymmetric cryptography.

| Statement | Symmetric | Asymmetric |
|---|---|---|
| Uses one key to both encrypt and decrypt the data |   |   |
| Uses a matching pair of keys |   |   |
| Only one of the keys is shared with others |   |   |
| The same key must be shared with everyone who needs to read the data |   |   |
| Is usually the faster process |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Statement | Symmetric | Asymmetric |
|---|---|---|
| Uses one key to both encrypt and decrypt the data | **✓** |   |
| Uses a matching pair of keys |   | **✓** |
| Only one of the keys is shared with others |   | **✓** |
| The same key must be shared with everyone who needs to read the data | **✓** |   |
| Is usually the faster process | **✓** |   |

All five rows correct **[2]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **2 marks** for all five rows correct
> 
> **1 mark** for four rows correct
> 
> Do not accept a row with a tick in both columns

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common mistake is to think that in asymmetric cryptography the sender has one key and the receiver has the other. Both keys in a pair belong to the same owner. The owner shares the public key and keeps the private key.
> 
> Students also tick "faster" for asymmetric because it sounds more advanced. Symmetric cryptography is the simpler process, so it is usually faster. Asymmetric cryptography is more complex, so it is slower.

parts.problemMd:
Two offices of a company send files to each other over the internet. The files are protected using symmetric cryptography.

Describe how a file is encrypted and decrypted using symmetric cryptography.
parts.solutionMd:
The sending office uses a key to encrypt the file (the plain text) into cipher text **[1]**

The same key must be shared with the receiving office **[1]**

The receiving office uses the same key to decrypt the cipher text back into plain text **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any three from:**
> 
> - a single key is used for both encryption and decryption
> - the file / plain text is encrypted using the key (and an encryption algorithm) to produce cipher text
> - the key has to be shared with / given to the receiving office
> - the receiving office decrypts the cipher text using the same key (to get the plain text back)
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Accept "secret key" for "key"
> 
> Do not accept the receiving office decrypting with a private key, or the sending office encrypting with a public key, because public and private keys are used in asymmetric cryptography

> **[exam-tip]**
> Weak answers say "the file is encrypted, sent, then decrypted" and never mention the key. Every mark here depends on naming the key and making clear it is the same key at both ends.
> 
> Notice the step that makes symmetric cryptography risky: the key itself has to reach the other office. Anyone who obtains that key can decrypt every file encrypted with it. This is why the risk of compromise is higher with symmetric cryptography than with asymmetric cryptography.

parts.problemMd:
An online shop has thousands of customers. Each customer sends their payment details to the shop over the internet. No customer must be able to read the payment details of another customer.

Explain why the shop uses asymmetric cryptography rather than symmetric cryptography for these messages.
parts.solutionMd:
With symmetric cryptography, the single key that encrypts and decrypts the data would have to be shared with every customer **[1]**

So any customer, or anyone who obtained that key, could decrypt the payment details of other customers **[1]**

With asymmetric cryptography, the shop shares only its public key, and each customer encrypts their payment details using the shop's public key **[1]**

Only the shop's matching private key, which is never transmitted, can decrypt the cipher text, so a customer who holds the public key still cannot read another customer's details **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any four from:**
> 
> Symmetric (max 2)
> 
> - the same single key encrypts and decrypts, so it would have to be shared with every customer
> - any customer / anyone who obtains the key could decrypt every other customer's message // the risk of compromise is higher
> 
> Asymmetric (max 3)
> 
> - the shop generates a matching pair of keys, a public key and a private key
> - the shop's public key is shared with all customers
> - each customer encrypts their payment details using the shop's public key
> - the cipher text can only be decrypted using the shop's private key, which is kept secret / never transmitted
> - so holding the public key does not allow a customer to decrypt another customer's message
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> Accept "recipient's public key" / "receiver's private key" for the shop's keys
> 
> Do not accept each customer encrypting with their own private key, because anyone with that customer's public key could then read the details
> 
> Do not accept "asymmetric cryptography is faster", because it is the slower process

> **[exam-tip]**
> The question says "rather than", so the examiner is looking for both sides. Many students describe the asymmetric process in full and never say what would go wrong with symmetric cryptography, which limits them to 3 marks.
> 
> Writing "asymmetric is more secure" is not enough by itself. Say why: with symmetric cryptography the one key has to be given to everyone, but with asymmetric cryptography only the public key is shared and the private key never leaves the shop.

parts.problemMd: Explain what is meant by **Deep Learning **in relation to Artificial Intelligence (AI).
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One **mark per mark point (**Max 3**)
> 
> MP1 Deep learning learns by finding hidden patterns that are **undetectable to humans**.
> 
> MP2 It structures algorithms in layers: **input **layer, **hidden **layers and **output **layer.
> 
> MP3 … to create an artificial neural network to learn and make intelligent decisions on its own.
> 
> MP4 It is trained using large quantities of unlabelled data.
> 
> MP5 Deep learning requires/uses a **large number of** hidden layers.
> 
> MP6 … the larger the number of layers, the higher the level of success.

parts.problemMd: Explain what is meant by **Reinforcement Learning **in relation to Artificial Intelligence.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One **mark per mark point (**Max 3**)
> 
> MP1 Reinforcement learning is a machine learning technique based on feedback / rewards / punishment.
> 
> MP2 … in which an agent learns to behave in an environment by performing the actions and seeing the results of the actions.
> 
> MP3 … for each good action, the agent gets positive feedback / reward and each bad action receives negative feedback / punishment.
> 
> MP4 The agent learns automatically using feedback without any labelled data / specific instructions.
> 
> MP5 Adjust node weightings to achieve the correct outcome. // Using feedback to improve its performance at accomplishing similar tasks.

parts.problemMd:
Artificial neural networks have played a significant role in the development of machine learning.

Explain what is meant by the term **artificial neural network**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One** mark per mark point **(Max 4) **
> 
> MP1 An artificial neural network is the component of artificial intelligence that is meant to simulate the functioning of a biological brain.
> 
> MP2 Artificial neural networks are a key component of machine learning.
> 
> MP3 They can solve problems that would prove impossible or difficult for humans // Artificial neural networks have self-learning capabilities that enable them to produce better results as more data becomes available
> 
> MP4 Artificial neural networks can be layered (input, hidden and output layers) // Artificial neural networks have many interconnected layers, some / many of which are hidden
> 
> MP5 Weights are assigned between nodes
> 
> MP6 Weights are adjusted through training to give a more accurate result
> 
> MP7 More complex learning capabilities / more accurate results are available with larger numbers of hidden layers

Show your working and write your answers in the table provided.
