> Remember the + 1 and - 1. After 36 is checked, the new lower bound is index 9, not index 8, because element 8 has already been compared. Leaving out the + 1 or - 1 gives a different sequence of values.

parts.problemMd:
A library system stores 1000 book titles in a 1D array, sorted into alphabetical order. The number of titles is going to increase to 2000.

When the array holds 1000 titles, a binary search makes at most 10 comparisons to find a title or to decide that it is not in the array.

Explain how increasing the number of titles to 2000 affects the maximum number of comparisons made by:

- a binary search
- a linear search.
parts.solutionMd:
Binary search: the maximum number of comparisons increases by only one, from 10 to 11 **[1]**

This is because each comparison halves the part of the array still being searched, so doubling the number of items needs just one more comparison / the number of comparisons increases logarithmically **[1]**

Linear search: the maximum number of comparisons doubles, from 1000 to 2000, because every item may need to be checked / it increases linearly with the number of items **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for binary search: the maximum increases by one // increases from 10 to 11
> 
> **1 mark** for the reason: each comparison halves the search area // the time to search increases logarithmically as the number of items increases
> 
> **1 mark** for linear search: the maximum doubles // increases from 1000 to 2000 // increases linearly with the number of items
> 
> Accept O(log n) for binary search and O(n) for linear search only when the effect of doubling is also described
> 
> Do not accept "the binary search takes twice as long". Doubling the number of items adds only one comparison
> 
> Do not accept "the binary search stays the same". It needs one more comparison

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use the numbers in the question. Many answers only say "binary search is faster". This gains no marks here, because the question asks how the maximum number of comparisons changes when the array grows.
> 
> You can check the binary search figure without a calculator. 2 to the power 10 is 1024, which is more than 1000, so 10 comparisons are enough for 1000 items. 2 to the power 11 is 2048, which is more than 2000, so 11 comparisons are enough for 2000 items.

parts.problemMd:
The 1D array `Values` is declared as `ARRAY[1:6] OF INTEGER`. Before sorting, it holds:

3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 2

The array is to be sorted into ascending order. Two algorithms are being compared.

**Algorithm A: bubble sort**

**Algorithm B: insertion sort**

A comparison is one check of whether a value in `Values` is greater than another value in `Values`. In Algorithm B, when `Pos > 1` is `FALSE`, assume that the rest of the `WHILE` condition is not checked.

Complete the table to show the number of comparisons each algorithm makes to sort this data. Then explain why Algorithm B makes fewer comparisons than Algorithm A for this data.

| Algorithm | Number of comparisons |
|---|---|
| A: bubble sort |   |
| B: insertion sort |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Algorithm | Number of comparisons |
|---|---|
| A: bubble sort | **15** |
| B: insertion sort | **9** |

Algorithm A: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 **[1]**

Algorithm B: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 5 = 9 **[1]**

The values 3, 5, 6, 8 and 9 are already in order. In the insertion sort, each of 5, 6, 8 and 9 needs only one comparison, because the loop stops as soon as the value to its left is smaller. **[1]**

The bubble sort can move the 2 only one place towards the front in each pass, so it needs five passes, and each pass compares again pairs that are already in order. The insertion sort moves the 2 to the front in a single iteration. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for 15 comparisons for Algorithm A
> 
> **1 mark** for 9 comparisons for Algorithm B
> 
> **1 mark** each for any two of these points, to a maximum of 2: in the insertion sort, a value already in the correct place needs only one comparison, because the `WHILE` loop stops as soon as a smaller value is found to its left; the insertion sort moves the 2 to its final position in one iteration of the `FOR` loop; the bubble sort moves the 2 only one place per pass, so five passes are needed; the bubble sort compares again pairs that are already in order in every pass
> 
> Do not accept 25 or 30 for Algorithm A. Those totals assume five comparisons in every pass, but `Boundary` is reduced by 1 after every pass, so each pass makes one comparison fewer than the pass before. The algorithm does start a sixth pass, but `Boundary` is then 0, so the `FOR` loop does not run and no comparison is made.
> 
> Do not accept 10 for Algorithm B. When `Pos` reaches 1 the 2 is at the front of the array, and there is no value to its left to compare it with.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often expect the bubble sort to be quick here because the data is almost in order. It is not. A small value near the end of the array moves only one place per pass in a bubble sort, so a single value in the wrong place can force the maximum number of passes.
> 
> When you explain a difference in performance, refer to the actual data in the question. "Insertion sort is more efficient" earns nothing on its own. Say what each algorithm does with this data: how far the 2 moves in each pass or iteration, and which comparisons are repeated.

parts.problemMd: Describe how an insertion sort puts the values in a 1D array into ascending order.
parts.solutionMd:
The first value is treated as a sorted list of one item, and the sort starts with the second value. **[1]**

Each value in turn is compared with the values to its left. Every larger value is moved up one place, and the value is inserted into the gap that is left. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any two from:**
> 
> - The first value is treated as sorted // the sort starts at the second value
> - The next value is taken and stored in a temporary variable
> - It is compared with each value to its left / in the sorted part, in turn
> - Each value that is larger is moved up / to the right one place
> - The value is inserted into the gap // when a smaller or equal value, or the start of the array, is reached
> - This is repeated for every value until the end of the array is reached
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Do not accept a description of comparing adjacent pairs and swapping them over a series of passes. That describes a bubble sort.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common way to lose both marks is to describe a bubble sort. An insertion sort does not make passes through the whole array. It takes one value at a time and inserts it into the correct place in the part of the array that is already sorted.
> 
> Use the word "inserted" or "inserts" in your answer. It shows the examiner that you know what makes this sort different.

parts.problemMd:
A school stores the names of 200 students in a global 1D array `Names`.

The names are stored in ascending alphabetical order. Each name appears only once.

A function `BinarySearch()` is needed. It:

- takes a string parameter `Target`
- performs a binary search on `Names`
- returns the index of the element that matches `Target`
- returns -1 if `Target` is not in the array.

Write pseudocode for the function `BinarySearch()`.
parts.solutionMd:
Function header with parameter and return type **[1]**

Lower and upper bounds initialised to 1 and 200 **[1]**

Loop that stops when found or when the lower bound passes the upper bound **[1]**

Middle index calculated with DIV **[1]**

Lower bound moved to Mid + 1 or upper bound moved to Mid - 1 after the comparison **[1]**

Mid returned if found and -1 returned if not **[1]**

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any six from:**
> 
> - function header with the parameter `Target : STRING` and `RETURNS INTEGER`, ending with `ENDFUNCTION`
> - initialising the lower bound to 1 **and** the upper bound to 200
> - a conditional loop that stops when the name is found **or** when the lower bound is greater than the upper bound
> - calculating the middle index using `DIV 2` inside the loop
> - comparing `Names[Mid]` with `Target` and setting a flag or returning when they are equal
> - if `Names[Mid]` is less than `Target`, setting the lower bound to `Mid + 1`
> - if `Names[Mid]` is greater than `Target`, setting the upper bound to `Mid - 1`
> - returning `Mid` if found **and** -1 if not found
> 
> **[6 marks]**
> 
> Accept `RETURN Mid` inside the loop when the names match, followed by `RETURN -1` after the loop
> 
> Accept a middle index calculated as `Lower + (Upper - Lower) DIV 2`, or with + 1 added before the `DIV`, provided it is used consistently
> 
> Accept a `REPEAT ... UNTIL` loop with an equivalent condition
> 
> Do not award the middle index mark for `(Lower + Upper) / 2`. The `/` operator gives a REAL value, which cannot be used as an array index
> 
> Do not award the bound marks for `Lower ← Mid` or `Upper ← Mid`. This can cause an infinite loop when the name is not in the array

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error is the loop condition. A loop that only tests `Found = FALSE` never ends when the name is not in the array. The search must also stop when `Lower` becomes greater than `Upper`, because there are then no elements left to check.
> 
> Use `DIV` for the middle index. An array index must be an integer, and in the Cambridge pseudocode `/` always gives a REAL result. Strings can be compared using the less than and greater than operators in the same way as numbers, which is what makes a binary search on names possible.

parts.problemMd:
An insertion sort is used to put the six values in the 1D array `Numbers` into ascending order. `Numbers` is declared as `ARRAY[1:6] OF INTEGER`.

Complete the table to show the contents of `Numbers` at the end of the iterations of the `FOR` loop when `Index` is 2, 3 and 4.

|   | Numbers[1] | Numbers[2] | Numbers[3] | Numbers[4] | Numbers[5] | Numbers[6] |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Before the sort | 16 | 4 | 11 | 2 | 19 | 7 |
| Index = 2 |   |   |   |   |   |   |
| Index = 3 |   |   |   |   |   |   |
| Index = 4 |   |   |   |   |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
|   | Numbers[1] | Numbers[2] | Numbers[3] | Numbers[4] | Numbers[5] | Numbers[6] |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Before the sort | 16 | 4 | 11 | 2 | 19 | 7 |
| Index = 2 | **4** | **16** | **11** | **2** | **19** | **7** |
| Index = 3 | **4** | **11** | **16** | **2** | **19** | **7** |
| Index = 4 | **2** | **4** | **11** | **16** | **19** | **7** |

Index = 2 **[1]**

Index = 3 **[1]**

Index = 4 **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the row for Index = 2: 4, 16, 11, 2, 19, 7
> 
> **1 mark** for the row for Index = 3: 4, 11, 16, 2, 19, 7
> 
> **1 mark** for the row for Index = 4: 2, 4, 11, 16, 19, 7
> 
> Each row must be fully correct to gain the mark.
> 
> Follow through: if one row is wrong, you can still earn the mark for a later row that is correct for one iteration of the algorithm applied to your previous row.
> 
> Do not accept a row in which 19 or 7 has moved. The `FOR` loop has not reached `Numbers[5]` or `Numbers[6]` by the end of the iteration when `Index` is 4.

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is tempting to swap two neighbouring values and move on, as you would in a bubble sort. In an insertion sort the value in `Item` keeps moving left until it meets a smaller value or reaches `Numbers[1]`. When `Index` is 4, the 2 moves past 16, 11 and 4 in one iteration and goes straight to the front.
> 
> Remember that the values to the right of `Index` are untouched. Copy them across unchanged, and only change the part of the array from `Numbers[1]` to `Numbers[Index]`.

parts.problemMd:
A race organiser stores the results of 40 runners in two global 1D arrays:

- `RunnerID` is declared as `ARRAY[1:40] OF STRING` and holds the ID of each runner
- `FinishTime` is declared as `ARRAY[1:40] OF INTEGER` and holds the finishing time of each runner, in seconds.

The runner whose ID is in `RunnerID[N]` has the finishing time in `FinishTime[N]`.

Write pseudocode for a procedure `SortResults()` that uses an insertion sort to put `FinishTime` into ascending order. The IDs in `RunnerID` must be put into the same order, so that each ID stays with its finishing time.
parts.solutionMd:
**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Max six from:**
> 
> - **MP1** Use of a `FOR` loop from 2 to 40 to take each value in turn
> - **MP2** Temporary storage of the finishing time being inserted
> - **MP3** Temporary storage of the matching runner ID
> - **MP4** Use of a `WHILE` loop with a correct exit condition: stops at the start of the array or when a time no greater than the stored time is found
> - **MP5** Moving both the time and the ID up one place inside the loop
> - **MP6** Correct updating of the position variable inside the loop
> - **MP7** Final insertion of both the stored time and the stored ID at the correct position
> 
> **[6 marks]**
> 
> Accept a `FOR` loop from 1 to 39 that inserts the value at position `Index + 1`, with the matching changes to the other statements.
> 
> Accept the `WHILE` condition written with `>=` in place of `>`. The array is still put into ascending order, although runners with equal times change places.
> 
> Do not award MP5 or MP7 if `RunnerID` is not moved in step with `FinishTime`. Each ID would then no longer match its finishing time.
> 
> Do not award MP1 or MP4 for an algorithm that makes repeated passes through the whole array, swapping adjacent pairs. That is a bubble sort, not an insertion sort.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mark that students lose most often is the one for the second array. Every time a finishing time is stored, moved or inserted, the matching ID must be stored, moved or inserted in the same way. If you forget one of these lines, runners end up with the wrong times.
> 
> A second common error is to write over the value being inserted before it has been saved. Store both `FinishTime[Index]` and `RunnerID[Index]` in temporary variables before the `WHILE` loop starts, because the first move copies a value into that position.

parts.problemMd:
An ordered binary tree stores the names of cities in alphabetical order.

The tree is implemented as a 1D array of records, `BinTree`. Each record contains a left pointer, the data and a right pointer.

- `RootPtr` points to the root node.
- `FreePtr` points to the first unused record. Unused records are linked together through their `LeftPtr` field.
- -1 is used to represent a null pointer.

The table shows the contents of the array.

| Index | LeftPtr | Data | RightPtr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | Lima | 2 |
| 1 | 3 | Cairo | 4 |
| 2 | 5 | Quito | -1 |
| 3 | -1 | Accra | -1 |
| 4 | -1 | Delhi | -1 |
| 5 | -1 | Oslo | -1 |
| 6 | 7 |   | -1 |
| 7 | -1 |   | -1 |

RootPtr = 0 and FreePtr = 6

The tree is searched for the city Nairobi. The search starts at the node pointed to by `RootPtr`. At each node it follows the left pointer if the item searched for comes before the data in that node, and the right pointer if it comes after. The search returns the index of the node if the item is found, or a null pointer if it is not found.

Identify the index of each node visited, in the order they are visited, and state the value returned by the search.
parts.solutionMd:
Nodes visited: **0, 2, 5** (Lima, Quito, Oslo) **[1]**

Value returned: **-1** (a null pointer, because Nairobi is not in the tree) **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the indexes 0, 2, 5 in that order and no others
> 
> **1 mark** for -1 / null pointer as the value returned
> 
> Accept the data values Lima, Quito, Oslo in that order for the first mark
> 
> Do not accept any list that includes 1, 3 or 4, or that visits the nodes in row order: the search must follow the pointers
> 
> Do not accept 5 as the value returned: Oslo is the last node visited, not a match
> 
> Do not accept 6 as the value returned: that is the value of `FreePtr`, not the result of the search

> **[exam-tip]**
> The rows of the array are in the order the items were added, not the order of the tree. Do not read down the Data column. Start at the index held in `RootPtr` and use the pointers to jump from row to row.
> 
> At Oslo, Nairobi comes before Oslo, so the search takes the left pointer. That pointer is -1, which means the item is not in the tree. The search stops there and returns the null pointer. It does not return the last index it visited.

parts.problemMd:
An ordered binary tree stores integers. It is implemented as a 1D array of records, `BinTree`, with indexes 0 to 7. Each record contains a left pointer, the data and a right pointer.

- `RootPtr` points to the root node.
- `FreePtr` points to the first unused record. Unused records are linked together through their `LeftPtr` field.
- -1 is used to represent a null pointer.

A new item is always stored in the record pointed to by `FreePtr`. It is then joined to the tree as a new leaf node.

The table shows the contents of the array before any more items are added.

| Index | LeftPtr | Data | RightPtr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 48 | 2 |
| 1 | 5 | 25 | 3 |
| 2 | 4 | 71 | -1 |
| 3 | -1 | 36 | -1 |
| 4 | -1 | 59 | -1 |
| 5 | -1 | 12 | -1 |
| 6 | 7 |   | -1 |
| 7 | -1 |   | -1 |

RootPtr = 0 and FreePtr = 6

The integer 30 is added to the tree, and then the integer 64 is added.

Complete the table and the values of `RootPtr` and `FreePtr` to show the contents after both items have been added.

| Index | LeftPtr | Data | RightPtr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 |   | 48 |   |
| 1 |   | 25 |   |
| 2 |   | 71 |   |
| 3 |   | 36 |   |
| 4 |   | 59 |   |
| 5 |   | 12 |   |
| 6 |   |   |   |
| 7 |   |   |   |

RootPtr = ..........

FreePtr = ..........
parts.solutionMd:
30 goes left of 48, right of 25, then left of 36, so it becomes the left child of 36.

64 goes right of 48, left of 71, then right of 59, so it becomes the right child of 59.

| Index | LeftPtr | Data | RightPtr |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 48 | 2 |
| 1 | 5 | 25 | 3 |
| 2 | 4 | 71 | -1 |
| 3 | **6** | 36 | -1 |
| 4 | -1 | 59 | **7** |
| 5 | -1 | 12 | -1 |
| 6 | **-1** | **30** | -1 |
| 7 | -1 | **64** | -1 |

Row 6 holds 30 with both pointers -1 **[1]**

Row 3 LeftPtr set to 6 **[1]**

Row 7 holds 64 with both pointers -1, and row 4 RightPtr set to 7 **[1]**

RootPtr = **0**

FreePtr = **-1** **[1]**

The cells in bold are the ones that change.

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for row 6 correct: LeftPtr -1, Data 30, RightPtr -1
> 
> **1 mark** for row 3 LeftPtr changed to 6
> 
> **1 mark** for row 7 correct (LeftPtr -1, Data 64, RightPtr -1) **and** row 4 RightPtr changed to 7
> 
> **1 mark** for FreePtr = -1 **and** RootPtr = 0 **and** rows 0, 1, 2 and 5 unchanged
> 
> Do not accept row 6 with LeftPtr 7: that is the old free list link and must be replaced by a null pointer when the record joins the tree
> 
> Do not accept 8 for FreePtr: there is no record 8, and the free list ends at -1

> **[exam-tip]**
> Adding a node changes two records, not one. You fill in the new record, and you also change one pointer in its parent. Students often write 30 into row 6 and forget to point row 3 at it, so 30 can never be found.
> 
> Before you use a free record, read its `LeftPtr`. That value becomes the new `FreePtr`. Then overwrite the new record's `LeftPtr` with -1, because a new node is always a leaf.

parts.problemMd:
A program stores integers in an ordered binary tree. The tree is implemented as a 1D array of records. No two items in the tree have the same value.

- `BinTree`, `RootPtr` and `FreePtr` are global.
- -1 is used to represent a null pointer. `RootPtr` is -1 when the tree is empty.
- `FreePtr` points to the first unused record. Unused records are linked together through their `LeftPtr` field. `FreePtr` is -1 when there are no unused records.
- An item that is smaller than the data in a node is stored in that node's left subtree. An item that is larger is stored in its right subtree.

Write pseudocode for the procedure `AddNode(NewItem : INTEGER)`.

The procedure must:

- output "Tree full" and add nothing if there are no unused records
- otherwise store `NewItem` in a record taken from the free list, and join that record to the tree as a leaf node in the correct position.
parts.solutionMd:
The model answer earns the marks as follows.

Checks `FreePtr` for -1 and outputs "Tree full" without adding the item **[1]**

Takes the record at `FreePtr` and moves `FreePtr` to that record's `LeftPtr`, before the record is overwritten **[1]**

Stores `NewItem` in `Data` and sets both pointers of the new record to -1 **[1]**

If the tree is empty, sets `RootPtr` to the new record **[1]**

Starts at `RootPtr` and moves left or right at each node, remembering the previous node, until a null pointer is reached **[1]**

Sets the left or the right pointer of the previous node, as appropriate, to the new record **[1]**

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for checking whether `FreePtr` is -1 and, if so, outputting "Tree full" and not adding the item
> 
> **1 mark** for storing the index held in `FreePtr` and then updating `FreePtr` to `BinTree[FreePtr].LeftPtr`
> 
> **1 mark** for storing `NewItem` in the `Data` field and setting the new record's `LeftPtr` and `RightPtr` to -1
> 
> **1 mark** for setting `RootPtr` to the new record's index when `RootPtr` is -1
> 
> **1 mark** for a loop that starts at `RootPtr`, follows `LeftPtr` when the new item is smaller and `RightPtr` when it is larger, stops at a null pointer, and keeps the index of the previous node
> 
> **1 mark** for setting the correct pointer (`LeftPtr` or `RightPtr`) of the previous node to the new record's index
> 
> Accept a pre-condition loop (`WHILE`) in place of `REPEAT ... UNTIL`
> 
> Accept any identifiers for the local variables
> 
> Accept deciding left or right after the loop by comparing `NewItem` with the data in the previous node, instead of using a `BOOLEAN`
> 
> Accept an equivalent recursive solution that meets the same marking points
> 
> Do not award the second mark if the new record's `LeftPtr` is set to -1 before `FreePtr` is updated from it: the rest of the free list is lost

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of the first few statements matters. The new record's `LeftPtr` is also the link to the next free record. Read it into `FreePtr` first, and only then set it to -1. If you do it the other way round, `FreePtr` becomes -1 and every other unused record is lost.
> 
> When the loop ends, the current pointer is -1, so it cannot tell you where to attach the new node. Keep a second pointer to the node you have just left. That node is the parent, and it is the one whose pointer you change. Also remember the empty tree: with no root there is no parent, so `RootPtr` itself must be set.

parts.problemMd:
A food delivery company holds customer orders in a queue Abstract Data Type (ADT) until the kitchen is ready for them. The number of orders waiting changes a lot during the day. Late at night the queue is often empty, but at lunchtime several hundred orders can be waiting.

The queue can be implemented using a 1D array or using a linked list.

Justify the use of a linked list instead of a 1D array to implement this queue.
parts.solutionMd:
A linked list is a dynamic data structure, so nodes can be added and removed as necessary and the queue can grow at lunchtime and shrink late at night **[1]**

A 1D array is a static data structure with a fixed size, so when the array is full no more orders can be added to the queue **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a point about the linked list, from:
> 
> - a linked list is a dynamic data structure // is not restricted in size
> - nodes can be added or removed as necessary, so the queue can expand or contract as the number of orders changes
> - items are added and removed by changing pointers, instead of moving the data
> 
> **1 mark** for a point about the array, from:
> 
> - an array is a static data structure // is fixed in size
> - when the array is full, the queue cannot be extended any further // no more orders can be added
> 
> Accept for the array mark: the array must be declared for the busiest time, so most of its elements are unused when the queue is short
> 
> Do not accept "a linked list uses less memory". Each node also stores a pointer, so a linked list holding the same orders needs more memory, not less
> 
> Do not award both marks for two points about the linked list only. One mark must come from the array

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Justify the use of X instead of Y" is a two-sided question. Many students write two good points about the linked list and nothing about the array, and they score only 1 mark. Make one point about why the linked list suits the queue and one point about what goes wrong with the array.
> 
> Use the scenario. The question tells you the queue is sometimes empty and sometimes holds hundreds of orders. That is the clue: the size of the queue is not known in advance, and a dynamic structure copes with that while a static one does not.

parts.problemMd:
A print server stores print jobs in a queue Abstract Data Type (ADT). The queue is implemented using two stacks, `StackA` and `StackB`.

- `StackA` holds the queue. The item at the front of the queue is at the top of `StackA`.
- `StackB` is empty except while a new item is being added.

To add a new item to the queue, these three steps are carried out in order:

1. Every item is popped from `StackA` and pushed onto `StackB`, until `StackA` is empty.
2. The new item is pushed onto `StackB`.
3. Every item is popped from `StackB` and pushed onto `StackA`, until `StackB` is empty.

The queue currently holds the print jobs 104, 105 and 106. Job 104 is at the front of the queue and job 106 is at the rear.

Job 107 is now added to the queue.

Complete the table to show the contents of each stack after each step. Write the items in each stack in order from the **bottom** of the stack to the **top**. Write "empty" for an empty stack.

| Stage | StackA (bottom to top) | StackB (bottom to top) |
|---|---|---|
| Before job 107 is added | 106, 105, 104 | empty |
| After step 1 |   |   |
| After step 2 |   |   |
| After step 3 |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Stage | StackA (bottom to top) | StackB (bottom to top) |
|---|---|---|
| Before job 107 is added | 106, 105, 104 | empty |
| After step 1 | **empty** | **104, 105, 106** |
| After step 2 | **empty** | **104, 105, 106, 107** |
| After step 3 | **107, 106, 105, 104** | **empty** |

- After step 1, job 104 was popped first, so it is at the bottom of `StackB`. The order has been reversed **[1]**
- After step 2, job 107 is on top of `StackB` **[1]**
- After step 3, the order is reversed again, so job 107 is at the bottom of `StackA` and job 104 is still at the top, ready to be removed first **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the "After step 1" row: `StackA` empty and `StackB` 104, 105, 106
> 
> **1 mark** for the "After step 2" row: `StackA` empty and `StackB` 104, 105, 106, 107
> 
> **1 mark** for the "After step 3" row: `StackA` 107, 106, 105, 104 and `StackB` empty
> 
> Each row must be fully correct in both columns to earn its mark
> 
> Follow through: award the step 2 mark if 107 is correctly added to the top of an incorrect `StackB` from step 1
> 
> Do not accept an item order written from top to bottom, for example 106, 105, 104 for `StackB` after step 1

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error is to copy the order across without reversing it. When you pop from one stack and push onto another, the first item popped (the top) becomes the first item pushed (the bottom). So every transfer reverses the order.
> 
> That double reversal is the whole reason two stacks are needed. The first transfer puts the rear of the queue on top, so the new item can be placed behind it. The second transfer puts the front of the queue back on top of `StackA`, so the next item removed is still job 104.

parts.problemMd:
A queue Abstract Data Type (ADT) of strings is implemented using two stacks. Each stack is a 1D array with its own top pointer. The global declarations are:

A stack is empty when its top pointer is 0. `StackA` holds the queue, with the item at the front of the queue at the top of `StackA`. `StackB` is empty except while a new item is being added.

These modules are already written:

- `PushA(NewItem : STRING)` pushes `NewItem` onto `StackA`
- `PopA() RETURNS STRING` removes and returns the item at the top of `StackA`
- `PushB(NewItem : STRING)` pushes `NewItem` onto `StackB`
- `PopB() RETURNS STRING` removes and returns the item at the top of `StackB`

`PopA()` and `PopB()` are only called when that stack is not empty.

Write pseudocode for:

- the procedure `Enqueue(NewItem : STRING)`, which outputs "Queue full" if `StackA` holds `MaxSize` items, and otherwise adds `NewItem` to the rear of the queue
- the function `Dequeue()`, which outputs "Queue empty" and returns an empty string if the queue is empty, and otherwise removes and returns the item at the front of the queue.
parts.solutionMd:
- Test whether `StackA` is full and output "Queue full" without adding the item **[1]**
- Loop while `StackA` is not empty **[1]**
- In the loop, pop each item from `StackA` and push it onto `StackB` **[1]**
- Push `NewItem` onto `StackB`, then pop every item from `StackB` and push it back onto `StackA` **[1]**
- In `Dequeue()`, test whether `StackA` is empty and, if so, output "Queue empty" and return an empty string **[1]**
- Otherwise pop the item from `StackA` and return it **[1]**

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for testing `TopPointerA = MaxSize` and outputting "Queue full", with no item added in that case
> 
> **1 mark** for a loop that repeats while `StackA` is not empty, for example `WHILE TopPointerA > 0`
> 
> **1 mark** for popping from `StackA` and pushing onto `StackB` inside that loop
> 
> **1 mark** for pushing `NewItem` onto a stack and then a loop that moves every item from `StackB` back onto `StackA`
> 
> **1 mark** for `Dequeue()` testing whether `StackA` is empty and, if so, outputting "Queue empty" and returning an empty string
> 
> **1 mark** for otherwise returning the value popped from `StackA`
> 
> Accept `NewItem` pushed onto `StackA` instead of `StackB` after `StackA` has been emptied. The order is still correct after the items are moved back
> 
> Accept any equivalent loop condition, such as a test that the top pointer is not equal to 0, or a post-condition loop that is only entered when the stack is not empty
> 
> Accept the pop and the push in one statement, for example `CALL PushB(PopA())`
> 
> Accept `Dequeue` written without the empty brackets
> 
> Do not award the fourth mark if the items are left in `StackB`. The front of the queue must be back at the top of `StackA`, or the next `Dequeue()` removes the wrong item
> 
> Do not award the third mark if the loop also changes `TopPointerA` or `TopPointerB` directly, because the modules already update them and the pointers are then changed twice

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often push the new item onto `StackA` straight away, as if `StackA` were a queue. It is a stack, so that puts the newest item on top, and it becomes the next item removed. The reason for the second stack is to reverse the order, add the item behind the others, then reverse it back.
> 
> Use the modules the question gives you. You do not need to write array code for the stacks, and you should not change `TopPointerA` or `TopPointerB` yourself. `PopA()` and `PushB()` already update them.

parts.problemMd:
Two different algorithms can perform the same task.

State **two** criteria that can be used to compare the two algorithms.
parts.solutionMd:
The time taken by each algorithm to complete the task **[1]**

The amount of memory used by each algorithm **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for the time taken to complete the task // the number of steps / comparisons / iterations the algorithm needs // time complexity
> 
> **1 mark** for the memory used // the amount of storage space the algorithm needs // space complexity
> 
> Do not accept two answers that both describe time, such as "speed" and "time taken". They are the same criterion and earn one mark
> 
> Do not accept the speed of the processor or the hardware used. That is a property of the computer, not of the algorithm

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students write "speed" and "time taken" as their two criteria. Both describe how long the algorithm takes, so they earn one mark between them. Learn the pair that the syllabus gives: the time taken to complete the task and the memory used.
> 
> Keep your answer about the algorithm. The same algorithm runs faster on a faster computer, so "it depends on the processor" does not help you compare two algorithms.

parts.problemMd:
A delivery company stores the details of 800 parcels in a 1D array. The array is **not** sorted.

Parcels are added to the array and removed from it many times each minute, in no particular order. After each change, the program searches the array **once** to find one parcel ID.

A binary search usually checks far fewer items than a linear search.

Explain why a linear search is more suitable than a binary search for this program.
parts.solutionMd:
A binary search can only be used if the data in the array is sorted. **[1]**

This array is not sorted, and it changes after every search, so it would have to be sorted again before every binary search. **[1]**

A sort must look at every item at least once, so sorting the array takes at least as long as a linear search, which checks at most 800 items and needs no sorting. The binary search would not save any time. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a binary search requires the data to be sorted // a linear search does not require the data to be sorted
> 
> **1 mark** for the array would need to be sorted (again) before each search // because the data changes between searches
> 
> **1 mark** for the time taken to sort the array is greater than the time saved by using a binary search // sorting must look at every item at least once, and a linear search checks at most 800 items
> 
> Do not accept "a linear search is faster than a binary search". In general it is not. The linear search is more suitable here because of the time needed to sort the data first
> 
> Do not accept "a binary search cannot find an item that is not in the array". A binary search can report that an item is not found

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most students gain the first mark and stop. Stating that a binary search needs sorted data is not enough on its own. You must use the scenario: the data changes all the time and each version is searched only once, so the cost of sorting is paid again and again.
> 
> Do not claim that a linear search is simply faster. The question tells you that a binary search usually checks fewer items. Your answer must explain why that advantage is lost in this program.

parts.problemMd:
The 1D array `IDs` is declared as:

Each element holds a student ID between 1 and 1000. A program must find out whether any ID is stored more than once. Two algorithms are being considered.

**Algorithm P**

**Algorithm Q**

Algorithm Q uses a second array, `Seen`, which is declared in its first line.

Compare the suitability of Algorithm P and Algorithm Q for this task, in terms of the time taken and the memory used.

Your answer must include the number of times the `IF` condition is evaluated by each algorithm.
parts.solutionMd:
Algorithm P evaluates the `IF` condition 499 + 498 + ... + 2 + 1 = **124 750** times. **[1]**

Algorithm Q evaluates the `IF` condition **500** times. **[1]**

Algorithm Q takes much less time. Even with the 1000 assignments needed to set every element of `Seen` to `FALSE`, it carries out far fewer steps than Algorithm P, which compares every ID with every other ID. **[1]**

Algorithm Q uses more memory, because it needs a second array of 1000 Boolean values. Algorithm P needs no extra array, only the two loop counters. **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for 124 750 for Algorithm P
> 
> **1 mark** for 500 for Algorithm Q
> 
> **1 mark** for Algorithm Q takes less time / carries out fewer steps // Algorithm P takes longer because each ID is compared with every other ID // the time taken by Algorithm P increases much faster as the number of IDs increases
> 
> **1 mark** for Algorithm Q uses more memory because of the extra array `Seen` (of 1000 elements) // Algorithm P uses less memory because it needs no extra array
> 
> Accept 124750 or 124,750 for Algorithm P
> 
> Do not accept 250 000 or 249 500 for Algorithm P. The inner loop starts at `I + 1`, so it runs 499 times when `I` is 1, 498 times when `I` is 2, and only once when `I` is 499
> 
> Do not accept 1500 for Algorithm Q. The loop that sets up `Seen` contains no `IF` condition
> 
> Do not accept "Algorithm Q uses less memory". It stores 1000 extra values that Algorithm P does not need

> **[exam-tip]**
> The common error is to multiply the two loop limits and write 500 × 500 or 499 × 500. Look at where the inner loop starts. Each pair of IDs is compared only once, so the counts are 499, 498, 497 and so on, down to 1.
> 
> A good comparison names both criteria and says which algorithm is better on each. Here there is a trade-off: Algorithm Q is much faster but needs more memory. Also notice why Algorithm Q is possible at all. It works only because every ID is known to be between 1 and 1000, so each ID can be used as an index into `Seen`.

parts.problemMd:
A linear search has a time complexity of O(n) in Big O notation.

(i) State what Big O notation is used to indicate about an algorithm.

(ii) State what O(n) shows about how the time taken by a linear search changes as the number of items in the array increases.
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The time complexity or space complexity of the algorithm // how efficient the algorithm is **[1]**

(ii) The time taken increases linearly with the number of items. For example, if the number of items doubles, the maximum time taken doubles. **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for (i): the time complexity / space complexity of an algorithm // the efficiency of an algorithm // how the time or memory needed grows as the amount of data grows
> 
> **1 mark** for (ii): the time taken increases linearly / in direct proportion as the number of items increases
> 
> Do not accept for (i) "the exact time the algorithm takes, in seconds". Big O describes how the time grows with the number of items, not a measured time
> 
> Do not accept for (ii) "a linear search is slow". This does not describe how the time changes

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (ii), use the word "linearly" or describe the link between the two quantities: twice as many items means up to twice as many checks. Words such as "slow" or "inefficient" do not show that you know what the notation means.
> 
> Remember that the `n` in O(n) stands for the number of data items. Big O never tells you the actual running time, because that also depends on the computer.

parts.problemMd:
The 1D array `Heights` is declared as `ARRAY[1:N] OF INTEGER`. The values in `Heights` are in ascending order.

**Algorithm A** finds the total of all the values in `Heights`.

**Algorithm B** finds out whether the value `Target` is stored in `Heights`.

Identify the Big O time complexity of each algorithm. Justify your answer for Algorithm B.
parts.solutionMd:
Algorithm A: O(n) **[1]**

Algorithm B: O(log n) **[1]**

Each time the `REPEAT` loop runs, Algorithm B discards the half of the remaining array that cannot contain `Target`. So doubling the number of items adds only one more iteration. **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for Algorithm A is O(n)
> 
> **1 mark** for Algorithm B is O(log n)
> 
> **1 mark** for the justification: the number of items still to be searched is halved on each iteration // the search area is repeatedly halved // the time taken increases logarithmically as the number of items increases // doubling the number of items adds only one iteration
> 
> Accept O(Log2 n) or O(log₂ n) for Algorithm B
> 
> Do not accept O(n) for Algorithm B. It contains one loop, but that loop does not run once for every item

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not decide the Big O by counting loops. Algorithm B has one loop, just like Algorithm A, but it is not O(n). What matters is how many times the loop runs. Algorithm A visits every item once, so its time grows linearly with `N`. Algorithm B halves the part of the array still to be searched each time, so it runs only about 10 times for 1000 items.
> 
> You may recognise Algorithm B as a binary search. Naming it is not enough for the justification mark: say what happens to the search area on each iteration.

parts.problemMd:
A developer tests two search algorithms, X and Y, on arrays of different sizes. The table shows the maximum number of items each algorithm checks before it finds an item or decides that the item is not in the array.

| Number of items in the array | Algorithm X | Algorithm Y |
|---|---|---|
| 16 | 16 | 5 |
| 256 | 256 | 9 |
| 4096 | 4096 | 13 |
| 65536 | 65536 | 17 |

(a) Identify the Big O time complexity of each algorithm. Use the data in the table to justify each answer. [3]

(b) The number of items is increased to 1 048 576, which is 16 times the largest array in the table.

State the maximum number of items that Algorithm Y will check. [1]
parts.solutionMd:
(a) Algorithm X is O(n), because the maximum number of items checked is equal to the number of items / increases by the same factor of 16 from row to row. **[1]**

Algorithm Y is O(log n). **[1]**

Each time the number of items is multiplied by 16, Algorithm Y checks only 4 more items. The number of checks increases linearly while the number of items increases exponentially. **[1]**

(b) **21** **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for Algorithm X is O(n) with a justification from the data: the number of checks equals the number of items // rises in proportion to the number of items // is multiplied by 16 when the number of items is multiplied by 16
> 
> **1 mark** for Algorithm Y is O(log n)
> 
> **1 mark** for a justification from the data for Algorithm Y: the number of checks increases by 4 each time the number of items is multiplied by 16 // the number of checks increases linearly as the number of items increases exponentially // the time taken increases logarithmically as the number of items increases
> 
> **1 mark** for (b): 21
> 
> Accept O(Log2 n) or O(log₂ n) for Algorithm Y
> 
> Do not accept O(n) for Algorithm X without a reason taken from the table
> 
> Do not accept 17 × 16 = 272 for (b). Multiplying the number of items by 16 adds 4 checks for Algorithm Y; it does not multiply the number of checks by 16

> **[exam-tip]**
> Look at how each column changes from one row to the next, not at the size of the numbers. The number of items is multiplied by 16 every row. Column X is also multiplied by 16, which is linear growth. Column Y goes up by 4 every row, which is how logarithmic growth appears in a table.
> 
> For part (b), continue the pattern rather than calculating a logarithm: 1 048 576 is one more row of the table, so Algorithm Y checks 17 + 4 = 21 items. Algorithm Y behaves like a binary search and Algorithm X like a linear search, but the question asks you to justify from the data, so quote the numbers.

parts.problemMd: Explain how a compiler makes use of a stack when translating recursive programming code.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One** mark per mark point **(Max 1)**
> 
> - MP1    The compiler must produce object code to
> 
> **One** mark per mark point **(Max 3) **
> 
> - MP2    …push return addresses / values of local variables onto a stack
> - MP3    …with each recursive call // … to set up winding
> - MP4    …pop return addresses / values of local variables off the stack …
> - MP5    …after the base case is reached // … to implement unwinding.

parts.problemMd:
The following recursive function is written in pseudocode. The line numbers are for reference only.

Identify the line number of the **base case** and the line number of the **general case** in the function `Total()`.
parts.solutionMd:
Base case: line 03 (reached when `N = 1`, it returns without making a recursive call) **[1]**

General case: line 05 (the function calls itself with `N - 1`) **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for base case: line 03
> 
> **1 mark** for general case: line 05
> 
> Accept line 02 or lines 02 and 03 for the base case, since line 02 holds the test that selects it
> 
> Accept lines 04 and 05 for the general case
> 
> Do not accept line 01 or line 07 for either answer; these are the function heading and ending

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common error is to give line 05 as the base case because it is the line that "does the work". The base case is the one that returns a value **without** a recursive call. Look for the line that does not mention `Total` on the right-hand side.

parts.problemMd:
The following function uses iteration to calculate the value of `Base` raised to the power `Exponent`. For example, `Power(3, 4)` returns 81.

`Exponent` is always 1 or greater.

Write pseudocode for a **recursive** version of the function `Power()`. The function heading must stay the same.
parts.solutionMd:
The test `IF Exponent = 0` identifies the base case **[1]**

The base case returns 1 without a recursive call **[1]**

The general case calls `Power()` with `Exponent - 1` **[1]**

The general case multiplies the value returned by `Base` and returns the result **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for a test that identifies the base case, `Exponent = 0` or `Exponent = 1`
> 
> **1 mark** for returning the matching base value: 1 when `Exponent = 0`, or `Base` when `Exponent = 1`
> 
> **1 mark** for a recursive call `Power(Base, Exponent - 1)`
> 
> **1 mark** for `Base * Power(Base, Exponent - 1)` returned in the general case
> 
> Accept an equivalent structure that assigns to a local variable and returns it once at the end, for example `Result ← Base * Power(Base, Exponent - 1)` followed by `RETURN Result`
> 
> Do not accept a solution that still contains a loop; this is not a recursive solution
> 
> Do not award the third mark if the recursive call does not reduce `Exponent`, as the base case would never be reached

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students write `Power(Base - 1, Exponent)`, reducing the wrong parameter. Ask yourself which value gets closer to the base case on each call: here it is `Exponent`, so that is the one that must change.
> 
> Another frequent error is to write the recursive call on its own line, for example `CALL Power(Base, Exponent - 1)`. A function is never called with `CALL`, and its return value must be used in an expression, otherwise the result is lost.

parts.problemMd:
The following recursive function is written in pseudocode.

In this function, `MOD` returns the remainder after integer division. `DIV` returns the whole-number quotient.

(i) Complete the trace table for the function when it is called as `DigitSum(4739)`. The first row has been completed for you. Rows where a call returns to an earlier call are shown with its call number in brackets.

| Call number | Function call | Number | Result | Return value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | DigitSum(4739) | 4739 | 9 + DigitSum(473) |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   |   |

(ii) State the purpose of the function `DigitSum()`.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

| Call number | Function call | Number | Result | Return value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | DigitSum(4739) | 4739 | 9 + DigitSum(473) |   |
| **2** | **DigitSum(473)** | **473** | **3 + DigitSum(47)** |   |
| **3** | **DigitSum(47)** | **47** | **7 + DigitSum(4)** |   |
| **4** | **DigitSum(4)** | **4** | **4** | **4** |
| **(3)** | **DigitSum(47)** | **47** | **7 + 4** | **11** |
| **(2)** | **DigitSum(473)** | **473** | **3 + 11** | **14** |
| **(1)** | **DigitSum(4739)** | **4739** | **9 + 14** | **23** |

Call number, Function call and Number columns correct **[1]**

Result column correct down to the base case, rows 2 to 4 **[1]**

Result column correct back up from the base case, the last three rows **[1]**

Return value column correct, ending in 23 **[1]**

(ii) It returns the sum of the digits of the integer passed to it **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i)
> 
> **1 mark** for the Call number, Function call and Number columns all correct
> 
> **1 mark** for the Result column correct in rows 2 to 4 (winding down to the base case)
> 
> **1 mark** for the Result column correct in the last three rows (unwinding from the base case)
> 
> **1 mark** for the Return value column correct: 4, 11, 14, 23
> 
> Accept the base-case row with an empty Result cell if the Return value is 4
> 
> Accept call numbers on the last three rows without brackets if they are 3, 2, 1 in that order
> 
> (ii)
> 
> **1 mark** for: it adds together / totals the digits of the number
> 
> Do not accept "it adds up the numbers" or "it counts the digits"; the answer must refer to the digits of the one number passed in

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error in a recursive trace is to fill the Return value column on the way down. No call can return a value until the call below it has finished, so rows 1 to 3 stay empty in that column. Values only appear once the base case is reached and the calls unwind.
> 
> A second error is to list the unwinding rows in the same order as the winding rows. The most recent call finishes first, so the unwinding rows run 3, 2, 1.

parts.problemMd:
A compiler translates a recursive function. When the program runs, the object code uses a stack to handle the recursive calls.

Name the process in which:

(i) the return address and the values of the local variables are pushed onto the stack with each recursive call, until the base case is reached

(ii) the return addresses and the values of the local variables are popped off the stack after the base case is reached.
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Winding **[1]**

(ii) Unwinding **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for (i) winding
> 
> **1 mark** for (ii) unwinding
> 
> Do not accept "pushing" or "popping" on their own; these name the stack operations, not the process

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often reverse the two terms. Winding happens first, on the way down to the base case, as each new call adds more to the stack. Unwinding happens after the base case, on the way back up, as each call finishes and the stack gets smaller.

parts.problemMd:
The following pseudocode shows a recursive function and a statement that calls it. The line numbers are for reference only.

In this function, `DIV` returns the whole-number quotient.

Each time `Steps()` is called, the return address (the line number the call was made from) and the value of the parameter `N` are pushed onto a stack.

(i) Complete the table to show the contents of the stack at the moment the base case is reached. Row 1 is the top of the stack. You may not need all the rows.

| Stack position | Return address | Value of N |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (top) |   |   |
| 2 |   |   |
| 3 |   |   |
| 4 |   |   |
| 5 |   |   |

(ii) State the value assigned to `Answer` on line 20.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

| Stack position | Return address | Value of N |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (top) | **05** | **1** |
| 2 | **05** | **3** |
| 3 | **05** | **6** |
| 4 | **20** | **12** |
| 5 |   |   |

Value of N column correct, 1, 3, 6, 12 from the top **[1]**

Return address column correct, 20 at the bottom and 05 in the three positions above it **[1]**

(ii) 3 **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i)
> 
> **1 mark** for the Value of N column: 1, 3, 6, 12 from top to bottom, with position 5 empty
> 
> **1 mark** for the Return address column: 05, 05, 05, 20 from top to bottom
> 
> Do not accept the stack in reverse order, with 12 and 20 in position 1; position 1 is the top of the stack, where the most recent call sits
> 
> (ii)
> 
> **1 mark** for 3
> 
> Do not accept 4 (the number of calls) or 0 (the value returned by the base case)

> **[exam-tip]**
> A frequent error is to put 05 as the return address of the first call. The first call was made from line 20, so that is where control goes back to when it finishes, and it sits at the bottom of the stack. Only the calls made by the function itself return to line 05.
> 
> In (ii), many students give 4 because there are four items on the stack. Count the values returned instead: 0, then 1, 2 and 3 as the stack unwinds.

parts.problemMd:
The following recursive procedure is written in pseudocode.

The procedure is called with the statement `CALL Show(5)`

(i) Write the output, in order, from this call.

(ii) The second group of values is output in the reverse order of the first. Explain, with reference to the stack, why this happens.
parts.solutionMd:
(i) 5, 3, 1 **[1]**

then 10, 30, 50 **[1]**

(ii) Each time `Show()` calls itself, the return address and the value of `N` are pushed onto the stack **[1]**

This winding continues until the base case is reached, when `N` is -1 and the condition `N > 0` is false, so nothing more is output **[1]**

The stack then unwinds, popping the most recent call first. The value of `N` is restored from the stack before the statement after the call runs, so `N * 10` is output for 1, then 3, then 5 **[1]**

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i)
> 
> **1 mark** for 5, 3, 1 in this order at the start
> 
> **1 mark** for 10, 30, 50 in this order after them
> 
> (ii) **Max 3 from:**
> 
> - Return address / value of `N` / values of local variables pushed onto the stack with each recursive call // winding
> - Calls continue until the base case is reached // until `N` is not greater than 0 // when `N` is -1
> - After the base case, return addresses / values of `N` are popped off the stack // unwinding
> - The stack is last in, first out, so the most recent call (`N = 1`) finishes first
> - The value of `N` popped for each call is the one used by the `OUTPUT` after the recursive call
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Do not accept an answer that says the values are output in reverse "because the procedure goes backwards" with no reference to the stack
> 
> Do not award the first mark of (i) for 5, 3, 1, -1; the value -1 is never output

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often output all six values in the order the calls are made, for example 5, 50, 3, 30, 1, 10. The second `OUTPUT` cannot run until the call before it has completely finished, and that call makes its own calls first. Trace every call down to the base case before writing anything that comes after a recursive call.
> 
> A second error is to output -1, or 0, from the base case. When `N` is -1 the condition is false and the procedure does nothing at all.

parts.problemMd:
A program is being developed to implement a game for up to six players. During the game, each player assembles a team of characters. At the start of the game there are 45 characters available. Each character has four attributes, as follows: | Attribute | Examples | Comment | |---|---|---| | Player | 0, 1, 3 | The player the character is assigned to. | | Role | Builder, Teacher, Doctor | The job that the character will perform in the game. | | Name | Bill, Lee, Farah, Mo | The name of the character. Messages are sent between computers as a string of characters organised into fields as shown: | Field name | Description | |---|---| | STX | a single character marking the start of the message (ASCII value 02) | | DestinationID | three numeric characters identifying the destination computer | | SourceID | three numeric characters identifying the source computer | | Data | a variable length string containing the data being sent (Minimum length is 1 character) | | ETX | a single character marking the end of the message (ASCII value 03) | For example, the following message contains the data "Hello Jack" being sent from computer "202" to computer "454": ` "454202Hello Jack" ` Each computer will run a copy of the same program. Each program will contain a global variable MyID of type string which contains the unique ID of the computer in which the program is running. The first two program modules are defined as follows: | Module | Description | |---|---| | `GetData()` (already written) | - returns the data field from a message that has been received
- If no message is available, the module waits until one has been received. | | `ReceiveFile()` | - takes a file name as a parameter of type string
- creates a text file with the given file name (no checking required)
- writes the data field returned by GetData() to the file
- repeats until the data field is "****", which is not written to the file
- outputs a final message giving the total number of characters written to the file, for example: `132456 characters were written to newfile.txt` | Write pseudocode for module `ReceiveFile()`. Module GetData() has already been written and must be used.
parts.solutionMd:
`PROCEDURE ReceiveFile(FileName : STRING)`

`    DECLARE FileData : STRING`

`    DECLARE CharCount : INTEGER`

`    CONSTANT Terminator = "****"`

`    OPENFILE FileName FOR WRITE`

`    FileData ← GetData()`

`    CharCount ← 0`

`    WHILE FileData <> Terminator`

`        WRITEFILE FileName, FileData`

`        CharCount ← CharCount + LENGTH(FileData)`

`        FileData ← GetData()`

`    ENDWHILE`

`    CLOSEFILE FileName`

`    OUTPUT CharCount (, " characters were written to ", FileName)`

`ENDPROCEDURE`

Mark as follows:

MP1 OPEN file in WRITE mode and subsequently CLOSE 
MP2 Conditional loop until terminator received 
MP3 ‘Attempted’ use of GetData() – Ignore CALL … 
MP4 Fully correct use GetData()to return the data in a loop 
MP5 Maintain CharCount in a loop 
MP6 Write each line to the file - except the terminator in a loop 
MP7 Final output of message giving number of characters written outside loop

parts.problemMd:

Problem .....................................................

Solution ........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
### Max 3 marks

**Problem:**

- If the file being sent contains a line equal to `"****"`
- Then the file written by `ReceiveFile()` will stop at that line and any subsequent lines will be lost.

**Solution:**

- Read the file at the sending end to count how many lines it contains.
- Send an initial message containing the number of lines to be transmitted.

**Alternative Solution:**

- The transmitter chooses a different terminator string/character that does *not* occur anywhere in the file.
- The transmitter sends this unique terminator *before* sending the first line of the file / before the transfer begins.

parts.problemMd:
A program asks the user to input two whole numbers. It then divides the first number by the second number and outputs the result.

Identify **two** different exceptions that could be caused by the data the user inputs while this program is running.
parts.solutionMd:
The user inputs 0 as the second number, so the program attempts to divide by zero **[1]**

The user inputs data of the wrong type, for example letters instead of a whole number **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for divide by zero // the second number input is 0
> 
> **1 mark** for an input of the wrong data type // a non-numeric input, for example typing "ten" when a whole number is expected
> 
> Accept "division by zero error" or "a run-time error caused by dividing by 0" for the first point
> 
> Accept "user error, typing an incorrect data type" for the second point
> 
> Do not accept "syntax error": a syntax error stops the program being translated, so it never runs and no exception can occur
> 
> Do not accept "logic error": a logic error gives a wrong result but does not interrupt the program
> 
> Do not award two marks for two versions of the same exception, for example "dividing by 0" and "the second number is zero"

> **[exam-tip]**
> Name the event that causes the exception, not what happens afterwards. "The program crashes" or "the program stops" is the result of an exception that is not handled, so it earns no mark on its own.
> 
> Make your two answers genuinely different. Both marks here come from two different inputs: a zero, and data of the wrong type.

> 
> - An exception is an unexpected event that happens while the program is running // an event that disrupts the normal flow of instructions
> - An example of an exception in this program: the file is not found // the storage device fails // hardware failure // the file is empty, so the mean calculation attempts to divide by zero // the end of the file is reached unexpectedly
> - Exception handling traps (some) run-time errors // responds to the unexpected event
> - It prevents the program halting unexpectedly // the program can continue running and the display is not left blank
> - It allows a meaningful error message to be produced
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Maximum 2 marks if no point refers to this program, for example the file, the storage device or the mean calculation

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not confuse exception handling with validation. Validation checks data that a user inputs. It cannot stop a file going missing or a storage device failing while the program runs. Those are the events exception handling exists for.
> 
> "Explain why" needs reasons, not just a definition. Give an exception that could happen in this program, then say what handling it achieves: the program does not halt unexpectedly, and it gives a meaningful error message.

parts.problemMd:
A program uses this pseudocode to find the average of some readings entered by a user. Line numbers are shown on the left.

Identify **three** different line numbers where an exception could occur when this pseudocode is run.

For each line, describe an event that would cause the exception.
parts.solutionMd:
Three lines, each with a matching event, for example:

| Line number | Event that causes the exception |
|---|---|
| **04** **[1]** | **The file Location.txt does not exist or cannot be found** **[1]** |
| **11** **[1]** | **The user input 21 or more at line 08, so Index reaches 21 and Readings[21] is outside the array bounds** **[1]** |
| **14** **[1]** | **The user input 0 at line 08, so the program attempts to divide by zero** **[1]** |

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> For each of three different lines (maximum 3 lines):
> 
> **1 mark** for a line number where an exception could occur
> 
> **1 mark** for an event that would cause the exception on that line
> 
> Accepted lines and events
> 
> Line 04: the file does not exist // is not found // the file name is wrong // the storage device fails (hardware failure)
> 
> Line 05: the file is empty, so there is no line to read // the end of the file has been reached // the storage device fails (hardware failure)
> 
> Line 08: the user inputs data of the wrong type // a non-integer, for example letters or 2.5
> 
> Line 11: the value of NumReadings is greater than 20, so the array index goes out of bounds // the user inputs data of the wrong type for a reading
> 
> Line 14: NumReadings is 0, so there is a divide by zero
> 
> The event mark can only be awarded for an event that matches the line number given
> 
> Do not accept line 12 for the out-of-bounds event: the exception occurs at line 11, which accesses the missing element first, so line 12 is never reached
> 
> Do not accept line 10 for a negative number of readings: the loop runs zero times and no exception occurs. A negative value also gives no exception at line 14, because only 0 causes a divide by zero

> **[exam-tip]**
> Trace what the program does with an unusual value before you claim an exception. A common mistake is to say that a negative number of readings breaks the loop at line 10. It does not: a count-controlled loop from 1 to -3 simply runs zero times.
> 
> Choose the line where the problem first happens. If the user asks for 25 readings, the error happens at line 11, when the program tries to store a value in Readings[21]. Line 12 would use that element too, but the program never gets there.

parts.problemMd:
A program uses four different files. For each task, complete the table by writing the file mode that the `OPENFILE` statement must use.

| Task | File mode |
|---|---|
| Add a new line of text to the end of an existing log file, keeping the lines already in it |   |
| Go directly to record 250 in a file of fixed-length records and replace that record |   |
| Output every line of a text file of product names, in order |   |
| Create a new text file to hold today's results, replacing any file with the same name |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Task | File mode |
|---|---|
| Add a new line of text to the end of an existing log file, keeping the lines already in it | **APPEND** |
| Go directly to record 250 in a file of fixed-length records and replace that record | **RANDOM** |
| Output every line of a text file of product names, in order | **READ** |
| Create a new text file to hold today's results, replacing any file with the same name | **WRITE** |

Two correct rows **[1]**

All four rows correct **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for any two rows correct
> 
> **1 mark** for all four rows correct
> 
> Accept the modes in lower case, for example append, random, read, write
> 
> Do not accept `WRITE` for the log file: `WRITE` mode creates a new file, so every line already in the log is lost
> 
> Do not accept `READ` or `WRITE` for record 250: the record must be read and then written back at the same position, and only `RANDOM` mode allows a record to be read or written at any position in the file

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error is writing `WRITE` for "add a line to an existing file". `WRITE` always starts an empty file, and `APPEND` is the mode that keeps the old data and adds after it.
> 
> A file is opened in only one mode at a time. If a task needs to both read and replace a record in the middle of a file, the answer is `RANDOM`, not "READ and WRITE".

parts.problemMd:
A hotel stores one record for each room in the random file `Rooms.dat`. Each record uses the user-defined data type `TRoom`.

This pseudocode changes the status of one room.

Describe the purpose of each of these commands in the pseudocode:

- `SEEK`
- `GETRECORD`
- `PUTRECORD`
parts.solutionMd:
`SEEK` moves the file pointer directly to record position 14 (the value of `RoomPosition`) in `Rooms.dat` **[1]**

`GETRECORD` reads the record at the file pointer and assigns it to the variable `ThisRoom` **[1]**

`PUTRECORD` writes the data in `ThisRoom` into the file at the file pointer, replacing the record that was stored there, so the file now holds the new status **[1]**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `SEEK`: moves the file pointer to the position / location / address given (record 14)
> 
> **1 mark** for `GETRECORD`: reads the record at the file pointer into the variable `ThisRoom`
> 
> **1 mark** for `PUTRECORD`: writes the record in `ThisRoom` to the file at the file pointer, replacing / overwriting the data that was there
> 
> Accept "record number 14" or "the 14th record" for the position
> 
> Do not accept "`SEEK` searches the file for the room": `SEEK` does not compare any values, it goes straight to the position it is given
> 
> Do not accept "`PUTRECORD` adds a new record to the end of the file": it replaces the record at the file pointer

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students read `SEEK` as "search" and describe a loop that checks each record in turn. No checking happens. The program already knows the position, and `SEEK` moves there in one step.
> 
> Also keep the text file and random file commands apart. `READFILE` reads the next line of a text file; `GETRECORD` reads one whole record, with all its fields, from the position the file pointer is at.

parts.problemMd:
The random file `Products.dat` stores one record at each position. Each record uses the user-defined data type `TProduct`. Only the `ProductCode` field is shown in the table.

Positions 1 to 5 hold records and position 6 is empty. The variable `NewItem` already holds a complete record with the `ProductCode` "P999".

A programmer wants to move the records at positions 2 to 5 up by one position each, and then insert `NewItem` at position 2. The programmer writes this pseudocode.

Complete the table to show the `ProductCode` at each position after the pseudocode has run. Then explain why the pseudocode does not do what the programmer intended, and state the change needed to the `FOR` statement.

| Position | ProductCode before | ProductCode after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A101 |   |
| 2 | B202 |   |
| 3 | C303 |   |
| 4 | D404 |   |
| 5 | E505 |   |
| 6 | (empty) |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| Position | ProductCode before | ProductCode after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A101 | **A101** |
| 2 | B202 | **P999** |
| 3 | C303 | **B202** |
| 4 | D404 | **B202** |
| 5 | E505 | **B202** |
| 6 | (empty) | **B202** |

Positions 1 and 2 hold A101 and P999 **[1]**

Positions 3, 4, 5 and 6 all hold B202 **[1]**

The loop works upwards from position 2, so each record is copied over the next record before that record has been moved. B202 is copied into every later position and C303, D404 and E505 are lost **[1]**

The loop must work downwards from the last record, for example `FOR Position ← 5 TO 2 STEP -1` **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for positions 1 and 2 correct: A101, P999
> 
> **1 mark** for positions 3 to 6 all correct: B202
> 
> **1 mark** for the explanation: a record is overwritten before it has been moved // B202 is copied forward into every later position // C303, D404 and E505 are overwritten and lost
> 
> **1 mark** for the change: the loop counts down from 5 to 2, for example `FOR Position ← 5 TO 2 STEP -1`
> 
> Accept a description of the change, for example "start the loop at 5 and go down to 2"
> 
> Do not accept `FOR Position ← 2 TO 5 STEP -1`: a loop from 2 to 5 with a negative step does not work from the last record down
> 
> Do not accept a change that starts at 6: position 6 is empty, and copying it to position 7 does not move any record

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often assume the code works because every line is a correct file command. Trace the file itself, one iteration at a time, and write down what each position holds after every `PUTRECORD`. The overwrite shows up on the very first pass.
> 
> To make space in a file, always move the record furthest from the gap first. The Cambridge Pseudocode Guide's own example of inserting a record uses a loop with `STEP -1` for exactly this reason.

parts.problemMd:
A club stores data about its members in the random file `Members.dat`. Each record uses the user-defined data type `TMember`.

The file has already been opened in `RANDOM` mode. The variable `ThisMember` has been declared as type `TMember`.

Write **two** pseudocode statements to read the record at position 12 of the file into `ThisMember`.
parts.solutionMd:
The `SEEK` statement moves the file pointer to position 12 **[1]**

The `GETRECORD` statement reads the record at the file pointer into `ThisMember` **[1]**

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for `SEEK "Members.dat", 12`
> 
> **1 mark** for `GETRECORD "Members.dat", ThisMember`, after the `SEEK`
> 
> Do not accept `READFILE "Members.dat", ThisMember`: `READFILE` reads one line of a text file, not a record from a random file
> 
> Do not accept `GETRECORD` before `SEEK`: the record read would be the one at the old file pointer position

> **[exam-tip]**
> Learn the exact order of the two items after each command. The file name always comes first, then a comma, then the position for `SEEK` or the variable for `GETRECORD`. Students who write `GETRECORD ThisMember, "Members.dat"` or `SEEK 12` lose the mark.

parts.problemMd:
A sports centre has 60 lockers. The random file `Lockers.dat` stores one record for each locker. The record for locker number 1 is at position 1, the record for locker number 2 is at position 2, and so on.

Each record uses this user-defined data type.

This pseudocode algorithm assigns a locker to a member. It reads the record for the locker, changes it, and writes it back to the same position in the file.

Complete the file handling pseudocode.
parts.solutionMd:
Opening the file: `OPENFILE LockerFile FOR RANDOM` **[1]**

Reading the record: `GETRECORD LockerFile, ThisLocker` **[1]**

Returning to the record's position: `SEEK LockerFile, LockerNum` **[1]**

Writing the changed record back: `PUTRECORD LockerFile, ThisLocker` **[1]**

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **1 mark** for each correctly completed line (max 4)
> 
> Accept `"Lockers.dat"` in place of `LockerFile` in any line
> 
> Do not accept `READ`, `WRITE` or `APPEND` as the file mode: records are read and written at a chosen position, which needs `RANDOM` mode
> 
> Do not accept `READFILE` or `WRITEFILE`: these are text file commands

> **[exam-tip]**
> Changing `ThisLocker` changes only the copy in memory. The file does not change until `PUTRECORD` writes the record back, and a common error is to stop after the assignment and leave the file untouched.
> 
> Always `SEEK` to the position again before `PUTRECORD`, exactly as Cambridge's own random file examples do before every `GETRECORD` and `PUTRECORD`. Then the record is certain to go back to the place it came from.

parts.problemMd:
A shop stores data about its stock in the random file `Stock.dat`. The file holds exactly 500 records, at positions 1 to 500. Each record uses this user-defined data type.

A procedure `Restock()` is needed. The procedure:

- takes one parameter of type integer, `Amount`
- checks every record in the file
- for each item whose quantity is less than its reorder level, adds `Amount` to the quantity and writes the updated record back to the same position in the file
- outputs the number of records that were updated, after all the records have been checked.

Write pseudocode for the procedure `Restock()`.
parts.solutionMd:
Procedure heading with an integer parameter, and `ENDPROCEDURE` **[1]**

File opened in `RANDOM` mode before the loop and closed after it **[1]**

Loop through positions 1 to 500 **[1]**

`SEEK` to the position, then `GETRECORD` into a `TItem` variable, in the loop **[1]**

Quantity compared with reorder level, and `Amount` added **[1]**

`SEEK` the same position and `PUTRECORD` the updated record **[1]**

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Any six from:**
> 
> - MP1 Procedure heading with an integer parameter, and `ENDPROCEDURE`
> - MP2 `OPENFILE "Stock.dat" FOR RANDOM` and subsequent `CLOSEFILE "Stock.dat"`
> - MP3 Loop for positions 1 to 500
> - MP4 `SEEK` to the loop position and `GETRECORD` into a variable of type `TItem`, in the loop
> - MP5 Test `ThisItem.Quantity < ThisItem.ReorderLevel` and add `Amount` to `Quantity`, in the loop
> - MP6 `SEEK` the same position and `PUTRECORD` the updated record, in the loop
> - MP7 Count initialised to 0, incremented for each updated record, and output after the loop
> 
> **[6 marks]**
> 
> Accept a conditional loop that counts from 1 to 500
> 
> Accept the file name held in a variable or constant
> 
> Accept `PUTRECORD` for every record, not only the updated ones, as long as `Quantity` is changed only when the test is true
> 
> Do not accept `READFILE` or `WRITEFILE` for MP4 or MP6: these read and write lines of a text file, not records
> 
> Do not accept a test of "less than or equal to" for MP5: an item exactly at its reorder level is not below it

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mark most often lost here is MP6. Adding `Amount` to `ThisItem.Quantity` changes only the copy of the record in memory. Unless the record is written back with `PUTRECORD` at the same position, the file is exactly as it was.
> 
> Also watch where the file is opened and closed. Opening it inside the loop, or closing it before the loop ends, means the file is not open for the next `GETRECORD`.

parts.problemMd:
A veterinary surgery wants to create a class for individual pets.

| PetType | STRING | type of pet assigned at registration |

State **one **reason why the attributes would be declared as PRIVATE.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> To ensure that the attributes are only accessible using the class’s own methods/within the class.
